Of course, nothing justifies what happened, and no one can be blamed, because everyone was responsible for what happened

But as a re-creation of what happened.

Robert Downey Jr. Excelled as usual, as did Cillian Murphy, and directed It was very creative, especially the nuclear explosions. Maybe I wanted more and expected better, but I haven't seen a movie in the cinema for a long time. So it's something promising for me.

Certainly not as cool as Interstellar.

Nothing beats it. It was a long time ago but I still love it.

8.title: Cillian!!!
8.content:
I will watch this again on my Home Screen. Even with ear plugs (I had heard people say it was too loud), the decibels of this soundtrack were uncomfortable for me. I could have paid more attention if I could control the sound.

That said, I went to see this movie because Cillian Murphy was in it.

After seeing his phenomenal performance in "Peaky Blinders", I was banking on his performance as being exceptional. I was not disappointed. His OSCAR nomination is well deserved.

I believe the editors, producers, and Christopher Nolan, could have easily done away with the intimate scenes. They were completely superfluous, gratuitous, and just plain idiotic.

Other than that, it was pretty good, not sure if I would categorize as best picture of the year, although I, as previously mentioned, will watch it again, and thankfully be able to skip over the parts that should not have been in there.

8.title: Great and timely movie, but missing an ingredient
8.content:
Some reviewers call tis an epic movie, and it certainly has ingredients for it.

The filming was outstanding. And the performance certainly from Cillian Murphy is worth an Oscar.

The storyline was for me a bit blurred with mixing the development of the A-bomb with the period after WW2. Maybe I get a bit old...but would have been more relaxed to do it chronological.

The music was great at some points but got a bit over the top in some key scenes.

As we are now in a period where there is an increasing nuclear war thread This movie makes you think. The dilemma that Dr. Oppenheimer was facing with the development of the bomb was clearly felt and added to the depth of the movie.

What was missing in my opinion was any capturing of the damage the first 2 A-bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki created.

Last few years I watched two excellent documentaries. The first one is called Threads made by the BBC. The second is the Day after. Both show the real devastating effects of a nuclear war.

If the producers had added some shots on the devastating effects in Japan the real message of this movie would have been much deeper. And this movie could have helped the raise the global awareness on this topic of Nuclear War and the real effects.

So that's why I give this movie 8 points!

8.title: Atomic men
8.content:
Such a good movie It's insane, my only problem with it Is I had the feeling that the music was really really overpowering. I mean it almost felt like a musical in how much the music method in every scene of the movie to set the pace and the feelings.

But this remarkable how much love and attention was put into every character the way they talk it's just filled put together and the way story is built up sort all comes together. It's just move so good.

The movie was 3 hours long, but it didn't feel like it it felt so fast paced and it's mostly people talking and the character making sad faces, but it works. I never felt like it was slow.

But the best part is Oppenheimer himself a conflicted man with many ties that bind him in different directions. A man willing to Bear the sins of the burden created for self.

Many times the more brilliant you are, the more flawed you are simultaneously.

8.title: Hard to shake off the darkness in this historical film!
8.content:
Introduction: This is the story of the American scientist J. Robert Oppenheimer and his role in the development of the atomic bomb. I would describe this as a visual masterpiece, with brilliant acting and a protracted storytelling. The movie is directed by Christopher Nolan, who I think can call himself a living legend at this point.

Acting: If we start with the acting. The Nolans have a unique ability to choose the right actors and get the best out of them. All I can say is that the cast of "Oppenheimer" is impressive. The role of J. Robert Oppenheimer is portrayed by the Irish actor Cillian Murphy. Murphy exceeds all expectations, his intense gaze and a slightly manic and nervous movement pattern results in us as viewers gaining a greater understanding of Oppenheimer's character. Downey, Jr, Matt Damon and Emily Blunt all give an outstanding acting effort that makes us as viewers engulfed in a world of science and politics.

Visual effect: Now for the visuals. Nolan has a unique flair for visually exciting imagery, this film is no exception. The idea of showing the film in color when it is from Oppenheimer's point of view and in black and white when it is from the perspective of his antagonist, the head of the AEC (Robert Downey Jr), is absolutely phenomenal.

"No matter how sophisticated your CGI is, if it's been created from non-physical elements and you haven't shot with the camera, it will feel animated."


Nolan's resistance to using CGI creates new possibilities and makes us viewers feel emotions never felt before. The movie feels more genuine and raw.

Music: It is the Swedish composer Ludwig Göransson who composed the music in the film. Nolan's only requirement was to base the music on the violin, from there Göransson had the power to compost his interpretation of Oppenheimer and what a success it was! The violins shift between a beautiful and romantic tone to a frenetic and manic sound in a millisecond. The violin as an instrument manages to describe Oppenheimer's character in a unique way, as he can switch between the two emotions in the space of a second. And one side driven by his creation and striving to create, but on the other side, the anxiety of what he actually managed to accomplish and the consequences of that.

"Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds."


Running time: The film is three hours long, a seemingly long running time. But Christopher Nolan's ability to constantly deliver quick clips results in his viewers never get bored as time flies. I argue that Nolan uses the running time carefully and proves once again that he has earned his reputation for always managing to tie up the ending in an incredibly neat way.

Conclusion: Christopher Nolan knows how to raise the temperature in a scene, indeed in an entire movie. But he does not use the simplest tricks, he drills into Oppenheimer's psyche and morals and also tells the story of how Robert Oppenheimer is elevated and then displaced in a post-war USA. Oppenheimer is a movie with brilliant acting, amazing visual effects and outstanding soundtrack. A lot of the negative reviews concern the truthfulness of the film. Many argue that the film is not 100 procent accurate to what really happened. Perhaps there is some truth in this. Perhaps Nolan took a few too many artistic liberties. But I think it is important to remember that it is not a factual report, but a film that touches on a real event, a big difference. Of course, creative licence had to be taken at points, to make a watchable film that we should all be able to appreciate at cinemas. This does not mean that the film is trash, on the contrary, I claim that it is an art to combine real history with hip scenography and artistic freedom.

8.title: Nolan does it again
8.content:
I went into the movie with high expectations and overall it did deliver well.

Pros: special effects, story, acting, casting, cinematography, soundtrack/music, ending was well done

Cons: the beginning was a little messy for me, the audio for the dialogue could've been clearer - it was hard to heard several scenes, the writing for female characters in the story could've been stronger

I do think Nolan missed a few good opportunities in terms of making this movie a masterpiece, but the acting by all the actors, the special effects and the story will be remembered by many viewers for years to come.

8.title: Cillian Murphy is phenomenal in this well done Nolan box office hit, but it isn't all sunshine and daisies.
8.content:
I am giving this film eight stars...because it was well directed, well acted, well scored, well scripted and well good in every way, BUT and there is a but the film is exceptionally long at the three hour mark and consists primarily of a lot of dialogue between men and some imagined images in the real-life Oppenheimer's head...and some political shenanigans some of which involve communism.

Cillian Murphy plays American scientist J. Robert Oppenheimer and the film depicts his involvement in and around the invention and use of the atomic bomb in bringing an end to WWII. The film is based on the biography American Prometheus The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer by Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherer'in. The film starts with the following quote about Prometheus:

" Prometheus stole fire from the gods and gave it to man. For this he was chained to a rock and tortured for eternity."

The casting is phenomenal as the camera lands on one star after the other...there really are some acting powerhouses that show up under Nolan's direction. Speaking of Christopher Nolan, he is what brought me and my husband to this film. My husband is a huge fan of his, with his Inception being my husband's second favorite movie of all time. I will say he did an amazing job building the tension in a story that we already knew the outcome of...and that was thanks in large part to a flurry of strings in the symphonic score.

"Atmospheric ignition. Remote. Chances are near zero."

I enjoyed the recreation of both the Los Alamos research "town" and the infamous test. Both were visual events and have left me wondering how close they were to the real thing and how much was for the cinematic effect or impact.

Regardless, the film really is well done and I encourage you to watch it. I do have to put a warning on that recommendation...it is very long and involves a lot of men talking. I can understand the criticisms of the film being boring and women have only the remotest small roles, the largest of which is played by Emily Blunt as Kitty Oppenheimer. She isn't portrayed in the best of lights either...former member of the Communist Party, working on her fourth husband when she marries Oppenheimer, completely uninterested or absentee mother who would rather abandon her children so she can drink, but even at that we get very little of their personal home life as the focus is on the science, politics and men.

I do think it was worth seeing, but I definitely wouldn't sit through it again.

8.title: Chain reaction
8.content:
We finally watched Oppenheimer with my wife. We could have done so for a few days but she begged to wait until she had readied herself psychologically to endure Christopher Nolan's unrelenting Wall of Sound and plethora of travelling back and forth in time. I guess anyone who ever made it in Hollywood never shied away from having a personal signature. Like, for example, an unrelenting Wall of Sound at a level much higher than the level of the sound of dialog that we are supposed to hear in order for us to understand what the characters are saying, and a plethora of cuts travelling back and forth in time to test our ability to know where in time and at which point in the storyline we find ourselves in, loud bang-bang-boom after loud bang-bang-boom. At least in this outing he helped us with Black & White for the present vs. Color for all of the several points in the past.

After watching it I feel a bit like J. Robert Oppenheimer myself, at the point in his life when he was trying to convince the world that the H Bomb was bad. I stand the same chances of convincing the world that their golden boy, Christopher, is wearing the King's new clothes.

If you straighten out the timeline a bit, add a tiny bit more information about the science at Los Alamos, and slide down the constant-music sound level by 70%, with the dialog level up by some 20%, the movie is not half-bad. In fact, it is quite good.

Casting was really good and Matt Damon as General Groves was one of the very few actors who did stand a chance standing next to Paul Newman's General Groves, from Fat Man and Little Boy (1989). Emily Blunt worried me throughout the movie because her part, as Oppie's wife, was, I thought, very badly written, but she made-up for it in her scene testifying towards the end of the movie. Cillian Murphy was an excellent, excellent Oppenheimer and Robert Downey Jr.'s Lewis Strauss delivered the perfect tragic figure of a mediocre man turned pathetic lunatic by his hatred of J. Robert Oppenheimer.

I really don't understand how Nolan's choice of standing out from the pack by torturing the ears and brains of his audience has caused said audience such Stockholm Syndrome. It's not personal, dear Christopher; it's only business, and how you duped so many to give it to you. And I only speak as an older man with an excellent stereo system and sensitive hearing.

Given the choice of re-watching the story of the Manhattan project, I, myself, would opt for Fat Man and Little Boy (1989). But don't let me stop you :-) Go ahead. Watch Nolan's Oppenheimer and praise it. Praising Nolan makes one sound cool. "Intelligent filmmaking", some call it. I am not cool by any stretch of the imagination.

8.title: Hold on to Your Oppenheimer Hat
8.content:
I have given it 8 out of 10 because it held my attention and was pretty good. But some things really annoyed me about it.

Nolan has a problem with pace. Everything is unrelentingly frenetic. He seems afraid of the quiet and the slow. He doesn't do lingering shots like Tarkovsky. When characters decide to have important conversations, they walk quickly in large groups through corridors accompanied by loud intrusive music so we can't overhear them. Even when Oppy merely thinks about particles, we are assaulted by phantasmagorical images and loud unpleasant noises.

The centrepiece of the film, the detonation of the first atomic bomb, is surprisingly unconvincing and underwhelming. Nolan apparently doesn't like CGI but he should have used it here. Hiroshima and Nagasaki are not depicted. A shame. I wanted to see spectacular nuclear explosions.

I don't think Cillian Murphy is as good in his role as some people are saying. He can't convey the depth and breadth of Oppenheimer's intelligence. He looks good when he puts Oppenheimer's hat on but any actor would. I felt he was outshone by Robert Downey Jr. Which slightly unbalanced the film in my view. This film should have at its heart the question of the morality of nuclear weapons. But Downey Jr is so good he makes it seem like the film is all about the petty grudges of a long-forgotten politician.

Tom Conti is preposterous as Albert Einstein. Conti always thinks that if he chuckles away to himself, we will be fooled into thinking he's a great actor.

And Nolan's non-linear narrative habit seems incurable now.

8.title: Watch it with Subtitles
8.content: I heard and read many reviews mentioning the broad character spread of the film and how it took away from overall flow/comprehension. Watching with subtitles was really helpful for me, as all of the characters names were present during lines and I was able to associate faces to names much faster and with far more consistency than if I'd been watching without subtitles. Given that the runtime is so long, covers so much time in history, and jumps those historical timelines, the subtitles really helped me continue placing characters and led to in-stride comprehension that made this film very enjoyable. A gripping story with a few unexpected turns, loaded with history, and very morally compelling. I definitely recommend this if you're in the mood for a full-fledged drama.

8.title: 1570 IMAX a must!
8.content:
I have now seen this movie twice, once in regular cinema and once in 1570 IMAX. Even though it was an outstanding movie in regular cinema, I highly encourage you to see it in 1570 IMAX. It wasn't just a completely different experience, it was eye opening how films can be shot and watched.

The obvious is that Cillian Murphy will take home the Oscar for best Actor in a leading role because wow he just destroyed every single scene!

I can't tell you who was the best support cast member because there were so many that deserve recognition from Downey Jnr to Gary Oldman as President Truman.

After watching the movie the first time I researched more and more about these events and it actually made the second viewing more enjoyable! I recommend watching it first without researching anything and then diving deep into the story and watching it again!

8.title: Murphy stars in a great movie
8.content:
Now this is a movie to savor. The story is fascinating enough - nuanced and complex, but very rewarding if you stick with it.

The writing is great, the driection superb and the acting peerless, especially the performance from the star, Murphy.

This came out at the same time as the movie Barbie and both did well at the box office. The difference between the two is that one is nuanced and profound, the other propogandist and shallow. Take one guess.

It is a real treat to watch a movie with substance, given the rubbish that we are fed most of the time (Barbie being a very good example of the latter.)

8.title: Short-Circuit
8.content:
The theme of 'Oppenheimer' is connection: the present to the past, of course, but more importantly, one individual to another. It attempts to show how the effects of one man's actions, for good or ill, radiated out like ripples on a pond to affect potentially millions of other people.

The primary aim of 'Oppenheimer" is thus not to teach the history of nuclear physics in the manner of a documentary, but rather to give viewers an experience - the experience of wielding god-like powers together with accepting the responsibility for the consequences.

It is for this reason that "Oppenheimer" takes the form not of a public, objective narrative, but of an interior, subjective personal interpretation. Everything on screen has been filtered through the consciousness of either Oppenheimer (color) or Strauss (B&W).

This accounts for the rapidity, the abrupt cutting, the condensed dialogue, the abundance of characters and the sheer length. The viewer, almost overwhelmed by the multitude of connections, feels scarcely able to keep up,

If there is a flaw in the movie, it lies in the lack of preparation for O.'s sudden comprehension of his debt to others. As it stands, it doesn't quite make sense. What triggered it?

Ultimately, though, this is more than the story of one man, it is a story of a nation, as relevant today as eighty years ago. It is also - potentially - the story of Artificial Intelligence (AI), as well.

8.title: A Technically brilliant film with a story most people probably know?
8.content:
I think this was undeniably technically brilliant, but I also am left thinking that, aside from the minutiae of the antagonistic relationship the doctor faced in hearings, post bomb-drop-it was a story most people already know? Maybe it's my benefit of being educated in Canada on the subject, but I generally knew the larger story and ramifications, again, just not the granular details of the main himself. Such as his womanizing and movements in adult life.

So, it's a story worth telling and it's well told. There wasn't anything to put it really high in the echelons of amazing films, some of which Nolan has made, I think. Perhaps the hype affected me. Maybe a home viewing in 4K HDR and surround sound loses something as well. But I can't say I was excited to see it in a theatre with its length. And I'm glad I made that decision now, to be honest. So, there it is.

8.title: 3 films in one. You should like at least one of them.
8.content:
That is, film one, his personal life and internal struggles, professional, philosophical and romantic. Film two, the development, building and use of the worlds first atomic bomb. Film three, the hearings regarding his security clearance and the machinations behind them.

Personally, I found film one a bit of a drag. Film two of course, was the meat of it. Film three, I knew nothing about, or had forgotten, and so found it to be engrossing.

This is a class film, three hours , but never found a need for any intermission, even though it was heavy on dialogue, and I found at times that the exposition led to a docudrama feeling, but then again, not many viewers will be up on their quantum physics, political skulduggery , or moral philosophy.

There were a few off kilter fantasy scenes added, I suppose to make various points or elicit some emotional reactions, but personally I did not find them necessary and maybe even a bit ham fisted. More Hollywood stars than you could shake a stick at, great cinematography and sound score, well directed and edited, so overall an 8/10.

8.title: Only one flaw
8.content:
Let me start by saying that I've loved all Nolans movies so far and most of them I've seen many times. This one is another great one, and like the others, the acting is spot on. You can tell Murphy was the right man for the job. It also puts him up there with the very best. He's performance is just phenomenal and they use closups very effectively.

The music and sound in general is also very good, but here we get onto my only complaint.

It's like they forget to turn the music down during dialog. I know, Nolan have done this before, but here it's just a bit too loud. Some dialogs you can't really hear very well. Obviously this can be fixed with subtitles, but it just took me out of the story a bit. I've seen clips online from the film and they didn't have those music scores running that loud so maybe it's more prominent in the cinema.

I like movies that are loud and this movie is not too loud at all . It's just when you have a courtroom scene with dialogue, and at the same time a symphony playing at full volume, It does get a bit much.

8.title: -Time flys-
8.content:
If like me you have been putting off watching this film due to its 3 hour run time, don't! I was truly sucked into the intricate smorgasbord of characters and well told story, actually leaving me wanting more once the credits hit. Visually it is beautiful without being to indulgent and the use of the Kodak black and white custom 65mm was stunning.

Huge cast as to be expected for a Nolan film with stand out performance from Emily Blunt and Cillian Murphy but Robert Downey Jr feeling a bit flat and maybe could have been cast better. This film will leave you frantically scrolling wiki researching all kids of facts and history.

8.title: A Rare Expensive Beast!
8.content:
I tend to gravitate towards fiction more than fact. Never been a big fan of war, true events or biographies and I wasn't sure about this one, especially with its three hour run time. Besides Dunkirk (skipped it for obvious reasons) I have yet to be disappointed by any of his works and took a chance. Yes, I even liked Tenet...

Robert J. Oppenheimer is often considered a controversial figure in the history of the US WWII. Dubbed as the father of the of the atomic bomb that claimed the lives of hundreds of thousands of people in Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the title would begin to weight heavy around his neck as he would try to unsuccessfully appeal to the president against further use. Hailed as a hero and then eventually tried as a potential spy for the Soviets, his loyalty would come under question as the eventual regret of his achievement and his past dealings with the communist party is weaponized against him by someone fairly close to him but who?

I went in expecting a non eventful history lesson but got a movie with a slight mystery, instead. I am happy to say in today's climate, where it has gotten increasingly hard to bank on well known actors and directors to deliver a good film, Nolan still remains a reliable source for quality. His penchant for presenting scenes out of order, a slow but intense build of music in the background and short and quick lines of dialogue managed to keep the pacing quite brisk despite the long runtime and the lack of any actual action of any kind, it is simply brilliant. Perhaps not seeing any of the trailers and looking at a handful of reviews might have tempered my expectations? Or maybe I just got lucky that I found it entertaining unlike some of the movie goers around me. Eitherway, I will point out while this movie is great, its not perfect. You do need to go in with a tempered expectations as it has no action sequence, a lot of talk of theory and calculations along with a court drama towards the end. If you are expecting any scenes of war or action, you will be disappointed. However, if you have slight interest in science and are only vaguely familiar with name and facts around Oppenheimer, there is a story with a slight twist this movie tells and its well worth the watch atleast once.

Speaking of expectations, a lot of reviews seem to point out a certain singular moment as a caution and its possible that the version I saw had been edited but I have to ask 'WHERE WAS THE LONG GRATITOUS SEX SCENE??" Was it the intense breathing as the camera slowly pans by a wall? The only signs of nudity was a brief seconds of Oppenheimer sitting in a chair with his legs crossed, having a conversation. If this is a cause for concern then we have definitely gone backwards from the days of the FCC censorship. Because the scene is less than thirty seconds and subtle in a way where you don't really take notice.

8.title: Nolan has now out-Nolaned himself for the second time in a row, with a different set of minor issues
8.content:
Even though Oppenheimer is far more cohesive and easy-to-appreciate than the divisive Tenet, the two films still share many Nolanisms: the ticking time-bomb scenario, scientific exposition, an intense, panic attack-inducing soundtrack (this is very much a sound-driven film), non-linear storytelling. How Oppenheimer varies from Tenet, and why it's a better film, has something to do with the acting. Cillian Murphy embodies Oppenheimer to the degree that it's impossible to imagine anyone else in the role, and he's buttressed by an impressive ensemble cast including Matt Damon, Emily Blunt, Robert Downey Jr (what might have been...had he not devoted the best years of his life to Marvel), and many others who will certainly look familiar, meriting a visit to the Wikipedia cast list. It even becomes difficult to keep track of all these characters. Oddly enough there is no Michael Caine.

Another point of improvement over Tenet comes, ironically, from the fact that Nolan is reforming what is by now the most stale and unremarkable Hollywood genre of all: the biopic. Oppenheimer has a better idea of what kind of film it is, what story it wants to tell, and how to tell it.

That being said, there is something missing in the depiction of Oppenheimer's moral quandary; much like in Luhrmann's recent 'Elvis', the film lacks the knowledge (maybe strength?) to give its protagonist the truly moving, epic/tragic dimension he deserves. The difference is that where Luhrmann was immoral (his Elvis was by turns redeemed and destroyed by profligacy) Nolan is more amoral (generally concerned with physics and technicalities over emotional resonance). Murphy completely sells Oppenheimer's horror at what he's created, but when the film switches to McCarthyist machinations it's anticlimactic, almost beside the point, proving that Nolan is more awestruck by the effects of the Bomb on humanity as a whole instead of on one man. It still works dramatically, (and Nolan's position is far more understandable than Luhrmann's) but, much like in real life, Oppenheimer himself gets a little lost in the magnitude of his work. You feel his pain, understand him, but are not emotionally moved---history merely marches on. It should come as no surprise that Emily Blunt, playing his wife, feels underutilized.

Putting all that aside, a striking feature of the film is Nolan's restraint: any other director would be desperate to spice the film up with violence and destruction, but we watch Cillian Murphy's reactions. The real climax of the movie is not Hiroshima, but the Trinity test, and it's here that the old cliche 'it must be seen in the theater' holds true. This scene HAS to be experienced on a huge screen to get the full effect. Home viewing or streaming will not come close to what I sat through in the IMAX theater, and I'll leave it at that.

Ultimately Oppenheimer is still a singular, worthwhile experience which I plan to see again in the theater. It goes without saying that it's a better film than the more popular 'Barbie', a movie so ridiculous that even its supporters contradict themselves, saying 'It's just a movie about a doll! You can't take it seriously!' and a few sentences later: 'subversive masterpiece!' Out of these two films, infamously released on the same day, it's easy to tell which one will endure.

Another quibble, coming at the expense of sounding too snobbish: Nolan and cinematographer Hoytema are far too obsessed with soft-focus compositions, which make up nearly every shot in the film. The innovative black and white Imax film looks incredible of course, but what's the point if it's shot in the same woozy fashion as the color sequences? One of the main effects of black and white film is an emphasis on shapes, forms, and position, which is how directors such as Orson Welles and John Frankenheimer were able to work such wonders with it. Nolan could have blocked his scenes more creatively and found something even more visually stunning than the practical effect nuclear explosion, but his depth of field is so narrow that it can barely allow two things to be in focus at the same time. This works when we're meant to be getting inside Oppenheimer's head, but for the entire movie?

8.title: Amazing
8.content:
This was an amazingly shot movie. Most if not all are practically shot without the use of vfx which I find quite amazing when visualising the thought process of Oppenheimer.

I recognised most actors even in small rolls which was quite amazing. Just shows that many actors wanted to be part of this amazing work.

Murphy puts in an amazing performance which so far I expect to do put him in contention for an Oscar for the leading actor position. I also suspect RDJ might walk away with a best supporting actor, if not he should definitely be on the nomination list.

All the actors did a fantastic job. The cinematography was amazing and the direction.

Some people complained about the dialogue, but I could hear everything fine.

This film kept me engaged for the entire runtime.

8.title: 8.3/10. One of the greatest movies of the last decade.
8.content:
I guess i am late to the party, but better late than never.

I was sure this is a good movie but its plot/running time made me a bit hesitant to watch it. I mean, i didn't care much about Physics nor Oppenheimer. Furthermore, the whole story about creating the bomb and the repercussions of it in his life, don't seem that intriguing. Maybe if it was shorter, but 3 hours about this? Why?

As it seems, i underestimated Nolan. And it's a goofy mistake if you underestimate one of the greatest directors of all time. I am a big fan of his work but i must admit that i didn't love DUNKIRK neither TENET. OPPENHEIMER is a different beast though. This movie grabs you by the throat and makes you care about things which you didn't even imagine that might interest you. It's not that easy to watch but if you are an average iq person, you will understand most of it. This movie respects its viewers and their intelligence. Beware, don't watch it if you feel tired because it requires your attention. But it rewards you in the end.

I can't say anything that has not already been said. So, i 'll say this in the end of my review : Every actor here did a good or a great job, however, Murphy was transcendental. This is one of the most glorious acting performances of all time. I think i understood everything he communicated with his eyes. All the pride and the shame and the remorse and the "Still, I would have done it again a thousand times" attitude. All of his contradictory feelings. Congratulations mr Murphy. You did the (almost) impossible.

8.title: Will It Ever End?
8.content: The only thing that kept me from giving this film a 9 instead of an 8 is the length. Not much shorter than the actual war. The directing was excellant and the cast is superb. The only one I had a small problem with was the choice for President Truman. I think in real life Truman was gruffer. Other than that, everyone was right on. I believe the story line was fairly accurate as was the locations. I strongly recommend seeing this film, if you can sit for 3 hours. So, pack a lunch, put your feet up and enjoy. I think you will not feel cheated and certainly not happy and upbeat but very informed.

8.title: Prometheus Bound
8.content:
A truly well made movie about the triumph and tragedy of physicist Robert Oppenheimer, the father of the atomic bomb. It is also a movie about Cillian Murphy who has established himself as a truly capable thespian having come a long way since the compelling "The Wind that Shakes the Barley", and the more recent tv series "Peaky Blinders" with the trademark chain smoking and careful straightening of the porkpie hat brim, also observed in "Oppenheimer". I'd be surprised if his latest flawless role execution didn't land him an Oscar, or at least a nomination for one. What perhaps might work against it, would be the enduring sensitivities surrounding the use of the atomic bomb and the vital role that Oppenheimer played in its development. But, his country asked him to do something and he did it brilliantly. He was a brilliant scientist after all, and in the world we don't only have scientists but we also have politicians. Take a guess who could be more dangerous.

Like Prometheus, in one of the legendary Greek myths, who stole fire from the gods and bringing it to humans to better their lives, but not without consequences, that also meant giving humans a moral choice to use the "tool" for good or for evil.

If there was a criticism of the movie, that would perhaps be the witch-hunt campaign directed against Oppenheimer and which, in my view, did not seem to jump out of the movie with the deserved poignance around this rather tragic part in his life and scientific career. Further, the movie stops very short of the impact the atomic bomb has had on its actual use. Over 100k people were turned into vapour and ashes in Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945. Many more suffered unspeakable horrific health conditions followed by death. A mention would have been a fitting short epilogue with a poignant message but unfortunately the opportunity was lost.

8.title: Was excited to see a Nolan film in 70mm IMAX, left with mixed feelings
8.content:
Saw the film this evening, found a theater (one of two in Texas - they even flew in a projectionist from San Francisco) that had it in Nolan's recommended format - IMAX 70mm. I spent the week watching and listening to Manhattan project related content...here are my thoughts:

1) Visually, it looks awesome. Seeing it in 70mm IMAX helped I'm sure - but the exterior shots that filled up the full picture looked awesome and really were impressive. Hopefully someday digital cameras will be able to replicate the scale and resolution so the same grand scale can be brought to indoor sequences.

2) Audio - heard some reviews saying the audio was too loud, at my theater they had it set up just right I think. I could clearly hear everything and was only startled by the blast of the bombing going off when that came to screen. Like other Nolan films however there are some words that are hard to make out...even though this didn't take anything away from the picture for me - I do feel that watching this with subtitles at home would bring about a better understanding of the movie as a whole.

3) Story - the first two hours were great and I could feel the whole theater was engaged. The third hour however had no action and was focused in on a big experience in Oppenheimer's life in relation to his relationship to the US government. Personally I found the final hour a bit boring but if you're into history and especially if you grew up in the Cold War then you'll find it cool and relevant.

Overall I think this is on-par with Nolan's Dunkirk - his movies prior to that are legendary so don't go in expecting that and you'll leave happy. It has amazing actors/actresses and has a compelling and important story. - just didn't nuke my socks off like I expected.

8.title: Could have been perfection
8.content:
This is more or less a feature documentary type of a movie made only for people who have the basic knowledge of Oppenheimer and the first atomic bomb.

The movie is NOT for people who'd rather watch an action-y type of a film nor for people who simply are not interested in this topic in general. The movie won't change their opinion.

As a person who knows enough about the man and the first atomic bomb and who knew that the movie will be in the style of a "documentary" I was definitely the target audience and I am glad I saw the movie in cinema.

With that being said the movie has no business being three hours long. There are so many scenes that kill the pacing and should have been cut. The movie should have been 2h30m maximum or they should have made a mini series if they wanted to properly explain all the "side characters" and certain events that happened during that time period.

8.title: "Oppy" was no hero
8.content:
Yes, the movie does an awesome job dramatizing the development of the A bomb and the politics that afflicted "Oppy's" later career, so enjoy the show! But don't fall into the trap of feeling sorry for the guy. So what if he got stabbed in the back later? It's not like he fled the country in fear of his life, like Einstein. Face reality; he wanted to build the bomb because it was going to help his career and give him personal power, not out of some vague desire to help humanity. No, it was a power trip, plus a chance for an extended nerd-science summer camp in the desert, and to shag old flames while being tailed by the FBI. Who wouldn't sign up for that?

Sorry, the man himself was utterly human, and not a particularly fine example of the species. He was vaguely communist in a way that was used against him later in his career. Yes, the movie was pretty vague about what EXACTLY he was doing at all those Commie soirees, except it was a great way to meet women. But here's what the movie conveniently ignores: just HOW exactly does a Commie science prof afford a horse ranch in New Mexico? Duh! He inherits a small fortune from his thoroughly bourgeois father, of course! It sure is easy to turn Commie when you can finance it with inherited wealth!

So enjoy the movie. Don't feel sorry for the character. He's not a particularly sympathetic figure.

8.title: "I am become death the destroyer of worlds"
8.content:
Indeed. A movie about a troubled man who later wrestels with his demons regarding his involvement in the Manhattan project and subsequent acts of violence in Hiroshima and Nagasaki. I'm not the judge of that since I don't know how the war in the Pacific would have gone if not for H and N. I'm not the moral arbiter to judge this man and his involvement. Although I believe he was used by the US military.

You see much of what I described in Cillian Murphy's acting. He portays a man with some huge demons to live with. The start of the movie is a bit ambigous about why Oppenheimer did what he did in studying in Europe. The movie does say he needed to study quantum mechanics there and I can really see the movie depcts him as a genius who's plagued by what he wants to solve. The sleepless nights at university etc. Later he tries to fight against the system that wants to create more of his devices and more devastating devices. In my opinion Oppenheimer was not responsible for H and N. The generals and president were. The pilots dropping the devices were. I also think that he's pictured to be the one to understand what has happened after the war while others celebrate that the war was won. But at what cost.

Act two is basically politics and what the government did to a man who tried going against the tide. They tried to silence him. Rob him of credibility. He is protrayed as the father of the nuclear bomb. (please IMDB that Time magazine, not me)

The movie subtly studies the idea and consequences of the actions of these devices. Not for everyone definitely. Though a personal note is good to point out. I've played a few Fallout games and probably been somewhat sensitized. Nevertheles this movie should be 16+ mostly because of some sex scenes which aren't that bad. Basically actors dry humping because that wasn't real. Multiple minutes of needlesly showing boobs on screen. We would have gotten the idea of those two people having an affair with less boobs. It was basically just the actress sitting on his lap and in a chair but that chair thing. Why not put the dress back on? Though, breast aren't genitalia so that's why I said 16+.

The other thing that I did not like was cutting too often, in my opinion, back and forth from two hearings to the Los Alamos place. Annoying a bit. They were used as plot devices but still annoying.

The thing is, while Oppenheimer helped make the nuclear device, he also helped make nuclear power. If I had to decide I would take nuclear power over coal. Yes, nuclear waste but no greenhouse gasses.

A multifaceted movie that does a good job in depicting a troubled man wrestling with demons of his own and the problems of the era. The 1940s were really dark era of mankind.

8.title: Science, War, Politics
8.content:
"Oppenheimer" is a captivating and thought-provoking cinematic masterpiece that delves deep into the complex life of J. Robert Oppenheimer, one of the key scientists behind the development of the atomic bomb during World War II. Directed by a highly skilled filmmaker, the movie offers a mesmerizing portrayal of Oppenheimer's journey from a brilliant physicist to a morally conflicted figure.

The film brilliantly captures the historical context and the ethical dilemmas surrounding Oppenheimer's work on the Manhattan Project. Through stunning cinematography and meticulous attention to detail, it paints a vivid picture of the frantic race between scientific progress and military urgency. The audience is given an intimate glimpse into the intense pressures faced by Oppenheimer and his colleagues as they grappled with the responsibility of creating a weapon that could reshape the course of history.

What sets "Oppenheimer" apart is its profound exploration of the human aspects of this story. The movie delves into Oppenheimer's personal struggles. This doubts, and his internal conflicts as he becomes increasingly aware of the devastating potential of their creation. The emotional depth and complexity of the protagonist's character are brilliantly brought to life by the talented actor in the lead role.

🎭 The supporting cast also shines, further elevating the film's impact and this master director used them for the right amount of time to maintain the balance, which is remarkable, Although Nolan's characterization is weak like the rest of his films, anyway, each character feels fleshed out and integral to the narrative, effectively conveying the moral gray areas and the collateral damage caused by the atomic bomb. The performances are powerful, engrossing, and create a palpable sense of empathy within the audience.

🎥 The cinematography is truly breathtaking. The film's visual style successfully captures both the grandeur of the scientific moments and the intimate moments of introspection. The use of light and shadow helps to create a haunting atmosphere, emphasizing the weight of Oppenheimer's decisions and actions.

✍ The screenplay is masterfully written, providing the audience with enough scientific exposition to understand the complexity of the Manhattan Project, while simultaneously delving into the personal struggles and moral dilemmas faced by Oppenheimer. The dialogue is poignant and intellectually stimulating, keeping viewers engaged and intrigued throughout.

Generally, "Oppenheimer" stands as a remarkable film that explores the human side of a pivotal moment in history and also prioritizing the truth regardless of any grudge that is one of the important points of the film, it skillfully navigates the intersection of science, morality, and personal sacrifice, this thought-provoking and visually stunning movie is a must-watch for those seeking both historical insight and a profound exploration of the human condition.

8.title: There are no actors who fail in this film
8.content:
If you look at the list of actors starring in Oppenheimer, it is certain that this film features an ensemble of actors who are not playing around. Big Hollywood names are included in the cast in this film, including Cillian Murphy who plays the main character, namely J. Robert Oppenheimer.

Anyone who already knows Murphy's acting in other films or series will certainly not doubt his acting abilities. In appearance, Murphy already has similarities with Oppenheimer. Then in terms of acting, Murphy really succeeded in telling all the anguish that Oppenheimer experienced during his lifetime.

What amazes me even more is that Nolan was able to direct all his big actors to get their shining moments, even though these actors only appeared briefly in Oppenheimer. While watching, I saw that all the actors who appeared in Oppenheimer performed optimally and none of them looked weak.

8.title: An Intense and Chilling Experience
8.content:
Like everyone else I was pretty hyped up for Oppenheimer, the latest flick from Christopher Nolan based on the 2005 biography ''American Prometheus'' by Kai Bird and Martin J Sherwin. And after watching it, I think it's safe to say it met almost all of my expectations. From a technical perspective, the film is brilliantly well made. The sound design, production design and the breathtaking cinematography are all top notch. On top of that it also has one of the best scores of the year from Ludwig Görranson.

Speaking of the performances, Cillian Murphy IS Oppenheimer. His line delivery, acting and chemistry with the other actors felt so real and natural. Not to mention how identical he looks to the real J. Robert Oppenheimer. But the real star is Robert Downey Jr. As Lewis Strauss. Aside from the lead actor he gets most of the screentime and boy did he chewed it up. His expressions, line delivery and particularly the third act meltdown are brilliant. The rest of the cast does a pretty good job especially Benny Safdie as Edward Teller. Just like the title the movie primarily focuses on J. Robert Oppenheimer and his role in developing the atomic bomb. The movie gives him a proper structure and development and is fully fleshed out.

Even though the film is brilliantly well made with fantastic performances from the cast, I couldn't help but feel like it dragged on. Now I was really invested in the first 2 hours but as the final hour approaches I was starting to somewhat lose my interest. If only it was trimmed a little then it could've been perfect. Another issue I have with the film is that it completely sidelines the female characters ( just like other movies from Nolan ) Kitty Katherine Oppenheimer, played by Emily Blunt and Jean Tatlock, played by Florence Pugh. They are being setup in the beginning and then are almost completely forgotten until the final hour kicks in. Especially Blunt who should've gotten more screentime as she's supposed to play Oppenheimer's mistress. They could've easily explored more about Oppenheimer's personal life as well. This felt like a missed opportunity

Overall, Oppenheimer is a brilliantly well crafted film from Christopher Nolan that depicts one of the most eerie, intense, haunting and terrifying events in the history of mankind and is easily one of the best biopics/historical movies of all time. Even though the movie is 3 hours long and might test your patience it is a chilling experience nonetheless. You do not want to miss this.

8.title: You don't get to see so many great actors playing a nerd.
8.content:
Despite Oppenheimer's patchy reputation, Nolan has put forward a reasonably fair assessment in this day and age. In the storyline, Louis Strauss acted as a counterweight to the heroic side of the father of the atomic bomb, and went on to reveal in a one-liner the possibility of a malicious side of the calculating physicist. What undergirds the complexity of the assessment harks back to a witty remark made by Albert Einstein, accompanied by a few amazing shots, that will make things 'click' into place. Though I also lament that nothing more comes out of the Prometheus analogy.

I do notice the back-and-forth switching between B&O and coloured clips which sets apart, of course, the chronology and also reinstates the mood change. This kind of nudge is helpful. It keeps me aware of the sorry condition that the aspect ratio 1.43:1 is not available where I am, for me to enjoy the enhanced white-hot scene. Pity.

To be sure, physicists are smart and most are funny in person like Richard Feynmann. However, some brilliantly written dialogues strike me as out-of-character. Even the entourage of Strauss could drop some vitriolic lines. Someone should have toned it down, not overshoot.

8.title: Movies are back. Packed theater and overwhelming praise for a Christopher Nolan film. Unfortunate it had to be this one.
8.content:
My first watch of this film was on opening day, second half of a double feature, and without the knowledge of critical response. This viewing was a few days later among friends in an IMAX theater. That viewing I was impressed with Christopher Nolan's technical ability and the performances are fantastic. I forgot how much folks overrate those aspects of movies until later in the day and the following days when I see this film being praised as one of the best ever.

It most certainly is not that great.

The politics are dumb and the storytelling choice is incredibly questionable. But to discuss the storytelling I feel it is important to break down the story.

This is a biopic about Julius Robert Oppenheimer, the father of the atomic bomb. How this guy went from a talented Jewish physics student to potentially the most influential scientist that has ever existed. From the start Nolan presents Oppenheimer as a gifted young man with a knack for understanding physics. We get the impression that this is the golden boy and a pure genius, everything wrong with stories about smart people. But after the start, we don't get much of that at all. Oppenheimer is then shifted away from gifted person to a leader who understands how to manage folks and does not pretend to be perfect and great at everything. Most of the science in this film is relatively silly dialogue that technically makes sense but I have no idea why they occur when and how they do, almost like Nolan doesn't really know how these places function. The film does get so far away from its initial presentation of Oppenheimer that it is regularly stated that this man does not participate in physics much anymore. Quite the contradiction that I think is done well enough and probably reflects the real story.

Where Nolan gets into trouble is the explicit discussion on politics, of which this film is deeply dependent on. Something that I expected given the historical J Robert Oppenheimer mixed with how questionable Christopher Nolan's politics seem to be.

I've touched on my interpretation of Nolan's politics in the films of his that I've watched so there really is no point in including those here as this film is more about how he understands politics that are different from his own. Capital-C Communism was almost the entirety of American politics from the end of WW1 until the fall of the Soviet Union. And really the height of its influence was probably in the years between WW2 and Vietnam, though its roots are much older, dating back to lower-case-c communism and the theorists of the 19th century. Oppenheimer very well was a communist in the academic sense of the word. He read all three volumes of Das Kapital, something that very much makes him more well read than almost all Communists, past or present. He even understood the concepts well enough to take his students to the massive labor strikes and union meetings that were a major part of global politics in the 1930s. This fact seems to be completely lost on Christopher Nolan as he presents communism, and subsequently Oppenheimer's politics, as a more academic incursion than it historically was. In fact most of the things that were later called "Communist" by McCarthyists were done by folks who were at the time, or later in life, opposed to Bolshevik theory. Much of the work done in the labor movement before 1918 was done by Anarchists and varying Left-Wing organizers, with only very few taking a positive stance on Vladimir Lenin's October Revolution once it occured. Only later, starting somewhere around the stock market crash, did the Vanguardist Capital-C Communist movement gain traction in large numbers in this country. It seems that the historical J Robert Oppenheimer was probably not a Vanguardist, judging by his disavowal of communism after the war, and instead one of the many people who supported the Socialist movement at the time that had genuine solutions to the problems caused by Capitalism.

One of those problems eventually ended up being fascism. Communists, Anarchists, Social Democrats, and all the other differing flavors of socialist rarely agree on much but they all could come together and oppose the rise of fascism and the culmination of this ideology in the Nazi regime. From the inception of left wing thought, authoritarian use of existing institutions were always used to quell the labor movement. In spite of the overwhelming force of monarchists and Liberal governments, Socialism persisted and labor struggles were won from time to time. So when fascism came knocking on the ruined doors in interwar Europe, all leftists understood the threat and what was at stake. One of the last efforts in the leftist struggle against fascism took place in Spain during the fascist overthrow of the republican (in the academic sense of the word, not the co-opted American sense) government. The father of fascism, Benito Mussolini, and Adolf Hitler supported Franco's fascists while the Republicans and Catalonia were supported by international leftist groups, trade unions, anarchists, and the Comintern. It was a precursor to WW2 where we had very clear sides with one being fascists and the other largely being working-class folks. And yet the Liberal governments of the time took a stance of neutrality because while fascism was a threat to civil liberties and minorities, socialism was a threat to Capitalism (the entire reason liberalism exists). You were either opposed to fascism or you aided it and as usual Liberalism's inaction allowed the strong centralization of fascism to blossom.

All of this nuance could have been presented in this film but that would require Christopher Nolan to understand worker's rights beyond the labels of "Communism, union, or left-wing" which I know he does not. Nolan understands these concepts in the post-FDR context that we all today are stuck with, unless for some reason you take an academic interest in communism.

In the film, Christopher Nolan presents trade unionism and Communism as somewhat intertwined. The Communists are treated as shady individuals and the Communist Party as a shady organization, even in the non-Strauss scenes. This is the framing of the McCarthyists and Christopher Nolan accepts it and presents it objectively. Nevermind the fact that historical J Edgar Hoover and McCarthyists were as racist and anti-communist as the Nazis. We get the presentation that Communists are somehow just as bad as Nazis, which is the incredibly asinine garbage one would expect to hear from post-FDR liberals and conservatives. We get a good deal of screen time devoted to Communist Party gatherings of professors at cocktail parties and (I think) just one union hall meeting of laborers, none of longshoremen strikes or factory workers that Oppenheimer also frequented were pictured, and almost no screen time of what the Communist Party was fighting against. It is all once again just presented as an academic exercise of talking about communism and none of the actual labor organizing that was very present throughout Oppenheimer's time at Berkeley. This is because Nolan wants to clearly indicate the difference between J Robert Oppenheimer and the Communist Party so he can present how unjust the trials against him were - which they were, but Nolan either doesn't understand why or doesn't agree with the reason why and wanted to substitute his own.

The Red Scare of the McCarthy era and the suppression and oppression of left wing movements were unjust because Socialism is not fascism. This is something that J Edgar Hoover (along with many powerful individuals) probably disagreed with and since his FBI was the leader of domestic investigation, they treated Socialism like it was a major threat to humanity when it was only a threat to the status quo. So when the war was over, the pivot back from fascism to communism was made and this time with all the tools and energy used to find fascists were used against leftists. So when Cold War era rhetoric (or modern day rhetoric for that matter) demonizes communism it is inherently and intentionally baseless because communism has always been a threat to Capitalism and the status quo. J Robert Oppenheimer was unfairly persecuted for his communist ties, not because he wasn't a communist (he definitely was), but because persecuting communists is wrong. But Nolan cannot admit that, either because he doesn't agree or because he doesn't want to agree.

All of that could have been avoided if Christopher Nolan didn't try to include a political thriller in this film. This could have been a movie about the moral implications of the atomic bomb (and it half is) but instead Nolan wanted to weave in the politics because that is what he was publicly attacked for in his day.

To mix in the political elements, Christopher Nolan reuses the non-linear storytelling he perfected in Memento (2000). While that film used it to portray faulty memory, this film almost uses it to portray faulty investigations. And I think it is deliberate, because if Nolan had made this film more linear then it would be very obvious how stupid it is to make two movies in one. But he did it this way and I think everyone can agree that the Strauss portion of this film is probably the most boring and unnecessary. Nolan probably only wanted it to undermine the criticism of Oppenheimer that was leveled against him in his day and to glorify the man for modern audiences. He wanted to whitewash the father of the atomic bomb.

And finally I can talk about what J Robert Oppenheimer is known for today: the Manhattan Project.

From all accounts, the science of the film and the progression of discovery on the way to the bomb are all very accurate and well done. Despite how silly I think a lot of the scientidic dialogue is, I cannot deny that everything about the Manhattan Project, Los Alamos,

8.title: A Stunning Return to Form from one of Hollywood's Greatest Directors.
8.content:
I've been a big Christopher Nolan fan for a while (surprising, considering I'm a film bro, I know), but can't help but feel most of his offerings in the 2010s have been...in my opinion, weaker than his previous work. For me, films like Dunkirk and Tenet come off as cold nd lifeless, more interested in intricate film making than telling a compelling story. Nolan seems to actively want to alienate the audience with these movies. Interestellar and The Dark Knight Rises, on the other hand, almost feel too sentimental, betraying Nolan's characteristic fixation on logical storytelling for endings that seem like studio encouraged "feel good" endings that aren't necessarily earned.

That's all to say Oppenheimer strikes the balance between Nolan's almost mechanical view of storytelling - with various parts moving in tandem to get to an end goal - with the heart and humanity to keep the audience invested. It's his best movie since Inception.

Despite being 3 hours long, Oppenheimer was never boring or slow to me. If anything, one of the biggest issues with the film is its pacing in the beginning; it does feel somewhat edited like a movie trailer, jumping from scene to scene as we attempt to get an understanding of Oppenheimer's life. It does feel a bit too fast for the first chunk of the movie, but it's all worth it in the end. Once the main plot gets going, the movie really picks up its energy and something truly special. If I had one big complaint about this movie, it's the opening act (and to me, it's significant enough to hold this movie back from being a true masterpiece).

Cillian Murphy is absolutely incredible as J. Robert Oppenheimer; he embodies the man to such an extent that he basically disappears into the role. He is Oppenheimer, by the end of the movie, just so total and compelling a depiction of this fascinating historical figure that it reminds me why biopics still matter, even if the genre itself has become a bit of a parody. Robert Downey Jr. Is also incredible in this movie, disappearing into the role of conniving head of the Atomic Energy Association and surely earning himself a Best Supporting Actor nod. I also really like Matt Damon in this movie; for such dense and sometimes difficult subject matter, he brought a warmth, charm, and charisma to his scenes that felt oddly comforting.

To say this movie is STACKED with notable faces would be an understatement; the amazing thing is most of these people pop into the film for a scene or two and often, have extremely memorable moments in their own right. Florence Pugh's scenes are jarring, seductive, and sometimes disturbing, but I felt she was so crucial to the narrative. Emily Blunt playing Kitty Oppenheimer wasn't super impressive to me...until her incredible scene with Jason Clark during the questioning. My God, were they on fire there. Josh Hartnett pops in and brings that "all-American boy" pathos to the film and he's absolutely excellent. I could go on and on about all the actors in this movie, some very famous, who clearly just enjoyed the opportunity working with Nolan.

If there was one performance I really disliked though, it was Gary Oldman as Harry Truman. Not only did he not really sound or look like him, but it was a rare "over performance" for this guy, who typically is fantastic as a character actor. I felt he was jarring and super distracting.

I loved this film's cinematography, especially towards the end. There are so many iconic, visually stunning moments that stuck with me days after watching the film (i.e. Oppenheimer walking down the hallway, the entire assembly scene). But it's also interesting how overall, this film is very laid back and small scale (despite dealing with highly weighty themes), and will probably disappoint some expecting Nolan bombast. I personally didn't mind, but I would've been okay with a scene or two exploring the context of WHY the atomic bomb seemed necessary (*cough* my male brain wants some WW II action scenes for the IMAX *cough*).

I also really liked how the film dealt with the politics and zeitgeist of the era; if you're fascinated by World War II and the early Cold War, as I am, you are in for a feast of references that only a history nerd could appreciate. It really captures what the time was like and how complicated our past really was. This is a movie that deliberately eschews the Great Man theory of history, instead putting Oppenheimer squarely within a social and political context that, even if he tries, he can never control or be above.

But, I hope that instead of rolling your eyes and saying "it was boring, it was confusing," it prompts audience curiosity and gets people to try and understand the history for themselves. Nolan does a tremendous job of distilling a complex man and a complex era into a historical epic; I really have to commend the man for having the confidence to make a 3 hour long, dialog heavy historical drama in the middle of summer, and have it be a BLOCKBUSTER.

They don't make many Christopher Nolans anymore. Protect this man at all costs.

8.title: Oppenheimer: Christopher Nolan's Epic Journey into the Complex Mind of a Scientific Giant
8.content:
Background: "Oppenheimer," directed by the visionary Christopher Nolan, is a historical biopic that delves into the fascinating life of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the renowned physicist known as the father of the atomic bomb. Set against the backdrop of World War II and the race to harness the power of nuclear fission, the film takes the audience on a riveting journey through Oppenheimer's personal struggles, scientific genius, and the profound moral implications of his groundbreaking work.

The Great Things:

Compelling Storytelling: Nolan's masterful storytelling weaves together three timelines, providing an in-depth look at Oppenheimer's life, from his formative years as a student to his role as the head of the Manhattan Project. The non-linear narrative adds depth to the character and keeps the audience engrossed.

Outstanding Performances: The film boasts an ensemble cast, with Cillian Murphy delivering a career-defining performance as Oppenheimer. His portrayal captures the complexities of the man torn between his scientific curiosity and the moral dilemmas posed by his creations. Robert Downey Jr. And Matt Damon also shine in their respective roles, adding depth and nuance to the narrative.

Thought-Provoking Themes: "Oppenheimer" is not just a historical account of a scientific endeavor; it explores profound themes of power, responsibility, and the consequences of scientific advancement. It forces the audience to ponder the ethical implications of groundbreaking discoveries and the toll they take on individuals and the world.

The Moderate Things:

Lengthy Duration: Clocking in at three hours, "Oppenheimer" is a demanding watch. While the film's intricate plot necessitates a lengthy runtime, some viewers may find it challenging to stay fully engaged throughout.

The Flop Things:

Confusing Chronology: The film's non-linear storytelling, while engrossing, can be confusing at times, especially for viewers unfamiliar with the historical events and characters. Some may find it challenging to follow the complex web of timelines.

Review from Various Aspects:

Plot: "Oppenheimer" presents a gripping and insightful narrative, but the complex structure might overwhelm casual viewers. Nevertheless, the compelling exploration of Oppenheimer's life and the political context surrounding the development of the atomic bomb is commendable.

Acting: The performances in "Oppenheimer" are nothing short of exceptional. Cillian Murphy portrayal of Oppenheimer is a career-defining triumph, with other characters also delivering standout performances.

Duration: The movie's extended runtime might test the patience of some audience members, but it is necessary to explore the complexities of Oppenheimer's life fully.

Special Effects: As expected from a Nolan film, the special effects in "Oppenheimer" are top-notch. The recreation of the Trinity test and other pivotal moments in the atomic bomb's development is visually stunning.

Music: Ludwig Göransson's haunting and immersive soundtrack complements the film's tense and emotional moments, elevating the overall cinematic experience.

Great Ending: In conclusion, "Oppenheimer" is a thought-provoking masterpiece that showcases Christopher Nolan's unparalleled filmmaking prowess. While its ambitious storytelling and lengthy duration may not be for everyone, the film offers a mesmerizing journey into the life of a scientific giant and the consequences of his discoveries. Cillian Murphy's powerful performance and Nolan's directorial brilliance make "Oppenheimer" a cinematic achievement worthy of acclaim. This film serves as a stark reminder of the complexities of human nature, the pursuit of knowledge, and the moral quandaries faced by those who hold the power to change the course of history. "Oppenheimer" stands as a landmark in biographical cinema, leaving a lasting impact on its audience and sparking deep contemplation long after the credits roll.

8.title: Everything about Oppenheimer
8.content: Oppenheimer is a rare sort of biopic that doesn't cut down the characters and events down to a single focused narrative. Instead, it covers just about everything about him - the development of the atomic bomb, the moral qualms about dropping it on Japan, his relationships, his post-war activism, his security clearance "trial" and more. It's a dizzying montage of events that skip from time period to time period with an incredibly fast pace but it works due to a clear subjective thread and deft editing. Due to this comprehensive scope, there's too much to comment on, but the acting and editing deserve the most praise. The main criticisms I have are that there's nothing in the film that warrants an IMAX viewing and the flags are historically inaccurate.

8.title: Oppenheimer directed by Christopher Nolan.
8.content:
Sensitivity alert: this movie has low minority and LBGT representation.

Ultimately this is the autobiography of a Director who is: an executional genius, compartmentaliser and, gets the very best out of his staff.

18 months ago I wrote: I was looking forward to this story to see: actors asleep for 80% of the movie, scenes repeated from different angles and in the wrong order, proving love is in the theory of relativity and, the a-bomb explosion leading to a chain reaction where the movie then plays backwards to the beginning.

What I didn't expect was Nolans best movie since Memento. We had more baddies than an Indiana Jones, more A-listers than the Daily Mail Celebrity page, and more minutes per ticket than ever.

He engaged his inner David Lynch, including a scene with Churchill in the oval office. Like Spielberg he'd been fishing for an in oscar the WWII pond. I think he nailed it along with Cillian Murphy, hopefully Matt Damon (love those Boston Boys) and maybe a nod to Jason Clarke.

The book "The God Particle" gives a great insight to the giant steps made in quantum physics at the turn of the 20th Century, an unsettling period best expressed in the art of the Impressionist/Classical Modernist (although I never noticed that particular paining in the Kunsthaus). It was great that Nolan abandoned his own interpretation of science and left it to the professionals this time.

For me art is about conveying emotion and is best done when we can relate to the artist i.e. Humans (not super-heros) in extraordinary circumstances (Spielberg). In this movie the emotion is menace, which I felt in the pit of my stomach.

A list of the threatening characters include: God, Hitler, Stalin, Japanese Fascism, Commies (who don't believe in god), McCarthy, espionage, love cheats, the swamp, the a-bomb.... did I miss anyone? And an epic rivalry, equal to that of "Amadeus".

It would be interesting to see the number of minuets cut and if the story eroded, if scenes ran in order with no overlapping, like they did with the Godfather franchise. In Memento the editing was brilliant because it allowed us to see the story from the point of view of the protagonist, but does the compartmentalisation in Oppenheimer relate to the protagonist or merely to tax the viewer?

I read many complaints about the soundtrack drowning the dialogue, I think it is more to do with movie houses having the equalizer badly tuned.

8.title: Brilliant dialogues. Keeps Engaged most of the times!
8.content:
Don't watch this movie if you want to see how the first Atom bomb was made or the WWII ended.

Watch it if you love brilliant dialogues. The dialogues are master piece and so is the switch from current time frame to the past and back.

The characters have played their roles brilliantly. Murphy and Robert have done justice to their characters, so has Matt.

The movie is long, 180 plus minutes and that is where it captures the details and the essence of the court room drama. Doesn't stay in one time frame for so long that you get bored and swaps to past frame to make it relevant and a bit confusing at the same time (don't get me wrong with confusing word as it might get tricky if you don't follow the dialogues).

This is not Interstellar, so don't go expecting to see space crafts and bombs and fights. The fight is in the courtroom for everyone to see.

8.title: Decent movie spoilt by over loud and intrusive background music/effects
8.content:
This could have been an excellent movie with a star studded cast and stand out performance by Killian Murphey. However on a film largely dependent upon dialogue I can't understand why the editors felt it necessary to have constant background music (it never stops throughout the movie) which was discordant and painful to endure. At times it was so loud that hearing what was being said was impossible and even at it quietest it made comprehension difficult.

That being said, the movie painted a good picture of Oppenheimers character and the duplicity of politicians and the ultimate dilemma between scientific advancement and humanity of dropping the bomb.

Certainly came away with food for thought!

8.title: Absolutely fantastic.
8.content: This movie was absolutely fantastic. Quick paced. The score was powerful and emotional. Acting was exceptional. The last 45 mins were a bit much for me, so I'll take away a star for that. Also the nudity was unnecessary. You could have communicated the romantic tension without it, so I remove a star for that as well. Doing a little research on the biography of Oppenheimer afterwards, I believe the movie was very faithful to his character and personal life. Over all, I believe Christopher Nolan's film was a masterpiece that will always be remembered positively. As long as that movie was, I can't wait to see it again.

8.title: Another (Almost) Perfect Christopher Nolan Film
8.content: This movie has some of the BEST cinematography and acting I've ever seen. Everything seems to be very accurate to history (wardrobe, sets, etc). Cillian Murphy is the perfect casting choice for Oppenheimer and he killed it. I do somewhat feel that certain characters should have been given more screen time but the film is already 3+ hours. I also felt the pacing was a little random. This will not be an easy watch, especially for younger audiences. The ending has to be one of the best I have ever seen. No matter how many times I rewatch, I always get chills. Contrary to what others have said, the trinity test scene is absolutely PERFECT and manages to feel different from all other movie explosions. This is definitely one you don't want to miss on the big screen. 70mm if possible!!!

8.title: A brilliant piece of art on first viewing. Rewatch needed
8.content:
They won't fear it until they understand it. And they won't understand until they've rewatched it. First watch will take you only so far.

A lot to take in and absorb. Cillian Murphy and Robert Downey Jr have given their best ever performance. Nolan delivers again with his team in Cinematography, Techniques and sound editing. It would definitely take a second viewing to completely appreciate and or understand every aspects.

The experience on first viewing is mostly positive and captivating. But Nolan being Nolan with his non linear storytelling and layered character study; this requires to be seen again at it's own pace to be fully grasped. 8.5/10 on first watch.

8.content: Awesome, NOLAN .. THANKS FOR THIS. WE REMEMBER THIS. Your cinematic brilliance . 1st half at some parts while charcters discussing little boring feeling i felt but except that genius of a cinema. Watched first time your film in theatre it's great .
