A 3 hours film length doesn't frighten me as long as the film flies by which only happens if a movie keeps you engaged the whole time. Unfortunately, I feel it was a little too long and should have ended soon after the atomic bomb was a success and Oppenheimer comes to grips with the powerful self-destruction creation he made. Instead Nolan chose to drone on about Oppenheimer's bureaucratic problems he encounters and beats a dead horse on the moral problems he comes to grip with. I felt it was answered enough in the previous 2.5 hours and I admit I was beginning to clock watch and wondering when it was gonna wrap up. All I can say is that Nolan is indeed the greatest director of this generation but peaked with Interstellar for me which was truly a top 10 film. That movie deserved multiple viewings with a similar runtime but keeps you engaged the whole time. This I feel comes up way short behind his other masterpieces such as Interstellar, Dark Knight, The Prestige, and Inception.

7.title: Confusing
7.content:
A True Nolan fan here...

What can i say about Oppenheimer... The first hour i liked the best.

The build up, the science, the visions of particals and Energy.

The second hour was also desent, but deviated more from the bomb and gravitated towards Oppenheimer himself.

The last hour, was to much of a politcal drama and that played out like a losing chess game.

I have to adres the elephant in the room.

The "big"'explosion was a big letdown. Even in IMAX, except for the sound it wasn't all that spectaculair.

The acting was top nodge, Oscar worthy, Maybe even more For RD jr than the others.

Music was briljant but overall it was not the bombshell i expected.

7.title: Amazing cast, two serious flaws
7.content: The acting in this film is fascinating and the cast is absolutely stellar. It's an interesting story and certainly would have deserved a 9 were it not for two major flaws that are common in movies these days but taken to absurd excess here. First, the sound. It was so muffled and echoey, and the music and sound effects were so overwhelming, that my friends and I missed at least a third of the dialog. Since the drama depended on the dialog, this was a serious error in judgment. At times, it was obvious something very humorous was occurring in the dialog, but the entire audience just sat in confused silence trying to figure out what was going on. And then there were the frequent changes in scene. Just as you are settling into a scene, suddenly the story jumps to a different city, with different people, in a different decade. Between the inaudible dialog and the frenetic changes in scene, the film was often difficult to follow. I look forward to watching this with subtitles to see what I missed.

7.title: Very good but WAY too loud
7.content: I don't understand Nolan's fascination with jacking up the volume of his films to a level that sometimes drowns out the dialogue. It's also not necessary to constantly play background music. I'm not a filmmaker but it's ok to let the dialogue speak for itself. At least with this one I could still hear the dialogue, unlike Insterstellar where much of the film's exposition was drowned out by banging music. I don't recall Nolan's earlier films being this way but I think it may have started around The Dark Knight Rises and definitely hit a crescendo with Interstellar. Anyway, clanging music aside, the film is very good. The acting is superb and the story, minus a couple frankly unnecessary sex scenes, is phenomenal. My favorite scene was the bomb test and the tension of expecting the loud bang that waits for a bit before it actually happens. There's an example where audio was used correctly. It was actually QUIET for what seemed like an eternity and then the loud bang kicked in at just the right time. I wish the music had been handled the same way for the rest of the movie. I also didn't have any problem with the length and while it was preachy at times, the story was still effective and I could see why Nolan has said it's a horror film. Fix the audio and this is a 10.

7.title: Dutch is not Deutch
7.content: Don't get me wrong, Christopher Nolan did a great job making this movie. It was a suspenseful, historically important movie. However, I am very disappointed that a movie that probably has cost a lot of money to make, did not even bother to check whether the Dutch (scene which was shot in Leiden) actually made sense. It was in fact, not Dutch, but German. This, especially considering that the timeline was during WW2, is shameful. WW2 was a difficult time for the Dutch, of which survivors, including my own grandma, are still alive. Older generations can take offence to this mistake, and it is just very sloppy.

7.title: I want to like it....
7.content: Firstly, fantastic acting by Cillian and Downey. Amazing cameo by Gary Oldman. Rest of the cast were good nothing extraordinary. But my personal problem was the story makes a lot of jump cuts which is fine, but before going in the movie audience is expected to do a little bit of homework. Two hearings were going on in the beginning and only much later we are explained what's going on, but by that time I got exhausted just keeping up. Also once the explanation is given I didn't care enough. I usually don't check time or speak with anyone during the movie but it was very hard not to. I liked Downey's acting better than Cillian btw.

7.title: It was alright
7.content: In the beginning of the movie, I kinda got bored, and was bored for half of the movie, I'm kind of disappointed at this point, but, the last hour saved it, in my opinion. The moment when oppie and his crew started building the atomic bomb, things got interesting. The movie idea was very cool, people say that most don't really understand the film, but, it is in fact hard to understand it, but in the end, I did catch the idea of how they were building it. By far, not the best movie Christopher Nolan has ever made, but, it's there, I give it a solid 7, not bad, but not too great. Kinda disappointed, I was very hyped too see this movie, but it kinda screw me over at the beginning.

7.title: Needed an Editor with the Guts to Say Too Much
7.content:
Take any single sequence of this film by itself, it's brilliantly done. Take it as a three hours long whole, it's overdone and self-indulgent. Visually stunning, albeit with a sometimes heavy handed script, Oppenheimer comes achingly close, but doesn't quite live up to the hype.

I knew that Oppenheimer was a brilliant scientist who had led the Manhattan Project that built the atomic bomb. I was also aware that there were reservations among those who developed the bomb about actually putting it to use. I was only vaguely away that Oppenheimer had gotten caught up in a McCarthy era controversy that essentially ended his career. Nolan could have cut an hour from the film and lost nothing of the narrative, characterizations and moral. It's too bad that there wasn't anyone who might have told Nolan that it's altogether too much. That being said, it's a tour de force of acting, especially by Cillian Murphy, Emily Blunt, Matt Damon. And Robert Downey, Jr.

7.title: Longggggggg!
7.content:
How can a movie about the apocalypse be so long? At 3 hours this thing is a nightmare. It could easily be 90 minutes. The 1989 John Cusack film fat man and little boy covers the same material but is infinitely more entertaining.

So let's see. Oppenheimer is asked to make the atomic bomb. And he spends an inordinate amount of time wondering if maybe the bomb is bad or Communists are bad or whether he should sleep with another woman. And Iron Man pops up and decides he doesn't like Oppenheimer so he tells everyone that Oppenheimer is bad. And in the end everybody gets fired. Seriously why did this have to take 3 hours?

The cinematography was nice all of the technical stuff was nice. And half of Hollywood seems to be in the movie. I guess after covid everybody's dying for work any work. But honestly I would suggest that you just look up fat man and little boy and watch that instead.

Yawn. How did they make a movie that made me almost want to fall asleep while they're setting off an atomic bomb? That's what I'd like to know.

7.title: I feel tricked...
7.content: The movie is good but all that noise about seeing it on the biggest screen possible (I did) is unfounded. It's a procedural and you can see it on any screen you want. I was more impressed with the sound than the visuals. FX are secondary and spare, while the framing of individual shots is rather standard and the cuts so quick as too make it practically inconsequential anyway. It's still worth seeing in a movie theater, and it is a good film with some stellar performances. It's almost a shame there are so many name actors in it because it snaps you out of the story when you keep recognizing people in what amounts mostly to bit parts. It's not Nolan's best but it is a decent drama.

7.title: Not Christopher Nolans strongest film but it delivers.
7.content:
3.5 out of 5 stars.

Oppenheimer is a pretty fair biographical thriller film about Robert Oppenheimer and his invention of the nuclear bomb.

First of all it is a Christopher Nolan film which he delivers a non linear story structure which follow Oppenheimer. And than a black and white sequence which follows Lewis (Robert Downey Jr.) perspective. It is a strong biographical film. Nolan mastered himself at telling the story with a moving script.

The film builds the suspense with Oppenheimer rising to building the first nuclear bomb. After the first bomb test which does fail to be cinematic or spectacular that the direction tries to aim for.

Cillian Murphy, Robert Downey Jr., Emily Blunt, and the rest of the cast ensemble did great. It does have a variety of familiar faces. The performance is great.

What disappointed with the film is the film drags after the bomb test. It flashes between sequences with Lewis testifying against Oppenheimer. Talks of him being a communists or a spy. It just falls into one long hour of back and forth talk of his side of story and Lewis. It falls very flat. Especially it is a three hour film. The suspense and build up leads to a disappointment of one long dull film.

Nolan tries to entertain the audience with his loud music or noise in the background of thumping noises or flashes of the atoms exploding. The music score was also okay but nothing special. I am a huge Chris Nolan fan of all his films. This film falls right with Insomnia with being the weakest. It has a great cast and story. And direction. The script falls flat in the last hour which is more frustrating viewing than actually watching a strong film.

Oppenheimer is an okay film and a one time watch kind of movie and forgotten after it ends. I was a little disappointed.

7.title: Epic but too long and wrong focus
7.content: Fantastic film in so many aspects, such as acting and craftmanship: One of the greats in that aspect. However, as a viewer, I would have wished for a shorter film, possibly around two hours, and one that was focused more on the creation and testing of the bomb. I realise that the name of the movie is "Oppenheimer" and not "The Bomb", but it would still have been more interesting than following a quite tedious political game, the cancel culture of it's time. As it stands now it should have ended after the Trinity test. Everything beyond that point is where most of the excess time and not so interesting things where.

7.title: I wanted to like this
7.content: This movie was HUGE on dialog and nowhere near enough real action. Probably afraid to hurt anyone's feelings. The layer of music over top of the voice track was too much and made for too many missed words. All along I kept wishing for closed captioning so I could follow the story. For a 3 hour movie I completely expected more action. Sound decibel level was impressively loud. I expect some cinema grade loudspeakers got blown and probably startled a few Barbie movie goers in the theater next door. Time will tell if this was a hit. Might catch more streaming views so we can follow all the spoken words.

7.title: sloppenheimer
7.content:
Maturing is realising that christopher nolan isn't your favourite director anymore. Starting out as a film kid, you either go the wes anderson route, the nolan route, or the edgar wright route, and i was definitely a big nolan fan. I used to love the dark knight, inception, interstellar, but those films upon rewatch became draining. The style become so irritating, cringe in the way it took itself so seriously. While they were conventionally good films, i became disenchanted with most of his work. Comes tenet and i'm pretty much done with nolan, little faith left in him as a director, with his own films becoming a pastiche of nolan's ideas and conventions.

Needless to say, i went into oppenheimer reluctantly, though it would be disingenuous to say that i didn't have a morbid curiosity about the film. Biopics are my least favourite type of films, though right off the bat, oppenheimer doesn't strike as a conventional biopic, and thats mostly due to nolan fully maturing in his style and voice. This feels so nolan while at the same time feeling incredibly dissimilar to his previous work. Wordy dialogue that doesn't come off as robotic or blatantly expository, even though 90 percent of the dialogue is exactly that. There is life and character poured into this film, making this nolan's most human film, the most relatable even though it's not intrinsically relatable in subject matter. This is nolan at his most emotive, only really challenged by interstellar, which i would say is his other most human film.

Dialogue is good again, and it's helped with the fast-paced editing that nolan loves to use. Quite often the score will envelop the mix, making conversation hard to hear, which is still an issue that nolan is seemingly all for, though he definitely shows restraint. This is nowhere near as bad as tenet or dark knight rises, it's quite manageable this time round and it actually works, really putting you inside oppenheimer's head. Overall nolan's style fully matures, and it's used for a biopic, a type of film generally associated with the driest of dry and the utmost safest type of filmmaking. Obvoiusly nolan isn't here to make that movie, it's almost as though that this isn't non fiction, rather a character and a story completely made up in nolan's mind. And with that said, it's one of the more engaging stories he's told.

Performances are good though cillian murphy is the fucking star of the show, obviously. In fact he kind of outweighs the rest of the cast. I thought matt damon was actually quite bad, though i've never really been a fan of him. Big actors with small screen time and small roles was such a good decision and makes everyone feel so important, and the actors mostly disappear into their roles, if it's not for a few exceptions (matt damon). All-time best performance from murphy, though once again he's almost too good for the rest of the cast.

This movie is a lot, and i would consider it a bit uneven quality wise. A film on this scale simply doesn't sustain that type of magic that is present in certain sequences of this film. Though with that said, this film reminded me why i liked nolan in the first place.

EDIT: 4/5 -> 3.5/5 a lot of stuff has irked me when thinking about this film, and i think i'll need a rewatch to truly know how i feel about it all.

7.title: Too long but good movie.
7.content: Five Golden Globes for Oppenheimer, so that was the main reason I wanted to see it, to see what the fuzz is about. It's not a bad movie but personally I wouldn't have giving it any award. The cast was phenomenal, and by that I mean a lot of well known good actors and actresses, so nothing bad to say about the acting. I really like writer/director Christopher Nolan but Oppenheimer is certainly not better than Interstellar, Inception, The Prestige, Memento or Dunkirk for example. Three hours to tell Oppenheimer's story is just too long, especially when there is a lot of talking and debating and not a lot of action. The story is just dragged out and could have been told in two hours max. But yes it's a good movie, with a lot of good actors, it's just not award worthy as I've seen much better movies in that year.

7.title: Worthy but It was really a total bore from start to finish
7.content:
Oppenheimer

Perhaps I have been living under a rock but I had never heard of this man prior to the movie, of course I had heard of Einstein's theory of splitting the atom, and first done by Rutherford in the 30s, but apart from that I knew nothing.

This was a very mixed bag of a movie, when it appears the subject of the movie was the coordinator of the team in the desert that made the two nuclear devices that bombed Japan, at the end of the Second World War in Hiroshima and Nagasaki. As such it is a very American movie we Brits had nothing to do with it apart from supplying several of the scientists.

The movie was mainly about the politics and the secrecy and keeping secrecy around the project they were all working on, and as such, it was as dry as dust. The movie moved backwards and forwards in time, and it was very difficult to keep track of it. You only knew you were in the 60s when it was shot in black-and-white, but really, it was quite confusing.

Did I enjoy the movie? No, not really, I've just experienced it, did we have some stellar performances from the actors, it's difficult to tell as the roles were so very constrained. Clearly it is a worthy movie, and as such no doubt it will try and do well at the Oscars, but to my mind, there was nothing winning here.

I'm going to give this a 7 out of 10 for the way they managed to turn something so dry into something vaguely watchable but in terms of entertainment it was at best 3 out of 10. I am glad I saw it, but I never want to see it or hear it ever again.

7.title: An absolute low point
7.content: Oppenheimer is a well made film. The music is amazing. The acting is phenomenal. The story upon which it is based is really interesting as well. The adaptation for the screen, however is blatantly somniferous. Taken into account the upward trend of magnificence in each consecutive Nolan film, this is an absolue low point. It contains the usual tricks: black and white different time lines; flashbacks to a happening undisclosed until the end; ticking tacking music; silence before complete blasting of your eardrums. But now with an A24 vibe... I can't imagine this film has lived up to anybody's expectations.

7.title: Nolan hasn't done a world class film since interstellar
7.content:
Yes I'm giving this a 7 for its achievements with the whole production, acting, cinematography, score and above all the difficult biopic choice. It is an interesting story and I am a huge history fan. Which helped a lot with heaps of the other side characters.

The run-time was not an issue for me .

I will however say I want more vintage Nolan next. He's tried two movies in this historical genre Dunkirk which I don't rate at all and now Oppenheimer which I feel is a huge redemption.

Tenet was far too confusing and average compared to other Nolan epics. You've done well Nolan I salute you, it's time to go back to what you do best.

7.title: Exhausting is the Nolan style
7.content: "Oppenheimer" comes three years after "Tenet," which is clearly well-made but I do not like. "Oppenheimer" straddles the same criticism but at least, this one has a star-studded ensemble that slightly makes up for overly stylized filmmaking to the point that the viewer cannot catch their breath and feels lagging behind the whole time. There are very important historical nuggets in this movie, and if you are not familiar, it is best that you pay close attention, as it is something real and something potentially devastating to humankind. In some way, that makes this movie an exhausting way to be educated on this topic, when you can extract the same or more information from a more straightforward documentary.

7.title: Why is this such a hit?
7.content:
I had high hopes for this movie going in. I love all of Nolan's other movies, and I actually worked as a scientist at Los Alamos for several years (many years after the Manhattan project), and so I'm very familiar with the underlying physics, the New Mexico landscape, and the constant tension between scientific research and security concerns. If anyone was going to enjoy this movie, it was me!

And to be fair, I did basically enjoy it, mostly. Seeing a story I thought I knew fairly well brought to life, including many extra details that I didn't know about, was definitely interesting. The acting is undoubtedly top notch. But is it a Great Movie? Well, no.

The main issue here is that the central thread that the movie hangs on is the meeting to determine whether Oppenheimer's security clearance should be renewed. A secondary thread is the review as to whether Strauss should be appointed commerce secretary. Both of these threads are essentially courtroom dramas with a lot of talking back and forth, which can be pretty dry. But more importantly, the stakes don't feel that high (it's not life or death), and the arguments for and against the people concerned are not that interesting. I get that the movie uses these things as framing devices to cover a lot of more interesting topics, in the form of flashbacks, but it just feels like the balance is off. There's just way too much time spent in the courtroom, especially towards the end of the three hours, and the rest of the content feels fragmented and rushed.

And the famous Trinity test explosion scene that doesn't use any CGI? Yeah, it shows, and not in a good way.

In conclusion, an interesting study of an interesting guy, well acted, and nicely shot. But a bit unfocused and probably 30 minutes too long. 7/10, though I might have given it 8/10 I didn't feel it was so over-rated...

7.title: Historically solid, but a bit too much Nolan
7.content:
This is a fantastic bit of historical drama/biopic. The cast is universally flawless, and the film does an excellent treatment of the complex personalities involved. I thought they got Teller and Szilard particularly well, after Oppenheimer himself. They also did a great job with Bohr and Lawrence, and even the small bits of Feynman's history are easy to see here. If you know this topic from the histories that have been written of it, you will recognize everyone. I'm surprised to say that I found Damon to be the weakest in his portrayal of Groves, but that could be the writing, as Groves was both a famously difficult man to work with and an overweight slob of a human. It would be difficult for anyone except perhaps someone like John Goodman to portray him effectively.

My biggest complaint of the film is that it is too long. Its presumed climax is followed by a good 45-60 minutes of plot that is essentially courtroom drama, but devolves into a Nolan-style psychological thriller. Perhaps it was the cinema I was in, but I found the dialogue in these sections to be very difficult to follow, and sometimes even a bit difficult to hear/understand properly. I'll look forward to a rewatch with subtitles.

I've seen some people complain that the film is glamorizing a monster, and that no Japanese people are portrayed. I think this is a profoundly shallow interpretation of history. Oppenheimer was (and is shown to be) extremely conflicted, as were most of the people involved in this project. The stark reality is that once nuclear weapons were possible, someone was going to make them. I think we are lucky it was the Manhattan Project first. As for the Japanese, perhaps consider the plight of the Chinese and many other peoples who the Japanese conquered, tortured, raped, and pillaged first.

7.title: Three average movies, combined into an unsatisfying film.
7.content:
So the first third is so strangely cut and with such poor dialogue that it feels more like a trailer for a film. The second part is a classic action packed "let's build a thing!" Which at least gives us a moment of satisfaction from finally seeing the bomb do its thing. Ultimately disappointing as it's a bit of a fizzer. The final part is just a government bureaucratic drama that was so boring and pointless I wanted to die.

Let's put aside the fact that Nolan not only seems to never have had sex with a woman, or the fact that he cannot write a female character that has a greater depth than a puddle. The fact that he couldn't even bring himself to allow even say 10% of the masse of background characters to be women was just mind blowing to me. Especially when we know historically there were many women involved.

There were some parts that were genuinely beautiful and his effects with sound and the times he tried to visualise the thoughts and theories of quantum physics were captivating. But again, it just didn't combine into something solid. There was endless time shifting back and forth but the benefit of it was lost on me. It added almost nothing to it other than confusion. But I guess it was something to do while we waited and waited and waited for it to be over.

7.title: Expected much more
7.content:
Personally this was the most anticipated movie this year, if not the most anticipated in the last 5 years. Considering the pile of ... subpar production that is overflowing the industry lately it definitely deserves your attention, however I was left with the feeling that it could have been so much more, and sadly it wasn't. Since I am not an expert, I am not going to delve deep into the cinematography and I am pretty sure there aren't many people that are in position to criticize or evaluate Christopher Nolan when it comes to that. For me, personally, the action felt too fragmented at times, which disrupted the flow of the whole movie too much and left me with this unsettling feeling that the story could have been told better. I understand the logic behind the retrospection and I know that this technique has served Nolan beautifully on previous occasions, nevertheless I reckon it was exploited too much here. Moreover, the soundtrack was too intrusive at times and it was forcing your attention into the moment instead of guiding it.

Robert Downey Jr. Was great, probably one of his best works so far. Cillian Murphy also did a nice job in portraying the complex and disturbed nature of the person who brought to existence the deadliest weapon known to man.

As a science and physics geek I did expect the story to be more centered around the science breakthrough and philosophical implications of the nuclear weapons, but unfortunately it was more about ideology and political maneuvering within the Atomic Energy Commission.

It was a nice cinematic experience as a whole, but I wouldn't rank this among Nolan's best.

7.title: An Intriguing War Film with Stellar Performances
7.content:
Oppenheimer is a captivating war film that takes its audience on a mesmerizing journey through the life and times of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the brilliant physicist and key figure in the development of the atomic bomb. The movie's standout feature is undoubtedly Cillian Murphy's exceptional performance, which is nothing short of remarkable. His portrayal of Oppenheimer brings depth and intensity to the character, elevating the overall impact of the film.

The storyline and underlying theories explored in Oppenheimer are praiseworthy. The movie delves into the moral and ethical dilemmas faced by scientists involved in the creation of such a powerful and devastating weapon. It deftly highlights the inner conflict within Oppenheimer and his colleagues as they grapple with the consequences of their actions.

7.title: Interesting But Slow
7.content:
I saw Oppenheimer, starring Cillian Murphy-Peaky Blinders_tv, the Dark Knight movies; Emily Blunt-Jungle Cruise, Edge of Tomorrow; Matt Damon-Air, We Bought a Zoo and Robert Downey Jr.-Dolittle, the Marvel movies.

This movie is based on the true story of Robert Oppenheimer and his part in creating the Atomic bomb. It's directed by Christopher Nolan-Tenet, Dunkirk, the Dark Knight movies-and stars Cillian as Oppenheimer. It covers his attributes and brilliance in science, as well as his not so noble faults, like his womanizing-he had affairs while still being married. Emily plays his wife. There were also accusations of Cillian being a communist, which were investigated when the US government approached him to head up the project of creating a bomb to end WW2. Matt plays the soldier in charge and Robert plays a politician. There are several other cameos of recognizable actors in smaller parts. It is an interesting story but a little slow for my tastes. My brother liked it more than I did.

It's rated R for language, smoking and sexual content-including nudity-and has a running time of 3 hours.

It's not one that I would buy on DVD to watch over and over again but if you are interested in the history of it, it would be a good one to stream.

7.title: Tooooo slooooowwwww
7.content:
Great story and I learned a lot but...

There's absolutely, positively no reason this movie needed to be three hours long. The first hour was beyond boring and unbearably slow. I get it. We need to know his backstory but did we really need to know every little tidbit? For example, we had a whole scene that ended with them temporarily giving their baby away. Did that impact anything later in the film? Not that I noticed. Ok, he cheated on his wife. Did we need to have sex scenes and a fully nude Florence Pugh? No. Completely unnecessary. Did it matter that his first class initially only had one student? Nope. I'm surprised the movie didn't start with Oppenheimer's conception and show every time he went to the bathroom. Yeesh! Just tell us what we need to know for the rest of the movie to make sense and move on!

I'm not a fan of time jumps either. It probably could've been told just as well linearly.

The movie has an excellent supporting cast with many big name actors who only had bit parts. Blink and you'll miss them. Which is really a shame given that we're stuck looking at Cillian Murphy in every scene for three loooong hours. Ugh!

7.title: It's rare that a movie of this length would keep me engaged
7.content: It wasn't just a good film, it was masterful. The photography, the script, the acting, the special effects, often practical, everything came together perfectly. The incredibly accurate historical references and their very special ability to entertain, even if in a documentary. The experience of watching every moment is almost indescribable, and it will certainly be a film that, in the future, I will watch once, twice, three, and many more times. I'm suspicious when I say this, because I'm a big fan of both Cillian Murphy, who plays Oppenheimer, and the eccentric but surgical director, Christopher Nolan, however, this one who appeared on this year's posters is certainly a heavyweight in films, which I enjoyed as much as, if not more than, the revered director's "best work" (Interstellar). If it were me, a simple evaluator, to describe such a work in a title, I would call it "Christopher Nolan's Silent Orchestra".

7.title: Clumsy narrative with great actors, great history, great filming
7.content:
I really wanted to like Oppenheimer -- it's a story that has needs retelling to each generation. These are some of my favorite actors, and the filming is incredible. However, the dramatic arc really fails, making essentially two disjointed storylines in one that fail to meld despite multiple flashbacks and foretellings. It's not that it makes the plot line confusing to the attentive viewer -- it's that the film itself doesn't make clear what the emotional plot line is, and sabotages its own dance with moral ambiguity. The latter quarter is more of a contrived 'who dunnit' with a simplistic political villain -- almost a laughable attempt to give us a feel good ending as the bad guy gets his just desserts in the end -- pretty much portraying the opposite of the complex reality. I was left feeling WTF.

I haven't cared much for Nolan since Memento -- one of my all time favorites, and a film in which the viewer confusion was part of the taut plot line itself. This -- the opposite.

Nonetheless worth a watch for the history, good visuals, good acting, and ambitious effort.

7.title: Good
7.content:
Movie is good but a mini series like Chernobyl would have made more sense for this story. The story telling could have been better, and not all characters were good in acting.

Not worth watching in IMAX though, there are no visually pleasing scenes that would make it worth watching on a huge screen, movie is like a documentary with lot of talking.

This text is to fill the minimum character requirement, please ignore it. I am running out of words to write anything more about this movie, the lead character was best in acting, everyone else was average. Finally this is the last sentence to fill the review, hope their AI won't block it.

7.title: Glorified documentary
7.content:
This movie had the potential to be a powerful and moving piece of cinema, but unfortunately it fell short in several key areas. Despite being based on a true story to make it more a compelling storytelling, the film delivered more like a documentary type of portraying things. The emotional excitement that one would expect from Nolan's films was lacking, leaving my feeling somewhat underwhelmed.

One of the main issues with the movie was the lack of character development. The characters felt flat and one-dimensional, and their motivations and actions were not always clear. This made it difficult for me to connect with them on an emotional level.

Additionally, the use of jumpscare sound effects felt unnecessary and detracted from the overall experience. Rather than adding to the tension and suspense, these sound effects felt jarring and a little bit out of place.

In conclusion, while this movie had potential, it failed to deliver in several key areas. The lack of emotional excitement, poor character development, and unnecessary use of jumpscare sound effects all contributed to a less than satisfying viewing experience.

7.title: Bloated but full of greatness
7.content:
My first impression of Oppenheimer was just how loud it all was. Not to criticize the beautiful tones found throughout, but the heaviness and intensity of the music never relented, except for an inevitable central sequence when we finally, mercifully, get a moment of silence. Silence between the pieces of score, and silence between hours of continuous, hyper-paced dialogue and sound design, which all combined sometimes approaches cacophony.

The noise of it all sometimes seems an attempt to compensate for a misplaced idea that an audience wouldn't be able to sustain interest in this material without the distraction of a continuous soundtrack. I wish it would have appreciated more moments of quiet. And ironically, in spite of its relentlessness, Oppenheimer ends up the slowest, and most demanding of all Christopher Nolan films.

This is not a bad thing. This film is full of smart, engrossing material and succeeds as a rich retelling of Oppenheimer's legacy and the vast network of brains who helped make his Manhattan Project a reality. Multiple viewings are warranted. The cast is spectacular and good use is overall made of them (when we can pin an actor down long enough to even notice their presence), and I can't really blame Nolan anyway, for wanting to spruce up hours of granular physics, debates and testimony into something as awesome as possible.

Nolan's movies are gorgeous contraptions, made with exquisite care and a love of an old school sort of practical filmmaking, and they're always ambitious, always outsized. This movie left me with an odd feeling, which is that it was both too long and not long enough. Not long enough to really pierce the enormous scope of what Oppenheimer's life stood for against history, and yet full and stylized almost beyond the brim.

7.title: Decent movie but it gets pretty boring in the second half
7.content: This movie has great acting, great production, and the story is decent, which is why I gave it a 7, but it becomes a drag after the 2 hour mark. It becomes tedious to watch with all of the exposition. I stopped caring about the story after the bomb was tested and it goes into Oppenheimers trial. The film also jumps around to different timelines quite a bit. It feels a bit jarring. If I'm being honest, I think the movie is a bit overrated in it's rating. The acting is what really saves this film but but that can only take it so far. The story isn't necessarily dull but the execution of it in this film is. All in all this movie was boring and I was counting down the minutes until it ended. I wouldn't care to watch it again.

7.title: Go and watch it, but dont expect too much.
7.content:
Huge Nolan fan here, but I was expecting more. More engaging history, a trial? He commited a crime? I didnt get that, I needed to chek goggle to know why this movie spend so much time in the trial. Was the trial a third of Oppie life?

Really?

I have seen this with Oliver Stone?

Was Nolan confuse with this movie?

Does the book digested all of Oppenheimer issue?

I get out of the cinema with more questions than answers. Was that Nolan´s objetive? Sorry for my english.

I think the three parts of this movie where mot in touch in some points, I didnt know who where who. I was confused to the point to ask myself: why i am still here. This looks like a documentary or a realiity show.

7.title: Nolan, please return to the science fiction and adventure genres
7.content:
Oppenheimer is a good drama and biopic, but not an extraordinary movie like Nolan has done previously. As a fan, I would highly encourage him to return to his unique genres.

This movie has good drama and music, as we all expect from Nolan and Ludwig, along with good twist in second half. Oppenheimer also captured the post- and pre-events of the Manhattan Project. However, I was expecting another Inception, Interstellar, or Tenet. I guess it was my naiveté that, even though I knew it was a biography, I was still expecting those things. However, I would expect the next movie from Nolan to be another Inception, Interstellar, or Tenet.

7.title: Technically brilliant, but lacking in emotional beats.
7.content:
Nolan's films are usually a hit or a miss for me. However no one can deny the brilliance of his filmmaking. This film takes its time and then some to tell its story, and I believe it could have benefited from a shorter run time.

Most of which is taken up by men talking in rooms.

Which will definitely not be for everyone.

One of the weird things about Nolan's screenplays and characters, especially with this one, is that most of the time, the people talk like they are characters in an epic novel. The extreme cerebral nature of their dialogue and interactions lack a certain emotional resonance, and it's left to the horror of its themes to make the audience sympathise with them.

Robert Downey Jr. Was absolutely brilliant in this, and I've forgotten how much of a great actor he really is, after seeing him only as Tony Stark in the Marvel films for the last ten years or so.

Nolan's female characters unfortunately don't get anything to do in this film, other than make the main character feel bad, providing some down to earth consequences of his misdeeds.

The creation of the atomic bomb and its eventual detonation is cool to watch. There is also a deeply frightening scene involving a cheering crowd, which is probably one of my favourite moments in the film.

But other than that, it's not the masterpiece that everyone says it is.

7.title: Christopher Nolan's Cinematic Bomb Blasts On And Off Screen
7.content:
Oppenheimer (2023) : Movie Review -

Oppenheimer Review : Christopher Nolan, one of the greatest filmmakers in the World with the most consistent filmography, brings a new cinematic treat, "Oppenheimer". Based on the life of a physicist named "J. Robert Oppenheimer," this one is easily the most human-driven story ever told by Nolan. There is less action, more drama; there is less complexity, more tension; there is less soul, more characteristics, there is less everything of known-Nolan, but finally we have conversions in a Nolan movie. Oppenheimer is anything but a trademark Nolan film. When you look at his filmography, you see these things: Following was a low-budget banger with a classic twist; Memento is pathbreaking storytelling; Insomania is his attempt at psychological tension; Batman Begins is a revolution in the Superhero genre; The Prestige is a magical thriller; The Dark Knight is an Intellectual face off between the hero and the villain; Inception is a next-level sci-fi thriller; The Dark Knight Rises is a fulfilling send-off to the greatest superhero trilogy ever; Interstellar is an expansion of sci-fi Epic beyond infinity; Dunkirk is the most human-friendly and technically brilliant war drama; and Tenet is a fine example of time-breaking theme meeting groundbreaking visuals. After serving us something of the Nolan-fied genre in his every movie, the man finally enters the human drama genre, and how? If you think that Oppenheimer will be talking about the invention of the atom bomb and will take you to a laboratory to see the practicals behind its making, then you are wrong. Apparently, I was thinking of the same stuff, but I was wrong. The film is all about its title - Oppenheimer. It's the journey of a man who was excited to create a power that would make his country survive, but soon he realises that it is making some people lose their lives. The excitement, the trauma, the shivering, the lifelong guilt everything is there. There is blood on his hands, and he can't wash it. It's a textbook on Oppenheimer's life, but in a 3-hour brief. One thing is sure, after watching this film, you'll never forgive the name of J. Robert Oppenheimer, not because he achieved something in his life but because of what he lost.

As we know, Nolan does not believe in simple linear equations, so he has a non-linear narration again. One of them runs in black and white, indicating that the world is colourless after the fruit has spread its fire all over the world, not just Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Lieutenant General Leslie Richard Groves (Matt Damon) trusts J. Robert Oppenheimer (Cillian Murphy) to create a miracle for the American Government. Robert is appointed director of the project's Los Alamos Laboratory in New Mexico, tasked with developing the first nuclear weapons, four years after the start of the German nuclear weapons programme. Robert and the team achieve success at the Trinity test, and the president soon sends the bombs to be dropped on Japanese soil. Robert's celebration soon turns into a trauma, and he realises that the world might never be the same. He is framed for being a Soviet Spy, and the legal fight is not in his favour. How the most important man in the world at that time is trapped against the odds and how his acquaintances turn their backs on him is all that you get to see in the latter half.

A three-hour runtime frightens me for sure, but not when the director is Nolan or Cameron. A three-hour movie does not feel boring, if it's Avatar 2 or Oppenheimer. The screenplay is on the job there, and it makes every minute worth it. Oppenheimer is pretty slow in the beginning as the characters are new and a lot of Robert's personnel are discussed on the screen. So he was a womaniser, a communist, and not a brilliant man, but do we have to see it all? And for so long? Oppenheimer loses the character's grip there. Robert's complicated illicit affair with Jean Tatlock (Florence Pugh) is too detailed and bare. I know a lot of Indians are curious to know whether that Bhagwadgita phrase is used in the film or not, so let me tell you, yes, it is used, and twice. The first use of "I am become death, the destroyer of the world" might offend some religious people here. It might even become a big controversy in our country today. In those old times, when they told us the biopics of legendary inventors with "The Story of Louis Pasteur" (1936), "Edison The Man" (1940), "Dr. Ehrlich's Magic Bullet" (1940), "Madam Curie" (1942), and a few others, they never showed the protagonist in a bad light. But that era is gone, and today we have to deal with several intimate facts that need to be shown in the film, so it's okay. The slow start does an effective trick to let us know the characters, but even 3 hours feels too short for them to fit well.

Cillian Murphy is flawless as J. Robert Oppenheimer from start to end. You might have seen him in many good roles and solid performances, but this one surpasses them all. The tension, the fear, the excitement, the enthusiasm, the pressure, the guilt, and many more things, but this man carried full loads on his shoulder. Out of 3 hours, this guy hooks you to the screen for about 2 and a half hours, while all the others get half an hour of their own. It was such a big responsibility, and he did a great job. It's not just about facial expressions and dialogue delivery; Murphy had to look like Oppenheimer. For people who haven't seen Robert Oppenheimer in real life, Cillian Murphy is Robert Oppenheimer. Emily Blunt's shovelling testimony will win your heart, but there is nothing much to do for her there. He is there for 20 minutes, or maybe 30, but the way Robert Downey Jr. Has brought Lewis Strauss to the screen is simply amazing. Matt Damon's general is rough and tough, Josh Harnett's Lawrence is noticeable, Kenneth Branagh and Casey Affleck are fine, Rami Malek's cameo will have you clapping, and Tom Conti's Einstein is impeccable. Florence Pugh looks solid and drippy (as the character demands), while the big supporting cast of Benny Safdie, Dylan Arnold, Matthew Modine, Michael Angarano, Jack Quaid, Josh Peck, Olivia Thirlby, David Krumholtz, Dane DeHaan, David Dastmalchian, and others have been extremely encouraging.

Oppenheimer is technically a powerful film, but not as great as some of Nolan's previous works. The background score will have your heart pumping Faster on many occasions, and that disturbing score with lapses will have your throat choked. Watch out for the Trinity test sequences and Oppenheimer's testimony scene, and I am 100% sure you are gonna be blown away by the impact of the BGM. Hoyte van Hoytema's cinematography is very fine, especially the nuke scene. Nolan usually believes in practical effects and 2D viewing, and he also made this film without any CGI segments. Oppenheimer does not have anything groundbreaking as such, but the realistic effects do work on the IMAX screen. For instance, the bomb explosion scene. You expect it to be loud from the start, but you get a low sound and literally silence there. It makes practical sense, as we know sound takes time to travel, and by the time it reaches you, you are completely unaware of its existence. That's a masterstroke. A technical brilliance that everyone should notice. Christopher Nolan's storytelling goes through a change here. As mentioned above, Oppenheimer has nothing stone-breaking to offer, and frankly, it gets confusing sometimes with the new characters talking about something terribly new that you aren't aware of, but it's such a pleasure to see Nolan trying a simple human story with his extraordinary vision, of course. Robert's speech scene after the successful bomb test is artistically wonderful. The man has to speak about celebration and all happy things, and he does that, but his inner world is destroyed in those moments. How to describe two different emotions, happiness and sadness, at the same time is what you learn from Master Nolan here. See that framework, man. Oppenheimer is about Nolan attempting a complete character study, and for this reason, it is a must-see. The feel of the docudrama takes away the mass appeal of the film, but did Nolan ever care about that chunk of audiences? No. He didn't. He has his own audience, which is smart enough to understand his cinema. That's what you get here. Nolan's latest cinematic bomb blasts on the screen and leaves you burning off screen with its traumatic consequences. One bomb blasts there on the big screen, and the other one blasts outside the screen-that's inside you.

RATING - 7/10*

7.title: I may need to watch it again
7.content: This movie being shot in 70mm IMAX film doesn't make any sense once I watched it, the movie itself isn't very cinematic. Additionally the film throws around so many names and characters it makes it very hard to follow dialogue and story. I walked out being confused and a little underwhelmed. Near the end, the movie will lose most of the audience with all of the concepts, characters and lawsuits style scenes the last for a third of the movie. Personally the movie got worse and worse, with looser plot and story as it went. The one thing I well give Nolan is the sound design and ost, so goddamn good, it's my favorite part. Lastly, it felt like the whole movie revolved and written around the ending quote in the movie.

7.title: A masterpiece of cinema
7.content: I really enjoyed this movie, although it kept switching back and forth from the present to flashbacks. Usually when movies do this I notice it right away so it doesn't faze me, but in this movie it was kinda trippy. Very well put together, keeps you running in multiple timeframes. TBH, they could have ended in after 2 hrs with the successful test and it would have still been a very good movie. Went on longer than needed. The film was very loud in some parts which made it impactful but people with sensitivity to sound might want to wear earplugs. This film was very good and so important to show to a wide audience. As someone who has family that lived through the bombings in Japan, I think I was important to see the history behind the attacks. It stirred me emotionally in a way I didn't expect and I'm glad I had that experience. It was definitely heavy though.

7.title: Chaotic and powerful
7.content:
You really need your wits about you to follow this film. There are frequent and often quite rapid cuts to different time periods, perhaps a little overdone at times. Nolan helps by filming all of the Lewis Strauss (played beautifully by Robert Downey Jnr) scenes in black and white.

The pace is relentless yet I still felt the film was just a little bit too long - the first hour in particular was at times even a little boring. Once we get to the Trinity test, the film absolutely soars - although everyone knows what happened, the film becomes breath-taking and powerful. The subsequent scenes involving the witch-hunt against Oppenheimer and the senate hearings to confirm Strauss's cabinet position are impressive.

The acting is uniformly good, especially RDJ. I thought Cillian Murphy's portrayal of Oppenheimer was good but just a little too quixotic - you're never quite sure exactly what he believes, especially in the first half. It was great to see Tom Conti again, although maybe a little miscast as Einstein. Florence Pugh was given a few rather gratuitously explicit sex scenes, which I thought were just a little too bizarre. And as usual there were very good performances from Emily Blunt and Matt Damon.

Another major gripe is the soundtrack - appropriate in style but way too loud, detracting from the visual experience at times.

All in all a powerful but imperfect movie, certainly worth seeing, but it will require your intense concentration to keep up with the chaos at times. Not quite a masterpiece in my book.

7.title: A snooze and then lip read
7.content: Chopping back and forth eras during the story was annoying and completely unnecessary but what was most annoying was that the dialogue was overwhelmed by background 'music' so the ability to lip read was an advantage. I beg you to refrain from adding 'music/noise' when the excellent actors were speaking as it degrades the product. Undoubtedly the acting and actors were superb as, could have been, the story line. In my opinion the film could have been 140 minutes long. Again, I feel compelled to add that, at times, it was extremely difficult to hear the dialogue. Please consider the audience of all ages.

7.title: A good watch that could have been great
7.content:
Oppenheimer is truly a complex character and it feels and reflects in the Christopher Nolan's adaptation. The film largely works and the 3 hour run time doesn't bother you too much. Acting masterclasses are on display in Cillian Murphy and RDJ and excellent support from Matt Damon.

Only gripe is that the film only explores only one side of Oppenheimers character. Some of his real brilliance hasn't been shown at all and assumed the viewer would come prepared.

Also the film, even though dark, doesnt quite bring out why the Truman govt tried to defame their national hero at the time. Its probably again left on viewers to educate themselves.

7.title: Interesting examination of Oppenheimer but not exciting
7.content: This is a 3 hour movie and focus is mainly on Oppenheimer I grew up in the 1950 and I am aware of the historical story of Oppenheimer It is somewhat organized story and trying to do snippets in time events is not a great approach for three hour movie At times it is boring but acting is extremely well done It is not the best movie of the year and trying to call it is an Oscar because of what happened to Oppenheimer is really not interesting. It is sad but is not riveting The basic tenet of any movie should have interesting beginning middle and ending and the ending is probably the most interesting part of the movie Oppenheimer will always be remembered as the man along with Leslie Groves for running the Manhattan project The reality is that story should have focused on the development of the atomic bomb and men who created it and the struggles they had I found the movie with Paul Newman about Leslie Groves more interesting than this movie in certain aspects. In this era I think very few people would be interested to know what happened to Oppenheimer Also trying to look at what happened to him in the 1950 from a perspective of the 21st century is also flawed because of the adversary of the Cold War In reality Oppenheimer did give somewhat conflicting testimony as regards to certain events Of course he will be also regarded a hero and certainly was not a communist sympathizer by any means and loyal to his country He is a remarkable man who brought this project to success Cilian Murphy gave an outstanding performance and in some ways his personality personifies Oppenheimer (Does he ever smile in real life.)

7.title: Unfocused
7.content:
In my humble opinion, 'Oppenheimer' is a messy, non-linear and overlong missed opportunity, which meets neither the expectations of film and history buffs nor those of dedicated educators, who hoped to make it an educational tool to be shown in class.

Because the essential message and excellent acting performances are unfortunately drowned out with floods of words, a haphazard production design, a frenetic editing saturated with immersive sounds, and a lackluster cinematography.

The glowing superlatives surrounding the theatrical release therefore do not apply. And, in the absence of the "Best Film of the Year" that I expected, 'Oppenheimer' remains an interesting average film, nothing more and nothing less.

7.title: Uncertainty is the principle
7.content:
As auteurs so often must do, whether by choice or by some deep sense of selfishness, they must decide which three hours, out of so many more, to create from a source material that could be combined or split into discrete parts, maybe eventually a miniseries or podcast. As Julius Caesar once wrote, as the victor of the Gallic Wars, all of Gaul is divided into three parts. I have no doubt that Caesar struggled to decide which to write about most, and with what spin.

I also have a near-zero doubt that Christopher Nolan struggled to determine which parts of J. Robert Oppenheimer's life to slather together into a three-hour tour of a not-so-subtle reminder that of all the existential threats we humans ignore, it is probably total nuclear war which should be relatively high on the list.

Fine acting. Fine dialogue. Cillian Murphy survives through a joyless task of portraying a deeply troubled man, especially when it comes time for an important public talk or a public demonstration of just how big a bomb could be, at least based on current efforts.

How many presidents will Gary Oldman portray? Why do we get a third act filled with uncertainty and no intermission? What on Earth has kept us from mutually assured destruction?

Or were we always sauntering on borrowed time?

7.title: Quite certainly not Nolan's best work
7.content:
I'm fully aware that critiquing the work of an auteur like Christopher Nolan could be perceived as snobbish. Hence, I'd try to be objective in this review.

Firstly, it's a biopic. There's nothing quite unique about a biopic as the imaginative works of Nolan like the Inception or Interstellar. Hence, there is only so much he can do to be creative in directing Oppenheimer. It's just history, and there is nothing much to spoil there. This movie is a take on the personal predicaments and political persecution of scientist Dr. J Robert Oppenheimer who headed the Manhattan Project which resulted in the creation of the atomic bomb and as a consequence millions of innocent people lost their lives in the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

Secondly, there is a known pattern of human behavior which always targets the best of us when their job is done. Meaning, eminent scientists being harassed by the system once they have achieved great success is a recurring theme. We find that in the story of Alan Turing in the Imitation Game, in the story of Nambi Narayanan in Rocketry and so many others. It is common to find scientists working on technologies of strategic importance being framed for treason or similar cases and then being questioned for their loyalty to their nation. It's simply an occupational hazard. What can I say? Never build things for the government!

Thirdly, movies about American supremacy growing out of the Second World War and the subsequent cold war are stereotypical. We are quite over them. We just see them in different light now. President Truman's two bit rebuff of Oppenheimer is as asinine as it can get. It's cartoonishly evil. Perhaps it serves as the explanation of why no one ever committed suicide for being part of the decision to drop those bombs. Instead everyone just kept bickering over bruised egos for not being amply credited for the wonderful devastation which brought an end to the war.

Also it feels like Nolan is showing off by bringing on-board every brilliant actor out there for minor roles and cameos. Additionally, it could be a nerd's wet dream to see the glimpse of every founding genius of particle physics being name called and paraded as part of the plot but as a student of physics myself, I'm cringing.

Furthermore, the use of Bhagwat Gita reference was not given justice. The reason why Oppenheimer quoted those famous lines about becoming "destroyer of worlds" could have been treated better and not in a clichéd scene which could just be dismissed as some orientalist's curiosity with foreign religion. The movie didn't soak in the actual philosophy of which Oppenheimer was a keen student in real life.

The idea of a scientist who created the ultimate weapon of mass destruction growing a conscience and getting punished for that is a bit of a routine drag. I think this is where Oppenheimer contrasts with Heisenberg. While Oppenheimer set aside all his personal doubts to create the atom bomb for US government knowing well that he won't have any say in its use (In-fact he was highly enthusiastic about it initially) Heisenberg and his team of scientists working on the same project for the Nazis did not show that same motivation. I believe that's where Heisenberg's character far exceeds Oppenheimer's. Let's not delve in assessing such historical giants with our current worldview.

You can watch a movie called 'The Catcher was a Spy' on how USA deployed a baseball star to spy on Heisenberg to know if he's close to creating the atom bomb and if so, assassinate him. Critics didn't like the movie much. However I like it better than this.

Comparing with the body of work of Nolan, Oppenheimer does not feel like his best. It's an over emphasized effort to dazzle the world with the scale of production. We are sitting on the verge of a world war III with very real threat of a nuclear annihilation and we still don't care if the world will come to an end.

7.title: Over rated
7.content:
Not sure why people are giving this a perfect 10, I'm also not sure why it's made nearly a billion dollars at the box office.

I typically base my enjoyment of a movie on how badly I want to see a movie a second time after I've watched it. Oppenheimer is a movie I will never watch ever again. Much like Tenet before it.

It's an absolute struggle to sit through. The entire film is one scene after another of people talking. The anchor of the film is Oppenheimer himself. Who in my opinion doesn't have an interesting enough story to really root for and because I don't give a $hit about this person and his struggles with possible communist collusion I don't care about the movie.

Take scorceses the Aviator. The character of Howard Hughes is fascinating. He's talented, driven, charming, and also tragic. He's a character people want to know more about.

I will say this about Oppenheimer, it's well directed, with great cinematography and acting.

So it gets a 7 from me. But it's no where near on the same level as Nolan's other works.

7.title: Not blown away
7.content:
Music, cinematography, acting 10/10!

The actual story was 7/10 at best! I really like Nolan but this was not it!

First hour was a bit confusing with all the names and timelines but ok, it's a buildup!

Second hour was very good! My favourite!

Last hour I was looking for toothpicks around cinema to hold my eyelids open! Couple in front if me had a bottle of wine and fell asleep long time ago! One whole hour too long! I feel it could've been told in more interesting way!

If you like drama with lots of political and scientific chat, you will love it! I just need to feel more entertained at the cinema!

7.title: Oppenheimer - the tangled and bewildering tale of the father of the atomic bomb (I recommend it if you don't have anything better to watch)
7.content:
I admit I have very conflicting feelings about the movie. It just doesn't click for me. Christopher Nolan crammed biographical milestones of the physicist, mixed with the depiction of Robert Oppenheimer's greatest achievement (Cillian Murphy), namely overseeing the Manhattan Project which produced the first atomic bomb.

Amidst all of this, the story of a certain Admiral Strauss (Robert Downey Jr.) emerges, who politically speaking, was somewhat of an arch-nemesis of Dr. Oppenheimer and orchestrated his investigation for alleged acts of espionage for the Soviets.

I suspect there was an attempt to develop the narrative on three more or less parallel planes.

The personal plane where Oppenheimer is a bit leftist and somewhat promiscuous, bordering on the Communist Party where his wife had been a member, and his mistress was a staunch activist.

The professional plane of a highly successful physicist with managerial skills which led to his appointment to oversee the Manhattan Project.

And there's the political plane, where after using the scientist, the homeland investigates him under suspicion of treason, and here Admiral Strauss comes into play.

If you find it hard to understand as you read, know that it's the same when you watch the movie. My overall impression is that it's a well-made artistic documentary, but that's about it.

Honestly, I don't think it deserved the Oscar, but it was a case of the one-eyed leading the blind this year, although in my opinion, the clear winner should have been American Fiction. I suspect its status as a blockbuster and the impressive distribution in terms of Hollywood stars brought it the statuette.

7.title: Bob and the Bomb
7.content:
I didn't know too much about the life and times of American nuclear scientist J Robert Oppenheimer, although I suspect few others will too, but after watching Christoper Nolan's three hour long bio-pic, I'm certainly a lot more informed now. Oppenheimer or Oppie as he's irritatingly called frequently throughout the film, was the man who headed up the Manhattan project in World War II in the race to make a successful atom bomb as a means of ending the war. The film explores the dichotomy of a man who before the war displayed left-wing leaning, Communist sympathies, was in favour of unionisation and who supported the Nationalist forces in Spain's Civil War, with being the supremo of the team who produced the bomb to end all bombs which would be responsible for razing the cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki to the ground with over 100000 fatalities.

Some will say that being leftist and at the same time striving to stop the war by any means necessary isn't an inconsistent position and certainly didn't stop Oppenheimer's pursuit of his task, however there's no question that after the war, especially when the Communism of Soviet Russia became the new feared enemy in America, his lingering doubts about becoming "the destroyer of worlds" saw him publicly oppose the militarists who wished to go further and build the even more destructive H-bomb.

A man of his times, we see him in the film go from being feted as "the most famous man in the world", making the cover of "Time" and "Life" magazines and being thanked personally by President Truman to being hunted by the FBI and going through the indignity and eventual humiliation of losing his security clearance after undergoing tortuous private hearings by the authorities which seriously impacted his career. This appears to have been orchestrated by his erstwhile supporter and indeed employer Lewis Strauss (oddly pronounced "Stross") who, riding the wave of the post-war Communist witch-hunt, sees his opportunity to be the Iago to Oppenheimer's Othello and so bring him down, fuelled by a mixture of self-advancement and personal jealousy, apparently attributable to a perceived personal slight against him following an encounter between Oppenheimer and Albert Einstein years before.

Oppenheimer's gruelling excoriation by secret committee in a cramped meeting-room is contrasted with Strauss's later very public examination by Congress over his long-desired Cabinet posting in the new president Eisenhower's administration. In the end, events conspire to see Oppenheimer prevail and so commence his rehabilitation in U S. History, which this movie will no doubt presumably further advance in the public consciousness.

We also get insights into Oppenheimer's extremely colourful private life as he conducts more than one extra-marital affair while staying married to his supportive, long-suffering wife, the one highlighted being that with a card-carrying Communist party member called Jean Tatlock.

Writer / director Nolan again displays his by now trademark time-bending film structure, jumping back and forth in time, shifting between colour and black and white in the process. As you'd expect, this is a very talky, wordy film but while the exchanges during Oppenheimer and Strauss's trials are notable for their directness and clarity, I wish I could say the same elsewhere, in particular when Oppenheimer is romancing Jean. There's one particularly excruciating exchange between the two with them both sitting naked in chairs opposite each other after another of their clandestine meetings where both video and audio just scream pretentiousness.

The scenes showing the shock and awe of the bomb's test explosion and later its nightmarish impact on Oppenheimer's imagination when it's then dropped on Japan are brilliantly rendered, as you'd expect from this director who's well-served by his very starry cast including Cillian Murphy, even if his acting is sometimes a bit mannered for my taste, a for once iron-clad-less Robert Downey Jr, Matt Damon, Emily Blunt, Florence Pugh and Brit-cameos by Gary Oldman, Kenneth Branagh and Tom Conti, but thankfully not Michael Caine.

The film certainly commanded my attention and in today's world where there are growing whispers about the possibility of a third world war, the film hits a suitably sombre and cautionary note. At the end though, I probably left the movie more informed than entertained, even as I commend Nolan for a welcome change of pace and direction in his impressive but for me sometimes inconsistent body of work.

7.title: Music score killed it for me
7.content: Great acting, great scenery, great cast. But lousy, lousy, overbearing music and kitchy unnecessary special effects of atoms whizzing and exploding. Many scenes you could not hear what had been said as the music drowned it out. Obviously Oppenheimer had some mental issues but did it really need to be interpreted by a million stamping feet. Special effects are a tool to aid a movie not to become the movie. Acting on the other hand was spot on, who'd a thunk Robert Downie jr could play such a mean nasty guy so well. The Ciaran guy was good too. Many know him from Peaky Blinders which I never watched so I wasnt quite so enamoured. Loved Mat Damon and the nasty lawyer going after Oppenheimer was amazing. Mid 20th century backdrops captured well. Worth seeing but not again.

7.title: Great film, almost perfect
7.content:
There is much to be liked here and there are some incredible performances, especially from Murphy and Robert Downey Junior. Remar was a welcome addition and, despite his short appearance, brought a charm to the movie none of the others could do in all their screen time.

All in all, the casting was great. The location scouting and cinematography too. Much of the movie was well composed of emotionally charged takes with some subtle inputs by the DOP and director.

Where the film lacked was its on the nose quote "I have become death..." which everyone knows and due to its notoriety, could have been omitted from the final cut considering it isn't something everyone needs to be reminded of. These small additions let the movie down.

It is apparent Nolan was attempting an artistic insertion, but not well pulled off and came across rather eye rolling, such as the sex sequence in the panel room, the emulation of a nuclear blast in the room too later on.

But all in all, it's a great movie that is a must see. Though I can't imagine anyone watching it more than twice. Once in the cinema, once at home.

7.title: Oppenheimer: A Masterful and Thought-Provoking Epic
7.content:
Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer is a sprawling, ambitious, and visually stunning film that tells the story of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the scientist who led the Manhattan Project to develop the atomic bomb. The film is long and challenging, but it is also rewarding, offering a complex and nuanced portrait of a man who was both brilliant and flawed.

Cillian Murphy gives a tour-de-force performance as Oppenheimer, bringing to life a man who is both brilliant and tormented. Murphy captures Oppenheimer's intelligence, charisma, and idealism, as well as his deep sense of guilt over the creation of the atomic bomb. The supporting cast is also excellent, with Emily Blunt, Matt Damon, Robert Downey Jr., Florence Pugh, Benny Safdie, Rami Malek, Josh Hartnett, and Kenneth Branagh all giving memorable performances. Nolan's direction is masterful, creating a film that is both visually stunning and intellectually stimulating. The film is full of stunning visuals, from the vast desert landscapes of Los Alamos to the mushroom clouds of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Nolan also uses his trademark non-linear storytelling to great effect, creating a film that is both epic in scope and intimate in its focus.

Oppenheimer is not a perfect film. It is long and challenging, and it may not be to everyone's taste. However, it is a film that is sure to stay with you long after you have seen it. It is a film that is both thought-provoking and visually stunning, and it is a film that offers a complex and nuanced portrait of one of the most important figures of the 20th century. It is a film that is sure to be debated and discussed for years to come. It is a film that is both a masterpiece and a cautionary tale. It is a film that is both a triumph and a tragedy. It is a film that is both a product of its time and a film that is timeless.

Here are some of the things that I liked about Oppenheimer: -Cillian Murphy's performance as J. Robert Oppenheimer is masterful. Murphy captures Oppenheimer's intelligence, charisma, and idealism, as well as his deep sense of guilt over the creation of the atomic bomb.

-The supporting cast is also excellent, with Emily Blunt, Matt Damon, Robert Downey Jr., Florence Pugh, Benny Safdie, Rami Malek, Josh Hartnett, and Kenneth Branagh all giving memorable performances.

-Nolan's direction is masterful, creating a film that is both visually stunning and intellectually stimulating. The film is full of stunning visuals, from the vast desert landscapes of Los Alamos to the mushroom clouds of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Nolan also uses his trademark non-linear storytelling to great effect, creating a film that is both epic in scope and intimate in its focus.

-The film's depiction of the Manhattan Project is both accurate and harrowing. Nolan does not shy away from the horrors of nuclear war, and he shows the human cost of the atomic bomb in a way that is both powerful and disturbing.

Here are some of the things that I think audiences need to know about Oppenheimer: -The film is long and challenging. It is a film that requires your attention, and it is not a film that you can watch on a whim.

-The film's non-linear storytelling can be confusing at times. It is not a film that you can just sit back and enjoy. You have to pay attention to the details in order to understand what is happening.

-The film's depiction of the Japanese is somewhat problematic. Nolan does not show the Japanese as victims of the atomic bomb, and he presents them as a faceless enemy.

Overall, I enjoyed Oppenheimer. It is a film that is sure to be debated and discussed for years to come. It is a film that is both a masterpiece and a cautionary tale. It is a film that is both a product of its time and a film that is timeless. I give it a rating of 7 out of 10.

7.title: Good movie overall but not a masterpiece as many claim
7.content:
Don't get me wrong Oppenheimer is a good solid movie, but it does suffer from major problems that Nolan is incredibly stubborn about since Tennet (I consider tennet a satire on Nolan's own work, the movie was a total joke)

Now comes Oppenheimer, you can tell immediately as the movie starts Nolan has put in a solid effort and hard work here, the visuals, lightening and cinematography immediately come off as top notch. The storyline is well written and presented, but then there are many problems with this movie such as

it's loud, and I mean, extremely loud, lawsuit material loud, I could imagine number of hearing loss caused by this movie it is not necessary at all. Nolan increasingly is turning up the volume on his movies








Overall I cannot give this movie a masterpiece label, due to this issues. I do hope however Nolan keeps making movies, i do love his vision and mind. I guess tennet taught him a lesson and he seems to try harder now. However I don't know if we will ever see Nolan make something legendary, his last masterpiece was dunkirk and that was his peak.

7.title: An enjoyable historical drama if a little long and overhyped.
7.content: So let's start with the good bits: A fascinating story well told and easy to follow despite the usual non linear format of Mr Nolan. I also thought it ended well and had great acting and a brilliant cast. I would have given it more stars had it not been overhyped so much which left me with my expectations too high. Now for the bad bits (with spoilers!): Watching any film on a Cinema big screen with surround sound is a nice experience. However, I am not sure why this film was a 'must see' on a big screen. I am guessing for the overhyped bomb detonation taking place two hours into the three hour film. I was expecting so much more from the detonation sequence, I did not time it, but it seemed to be over so quickly with a flash, fireball and some shockwave bangs. Mr Nolan missed a trick here as he could have made it last so much longer with so many more effects. Then it was back to the slow but well told drama for the last hour. So, with the exception of a couple of minutes in the middle a big screen is no more a required for this film than for a courtroom drama.

7.title: Good Film and will Win Awards
7.content:
Good Film but I did find it slow in places, seems to build and build to a slight anticlimax.

Yes it's very good but I still feel it was missing a couple of ingredients in my view.

I did not find it as none stop thrilling film as it could have been but don't get me wrong it's an excellent film and loved the Albert Einstein story. Maybe a bit more WW2 action/context would have made it fly a little more.

Excellent acting by the main stars and amazing cast just falls shorts a little, maybe it was built up to much.

Some films can be 3 hours but don't feel like it's been 3 hours but sadly this did feel like 3 hours to me.

7.title: Experience the Brilliance and Struggles of J. Robert Oppenheimer in Christopher Nolan's Masterpiece, 'Oppenheimer' - A Must-Watch Historical Drama !
7.content:
"Oppenheimer" unfolds as a captivating portrayal of the life and achievements of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the brilliant mind behind the discovery of the atomic bomb. Christopher Nolan, once again, weaves his directorial magic in this mesmerizing masterpiece, although it does demand a considerable time investment with its three-hour runtime. Unlike typical action-packed thrillers, this film opts for a more profound approach, delving into pure drama and history.

While some viewers may perceive the movie as dialogue-heavy and scientific, it serves as an authentic representation of J. Robert Oppenheimer's life and the challenges he encountered. The narrative beautifully unfolds, highlighting the complexities and struggles faced by this extraordinary figure.

The climax of the film delves into the heart-wrenching reality of the atomic bombings in Hiroshima and Nagasaki, leaving a lasting impact on the audience. Cillian Murphy, an exceptional Irish actor, delivers a phenomenal performance in the lead role, bringing Oppenheimer's character to life with remarkable depth and emotion.

"Oppenheimer" emerges as a must-watch movie, especially for those who are unfamiliar with this significant piece of history. It serves as a powerful source of knowledge, shedding light on a remarkable individual and a pivotal moment in human history that shaped the course of the world. While it may not cater to everyone's tastes, this film undoubtedly stands as an insightful and enlightening experience for those willing to delve into the depths of history and human brilliance.

7.title: Lacking Nolans Cinematography
7.content:
