The scene with the bomb dropping was literally incredible, and the build-up made you sit on the edge of your seat. The speech scene after the bomb drops was probably my favorite scene in the movie, and it was honestly one of the creepiest things I have seen in a movie ever. Also, way too much background music which got kind of annoying in my opinion. The only other Christopher Nolan movie I have seen is Dunkirk, and I think it was a little better than this movie. Oppenheimer though is filled with great cinema.

7.title: I should have liked it, but I didn't
7.content:
It is hard to explain why I was disappointed, but the best way I can describe this movie is by saying it is like a bad version of Dunkirk. A shame really, considering my interest in Oppenheimer and the Manhattan Project. Take everything Dunkirk did wrong, or at least what I didn't like about it, and pack it into one movie. It seems the love interests and sexual scenes just try to breathe life into a somewhat lifeless story. I believe this is the film where we see the beginning of the end for Christopher Nolan. Maybe he's just lost his touch? Maybe he's been doing it so long, he's making the films more for himself than for his audience.

7.title: A big story, well told, but hard work.
7.content:
Oppenheimer is not a film to be taken lightly, a serious topic played out in a humourless 3 hour grind.

The story is secondary to the big philosophical questions it drops on you, was Oppenheimer a demon or a saviour, it's hard to tell.

Cillian Murphy was excellent, but like the plot he delivered it in a sad jumbled timeline, through flashbacks and memories, he seemed exhausted.

Some really annoying special effects done to mimic or highlight fission made their point a little too often. Overall about 30 minutes too long, post the big bang it was just sad & reflective.

So a big movie, well made, but not a fun outing, not all films should be but this one left me feeling a little hollow (and tired).

7.title: Poorly edited
7.content:
Grand story, really interesting plot. The movie is super long but it still feels many points were skipped over. The cinematics are gorgious. The main issue with the movie is bad editing or story telling. Especially in the beginning there are too many storylines at once, that are not properly ordered or put together. They could have used one of the story lines as the framing. And they do that later in the movie with the kangaroo court, but that is mising in the beginning, where we just get random cuts to four or five different timelines, where half of them are in black and white, to make them visually distinct, but often it is the future or the framing that is in black and white,making it rather disjointed.

Add to that the usual incompeting audio editing of dialogs, that is essentially Nolans calling card by now.

7.title: Science was overwhelming but movie was dull.
7.content:
The story is mainly about Robert Oppenheimer and his life into creation of first atomic bombs.

The story highlights Oppenheimer's personal life, his guilt, etc. In a peculiar way. Nolan chose the subject wisely but the movie was dull. It was 3 hours of eternity. I wish if it were less of court room drama. The science the scientists & people in charge were the highlights of movie.

Nolan has his own favorites set of actors. The thing is not everyone was great in this movie especially the scientists.

Final Verdict: Nolan, you don't have to make a movie that people would understand only after studying rocket science. Take a challenge to make a ten on ten movie which is family in nature.

As far as this movie is concerned I would say it to be Science was overwhelming but movie along with its length and courtroom drama was dull.

7.title: It's hard, strong, loud and chaotic
7.content:
I'm writing this a day after I watched this movie so I think it through)

this movie is hard, strong, loud and chaotic.

Nolan likes to play with time parallels so that's the thing that confused me in some way while watching.

After watching you have a lot of questions about Oppenheimer, project, his kids life, other scientists future etc. It means you have to make a research after. And for me this is about plot holes, because I don't want this quantity of questions after watching a movie.

"Oppenheimer" isn't the best Nolan's movie, for me it's not even in top 3 (maybe even 5; incomparable with "Inception" or "Interstellar") but directing is obviously good.

The cast is AMAZING (*love Matt Damon*), well played, incredible sound work, good picture quality.

Conclusion: movie isn't that great and interesting, it's good, maybe will rewatch one more time.

7.title: Very very good, with some shortcomings
7.content:
I want to love this movie as much as I do the other Nolan films, but I can't quite get there. First off, the acting is incredible, it does feel like a period piece, and the cast is A++. True to its name, this is really a film about Oppenheimer's life, with all the good and bad included. It does a very good job of showing the existential issues related to the bomb, and it is a heavy film in the way you would expect.

But there are some places where things could have been improved. First, the film is LONG, like really long. While everything is rightfully included for a reason, this film does not have the same rewatch value that other Nolan movies have. In the last part of the movie it feels like Nolan is kind of rushing to wrap things up, which I didn't appreciate. There's some pretty unnecessary nudity, which feels really out of place in a Nolan movie. I get that we need to explore all of Oppenheimer's life, but you can include that without being so explicit. The movie is an intellectual endeavor and takes some brainpower to watch, and while other Nolan films are this way, this one somehow feels different.

The trinity test is insanely cool though, and worth seeing in IMAX. Certainly a film for cinephiles, and like I said, the acting is superb with beautiful, expertly crafted sets. Overall, very good, but just so long and heavy.

7.title: Forgive Me For I Destroyed The World
7.content:
Nolan's Oppenheimer is a marvelous cinematic experience with stunning visuals, wonderful audio, good pacing and amazing acting performances. However, the film falls short in its underlying theme and story.

Oppenheimer is a technical masterpiece and should be considered as the new standard in the technical aspect of film making. The overall audio-visual experience that the viewer can experience in a proper IMAX cinema is without a doubt one the best movie experiences ever created. With stunning cinematography and a soul gripping score, I was fully immersed in my theatrical experience from the beginning of the film, right up until after the Trinity launch. As the Trinity launch was the culmination of the build up from the first two hours of the film, I was left wondering how the story would unfold further and what would it entail as we learn more.

To my slight annoyance, the third act revealed that the theme, and therefore the lesson of Oppenheimer was, that even the most brilliant minds cannot break from the shackles of governement control and must succomb to the necessities of the society they live in and the power that controls it. And yet, our most estemeed academics can forgive themselves for what they have created due to the fact that if they wouldn't make it, somebody else would and after all they only provide the gadgets, not use them as Truman told Oppenheimer. This theme echoes throughout the film and left a discouraged and sour taste in my soul.

As Oppenheimer was working to create his gadget, he was becoming more and more tormented by his own creation and what it would unleash upon the world. As a side note, Murphy has perfected his craft in playing a brilliant, yet tormented soul that draws you in his melancholy and pulls on your heart strings effectively, while still liking the character even through his many flaws. As a I was saying before however, this inner torment of Oppenheimer was not enough to make him stop his work but on the contrary, he pushed on to create the most dangerous deterrant the world has yet to see. The most he did to try to stop the making of these bombs was protest a little against the H-bomb. And even then went on to work on that protect. A brilliant physicist just could not stop working on atomic weapons. Now if that doesn't break down your spirit, I dont know what will. In addition, the sisua of responsibility is bridges of with the simple act of Truman telling Oppenheimer to get over it. As if scientists are not responsible for what their creations do to the world. Add to that the fact that the film demonstrated just how crooked and corrupt the American government is and I just can't make myself feel good about this movie.

From a Nolan fan I have to say that this film has the most grim message out of all the Nolan films and while the theme is important especially in these times, it would have been nice if the film would have offered some encouragement as well.

7.title: Enjoyable - could have been better
7.content:
I had really been looking forward to this movie as historical biopics based on real life events is one of my favourite genres. However I think the storyline and the 'A' list cast would have been better handled by a different director.

Nolan always seems to try to put his trademark on movies and they really shouldn't be about him and his style. This Nolan movie suffered badly from a lack of contextualisation around the two hearings from the outset. Who are these people? What is going on? How do they fit into the story? You have to work that out for yourself further into the movie, if you can.

As you are struggling to understand what is happening you are also bamboozled by Nolans favourite trick of monkeying around with timelines. Just like his Tenet and his Interstellar the movie jumped forwards and backwards at a dizzying pace, without really clarifying if you were in the past, present or future. Or when you were in the past or future, whether it was before or after the last point you went backwards or forwards.

Then there is the usual mumbled dialogue in places which is a feature of Nolan movies and one apparently that he is proud of. In the moment recordings I believe they are - but when the Artsy benefits detract from your ability to follow a film that should be straightforward but is already barely comprehensible it's just not helpful.

The score and cinematography were great, as were all the actors, and the story. Though to be honest history remembers Oppenheimer for the bomb, not the political fallout with a minor American politician, which added unnecessarily to the length of the movie and was a bit off-kilter in terms of where the plot and story should, and would have gone under a better director.

7.title: Well crafted and intriguing peak into history
7.content:
A very well crafted and intriguing look into the man who changed the world forever but it's not for everybody...

As a fan of Nolan and of all things history, I was excited to watch a film about J Robert Oppenheimer and prepared for it not to be a typical Nolan Movie. Whilst this is masterfully created and feels great in IMAX, it's not a movie that will resonate with everybody especially those who aren't interested in the subject matter.

Oppenheimer is a character study into the thoughts of the so called 'Father of the Atomic Bomb' leading up to the Manhattan project prior to when the atomic bomb was created and its aftermath when Oppenheimer had a bigger but different voice within the atomic energy scene.

I enjoyed insight into the world of a Theoretical Physicist and the dynamic between the science community and that of the US Army. Whilst this isn't a science based film that goes heavy into the detail, we did get to see Oppenheimer's rise through the field and several interesting discussions with his peers. We also get an insights into his personal life. Like many geniuses, he had a few skeletons in his closet.

The acting from Cillian Murphy and Robert Downy Jr was immerse as was most of the performances from the supporting cast. The sounds design was excellent and the testing of the atomic bomb was my favourite scene followed by the hearings. However my favourite part of the movie was Ludwig Goransson's dark, scientifical score. There were so many scenes where you felt the score elevating the mood or tension.

This movie is not for everybody. Whilst I enjoyed the movie and was especially intrigued by how Oppenheimer was viewed by those around him. It's a three hours long dialogue heavy character piece that I wouldn't necessarily recommend to all of my friends. I didn't find it slow but there are parts that are slower than others and viewers that aren't interested in the subject matter or who miss story beats may struggle to stay on board or remain invested. Whilst this isn't my favourite Nolan film, it's masterfully made and an intriguing, insightful work into a man who changed the world forever.

7.title: It could be much better.
7.content:
The film presents a compelling narrative centered around the father of the atomic bomb, blending historical elements with dramatization. While the storytelling is coherent, it lacks the intensity and excitement one might expect from such a profound subject. The cinematography, although aesthetically pleasing, follows a similar pattern of playing it safe rather than being truly invigorating.

A notable drawback is the film's reliance on CGI elements that seem superficially integrated. These elements are included primarily for visual enhancement but lack sufficient context or explanation, which feels like a missed opportunity to deepen the narrative impact. Moreover, the visual effects that are central to the story feel underwhelming, failing to match the gravity of the historical events depicted.

A significant omission in the movie is the lack of imagery or footage depicting the aftermath of the bombings in Nagasaki and Hiroshima. Including these could have profoundly enhanced the emotional weight of the film, making it more impactful and thought-provoking.

However, the creative decision to incorporate black and white footage is nice. It's important to note that the movie isn't just about the 'father of the Atomic Bomb' but mostly delves into themes of revenge.

The treatment of the Dutch element in the film is ridiculous. For a production of such scale and budget, the portrayal of the Dutch language is misleading, with the dialogue neither resembling Dutch nor German. This lack of attention to linguistic accuracy detracts from the film's overall credibility.

In conclusion, while the film is competently made and offers a unique perspective on a pivotal historical figure, it falls short in several areas, particularly in its visual storytelling and historical authenticity. It's a nice attempt, but it doesn't quite achieve the greatness it could have.

7.title: Great movie, just too long
7.content:
Being a topic I was interested in and know something about, with a great cast, director and all those awards, I was very excited about this movie. Then I saw the run time. 3 hours. Most movies do not need a 3 hour run time. Gone are the days of editors making a nice tight movie, cutting out anything that isnt needed to propel the movie forward.

Back in the day, the studios would chop up movies mercilessly. Then directors got a bit more power to keep what they wanted, but they still edited to a tight movie. Now that is gone and every director thinks he has 3 hours worth of a movie to make. Most dont.

This is a great 2 1/2 hr movie. The first hour could have been heavily edited to get things moving. The last hour was great.

7.title: An engrossing chronicle
7.content: An American-British biopic thriller; A story about physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, who was appointed to produce the first atomic bomb, and after his scientific team's work came to fruition, he faced the consequences of speaking truth to power. The film is a character study of political history based on the biography American Prometheus by Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin. The narrative deals with what he does and how he is treated by others - a meticulous, fact-based psychodrama. Its theme is how contradictions inherent in human personality bear a great burden for one and all and how we cannot know truth with perfect accuracy, much like the Uncertainty Principle in physics. Cillian Murphy is a tour de force who harnesses the anguish, guilt, gloom, and haughtiness of the title character in a layered performance. The optics captivate, which they must, and they haunt, as they should, given the enormity of real-life events. It is brilliant at showing how ambition and morality can end up in silos. Exposition was critical for the plot, so great minds of the age who had varied involvement in the arms race were introduced. Nevertheless, it ignored the crucial roles that British science played a part in jump-starting the quest and the importance of Australian physicist Dr Mark Oliphant to the work. As a drama, the first forty-five minutes worked hard with biographical detail. Music became a distraction, though. A hiatus in the near-constant accompanying musical score led the way for suspense to build to a gripping centrepiece sequence wherein the director's expertise in choreography was evident. Long-feature films need to earn emotional engagement - the third hour's pacing, with its long governmental hearings and political scrapping, was dense. Overall, it is a bold film about a complicated legacy with many strong performances. Visually it was arresting, and sound design was brilliant. As an aside, the film is bound to invite criticism of what it did not cover biographically, but a screenwriter has a prerogative to tell the story they want to tell and be judged solely on its theme, not the subject.

7.title: the weakness shows up on the small screen
7.content:
This movie must have been fun to watch in the theater, with trippy cosmic scenes and a big nuclear explosion. It's obviously made for the big screen experience, and was rewarded with big box office and awards.

However as a biopic, it fails, and it's obvious when you watch at home, where the glitz can't disguise the narrative chaos or Nolan's inability to actually bring out Oppenheimer as a character.

We're told that Oppenheimer was a womanizer but his relationships with women seem oddly dispassionate. I never fathomed why he bothered to have affairs at all, he just seemed to be going along with it. His relationship with his wife (excellently played by Emily Blunt) seemed grudging and harried, as she got increasingly frustrated by what a milquetoast he was.

The animus between Oppenheimer and Strauss was muddled and unconvincing. The scenes about that animus, and about the McCarthy witch hunt in Washington DC, were also muddled. How much did one plot thread influence the other? Was it all just stupid politics and stupider professional rivalry? Is any of this actually worth spending half the screen time on? Should have been cut way back.

The morality of the bomb was also muddled. Oppenheimer apparently washed his hands of it, the military and Truman were happy to take the morality off his hands. Oppenheimer felt bad about it, but that's about it.

And why was Truman portrayed as a creep? He made a tough decision to use the bomb but he was no villain. He was an authentic leader with a true moral sense of the type that seems entirely gone now. I wish we had a Truman to vote for in 2024.

However, this movie has a helluva cast, acting their heads off, with some notable actors popping up even in minor roles for a few minutes of screen time.

7.title: Stellar Cinematography
7.content:
"Oppenheimer" emerges as a cinematic triumph, boasting stellar cinematography that elevates its visual narrative to an unparalleled level. The meticulous attention to historical accuracy weaves a compelling storyline that aligns seamlessly with real-world events. The ensemble cast's performances are noteworthy, breathing authenticity into the characters, complemented by a captivating soundscape that enhances the overall viewing experience.

However, the film grapples with a notable downside-its extensive three-hour runtime. This lengthy duration poses a hurdle to the movie's rewatchability, a crucial factor for sustained audience engagement. Despite the movie's undeniable brilliance, the reluctance to revisit such a time-intensive piece may limit its enduring appeal.

The silver lining lies in the film's undeniable impact, underscoring the dedication of the actors, the prowess of the production team, and the immersive quality of its storytelling. While "Oppenheimer" might not clinch the title of your favorite, its cinematic merits and historical resonance position it as a formidable entry in the realm of filmmaking.

7.title: Compelling biopic of Oppenheimer, but overproduced
7.content:
It's a partial biopic of J. Robert Oppenheimer, who helped with the theoretical research for the atomic bomb and led the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos, New Mexico. It's set from the mid-1920s to 1958 in many places, with the most significant time in Los Alamos.

J. Robert Oppenheimer (Cillian Murphy) is portrayed in a jumbled timeline that touches on his early scientific education, his political interests and relationships, the influential women in his life, his interactions with a vast array of scientists in the development of the atomic bomb, the post-war controversy aroused by his political sympathies and family relationships, and his reflections on the implications of the nuclear bomb for humanity.

The most important figures who relate to Oppenheimer in the film include Jean Tatlock (Florence Pugh), Kitty Puening Oppenheimer (Emily Blunt), General Leslie Groves (Matt Damon) of the Manhattan Project, Commissioner Lewis Strauss (Robert Downey, Jr.) of the Atomic Energy Commission, and Edward Teller (Benny Safdie). Other prominent historical figures like Albert Einstein (Tom Conti) and Harry Truman (Gary Oldman) make cameo appearances, as do many scientists.

"Oppenheimer" is a compelling movie. My favorite scenes were Kitty Oppenheimer refusing to shake Edward Teller's hand late in the film and Harry Truman's brusque treatment of Oppenheimer and his demand that they "don't let that crybaby in the door again" after Oppenheimer raised concerns. The film brilliantly portrays Oppenheimer's complex personality. Unfortunately, almost everyone else is an incomplete character. The movie is overproduced with a few valuable gimmicks and too many that are simply distracting. The time lapse between the flash of the first test explosion and the sound reaching the scientists a short distance away was silly. And I doubt Oppenheimer climbed to a high platform to examine the bomb in a suit and tie.

Some characters seem exaggerated, as is wont to happen in such biopics. Lewis Strauss's villainy seems overdrawn, especially since his failure to get a cabinet seat occurred years after the conflict with Oppenheimer. John F. Kennedy's vote as a senator against Strauss joined 56 other Democrats.

Still, "Oppenheimer" is well worth seeing. It raises good questions about nuclear weapons and the meaning of international arms races. Oppenheimer's final words are not optimistic.

7.title: Not Nolan's best. And just too long.
7.content:
When the Oscars come round I don't think it will be Cillian Murphy that gets his shoulder tapped I think it could be Emily Blunt and Robert Downie Jr who plays Oppenheimer's would be nemesis, Lewis Strauss. Don't get me wrong, Murphy is good, just not truly great.

And that about sums up this overlong movie, good just not truly great.

The plot wriggles and writhes through timelines in such a way as to satisfy Nolan's trademark need for complexity and I have to confess to being confused for much of its three hours.

Also, if I was watching this as a Japanese viewer I'd be gritting my teeth at the overall celebration of the outcome of Oppenheimer's technical success. It treads a fine line between glorification and condemnation of the A Bomb that was dropped on Nagasaki and Hiroshima killing over 200,000 Japanese civilians.

And while Nolan coaxes a degree of remorse out of his central character I wasn't 100% convinced that he really did regret his actions. Sure he denounces them, to an extent, but he didn't go into this in wide eyed innocence, Oppenheimer absolutely knew his objective. The ethics are pretty muddled, like a lot of the plot in my view.

Ach, it's a hard one to deconstruct. I'm a little surprised at the ratings this movie is attracting because it's a long hard slog with a LOT of dialogue and not a great deal of action.

Perhaps the best scenes are the test sequences in the desert, the senatorial election drama at the end and the creepy but well handled rabble rousing reception Oppenheimer receives from his team on the news that Hiroshima has been obliterated. At least in this scene Nolan convinces us that it's not a celebration of the bombing, but an indictment.

Oppenheimer's vilification as a possible Communist is a central theme of the movie and is key to Strauss's objections and the 1954 kangaroo court FBI security clearance meeting which anchors the plot. There seems little evidence that he was a Commie, but the McCarthy regime at that time seemed to put little store in hard evidence and he clearly fared badly in this terrible stitch up.

Perhaps my favourite moment in the movie is the look of schadenfreude on the face of Strauss's advisor towards the end of the movie.

It's a delicious moment in a banquet that sadly has more plain fare than delicacies.

7.title: It's A Good Movie. How Good IS HArd To Say.
7.content:
Oppenheimer isn't a bad movie. It's a good movie. It's just difficult to know just how good it is since the dialogue is constantly interrupted either by over the top sound effects or a self important and intrusive soundtrack by Ludwig Göransson. It isn't that Christopher Nolan thinks he's Michael Bay. There's only one explosion, but it is a big one. It's just that he might as well have been Michael Bay, exchanging explosions on the screen for an explosive soundtrack. I don't know if Ludwig Göransson thinks he's the new Vangelis or the next Hans Zimmer, but he is neither. They must have a great sound system in the studio's mixing room. It's just too bad the average Cineplex can't quite match it.

I think he would have been better served if he had brought Zimmer onboard to do the soundtrack. He brought other people from the Batman movies. Gary Oldman is almost unrecognizable as President Harry Truman and Tom Conti is totally unrecognizable as Professor Albert Einstein. There are other Hollywood Heavyweights in other cameos as well. But they're all overshadowed by the intrusive overbearing soundtrack.

If only Christopher Nolan had more respect for the audiences intelligence he might have given the dialogue a more prominent place in his film. Quantum Mechanics and Nuclear Physics are difficult enough subjects to tackle when you can hear and understand every word being said clearly and distinctly. But when you have music that is trying to create a sense of urgency and tension even in scenes where there is none, it's a bit like the snow he inserts into scenes where it isn't cold enough to see the actors breath. Obviously he is foreshadowing nuclear winter and fallout, but again, it's as intrusive as the persistent soundtrack, and more than a little ham-handed. Muck like the inserted nudity and sex scene trying to allude to Oppenheimer's life being laid bare before his detractors.

Cillian Murphy's performance is excellent. Had this film been made a decade or two ago his part might well have gone to Peter Weller. He would have fit right in as the Doctor Buckaroo Banzai of the 1940s, especially when Naked Lunch like sexual and atomic hallucination intrude into the story almost as much as that bombastic soundtrack.

Perhaps all the blasts of music, sound effects and shocking imagery are to keep the audience awake since you can't always hear the dialogue. Or, maybe, he thought the dialogue itself would put people to sleep, especially after the bomb is made and shipped off to Japan and the movie is only a little more than half over and the film degenerates into a courtroom drama against Oppenheimer by a Robert Downey Jr.'s bitter character, since it's filled enough science and political science to put the audience to sleep even with the intrusive music and hallucinations. It's hard to say for certain since I couldn't hear a lot of it.

So I hope when the DVD comes out there will be instead of a Director's Cut, a Viewer's Cut, complete with options like a soundtrack that can be turned down. At least there will be Closed Captions, hopefully accurate ones, and not like the ones that seem be written for the deaf by the deaf. No, good ones where you can read what's actually being said. Only then will I be able to determine just how good this good movie really was. It was certainly better than the theater's sound system as it struggled to keep up. Perhaps they should resurrect the of Sensurround System from the 1970's that they used for movies like Earthquake and Midway with enough Cervwin-Vega speakers for a Grateful Dead concert. Maybe that would allow the audience to hear the dialogue above the intrusive score and atomic blasts. Otherwise it's like trying to watch a combination of a dramatic Broadway play with the entire New York Philharmonic on stage with the actors, punctuating their every line with fanfares and flourishes.

Does this review seem overly long and monotonous? Well then Oppenheimer probably isn't your cup of tea. The "courtroom stuff" makes the "math stuff" seem interesting by comparison. It seems that Christopher Nolan wanted to give us an epic. It's certainly long enough to be one. But most of the film isn't IMAX worthy, even if the soundtrack requires their sound system. This could have been a Smart Movie, but I think Nolan made it just smart enough for intellectually challenged pretentious people to think it is. Or maybe I'm wrong and it's just me. But if I were you, I'd wait for the DVD, or Stream it. That way you can rewind missed dialogue and take breaks as needed in order to find out.

7.title: The explosion trial scene makes it a memorable watch.
7.content:
"Oppenheimer." like previous Nolan's films, the screenplay was ingeniously crafted in a non-linear format, challenging the audience to piece together the narrative puzzle seat.

The explosion trial scene, undoubtedly the movie's highlight, which left me on the edge of my seat.

However, for me personally "Oppenheimer" leaned heavily towards a documentary-like experience. While this approach might be lauded by some for its historical accuracy and attention to detail, for me personally, it detracted slightly from the overall cinematic experience I have come to expect from Nolan's works. I was hoping for a more seamless blend of historical events with his trademark mind-bending storytelling.

Overall "Oppenheimer" was a good movie, but it fell short of making it to my list of favorite Nolan films. The explosion trial scene alone makes it a memorable watch.

7.title: A bit waste of energy
7.content:
Nolan hit the top with Interstellar, a film that could be considered the best science fiction film ever made, and since then he seems to struggle to find a way to repeat his triumph. But his work, following Interstellar did not meet the expectations, which -granted- are pretty high. Oppenheimer, though better than Dunkirk and definitely way better than Tenet, cannot put Nolan back to the top.

While Tenet was a pretty lazy movie, since it was obvious that Nolan did not do his homework, Oppenheimer suffers pretty much from the opposite. Too much information, too may representations of the biography which lead to a needlessly long film.

Surely, the father of the atomic bomb is a subject worth investing, worth representing all its aspects. But way too much weight was given in his alleged affiliations with the Communism rather than the moral dilemmas concerning the construction of the atom bomb, for example, on which we see a quite neutral position, attempting even to whitewash Oppenheimer from his responsibilities, at some points. Concerning the views of other respected scientists of the time on the Manhattan Project such as Einstein and the famous Einstein-Szilard letter is simply a sub-note lost in the noise.

Other aspects of his personality are lost as well. His pioneer work in quantum mechanics, his teachings, even his interest in mysticism, all seem to pale in front of whether Oppenheimer was a communist and the attempt to present him as an innocent martyr of the Manhattan Project.

And, of course, you can't have a proper martyr without a proper villain. In the tradition of Hollywood, every movie, even a biographical epic of a physicist, needs a antagonist of the main character, an one-dimensional, pure-blooded villain with completely selfish motives, no remorse, driven by emotions. As such, the film focuses a great deal on Lewis Strauss, a character more fitting to be a sub-note than Einstein or Szilard. There are times that one completely forgets that this is a biopic about Oppenheimer and think that they are watching a political thriller, about an ambitious, arrogant politician which finally meets his much by the most out of subject reference in the film: Kennedy... Because, apparently there can't be a film about the era when Kennedy was alive without yet another attempt to glorify him.

Speaking of one-dimensional characters, Nolan once again proves that he has no idea how to develop an interesting female character. Nothing we haven't seen in literally every Nolan film ever made. The women are irrational, driven by emotions, superfluous, a thorn at the hero's side. Such a shame for such a talented director and screenwriter.

Directionaly speaking, the film has much more merit than the overloaded, out-of-subject plot would lead one to believe. There you can actually see the talent of Nolan. Powerful images, beautiful close-ups which light up every detail of the expressional face of Cillian Murphy, atmospheric built-ups. Even in the noise of this narrative, which fails to focus on the atomic bomb, Nolan manages with his excellent direction to appeal to the existential dread of a nuclear holocaust. He leads the viewer to sympathize with the protagonist, to feel his anguish, his agony.

Of course, it will be unfair to give credit for that only to Nolan. Cillian Murphy once again gives everything to his assigned role. His expressions are way more powerful than his words, his gaze full of agony. His metamorphosis to Oppenheimer is almost too perfect. But nothing less can be expected of such a talented actor. He invest equally in every aspect of his character, and if one look up closely, they can see it in the movie, even of the plot does not focus on that.

Commendable is also the performance of Robert Downey Jr. If we consider that he didn't have the same chances to prove his work, since his character was awfully one-dimensional and full of unbearable cliches, we could say that his performance was equally powerful as that of Cillian Murphy.

We shouldn't overlook the other performances. The cast was full of talented actors, so talented that they seem wasted to the assigned role, beginning with Emily Blunt who had to suffer the one-dimensional, derogatory female lead character to Gary Oldman who appears in just one, pretty much unnecessary scene that lasts only a few seconds. In between you can see Kenneth Branagh and Jack Quaid. But I would like to take a minute to commend on the performance of Josh Hartnett and Florence Pugh. Because much was expected and much was delivered from Cillian Murphy and Robert Downey Jr. But I must admit that I didn't expect to see such pleasant performances from Josh Hartnett and Florence Pugh. The first ones seems to have matured in silence, he convinced me in every turn and his performance was quite substantial. The latter proves in every opportunity that is given that she is a young talent, worth noticing that makes the best of every given role. And once again, I should note that she too had too suffer a one-dimentional, derogatory role.

Lastly, we shouldn't forget to commend the excellent work of the make-up department. It was really convincing, subtle work that helped the actors transform completely to their assigned character. The attention to detail was worth-noticing.

Overall, It was an excellent effort from a directional aspect, the cast was rich and talented, committed to their work, the make-up and visual effects amazing. But all of that seemed wasted in a script full of noise, focused in indifferent or even out-of-subject topics while disregarding the vital aspects of the biography. Good thing it wasn't nuclear waste...

7.title: according to my opinion
7.content:
Cillian Murphy delivers a standout performance as Oppenheimer, capturing the character's intellectual brilliance and the emotional burden he carries as he grapples with the consequences of his creation. The supporting cast, including Robert Downey Jr. And Emily Blunt, adds depth to the narrative, each portraying key figures who influenced Oppenheimer's life and decisions.

Nolan's direction is meticulous, with a narrative structure that interweaves different timelines, providing a comprehensive view of Oppenheimer's life and the events leading to the bomb's creation. The film is visually stunning, with cinematography that captures both the grandeur of the scientific achievements and the stark reality of the bomb's destructive power.

The screenplay is dense with dialogue that reflects the intellectual debates and ethical questions of the time. Nolan does not shy away from exploring the moral implications of the atomic bomb, making the film a thought-provoking experience. The pacing is deliberate, allowing the audience to absorb the gravity of the historical events being depicted.

However, the film may not appeal to all audiences, especially those expecting a more straightforward biopic or action-driven plot. The non-linear storytelling and the focus on dialogue and character development might be challenging for some viewers.

Overall, *Oppenheimer* is a powerful and thought-provoking film that explores the complexities of a man who changed the course of history. Nolan's direction, combined with strong performances and a compelling narrative, makes it a must-watch for fans of historical dramas and those interested in the ethical questions surrounding scientific discovery.

7.title: It could have been 70 minutes shorter...

...or a TV show in 5 parts.

+ Cillian Murphy is amazing, though. He should get an Oscar nomination for this.

+ As a non native English speaker, I hate the fact that some of Nolan's movies are a bit hard to understand due to some questionable sound editing choices.

+ It is definitely one of Nolan's most conventional movies so far.

+ It came to my attention that the upsetting story of Los Alamos wasn't told in its entirety. Apparently hundreds of families living off that land were ressetled and their livestock killed. People living in the surrounding areas got cancer and leukemia in the years that followed. Same happened with the people of color - mostly hispanics - who worked in the area without the appropriate gear.

I think Nolan lost a good opportunity to show some of the implications those other Americans faced (and apparently are still facing.) Oppenheimer is portrayed as a victim during the second half of the film, but going beyond his inner circle to show how that whole thing affected other Americans in New Mexico would have benefitted the film greatly. Without that, it's a veeeery long odyssey about a bunch of white men playing god and making questionable decisions, which is fine, but it's 2023 and we can do better, no?

7.title: A Brilliant Performance
7.content:
Oppenheimer is a film that boasts amazing directing and clean visuals. Cillian Murphy delivers an amazing performance, one that truly deserves an Oscar. The dialogues of the movie are particularly noteworthy.

However, the film is not without its flaws. The use of black and white shots doesn't seem to add much to the story, and the fast-moving timeline can be difficult to follow. It might have been more effective if the story was told year by year, with the trial and future scenes in black and white for better understanding.

Additionally, while all of Nolan's films come with high expectations, Oppenheimer doesn't quite live up to them - with the exception of Interstellar.

Overall, it's still a film worth watching for its amazing visuals and Cillian Murphy performance.

7.title: Felt like watching a 3 hour long trailer.
7.content:
Not enough dialogue and not.. very good dialogue at that, way too many cuts and waaaay too loud score and why did every single scene need a score at all? Let the actors do their job. Let the sets speak for themselves. It's a drama film about a physicist, not Batman.

I didnt really enjoy the film. I think it was an OK film that could have been a great film, if it had another director-writer. I love Nolan usually, but.. a drama film that should be dialogue-driven is not really his area of expertise, in my opinion. He isnt a very good dialogue writer. Good actors ruined by all those fast cuts.

Feels like a drama film for people that usually watch 1.30h action movies and hate drama.

Still be prepared for numerous time hops that can be a bit confusing, something to identify the timeline would have been helpful. I appreciated the moral dilemma, but also know that one needs to find comfort in the greater good.

Some of the liberties taken were slanted...certainly didn't make Truman look too good. Even if it was subtle, the spin was there....poor Hollywood can't help itself. Can we not just have a factual movie without the "message" ?

Unfortunately this movie is very poorly written. But because of the interesting topic it touches and good acting I give it a 7, as in it's intertaining. But wouldn't recommend people waste money on it in cinema.

7.title: Very good but maybe not exceptional
7.content: Here's what I liked. The acting was superb. Cillian Murphy (Who is this guy?) was outstanding. Oscar winning performance. The supporting cast was terrific including Robert Downey Jr. You felt the characters were real. Only Matt Damon's role felt forced. The script was intelligent (for the most part) and it's a good story. Nuclear weapons is admittedly a touchy subject and the movie kept its balance until the last hour when it became a tad one-sided. The short scene making President Truman seem like a bumpkin was disappointing, for example, even though I read that a couple of quotes he said in the movie were true. Still, it made me wonder how historically accurate the movie was. From what I read, Oppenheimer was more flawed than the movie indicates, and I left the theater wondering what kind of man Oppenheimer really was, besides being a competent director and a womanizer. I also thought the use of imagery showing what Oppenheimer was thinking at times was too speculative and overdone. All said, this was a good film which offered a lot. However, it's not Nolan's best movie, in my opinion.

7.title: A Cinematic Journey Through Science and Politics
7.content:
I recently watched the film "Oppenheimer," directed by Christopher Nolan. The movie delves into the life of J. Robert Oppenheimer, an American theoretical physicist known for his pivotal role in developing the atomic bomb, ultimately leading to the devastating events in Hiroshima.

Starring Cillian Murphy as Oppenheimer, the film is a captivating blend of scientific exploration and political intrigue. It explores the complexities of Oppenheimer's life, his contributions to science, and the moral dilemmas surrounding the use of the atomic bomb.

The narrative unfolds in a lengthy yet engaging manner, providing insights into the scientific advancements and the political landscape of the time. The film not only highlights Oppenheimer's scientific achievements but also delves into the challenges he faced, including the need to protect him and his subsequent trial.

"Oppenheimer" offers thrilling sequences, particularly in its scientific aspects, and presents a nuanced portrayal of the ethical considerations surrounding Oppenheimer's work. Released in 2023, the film provides a fresh perspective on historical events while keeping audiences on the edge of their seats.

7.title: Well made, but disappointing and often tedious
7.content:
Having been a fan of Christopher Nolan's films for some time and after hearing all of the hype, I was so looking forward to this movie. Perhaps over expectation is behind some of the disappointment.

Oppenheimer has many of the components of a great Chris Nolan film: Intelligent writing, compelling story, stellar acting performances. Unfortunately it also suffers from an overdose of some of the often seen pitfalls: Overly-complicated, fractured pacing and a sound track that is sometimes just TOO LOUD. (This was a particular irritation for me - I have a decent 7.1 dolby surround set-up and had to spend ages tweaking the outputs to hear the dialogue properly without being blasted by the sub woofer!)

Aside from the problematic audio I really struggled with the structure and pace. The first hour, with it's constant jump cutting and flicking between time periods was just irritating. The middle hour, when the story finally settled down and it became possible to start understanding the characters and the narrative, was a great watch, and I finally found myself enjoying the film I had been expecting. Sadly in the final hour, we jumped back to a fractured and exhausting narrative, again jumping between time periods, between colour & B&W, again overshadowed by an unnecessarily loud and at times discordant sound track. For the first time ever in a Chris Nolan movie, I found myself checking the time, looking forward to the end.

I am frankly baffled by the majority of reviews and ratings. For me, this was Chis Nolan's weakest film yet. 7/10 for me in recognition of the scale and obvious achievement. But unlike every other Nolan film, this is not one that I have any desire to ever watch again.

7.title: A Movie More about the Man than the Bomb
7.content:
There have been numerous dramatizations about the building of the bomb. Certain movies were bombs themselves (Fat Man and Little Boy). I was expecting the movie to centralize around the work going into building the first atomic bomb. Instead, it is really only the backdrop for a biography about Oppenheimer. Nolan and the screenwriters spiced up his story, using a hearing with flashbacks as the narrative structure. That type of structure allows the film to jump around in time, following the impacts of a decision throughout his life. Jumping around is definitely Nolan's directing style. It keeps the pacing fast, and helps to parse out portions of the film that would have otherwise become static if told in linear fashion. This is the case of the hearing. It is conducted in a small and uninteresting room as a location. Same for the many many conversations about being engaged in politics.

One review mentioned the directing style resembling Martin Scorcese. The "Goodfellas" director was the pioneer of the hyper-pacing when telling a story. Nolan perhaps might feel that Michael Bay syndrome of quick cutting to force the audience to keep watching by subjecting them to some new stimulus every few seconds. Nolan probably justifies the quick cutting knowing that this is meant to be a summer tentpole film, which needs to resemble a roller coaster ride. So you get a lot of big music cues, big scenes, a big group of side characters, and just a little tiny bit of humour. Adding the right amount of humour is extremely important for a script that wants be a serious drama. Too many yucks can decrease the amount of gravitas to the story. Too little humour keeps the audience in an emotional rut. They need to have a bit of levity once in a while, especially when the movie gets heavy handed. Matt Damon plays the general in charge of the Manhattan Project. As seen in the trailer, his heavy handed character almost gets to the point of over-acting. Thankfully he is allowed to be more than one dimensional. There still is the memory of Paul Newman playing Damon's character in "Fat Man and Little Boy". That movie made many bad decisions, one was to make Paul Newman an overdrawn movie villain.

As I sat through the three hour running time, something occurred to me that was a revelation, I could actually hear and understand the dialogue! Finally someone convinced Nolan to turn the music down a bit. The music score must have been a huge undertaking. I think few people realise the amount of man hours it takes to go over footage only a few minutes at a time and carve out a music cue that encompasses many factors (character, story, location, time of day, mood, etc.), and not become derivative or repetitious. Ludwig Goransson displays a wide breadth of musical knowledge that Hans Zimmer never had. He uses a musical palette of many instruments and styles (including Zimmer).

So the story gets around to the actual event of setting off the atomic bomb. I don't know why, but Nolan didn't want a computer simulation. The practical version failed to really invoke a sense of awe. Unless... Nolan wanted this movie to be less about the bomb, and as such only give scant details on its production, along with the tedious aspects of testing for two years. This film finds a lot of good intelligent interaction with the supporting characters, many are whom are physicists. The final act of the film focuses on the aftermath of the birth of the atomic age. We see how those other characters react to the event as well as to the pressure of politics. The red scare back then made it easy to make scapegoats out of innocent people.

So of course you are asking, does it fail the two hour rule? Does this film justify its three hour running time? If you are Martin Scorcese, you can justify a longer running time, like "The Departed", because you are condensing an even larger story. Such is the case here, mostly. As important as politics are, I feel audiences don't find it entertaining.

The supporting characters do a fine job of filling out the scope of this film. The film jumps around from Europe to Ivy League college campuses to the New Mexico desert. Meaningful conversations are written with a certain eloquence in mind. In other words, a lot of thought was put into the dialogue to add more subtlety about the greater meaning of what they are saying. Robert Downey Jr. Does a great transformation into a man who was the first commissioner of the Atomic Energy Commission. Not a very exciting man, thus played in a relaxed fashion by Downey. Emily Blunt has very little screen time in this film. Not much is explored about their marriage, and she has few lines for such a prominent actress in a seemingly prominent role. There are other familiar faces that pop up, which I won't spoil the fun. Cillian Murphy plays the role of his career. By far, Oppenheimer is a complex character, and some odd behaviour is shown. Murphy seems to be always in deep thought, and somewhat disassociated with the kind of everyday life most people have. Like being a proper parent.

There was some light applause at the end of the nearly sold out showing I went to. Here is a chance to learn about an interesting piece of history, and in the process experience a refreshing break from the summer blockbuster sequel assembly line. I would only say some parts of the story could have been condensed even more, such as some of the politics. Nolan is certainly developing a reputation for retelling stories in a more exciting way. Many see Nolan transitioning into a serious director with Dunkirk and now this historical piece. Such as his inclusion of nudity (for the first time?) in one his films. There needs to be an artistic approach that makes sense when showing nudity, and Nolan shows that kind of maturity here.

7 out of 10.

No questions asked - it is one of the big films but the constant blasting of music, also during important conversations is totally annoying and distracting. At some stages it also creates a different "vibe" then the scene is about. Absolutely awful editing here. And if you think oh great 5 seconds without... it will start again with the next track.

Given the whole picture it is a shame that this happens at all. Music should be support the picture, but here it is a complete own thing and is not keeping the focus on what is shown. Some Scenes are wonderful and the music fits but these are rare to find sadly. I would have given a 9 but that was really... too much bad fitting music in too much scenes.

7.title: Nolan trying too hard as usual
7.content:
Nothing Christopher Nolan makes is easy to watch. Which I guess is one of his biggest charms, while also being his biggest downfall. You can't just sit and enjoy his movies, you have to surrender yourself to the fact that he wants to make you earn it.

This starts with his refusal to make a film with understandable dialogue. Oppenheimer was mildly better than Tenet in this regard. But seriously, if he wants us to have to concentrate and think, at least let us understand what the actors are mumbling, or add subtitles.

Having said all that, I'd still recommend seeing this movie once. It is a very good story, brilliantly acted, and incredibly shot. I saw it in a standard theatre, not Imax. But considering 90% of the movie takes place inside, I don't know why you'd need to film it for Imax anyway?

As I said, definitely see it once. But probably no need to see it twice....

7.title: A good but long watch

First of this is a good film and (as far as I can gather) generally accurate

With a plethora of stars, many in small parts, the acting is very good

The first 2 hours go by in a whiz as I was totally enthralled, totally absorbed

This film is beautifully crafted and acted where it (dare I say it) goes slighly awry, is it is just soooooo long.

I have to admit in the last 30 minutes I was wishing it would end. It's a bit of a marathon to watch and begins to run out of steam in the last part.

Therefore for the first 2 hrs 8/10 but overall 7.5/10

Movie is slow and little boring. If you less time and want some entertainment then don't watch it.
