This film was fire (Literally)

Oppenheimer (2023) is an extraordinary film that captivated my senses from start to finish. This historical drama, directed by the brilliant Christopher Nolan, weaves a mesmerizing narrative that delves deep into the life of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the brilliant physicist whose work changed the course of history during World War II.

From the moment the film begins, the audience is transported back in time to the tumultuous era of the 1940s, and Nolan's impeccable attention to detail immerses us into the historical setting effortlessly. The cinematography is awe-inspiring, and the breathtaking landscapes blend seamlessly with the authentic period settings, bringing Oppenheimer's world to life.

The casting is nothing short of perfection. Cillian Murphy delivers an Oscar-worthy performance as J. Robert Oppenheimer, capturing the complexity and inner struggles of the enigmatic physicist with unparalleled depth. His portrayal is nuanced and compelling, allowing us to empathize with Oppenheimer's moral dilemmas and the burden he carries as the father of the atomic bomb.

The supporting cast, including talented actors like Jessica Chastain, Michael Caine, and Tom Hardy, further enriches the movie, elevating it to cinematic greatness. Each character is beautifully crafted and contributes significantly to the story's emotional weight.

One of the most impressive aspects of Oppenheimer is its intelligent and thought-provoking script. Kudos to the screenwriters for expertly exploring the ethical questions surrounding scientific discoveries during wartime, the moral responsibilities of scientists, and the consequences of unleashing such powerful weaponry on the world.

The film's score, composed by the incomparable Hans Zimmer, is nothing short of a symphonic masterpiece. It amplifies the emotional impact of every scene, pulling at our heartstrings and enhancing the overall experience.

Christopher Nolan's direction is, without a doubt, a work of art. His ability to interweave historical events with human emotions and philosophical musings is nothing short of genius. He masterfully guides the audience through a rollercoaster of emotions, leaving us contemplating the consequences of our actions long after the credits roll.

Oppenheimer is not merely a historical retelling; it's a powerful reflection on the frailty of humanity, the pursuit of knowledge, and the consequences of playing with forces beyond our comprehension. This film will undoubtedly leave a lasting impression on anyone fortunate enough to witness it on the big screen.

In conclusion, Oppenheimer is an unparalleled cinematic experience that deserves every single one of its five stars. Christopher Nolan's visionary direction, outstanding performances, breathtaking cinematography, and emotional depth make this film a true masterpiece. It is a must-watch for anyone who appreciates the power of storytelling and the impact of historical events on the course of human history.

10.title: Oppenheimer sits alongside the best films ever made
10.content:
Oppenheimer, the film from Christopher Nolan has usurped Russians from Dream of the Blue Turtles as the leading edge of cultural awareness for "father of the atomic bomb". In that song, Sting flippantly introduced the subject as "Oppenheimer's deadly toy". In reality his relationship was much more complex with nuclear weapons than that; but kudos to Sting for introducing a name to millions of folks who otherwise wouldn't have heard it until now. Oppenheimer is a big film in the most Christopher Nolan manner possible. It's a three-hour dramatic tour de force that grabs viewers by their shirt collars and maintains its grip for the vast majority of its run time.

Unlike Nolan's other works, Oppenheimer is driven by dramatic sequences, tight dialogue, and acting that's top-notch. There aren't any big action sequences, but viewers who want a breathtaking overview of the Atomic Bomb, its creation and after-effects will be mesmerized. That's all the more amazing because there are about two dozen characters as the film jumps between a 20-year era in history. Those characters are all memorable and their role in Oppenheimer's life and work are always clear, unless they aren't.

This is a Christopher Nolan film after all, and some scenes are truncated or have certain lines of dialogue not audible. Those lines or scenes will be seen later in the film, but only when they need to be shown in order to crystallize plot threads. Nolan also uses black and white film to contrast the setting, tone, timing and perspective of the story in a near-perfect manner. There's a reason why some scenes are in color and others aren't. Some characters are shown in a flashback in black and white, then immediately shown in the current story in color, or vice versa. When you see the film, this effect is akin to a chess match that the characters are having.

As a film, Oppenheimer is very difficult not to look at. There are dozens of scenes that were filmed close-up, with the minute details of the actor's faces or bodies filling up the screen. And because this is a character-driven film, there are many more opportunities for people to fill the scenes than Nolan's other works.

The first act of the film is more of an artistic painter's approach to Oppenheimer as a person, than a traditional movie. There are short, chaotic cuts and close-ups of Cillian Murphy interspersed with micro close-ups of the stages of explosions, reactions and wires that are reacting to electrical charges. This part of Oppenheimer focuses on his early educational life as the background, but it's being presented in hindsight because he is currently being questioned by a Congressional panel.

He's a very gifted student who is well-networked, but also mischievous, too direct at times and keenly aware that he's usually the smartest person in the room. As a teacher, he wants to engage in theoretical physics and the concept of energy relating to collapsing stars and the blackness of space. He is also very open-minded, even to those with radical ideas on campus. Because of this, he makes numerous friends in a school communist organization, which unfortunately comes back to haunt him.

The classroom next to his is working on a machine that will research, and hopefully split, atoms. As the world's drumbeats to WWII get louder his classes get bigger and his knowledge of physics gets more useful.

The world's top physicists have been captured or are working with the Nazis. When they make a key breakthrough in nuclear power Oppenheimer realizes that the world is racing towards weaponizing this new technology. The lab next to his classroom is able to replicate what the Germans did and he's given the chance to form his own team.

Oppenheimer teams up with a U. S. General and they create their own research facility in Los Alamos. It's a city where they all live with their families and can conduct testing and research with minimal delay. The film does a great job of making the potentially incomprehensible process of nuclear reactions, bombs, and the science behind them something that non-tech folks can understand. When you see Benny Safdie as Edward Teller talking about a different delivery method for the bomb that could prove more efficient you're able to follow the logic.

The success of the bomb's testing starts Oppenheimer's concerns about responsibly using that power. The end of WWII brings even more issues as he runs afoul of certain politicians, which results in his inquiry that started the movie.

Oppenheimer is a powerful film that ranks alongside Schindler's List in terms of a war or combat film that will stand the test of time. It's impossible not to compare the two films in terms of quality and deftly telling a story to audiences that aren't familiar with its titular character. The final act of the film focuses on McCarthyism and communist hearing, where his past history, as well as that of his wife and peers, will resonate with folks today.

Could you really be held accountable for one meeting that you had with someone a decade and a half ago? Your actions have always been solid, but those who seek you harm are focusing on that meeting or perhaps the beliefs of a second-tier associate. Could you really be held accountable just for RT something on social media? Your actions are solid, but those who don't think like you do will do anything to cause you harm. McCarthyism and the public's zeal to believe or jump on the bandwagon of those who said something on social media that runs counter to what they believe have much in common.

Oppenheimer was an independent thinker who wasn't afraid to surround himself with people who question his work or beliefs. While the movie, Oppenheimer was indeed a fantastic piece of cinema, I hope that the irony of those who persecuted him isn't lost on all of audiences and the similarities that they might share.

10.title: Bad things can help to save the world
10.content:
"Oppenheimer" Movie Review

Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer is a cinematic masterpiece that masterfully weaves history, science, and human psychology into a gripping narrative. Released in 2023, this biographical drama offers a deep exploration of the life and legacy of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the physicist often regarded as the "father of the atomic bomb." With an all-star cast, stunning cinematography, and a haunting score, Oppenheimer is not just a film; it is an immersive experience that challenges viewers to reflect on morality, ambition, and the far-reaching consequences of human innovation.

The movie is based on the Pulitzer Prize-winning biography American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer by Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin. Nolan uses his signature non-linear storytelling to great effect, interweaving two primary timelines: Oppenheimer's rise as a brilliant physicist and his later struggles during the Cold War-era Red Scare. This dual narrative creates a dynamic tension, allowing viewers to see both the highs of scientific achievement and the lows of political persecution.

Cillian Murphy delivers a career-defining performance as Oppenheimer. His portrayal captures the physicist's complexity-a man of immense intellect and ambition, haunted by the moral implications of his work. Murphy's gaunt appearance and intense expressions reflect Oppenheimer's inner turmoil, making him a deeply compelling and human figure. Emily Blunt also shines as Kitty Oppenheimer, bringing depth and resilience to a role that could have easily been overshadowed. Matt Damon, as General Leslie Groves, provides a grounded counterpoint to Oppenheimer's idealism, while Robert Downey Jr. Offers a standout performance as Lewis Strauss, a figure central to Oppenheimer's later downfall.

The film's pacing is deliberate, allowing the audience to fully absorb the weight of each moment. Nolan dedicates significant time to the Manhattan Project, the secretive World War II initiative that developed the atomic bomb. The scenes at Los Alamos are a highlight, capturing the blend of excitement, camaraderie, and anxiety among the scientists. The eventual Trinity test-the first detonation of an atomic bomb-is a cinematic tour de force. Shot without the use of CGI, the explosion is both awe-inspiring and horrifying, a visual and auditory spectacle that leaves a lasting impression.

Nolan's choice to avoid traditional CGI effects underscores his commitment to authenticity. The practical effects, combined with Hoyte van Hoytema's stunning cinematography, create a visceral viewing experience. The use of IMAX cameras captures the grandeur and detail of the film's landscapes and interiors, immersing the audience in both the beauty and the destruction inherent in Oppenheimer's story.

The score, composed by Ludwig Göransson, deserves special mention. It is both haunting and evocative, blending classical and modern elements to reflect the film's themes of innovation and dread. The music builds tension in key moments, particularly during the Trinity test and Oppenheimer's later confrontations, heightening the emotional impact.

While Oppenheimer excels as a historical drama, it also poses profound ethical questions. The film does not shy away from the devastating consequences of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, though these events are shown indirectly. Instead, the focus is on Oppenheimer's personal reckoning. As he grapples with the realization that his invention could lead to unprecedented destruction, the audience is invited to ponder the responsibility of scientists and the morality of pursuing knowledge without considering its potential consequences.

However, Oppenheimer is not without its flaws. The dense narrative, laden with scientific and political details, may overwhelm some viewers. Additionally, the film's focus on Oppenheimer's internal struggles means that the voices of those directly affected by the bombings are largely absent. While this is consistent with the film's perspective, it may leave some audiences wanting a more comprehensive exploration of the bomb's human toll.

In conclusion, Oppenheimer is a profound and thought-provoking film that cements Christopher Nolan's reputation as one of the greatest filmmakers of his generation. It is a testament to the power of cinema to explore complex ideas and emotions, offering both a history lesson and a meditation on the human condition. While not an easy watch, it is an essential one, reminding us of the profound consequences of our choices and the burden of knowledge.

10.title: Nolan's Magnum Opus!
10.content:
Just when you think it can't get better than The Dark Knight or Inception, Nolan comes out with his Magnum Opus. The mind and skill required to craft this puzzle is truly extraordinary, and Nolan has cemented himself as one of the greats of all time with this movie.

The story strikes the right balance in so many ways by delicately depicting the puzzle that is the politics of war and national security, relative to the social good for mankind. At a surface level, the theme of war is not appealing, and many may not like Oppenhiemer's legacy, and that's the genius of this movie. Despite its length, it is engaging from minute one and the videography & use of background music leaves you glued till the 180th minute. It makes it a human story about Oppenhiemer, and yet gets under your skin and has you thinking about the perils of warcraft and the arms race. It has you asking should human technological development have boundaries? Who should decide those boundaries? And who should hold the key to the big red button? An extremely relevant topic in this new age of AI.

To top off Nolan's efforts are superlative performances by the cast -- too many to mention individually, but without question a career best performance by Cillian Murphy in the lead role. Nolan's craft elevated each and every one of the cast to raise the bar, and it was seamlessly woven together on screen.

This should be a must see for any and all, especially in this era where we seem to have forgotten about the horrific consequences of global warfare; precisely when we forget, are we at greatest risk thereof.

10.title: Nolan at the top of his game

Oppenheimer is viewed as a hero by so many but he knows how many people have died and because of his work so much more destruction is inevitable. The toll this takes on him as a character is fascinating and the desperation he has to try and change the future that he has already guaranteed is so interesting. Cillian Murphy brings such a wide range in his Oscar worthy performance, and really captures Oppenheimer perfectly. He is also supported by a wonderful ensemble cast. Emily Blunt, Matt Damon, and Florence Pugh all have some of their best work on display here, and Robert Downey Jr is the other real standout. Downey gets a chance to really show he can play so much more than Iron Man, and the twist that he was the one going against Oppenheimer was brilliantly done. It's one of the best movie reveals of all time in my opinion not just because of how it was written but because of the performance. Nolan is one of the best directors of all time and he clearly brought everything he had to this movie. The script is so solid and people are going go be quoting this movie for years to come. Nolan chose to tell this story in such a unique way and it really captures the urgency of the creation of the bomb as well as the panic of the aftermath. The editing is next level and the sound design is immaculate. Oppenheimer is a triumph on every single level. 10/10.

10.title: A Cinematic Masterpiece
10.content:
Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer is a sweeping, epic biopic that tells the story of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the theoretical physicist who led the Manhattan Project to develop the atomic bomb. The film is a visual and intellectual tour-de-force, with Cillian Murphy giving a tour-de-force performance as Oppenheimer.

The film begins with Oppenheimer as a young man, studying physics at Harvard. We see his early brilliance, his love of science, and his idealistic commitment to using his knowledge to make the world a better place. As the war progresses, Oppenheimer is recruited to lead the Manhattan Project, a top-secret effort to develop an atomic bomb. The film follows Oppenheimer as he leads this team of scientists, working day and night to create a weapon that could change the course of history.

The film is not afraid to show the dark side of Oppenheimer's work. We see the moral and ethical dilemmas that he faces, as he grapples with the implications of creating a weapon of such destructive power. We also see the toll that this work takes on him, both physically and mentally.

Oppenheimer is a complex and challenging film, but it is also a deeply rewarding one. It is a film that asks big questions about the nature of power, the responsibility of scientists, and the dangers of nuclear weapons. It is a film that will stay with you long after you have seen it.

**10/10**

**Pros:**

* Cillian Murphy's tour-de-force performance * Stunning visuals * Thought-provoking story * Powerful performances from the supporting cast * Christopher Nolan's masterful direction

**Cons:**

* The film is long (nearly three hours) * Some of the scientific jargon may be difficult to follow

**Overall:**

Oppenheimer is a must-see for fans of Christopher Nolan, Cillian Murphy, and historical dramas. It is a film that will stay with you long after you have seen it.

**Here are some additional thoughts on the film:**

* The film's visuals are stunning. Nolan uses his trademark IMAX format to great effect, creating images that are both visually arresting and emotionally powerful.

* The film's story is thought-provoking and challenging. It asks big questions about the nature of power, the responsibility of scientists, and the dangers of nuclear weapons.

* The performances from the supporting cast are also excellent. Emily Blunt, Matt Damon, Robert Downey Jr., and Florence Pugh all give memorable performances.

* Nolan's direction is masterful. He creates a film that is both visually stunning and emotionally powerful.

Overall, Oppenheimer is a must-see for fans of Christopher Nolan, Cillian Murphy, and historical dramas. It is a film that will stay with you long after you have seen it.

10.title: The cinematic masterpiece not to miss
10.content:
"Oppenheimer" is a mesmerizing and thought-provoking biographical drama that delves into the complex and fascinating life of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the father of the atomic bomb. Directed by Christopher Nolan, this film is a masterclass in storytelling, boasting outstanding performances, meticulous attention to historical detail, and a gripping narrative that explores the intricacies of human nature and the consequences of scientific discovery.

Cillian Murphy delivers a tour-de-force performance as Oppenheimer, capturing the scientist's intensity, charisma, and vulnerability. Murphy's portrayal is both nuanced and powerful, conveying the complexity of Oppenheimer's character and the moral dilemmas he faced in his pursuit of scientific knowledge.

The supporting cast is equally impressive, with standout performances from Emily Blunt as Katherine "Kitty" Oppenheimer, Matt Damon as Leslie Groves, and Robert Downey Jr. As Lewis Strauss. The chemistry between the actors is palpable, creating a sense of authenticity and depth that draws the viewer into the world of the film.

Nolan's direction is, as always, meticulous and masterful. He weaves together multiple storylines and timelines with ease, creating a narrative that is both cohesive and complex. The film's pacing is deliberate and measured, allowing the viewer to absorb the intricacies of Oppenheimer's story and the historical context in which he lived.

One of the standout aspects of "Oppenheimer" is its attention to historical detail. Nolan and his team have clearly done their research, recreating the world of 1940s Los Alamos with meticulous accuracy. From the sets and costumes to the music and cinematography, every aspect of the film is imbued with a sense of authenticity and period detail.

The themes of "Oppenheimer" are timely and thought-provoking, exploring the complexities of scientific discovery, the consequences of playing with forces beyond human control, and the moral dilemmas that arise when scientific progress conflicts with human values. The film raises important questions about the responsibility of scientists and the ethics of scientific inquiry, encouraging viewers to reflect on the implications of scientific discovery and its impact on human society.

In conclusion, "Oppenheimer" is a biographical masterpiece that is both a tribute to the life and legacy of J. Robert Oppenheimer and a thought-provoking exploration of the human condition. With its outstanding performances, meticulous attention to historical detail, and gripping narrative, this film is a must-see for anyone interested in science, history, or the complexities of human nature.

10.title: Thank you, Nolan!
10.content:
Nolan is my favorite director, second to none. I just love all his movies and I don't think there is a bad movie in his CV.

He is a real man because he makes the movies exactly the way he wants them, using the best possible technology at that moment for a real experience on the big screen, the way movies should be seen.

On the one hand, this is a slightly different film in his career. A three-hour biographical drama with no effects, no CGI, no big twist at the end of the movie is something we haven't seen from Nolan since... well, never. On the other hand, he stayed true to himself by using his signature and style, so we can see part of the film in black and white, that is, part of the action, the non-linear flow of the story, a great interest in physics, we have seen all of this to a certain extent in his films, such as Interstellar or Memento. I was delighted with the final product because, theoretically, I would not have been drawn to the cinema by a biopic about an American scientist who invented the atomic bomb, and on top of that, it lasts for three full hours. At no point was the film boring to me, I did not feel its true duration. That's a big compliment.

Right at the beginning, I noticed that the film will have a lot of text because, as expected, there is a lot of dialogue, but these dialogues take place at a slightly higher speed, there are not many breaks. This was fine with me because it drew my attention to follow more closely. To be honest, I didn't check this later, I'm just giving my personal impression. Also in the film there are a lot of events and characters over a long period of time, there are no unnecessary scenes, things change and I think that this contributed to the film holding attention throughout its duration.

The cast of the film is quite strong and diverse, and Cillian Murphy, who portrays the title character, had a career role, and I predict an Oscar nomination for him, at the very least. He carried the entire film on his back, and he is portrayed as a layered and complicated man, he is neither positive nor negative, he is neither good nor bad, but he has his virtues and flaws, his doubts and moral doubts, it is up to us as viewers to judge what he is like. Clearly, all of this would not be possible without the accompanying ensemble, which is also at the highest level. Robert Downey Jr., Matt Damon and Emily Blunt deserve all the praise who are in the best scenes of the film, showing their pure talent when there is no green screen next to them. I must also say that the film has very, very many characters, some of whom are proven actors and Oscar winners who appear literally in a cameo role, one or two scenes for a minute or so and that's it. Obviously when Nolan does something then everyone clears their schedule to be a part of such a project. I won't mention who they are because I didn't know that myself, so I was positively surprised when I saw them in the movie.

The film has several themes that it deals with and I think it balances them brilliantly. So we have biography, court drama, politics, history, physics, and moral doubts about whether something should be done just because it can be done. So much that I probably didn't manage to catch everything in one viewing, so I'm drawn to watch it again. In addition to all that, the film has a very important message.

Nowadays, this film is exactly what we need when we are bombarded with various blockbusters and franchises with countless sequels and heavy effects. That I can watch something a little different in peace, and yet that it is visually beautiful, with a great sound and soundtrack. I understand that there will be a good portion of people who will not like this movie, but that is a topic for another discussion. The fact that a three-hour drama will manage to make money in theaters in this day and age speaks volumes. I predict several Oscars in various categories. A movie with a capital letter, the movie we needed, not the one we deserved.

Thank you, Nolan!

10.title: A Movie Which Shows the Bleak Reality of Nuclear Weapons - Nolan Has Created Yet Another Masterpiece (MINOR Spoilers)
10.content:
Oppenheimer is, to put it short, a masterpiece. Christopher Nolan has once again rubber-stamped that he is the greatest living director of our time.

From the incredible cinematography, story-telling and acting; to the incredible score that was, once again, comprised by Ludwig Göransson.

Oppenheimer follows the story of J. Robert Oppenheimer, "the father of the atomic bomb"; the "Destroyer of Worlds"; the man who became "Death", during the events leading up to the end of America's fight with the Japanese during World War 2 and stars Cillian Murphy, Emily Blunt, Robert Downey Jr. And many others in this star-studded biopic.

At a run time of 3 hours and 9 seconds (Nolan's words, not mine) this film is full of intrigue, spectacle, tension and pure filmmaking brilliance. There's not a single character who did not feel important or integral to the film's plot, nor a single actor who felt out of place.

The common use of "time" in Nolan's films is used slightly differently compared to Nolan's previous work. Scenes are shown at different points in time simultaneously and are structured perfectly. It doesn't feel jarring, nor do you feel lost. It all blends together naturally and is paced out perfectly, which is what Tenet did suffer with at times. And I was a fan of Tenet, I still am as a matter of fact. But, with Tenet, I could easily see why some people would find that film overwhelming or jarring at times.

This movie also did away with the music above dialogue trait that Nolan's last few films have suffered with. The dialogue here actually felt important. Yes, this movie is LOUD (and there is a specific scene in this film that is EXTREMELY loud so be warned) but nothing felt drowned out.

This movie also hammers home the true devastation of nuclear weapons. Without going into spoilers, the American army and people see Oppenheimer as a hero towards the final act, but Oppenheimer is struggling to even comprehend what he has created and starts to see hallucinations and visions of the true devastation of the weapon he had manufactured. And it is horrifying, to say the very least. The use of this imagery was extremely unsettling - only Oppenheimer truly understood the impact he had on the world when creating the bomb and only he seemed to know just how awful it truly was. (Just in case, I will mark this review as containing spoilers. Just in case)

We also get a look into J. Robert Oppenheimer's and Lewis Strauss' strenuous relationship, which is a major theme throughout. By the end, again not spoiling anything, this film really hits home about the fact that nobody wins. Whether that's because of old feuds, or even in war. Especially when nuclear weapons of mass destruction are involved.

Oppenheimer is a beautiful piece of cinema in which I implore anyone and everyone who loves this industry to go and watch. We need more films like these and less cookie cutter MCU films and less remakes and sequels plaguing it.

Go support it and enjoy it.

Christopher Nolan, has once again, defied the film-making norm.

10/10.

10.title: A Resonant Cinematic Portrait: Oppenheimer (2023) Movie Review
10.content:
"Oppenheimer" (2023) is a visually captivating and thought-provoking cinematic exploration of the life and legacy of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the brilliant physicist whose pivotal role in the Manhattan Project forever changed the course of human history. Directed by Christopher Nolan the movie offers a fresh perspective on the complex character of Oppenheimer and the moral quandaries faced by those involved in the creation of the atomic bomb.

Cillian Murphy delivers a captivating performance as Oppenheimer, capturing the essence of a man torn between his scientific ambitions and the ethical implications of his work. The film does an excellent job of presenting the scientific challenges, the collaborative efforts of the era's brightest minds, and the tense political climate that surrounded the project. The recreation of the Manhattan Project's laboratories and the depiction of the rigorous scientific pursuits are both visually stunning and intellectually engaging.

What sets this movie apart is its focus on the human side of Oppenheimer. It delves into his internal struggles as he grapples with the profound impact of the atomic bomb on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The movie presents Oppenheimer as a figure whose brilliance was matched only by his moral weight, and the exploration of his efforts to promote arms control in the aftermath of the war adds a layer of depth to his character.

The film doesn't shy away from addressing the controversies and political conflicts that marked Oppenheimer's life during the Red Scare era. It highlights his clashes with government authorities and his association with politically charged individuals, painting a picture of a man whose intellect often put him at odds with the prevailing political climate.

In the end, "Oppenheimer" (2023) is a cinematic triumph that offers a resonant portrait of a brilliant mind grappling with the responsibilities and consequences of his groundbreaking work. It serves as a poignant reminder of the moral complexities that arise when scientific progress intersects with the realities of a world in turmoil. If you're interested in history, science, and the intricate moral fabric of the atomic age, "Oppenheimer" is a film that will leave a lasting impression.

10.title: The Man Who Dared Disturb the Universe: J. Robert Oppenheimer
10.content:
When I watched Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer, I never thought I would discover I had much in common with the "father of the atomic bomb" (apart from the fact that we had both studied at Cambridge). Our admiration T. S. Eliot and John Donne. As soon as I got home, I opened my poetry books and reread the lines mentioned in the movie, trying to understand how Oppenheimer was inspired by them. They all had a common theme: destruction & rebirth Let's take a look at Eliot's poem, Waste Land, which was published in 1921

April is the cruelest month, breeding Lilacs out of the dead land, mixing Memory and desire

April, which is the symbol of awakening and rebirth, is cruel because when the birds begin to sing and the fields begin to bloom, our narrator feels the darkness, death wish and fear more intensely. While he tells about death, destruction caused by war, loss of faith and hope, loneliness and barrenness with references to Dante, Shakespeare and mythological texts, he also gives signs of rebirth by making references to rain and the rooster that heralds the morning:

Only a cock stood on the rooftree.

Co co rico co co rico.

In a flash of lightning.

Then a damp gust.

Bringing rain.

Oppenheimer collects the particles of reality he finds in the middle of the wasteland and seeks ways to reassemble them differently, Maybe he was after a new and different state of being, like Eliot, like the cubist painter Picasso he admired.

Another poet who inspired him during the design and implementation of the Manhattan Project is John Donne. When General Leslie Grovers asks where the name "Trinity" comes from, Oppenhaimer replies in a letter to him: "There is a poem I love that John Donne wrote just before his death: Hymn to God, My God, in My Sickness. Invocation of My God)." This poem describes a man who is not afraid of death because he believes in rebirth... There is another poem: Batter my heart, three-person'd God'..."

Then he tells that Trinity got its name from this poem of John Donne's best known and most discussed. Trinity in Christian theology, the name given to the divine trinity consisting of the . In this poem quoted by Oppenheimer, the narrator begs the three-person'd God (Father, Son and Holy Spirit) to blow, bend, break him. Only if he is chained, he truly will be free, if he is burned and destroyed, he will be reborn.

Based on the assumption that rebirth is not possible without disintegration, destruction, burning, and extinction. And inspired by poets and painters, he "dares to disturb the universe",

10.title: Best movie in the history
10.content:
"Oppenheimer" is an awe-inspiring cinematic triumph that surpasses all expectations. Crafted with dedication, the decision to shoot entirely with IMAX cameras sets a new standard for visual excellence. Clocking in at a remarkable three hours, it boldly claims the title of the longest IMAX film ever, and rightfully so.

Christopher Nolan's directorial genius shines once more, elevating "Oppenheimer" above even his own acclaimed works like "Interstellar." This movie is undeniably a groundbreaking masterpiece in the history of cinema. It effortlessly weaves an enthralling narrative around the captivating true story it portrays.

The film's unique subject matter delves into the life and legacy of J. Robert Oppenheimer, whose contributions to history continue to reverberate to this day. Nolan's impeccable storytelling, coupled with a stellar ensemble cast, breathes life into the characters and transports the audience to a different era.

The breathtaking cinematography captures the grandeur of the Manhattan Project and the complexities of the human spirit. The use of IMAX technology elevates the visual experience to a whole new dimension, making "Oppenheimer" a visually mesmerizing spectacle.

The narrative's depth and emotional resonance leave a lasting impact on viewers, sparking contemplation and awe. As the story unfolds, you'll find yourself drawn into a world of passion, intellect, and moral dilemmas that grip your heart and mind.

With its seamless blend of historical accuracy and artistic vision, "Oppenheimer" becomes more than just a film; it becomes an immersive experience that stays with you long after the credits roll. Nolan's masterful direction and the cast's exceptional performances breathe life into the past, making history come alive on the silver screen.

In conclusion, "Oppenheimer" is a rare gem in modern cinema, an unforgettable journey into the depths of history and human ambition. Christopher Nolan's unparalleled storytelling, combined with the innovative use of IMAX, cements this film as a landmark achievement. For anyone seeking a captivating, thought-provoking, and visually astounding experience, "Oppenheimer" is an absolute must-see. Prepare to be enthralled and enlightened in equal measure as you witness this cinematic magnum opus that will undoubtedly be remembered for generations to come.

10.title: One of Nolan's Best Work
10.content:
I will regard this film as one of Nolan's finest cinematic achievements. This film seamlessly envelops the viewer in an atmosphere of palpable tension, mirroring the inner turmoil experienced by Oppenheimer himself as he grapples with the intricate dance between morality, politics, love, and war.

The film commences with a reference to Prometheus, the Greek deity who suffered exile for bestowing fire upon humanity, drawing a parallel to Oppenheimer and his bestowal of a similar power upon mankind.

Oppenheimer's magnetic presence effortlessly engrossed me in what felt like a fleeting three-hour masterpiece. A young scientist embarks on a harrowing journey, facing a multitude of trials-both metaphorical and achingly real-while bearing the weight of immense societal expectations and governmental pressures, all portrayed flawlessly by the talented Cillian Murphy. The raw humanity conveyed through Oppenheimer's courageous facade is truly captivating.

The film masterfully captures Oppenheimer's inner turmoil through decisive scenes and a meticulously crafted symphony of ambient sounds and music. Each moment adds to the mounting tension, leading inexorably towards the climactic moment of the detonation of the atomic bomb, as if the thrill of a mere countdown could be elongated into a two-hour cinematic experience. It was as though I too, were a part of this very first nuclear test.

While the creation and explosion of the bomb itself do not solely dominate the film's focus, they serve as a compelling backdrop against which Oppenheimer's adversaries maneuver in the shadows. These opponents, ranging from disagreeable figures to actively malicious forces, amplify the overarching narrative, providing an engrossing layer of intrigue and conflict.

10.title: Another Masterpiece of the Legend Christopher Nolan.
10.content:
"Oppenheimer" is a stunning film and easily one of the best of the century so far. Directed by the legendary Christopher Nolan, this movie excels in every aspect. The cinematography is breathtaking, capturing both the grandeur and the intimate moments with equal skill. The lighting is meticulously crafted, enhancing every scene's mood and tone.

The sound effects and film score are immersive, pulling you into the world of the characters and the tension of the storyline. The VFX and SFX are top-notch, seamlessly blending with the live-action elements to create a realistic and gripping experience. The CGI is impressive, used wisely to support the narrative without overshadowing the human drama.

Editing and color grading are handled with precision, ensuring a smooth flow and a visually cohesive film. Each actor delivers a remarkable performance, arguably the best of their careers, making every character memorable and impactful.

Christopher Nolan proves once again why he is considered one of the greatest directors of all time. His vision and execution are unparalleled, turning "Oppenheimer" into a true masterpiece. This is a film that demands to be seen, an experience you shouldn't miss. Watch it at any cost before you die - it's that extraordinary.

10.title: Christopher Nolan gets better and better with every new movie.
10.content:
There's always 3 sides to a story. In this case it will be, Oppenheimer's, then there is Christopher Nolan's version (based on the biography American Prometheus by Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin) and the truth. We hope and pray that what's shown is as close to the real story; magnified for cinema, but true to the events that happened.

Having said that, this is a brilliantly-made film and Christopher Nolan gets better and better with every new movie. Unlike the usual conventional biopics, he creates a wonderful layered examination of a man via all his great accomplishments and fundamental flaws.

Through a judicial committee interrogation, Oppenheimer is haunted by errors of his judgement, shown through flashbacks of pivotal moments in his life. We get a perspective of what his mind would've been processing through this harrowing period of his life where all his hard work could get mitigated by powerful government officials. Nolan manages to work his magic in the best possible way, striking a balance between showcasing the triumphant rise and tragic fall of an imperfect man.

The film presents Oppenheimer as neither a hero nor a villain, but a complicated man whose human qualities undermine what he will be remembered for. He can be viewed as a martyr and a scapegoat simultaneously, for the manner in which he managed to end the deadliest conflict in world history, while ushering in something even worse.

A career best performance from the consistently brilliant Cilian Murphy. He gives his all to the role of Robert J. Oppenheimer. And Robert Downey Jr shows that he hasn't forgotten acting post his 10 years' stint as Iron Man. This is one of his best roles. The rest of the cast, Matt Damon, Emily Blunt, Florence Pugh and Rami Malek, add significantly to the film's talent pool.

Having expressed his dislike about the use of Computer Generated Imagery, Nolan keeps viewers on their toes through good directorial proficiency. The creative use of editing keeps the story moving at a brisk pace, especially considering the movie's 3 hour run-time. The cinematography and soundtrack (mostly soundscapes) further create an unmatched cinematic experience.

10.title: The Best Biopic ever.
10.content:
It is a Nolan movie. It is a biopic. It is about the life of the most important man in the world at that time. His complexities, his flaws, his challenges and how he was treated. Those aspects cannot be changed by Nolan. It is based on a book. But Nolan takes the source material adds his flavor of intertwined timeline, epic visuals, brilliant dialogues (the best in any Nolan movie), mind-blowing sound and a fantastic screenplay.

Add to this the performance of a lifetime by Cillian. His eyes under the IMAX lens sucks us into the shoes of Oppenheimer. We feel the man. Intensely. Some of the scenes bring tears to the audience's eyes, but Cillian just stares into the camera and pierces our heart. He looks and feels like Oppenheimer. Even in the interviews promoting the movie, he still looks tired from the performance.

Robert Downey Jr shatters and breaks through his Iron man cage. You wont be reminded of his Marvel role at all. And that says a lot about the performance. His anger and ego comes out strongly as any other dramatic performance of the decade.

All the other cast also have given their best. Emily Blunt shines in the few scenes that give her the opportunity. Matt Damon is also striking and a relief for the audience. Rami Malek, many of the Nolan constants (NO, Micheal Caine is not there ehre) have all done complete justice. The performances take the movie a notch ahead.

The music is also brilliant and draws in the emotions from the visuals and fills our ears. Brilliant score, haunting where it has to be and epic elsewhere.

Cinematography is a new leaf for IMAX where the focus is not on huge sets pieces or scenery but on the performances of the cast.

Finally Nolan pulls of one of his most daring ventures. He challenges the audience to focus on every word and every visual, which is not easy for the people used to the short attention on their phones everyday. But it pays off. You get the experience of being in the World war era and in the shoes of the man who had to design to kill to save lives. And the fear and horror of Nuclear bombs is as relevant as it was then.

Watch with an open mind and 100% focus. You will be transported elsewhere. And it will take a while to return to your usual self. And that is how great movies leave the audience.

10.title: Spoiler free) Nolan's Masterpiece, it just wont be appreciated by all
10.content:
When the credits began to roll, I was speechless. An incredibly fast paced and stressful 3 hours flew by in what felt like an episode of television. I felt almost a sour taste in my mouth, and wanted to go curl up in a ball under my covers. My heart was still racing and mentally I was exhausted. A lot of my hope was gone. Still, my main thought was "unbelievable. I have just witnessed Nolan's masterpiece." Long has Nolan been a director I admire for his technical accuracy, complex topics, and what he reveals about humanity. This film was no different than his previous films in attention to soundtrack, visual affects, and filmography. Without the use of a big twist like in inception and the prestige, he still left a meaningful end impact.

Now, to address the title as to why it won't be appreciated. Like any semi-causal moviegoer, I instantly went to the reviews to see how others felt. Large criticisms were the dialogues were too complex, the trinity test too small, and overall a boring film. I chalk those reviews up to the type of people who watch a movie for only a dopamine release. I say that not in a pretentious way, but in a way as to why I thought this film beats the dark knight or other films. All I wanted to do after this film was debate and read more about this obviously flawed yet important man. The world I have lives in was challenged and I no longer felt as safe as before. This was marketed as a blockbuster must see, and while that is true that everyone should watch it for its obvious important matter, the satisfaction a moviegoer will derive is lessened if they are not ready to be confused and want to learn more after.

If you want an action movie, this is not for you. If you want a quick flick, I would definitely not recommend this. If you want to be challenged and stressed in ways that movies such as Inception, The prestige, Fight Club, Whiplash, and many more, then I couldn't recommend this movie more. I watched in UltraAVX and just bought weekend tickets for IMAX.

10.title: "Oppenheimer: A Haunting Glimpse into the Heart of Darkness"
10.content:
"Oppenheimer," Christopher Nolan's 2023 masterpiece, delves deep into the enigmatic world of J. Robert Oppenheimer and the creation of the atomic bomb, a pivotal moment that forever altered the fabric of history. As a historical drama with a haunting overlay of horror, the film navigates the complex moral and ethical dilemmas faced by those behind the Manhattan Project during World War II.

Nolan, known for his intricate storytelling and ambitious cinematic visions, embarks on a journey through the shadowy corridors of power, science, and human ambition. The film's slow burn start is a meticulously crafted preamble, setting the stage for the gripping narrative that unfolds, capturing the audience's attention as it accelerates towards the pivotal moment of the world's first nuclear explosion on July 16, 1945.

The portrayal of Oppenheimer and his cadre of brilliant scientists, led by Lt. Gen. Leslie Groves Jr., is nothing short of captivating. The cast's performances are profound, bringing depth and complexity to their historical counterparts. Their endeavor, culminating in the Trinity test, is presented not just as a scientific achievement but as a moment of profound existential reflection for humanity.

The film's pacing, which begins at a contemplative speed before catching momentum, mirrors the gradual realization of the consequences of their work. Nolan's direction ensures that the historical and personal ramifications of the Manhattan Project are felt with full force, making "Oppenheimer" not just a film about historical events but a profound commentary on the human condition.

The awards and accolades showered upon "Oppenheimer" are a testament to its impact, echoing the necessity of such a cinematic exploration. The Academy Award for Best Picture, among others, underscores the film's achievement in capturing a moment in history with both accuracy and emotional depth.

The narrative's extension into the post-war aftermath reveals the personal and societal struggles that follow groundbreaking scientific achievement. It touches on themes of integrity, the price of innovation, and the sometimes tragic fate of those who dare to lead progress.

"Oppenheimer" is more than a historical drama; it's a cautionary tale that resonates in the contemporary world. It serves as a reminder of the power of human intellect and the moral responsibilities that come with it. For fans of Christopher Nolan and cinema-goers intrigued by the complex interplay of science, history, and morality, "Oppenheimer" is an essential viewing experience. This film not only chronicles a monumental event but invites reflection on the impact of human achievements and the ethical considerations that should accompany them.

10.title: Maybe the best film of this decade so far
10.content: There are two words to describe Oppenheimer: cinematic masterpiece. None of the achievements of this film could be done without writer/director Christopher Nolan. The script is absolutely phenomenal. It's a dialogue heavy three-hour film, but the tension and master class writing created by Nolan keeps you on the edge of your seat the entire time. The score by Ludwig Goransson is fantastic, as it also helps build tension in almost every scene. The film jumps before, after, and during the testing of the atomic bomb, but it is surprisingly not too difficult to follow, and it is kept extremely interesting throughout. Another thing to note is the absence of CGI in the film, which is mind-blowing to think about after you've seen it. There are tons of shots showing close ups of the explosion, atoms, neutrons, etc., which you would think Nolan would use CGI for, but he doesn't, and all of these shots are visually stunning. It is just such an amazing accomplishment. Another key factor in this movie is the incredible acting from everyone involved. There are tons of A-list actors sprinkled throughout, some even just having one scene, and they all give great performances. One in particular is Tom Conti as Albert Einstein. Einstein is in a scene at the beginning, middle, and end, but the impact he has on the film is really memorable and impressive. Cillian Murphy as Oppenheimer just needs to win Best Actor. His performance summed up in one word is haunting. He haunts with his eyes, the way he delivers his lines, and the way he just stares. He really shows the audience how depressed and miserable Oppenheimer was particularly after Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Robert Downey Jr also shows how he isn't just Tony Stark, but an incredible actor with a wide range. Everyone involved absolutely deserves an award; the film is that great. Nolan's biopic Oppenheimer proves he is one of the great directors of all time.

10.title: All Timer
10.content:
Resounding applause for such a well crafted movie. This might be Christopher Nolan's best entry yet. Snappy, well thought and energetic, Oppenheimer never lets its foot off the gas. Cillian Murphy and Robert Downey Jr are absolute juggernauts. You feel each cut, each stare, each word said.

The stress expertly overwhelms the audience through insanely good edits and music. The sound design is exceptional. It just all feels so natural and earned. The tension is through the roof and you feel that with every nuance this film brings.

Cillian's looks and expressions are just perfect. This guy brings his A Game like never before, same for Robert. The security clearance bit is gripping and intense. It's pretty shocking to be honest. The drama is real and the tone is adequately overbearing and gloomy.

At the end of the film, you're just in awe. Truly a memorable experience and unforgettable achievement.

10.title: Nolan's Schindlers List
10.content: Take the artistry of Spielberg's Schindler's list and apply it to a psychological thriller about science and you have Oppenheimer. No doubt this will be to Nolan's pedigree what Schindler's list was to Spielberg's. It is a masterpiece of a film. The performances are perfect, the special effects all in camera (pls watch the bonus features!), they invented black and white IMAX film for this movie, and made an actual bomb to get the nuclear explosion right. The cinematography is breathtaking especially the black and white segments. The structure of the film is perfect for telling the story Nolan is aiming for (Nolan deserves more praise for film structure - consider Momento, Dunkirk, Inception, and Tenet). How can a movie about math and science be so intense? Chris Nolan, that is the answer.

10.title: EXCELLENT !
10.content:
The elements of our universe are truly miraculous. Tremendous insightful masterpiece.

Cillian is Outstanding, Excellent, Robert is exceptional, Emily is always good, and Matt is great no matter what role he plays.

Physicists and Scientists are remarkable in their intelligence, education, and understanding, in their pursuit to reveal the wonders of our world.

Human intelligence, given to us by God, is given as a gift, to allow us to discover the unfathomable depth of our World. Our human intelligence is given for our use.

When intelligence is used for understanding, wisdom and good, we have used it as it was intended. In the battle of good vs evil, sometimes it must be used so good prevails, and souls survive.

10.title: Historical Film Like None Other!!
10.content:
I will always remember the time that I went to see Oppenheimer. I look forward to looking back decades later and saying "I saw that in the cinema". I have heard many people say this about Star Wars etc, and never really got it until now.

Nolan has hit the peak of not only his craft but borrowed an element from every movie he has made up until this one and blended it perfectly into a gripping 3 hour magnum opus. I can only hope the success of this allows for other challenging but brilliant original IP being green lit. While there is a lot of uncertainty around strikes and the future of Cinema, this not only brought me to tears many times in its three hour runtime but gave me hope for the future of movies.

10.title: Ambitious Masterpiece well finished
10.content:
Always believe a great movie will leave the viewer a pounding heart after watching. The message or core value of the movie is conveyed through the story, music, scene, character themselves; gradual, hidden but so powerful which last almost forever.

The timing of the movie is quite crucial, we are at the intersection of world politics, and what a great reminder and time to pause to reevaluate our decisions.

I would not mention much more specific scenes. However, hope everyone would agree, each individual could feel the challenging, conflict and transition of the main character. And most importantly, the threat and disaster of the nuclear bomb.

10.title: The Untold
10.content:
The thing about Nolan is, his vast knowledge and wisdom about his projects is like a double-edged sword. It's a blessing and a curse and beyond comprehension for most people, therefore many can't truely connect with his work in some levels.

Needless to say different opinions should be respected but calling it 'boring' is something that i'd rather not discuss further.

Nolan has a great universal awareness and scientific vision that we need in motion picture industry to rise it to the occasion.

Now about Oppenheimer, we all know nothing is perfect, but the flaws makes it memorable. The story needed many more hours for political coverage and character development, so perhaps series would have been a better choice? But Nolan doesn't do series so thats that, and It's a movie people, not a documentry so we can take a step back.

For this review I focused on some issues that less people had talked about, everything else has been said by my fellow wiser reviewers. Good luck!

10.title: Nolan is the best filmaker alive
10.content:
It took me long enough to write this review, by now I've seen Oppenheimer 2 times at the cinema and I've come to the conclusion that Nolan is simply the best. He seems to be one of the few directors in history that keeps experimenting and tries to do something new for each of his movies and still keeps some sort of style in which you can recognise at any given time that you're watching a Nolan film. Very few directors get to actually get all the actors they'd like to have for their movies and Nolan gets to do it every time.

This time for Oppenheimer he takes a bit from each of his previous movies to construct this one. After not having a developed protagonist for his previous 2 films, he goes all out for this one as Cillian Murphy really becomes Oppenheimer and you get to experience with him his rise, fall, guilt, sadness and so many other emotions as he goes through his journey of becoming the most important man in the world. The cast is amazing, filled with great performances with Downey Jr and Damon as standouts. The music is great and gives so much impact to the important moments and makes them fill somehow epic, it helps build up tension and releases you when not needed.

Overall It is one of the most complete movies ever done by Nolan and it resonates with the international tension in the world today between Russia and USA. It is definitely the best film of the year so far, one of the best in the last decade or so and one of the most important films in the century.

10.title: Very difficult to make 3 hours of physics exciting, saw it 4 times
10.content: I think those who found this movie boring just do not understand how much went in to making this movie. It takes a lot for me to admit i could not have done it, even if true. The factual scenes were in black and white, the subjective ones in color. Oppenheimer saw beautiful abstract images of the universe until he realized what he had done and his visions become horrific. They had a techniques of keeping scenes short and dialog at a minimum. They would mention a character before he came on so you would understand the context. There is no way you could give me a character who was an elite nerd and do such an interesting job. Those who know nothing about him or the atomic era we live in or do not care, well do not go. For the rest of us it was just great acting, directing and writing too. There are movies I love and ones that are so good I am in awe.

10.title: Tense and haunting film
10.content: It's crazy how one of the most anticipated summer blockbuster films of this year is based on a historic figure...and it's directed by Christopher Nolan. I think this is the movie people been wanting for a while. Something not action-pack, not computer generated, not fun or silly quips, but something new or refreshing that us audiences haven't seen in a long time. Even with Nolan's style of filmmaking, this movie feels different from the rest of his work. It's basically a 3-hour movie about J. Robert Oppenheimer rises and fall of his fame as becoming the "father of the atomic bomb." It's mostly people talking throughout the movie, but the main focus is Oppenheimer which is more of a character study in his point of view and Lewis Strauss. The cast was fantastic, it was visually stunning, the music score is very tense like you were a part of that certain scene, the story was great as usual from Christoper Nolan. Sometimes the sound mixing can be loud between dialogues, but I can easily make it out what characters are saying. In the end, the movie will leave you in fear for what the future of a nuclear weapons will be and the consequences.

I could only expect an explosive genius as this to come from Christopher Nolan and not only his direction but having written the screenplay as well only personifies my love of his portfolio.

I would highly recommend watching this in the cinema as the bone rattling explosions can only be justified with surround sound. Failing that and you are watching this at home and you sense impending doom of what Oppenheimer created. Turn up your sound to the max! You won't regret it.

An eye-opening historical epic that not only takes the audience on a character driven journey into the psychology of America's very own Prometheus, but also an inquisitive commentary that places viewers in the witness stands, whilst Nolan expertly questions the morality, and ethics, of America's power driven politics.

With a keen eye for detail, delicate hands to guide, and a compassionate soul to lead, Christopher Nolan directs his latest gargantuan cinematic feat to perfection, immersing viewers in the mesmerizing beauty of auteur craftsmanship and the very art form itself, at every chance he gets.

There isn't a single moment throughout its three hour runtime, where you don't feel the insurmountable scale of what is happening before your very eyes. Every frame leaps from the screen, and burrows into your mind. Every sound ripples through your core. Every thunderous bellow of Ludwig's transcendent score sears itself into your soul. It's a marvellous achievement for the magical medium of cinema.

In this intricate three-hour tale, Christopher Nolan skillfully intertwines themes of inflated ego, fear, power, scientific breakthroughs, and moral dilemmas. It is, without any shadow of a doubt, Nolan's talkiest film to date, but don't let that worry you, because your attention will never wane. In fact, prepare to be entranced, for in "Oppenheimer," the mesmerizing allure of Cillian Murphy's chiseled jawline intertwines seamlessly with his Oscar-worthy portrayal of the enigmatic Oppenheimer. Yet, the film's spell extends far beyond Murphy's captivating presence. As the story unfolds, you'll find yourself drawn into a captivating exploration of the profound science of morality, a riveting journey bolstered by a stellar ensemble cast, led by the sensational Robert Downey Jr. The orchestration of emotions further intensified by a compelling score and unparalleled sound design. A feast for the eyes awaits with stunning cinematography, sweeping you into the grandiose portrait of a haunted man. And remarkably, these enthralling elements converge, granting you the privilege to savor an all-encompassing cinematic experience of epic proportions.

Immersed in the realm of cinematic brilliance, "Oppenheimer" achieves an enchanting fusion of narrative, visuals, and audio, akin to a symphony conducted to perfection. As the story unfolds, a kaleidoscope of sounds and images harmonize, gracefully transitioning through various tones and intensities, all the while gathering boundless momentum with every successive scene. The film's forceful and relentless crescendo propels the audience towards a climactic finale, leaving them captivated by the sheer artistry of this extraordinary cinematic experience.

Phew... Now all of that is out the way, I can finally leg my hair down, and just express my love and gratitude for particular aspects of the film. Benny Safdie is absolutely incredible, and I'm so happy he received a - slightly - bigger role than most of the other supporting cast members. I hope to see him in many more film's as he is yet to disappoint. Josh Hartnett is having his comeback moment, and I'm all here for it. He's sensational here and people aren't talking about him enough. RDJ turns in such a fine performance, I want a spin-off with him leading it. It's easily the best, most mature piece in his filmography. He demands your attention every second he's on screen, particularly when it's told from his POV. Hoyte Van Hoytema's cinematography is next level - but do we really expect to get anything less than an immersive masterclass with him at the lens. The sound design is unlike anything I've ever heard or FELT - like right up in my bum cheeks, rattling its way all the way uo my spine and out of my mouth. Now, my favourite aspect of the film, and perhaps my favourite score in a long long time. I was absolutely blow away, every single time it thundered in. There were moments where I felt like I had become one with the symphonies, momentarily closing my eyes just to live in that space. You don't just listen to this score, you feel it. Nolan is a king. What he, and his remarkable cast and crew has accomplished here, is truly something special.

My one and only qualm comes in the form of a nude, and absolutely stunning Florence Pugh, or rather, the two sex/nude scenes in which her character was involved. I felt they added nothing to the story, and were completely disconnected from the rest of the film. The first time was very jarring, and the second was more unnecessary than the first. To me it felt like it was the only way Nolan could notch this film up to a 15 rating, to attract an older audience. I understand Jean Tatlock played a pivotal part in Oppenheimer's life, I just wish she was incorporated into the story in a more natural way, that fitted with the rest of the film. However, this minor discrepancy can be forgiven, considering the many gleeming aspects outweigh the one.

10.title: Atomic movie making
10.content:
To begin with, Robert J Oppenheimer, the physicist who led the Manhattan Project, famously quoted the Bhagavad Gita after witnessing the first successful nuclear explosion at the Trinity test site in Los Alamos New Mexico. He said, "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds". Intentionally or unintentionally, he was just doing his karma, but the consequences were enormous as we have encountered in the past and possibly will in the future.

The movie is more about the political affairs of Oppenheimer. The science behind the nuclear fission is not covered in great detail, but moral dilemma experienced by him post invention and aftermath of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and his concern for the planet gives the moves a closure.

Murphy's acting is top notch. Nolan's direction is excellent, as always. This is Nolan's first biopic and he did the best work yet! It's a brilliant movie making, undoubtedly, especially given Nolan's top notch screenplay and direction, coupled with the IMAX cameras that give the viewer the best experience when watched on the biggest screen possible.

There are many references to quantum physics and a brief interaction of Oppenheimer with Einstein. A major part of the movie goes into the investigation of Oppenheimer's involvement in conspiracy to spy, and being a communist, which was more of a political will.

The basic idea and usage of powerful weapons like Brahmastra were mentioned in the Indian scriptures Ramayana and Mahabharatha, which gives the indication that the WMD might have been invented and used since antiquity. They might have already realized the power lying within each atom and used it for the good and seen it as the revelation of divine power then as opposed to the plutonium-239 and uranium-235 isotopes be used for evil purposes in this age.

Overall, it's a must watch for all science and movie buffs!

10.title: Nolan's best film?
10.content:
For me, this film cements Christopher Nolan's place among the greats of cinematic directors. Oppenheimer has built a heavy weight of expectation yet it grasps with both hands its opportunity to wow viewers.

As a big fan of all of Nolan's work previous work to varying degrees, I too was hopeful of being treated to a box office marvel and I leave the theatre feeling quenched of that thirst. As always I was impressed with the technical qualities of Nolan's work, his insistence on practical effects over CGI continues to deliver results too often lacking in films by his contemporaries.

The film was considered and showed admiral constraint in its use of shock and horror on a subject that could have otherwise delved into a macabre tale of gore seeking cheap engagement. Oppenheimer told a narrative of political drama as explosive as anything else on display which served as a fascinating allegory for the concept of mutually assured destruction. Set to the backdrop of an era of post-war anti-communism and McCarthyism, this piece tells a complex story of one of the most influential people in history and exhibits the internal conflicts within his life, attempting to explain his motivations and views.

The cast is stacked with talent, with notable cameos from a wide range of big names. I was thrilled to see Cillian Murphy cast as the leading man in a Hollywood blockbuster and he delivered a brilliant performance capable of exquisite expression and conflict. Robert Downey Jr provided a nice reminder to the world that he is capable of much more than Marvel and Matt Damon produced a solid outing as usual. Florence Pugh, in a more limited role than touted, graced the screen with her presence and I'd like to shout out Benny Safdie and Jason Clarke, both of whom I always thoroughly enjoy watching.

Minor criticisms include a feeling that at times the pacing lost some of the tension that Nolan was building too with shots perhaps cut too abruptly. I don't think some of the stylistic choices landed with much of an effect and at times the plot felt confusing. I always feel that 3 hour run times are superfluous, though I'm conflicted here as I also could have enjoyed another hour of the story which enjoyed an addictive quality.

For me, this film draws together the best of Nolans' precious works, particularly those more grounded in reality like Dunkirk and Memento, with the end result being one of the most complete films I've had the pleasure of watching.

10/10.

10.title: Christopher Nolan reaffirms his place among the very best of all time.
10.content:
Wednesday, July the 19th. Opening night in Paris. The audience exits the crowded room in dead silence, having witnessed yet another masterpiece from the director who doesn't require any introduction. While being so typically Nolan, Oppenheimer also separates itself from the rest of his filmography. No Tenet-like action sequences, no mind-bending elements, no confusing timeline. The movie unfolds slowly but surely, and the 3 hours go by without being felt. The final hour in particular, might just be the best I've witnessed in a long time.

As for the actors, the performances are as stellar as you could expect and probably have already heard. Cillian Murphy does an Oscar-worthy job at portraying a brilliant yet troubled Robert Oppenheimer, RDJ is (for the better) unrecognizable and delivers probably the most subtle and complex performance of his career. Emily Blunt oscillates between vulnerability and strengh masterfully, and the rest of the star-studded cast does an equally amazing job.

When it comes to the soundtrack, Ludwig Goransson's work is superb. Powerful at times, it can also be very subtle, almost fading into the background noises. But when it comes back at the front of the stage, it will give the viewer goosebumps and sink him into Oppenheimer's internal struggle.

Hindsight might be needed in order to properly judge this film, but it is my opinion right now that only The Prestige and Interstellar (maybe) surpass it in Nolan's work.

10.title: "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds"

"Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds"

Behind the battle of countries during World War II, there was a scientist who made history and ended the war. Unfortunately, he also created a weapon of mass destruction.

Robert Oppenheimer's story was unveiled thoroughly in this Christopher Nolan masterpiece. From how he got the idea to creating that idea and making history. Oppenheimer's success sadly was his tragedy as well. (SPOILERS AHEAD, well if they are) A series of hearings questioning his loyalty became his battle as he made his greatest invention. As a complicated yet a man of science, he made friends with fellow scientists. But his idea of this "ultimate weapon" also made him work with the military which was later used against him. His friends, colleagues soon turned against him. Notably, Lewis Strauss was the villain of his story, hiding in the shadows but already plotting on destroying not only his reputation but his life as a whole. Despite winning on having Oppenheimer lose his security clearance, Strauss still failed to secure the votes he needed to be a part of Eisenhower's cabinet. Thus, Oppenheimer is regarded as "Father of the Atomic Bomb."

The drama, the suspense, the thrill, the story, the science, the execution, everything in this movie is a masterpiece. Nolan knows what he's doing and he did it right. Cillian Murphy's performance as the great scientist was spot on. RDJ being the villain of this story was well executed as well and the whole ensemble cast was amazing in this film.

Shot in IMAX cameras, this movie is really BEST SEEN in IMAX theaters (but it won't be in 3D).

Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer is a 9.5/10 for me. Before or after watching the movie, do research for it to be understood more.

"It won't be for you. It will be for them." -Albert Einstein to J Robert Oppenheimer.

10.title: Life changing.

It's a very impactful visceral experience that makes you feel strong emotions of awe, concern and wonder. You think and feel about humanity throughout the film and it's difficult to stop thinking about these feelings after you leave the theater. The actors and story remind you what it means to be human, with people's everyday emotions and feelings like calm, hope, love, glamour, lust, sadness, empathy, jealousy, chaos and hatred. Yet you also feel the immense fragility of humanity due to our potential for barbarism, conspiracy and self-destruction at the level of the atomic bomb, while also feeling awe for our ingenuity, intelligence and glamour in our scientific and artistic pursuits in life. These contradictory feelings of the nature of human life are interwoven with each other and it makes you ponder how complex, beautiful, serious, grandiose, important and precious our lives are. The film is made all the more potent once you realize all of this, developing and using atomic bomb, and for the most part, happened, and this is who we are, and you are viewing, to some extent, reality, when you watch the bomb explode and observe the human circumstances arround it. Cillian Murphy does a great job as Dr. Oppenheimer, as do the others. I highly recommend seeing it in Imax to get a bigger screen and a louder Soundsystem to fully enjoy what I believe is a once in a lifetime achievement in cinematography, acting, soundtrack and sound editing.

10.title: Up there with The Dark Knight and Inception
10.content:
After watching this movie twice, it's safe to say this is a Nolan Masterpiece. There are a lot of reasons this movie works, the cinematography, the performances, the story, and last but not least the score. The shots in this movie are done so well the way they were able to capture weather in New Mexico and Britain, the way they were able to show the mind of Oppenheimer, and the way they were able to show us the two sides of this story was nothing short of amazing.

The performances were some career best. Cillian Murphy will no doubt receive a nomination for best actor and RDJ definitely deserves one for probably another career best. This movie flaunts it's dedication to characters by having hollywood heavyweights like Oldman, Affleck, Malek, and Branagh in such minor roles, but they nail the role so well that you don't even really acknowledge (especially with Oldman) that is that actor as you instantly get immersed in that characters role in this dynamic. Damon, Safdie, Dehaan, Hartnett, Conti, Peck, Bostick, Quaid, Pugh, Blunt, the list goes on of the characters who are sort of on the sideline throughout the story and although their roles are all minor as well they all blend in so well you feel a sort of realism to how these scientists really were and how this project really went. Krumholtz and Clarke were both stand out side characters along with Emily Blunt as characters who had a lot of great moments while Safdie stole a lot of moments at los-alamos. Conti as Einstein was also a really good casting. Honestly I could go on about how amazing the performances were so you're just gonna have to see it yourself to believe it.

The story is told in a very unconventional way but it works so well and they picked a very interesting way to tell several stories at once. By using the trial we are able to see the entire professional career of Oppenheimer while focusing on the Manhattan project and the fallout because of it which lead to the trial. Then it shows Strauss's view and his motives, but while it shows that and goes back to what the truth was we see the contradictions. Then it is unfolded as we see the truth of the trial and the small moments and instances that lead to this trial. If I get to into it I'd spoil it and as with most Nolan movies the timeline is hard to explain you have to watch it to see how good it is. Also the ending to this movie is the most profound ending I have ever seen in a movie it leaves you thinking and in a good way it's not all horror like some suggest it is. It is by far the best ending scene in a movie which says a lot because many movies best moments are the ending scene.

The score is the best since inception maybe even better it's insane. I have very few songs from a movie that I have listened to more than destroyer of worlds from this movie. This score hits every scene perfectly it brings the moments of tension to a whole new level of anxiety and intrigue. The triumphant moments are that much more triumphant, the ending is done masterfully. I can not say enough good about this movie's music.

What's wrong with this movie, well it has a few issues that are worth noting, mostly just unnecessary scenes, the sex scenes with Pugh are done for accuracy and for its importance to the trial, but there was no reason for them, we didn't see him bone Kitty or Ruthy, it was sort of just a scene to have. I don't even think they were bad the scenes were done tastefully, but unnecessarily. I also thought that some of his montages earlier in the movie were a little bit messy for pretty much no reason other than just to be there.

Overall this movie is the best Nolan has put out in 10+ years maybe ever 9.7/10.
