10.title: The Best Movie of 2023! Period!
10.content:
This film was my most anticipated film of the Summer, if not the year; and the film certainly did not disappoint! Christopher Nolan delivers the best movie of his career, without a doubt! It's a cinematic masterpiece, and I will be surprised if this movie DOESN'T win the Oscar for Best Picture of the year. It deserves that title. It's certainly is the best film I've seen this year, and takes the top spot on my list!

The film delivers a stunning, staggering, and sometimes scary look at the life of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the "father of the atomic bomb." The movie is based on the biography of Oppenheimer called 'American Prometheus' by Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin (which I read in a week last month to prepare for the film). Oppenheimer is portrayed by Cillian Murphy, whose performance is so riveting and nuanced and haunting that the 3 hour runtime of the film became an afterthought. His performance as the famous theoretical physicist who birthed the world's first nuclear weapons is haunting, so nuanced, and brilliant that I couldn't take my eyes off him the entire time he was on the screen! Murphy ought to make room on his shelf for the many awards that should be coming his way due to this incredible performance!

The other standout performances amongst this massive ensemble star filled cast is Robert Downey Jr as Lewis Strauss, a former political ally turned bitter rival of Oppenheimer. Downey commands the screen in a performance that allows him to stretch his legs and really gives him the respect he deserves as one of the best in the business, and he should receive a Best Supporting Actor nomination or award for his performance. Other superb performances in this are the the ladies in Oppenheimer's life, played by Emily Blunt and Florence Pugh!

The movie starts with the hammer down and doesn't let up, and will keep you on the edge of your seat till the very very last haunting shot, in which Oppenheimer contemplates the potential future world ending way his creation may be used to bring an end to human civilization.

The film, though 3 hours long (believe me, it doesn't feel like a 3 hour long film) is a masterpiece, and it could almost be broken down into 3 acts: Oppenheimer's origin story (where he almost sees things on a molecular level with molecules and atoms smashing and moving together, almost like a superhero), the second act begins with the start of the Manhattan Project, which begins an edge of your seat portion of the movie, depicting the scientist's race to beat the Nazis in the development of the atomic bomb (a race at the time during WWII Germany had an 18 month head start on the development of atomic weapons; act 3 begins after the successful Trinity Test (which is done with absolutely no CGI whatsoever). The 3rd act of the movie becomes a very tense and gripping courtroom drama as well as a bit of a psychological horror piece, as Oppenheimer and a few of the fellow scientists begin to contemplate the massive horror they've unleashed on the world. Christopher Nolan blends the 3 acts in the movie together in such a masterful way that those 3 hours go by pretty quickly.

The subject matter is of course pretty dark, but you can't take your eyes off of the spectacle and the epic story of a man whose innovation allowed us to save human civilization, but also haunted him for the rest of his life, and the phenomenal performances by all of the actors involved.

Some people may need a refresher on WWII and Cold War history before watching this film, but any cinephile and movie lover like myself should be more than happy to lose themselves in this film.

Chris Nolan masterfully weaves narratives from different time periods while exploring the character depths of a man whose actions altered the world's history and trajectory forever, for better or worse. Nolan brings us right into the mind and the complex psyche of Oppenheimer himself, and all the moral conflicts within him.

Every single thing in the movie is flawless, including the score and music by Ludwig Göransson. It truly deserves to be seen on the biggest screen possible. It's an unforgettable movie and my favorite film of the year! It's the best movie of 2023. Period!

10.title: The Production Is As Great As Its Subject is Massive
10.content:
Orlando Gardner says "...The screenplay is dense and layered (I'd say it was a thick as a Bible)...".

This is true. This is because every historically significant figure in the development of this weapon is in this film with a speaking role. From Seth Henry Neddermeyer who conceived chemical explosives driven implosion (yet utterly failed in the achievement of his own original idea), to George Bogdanovich Kistiakowsky, the Harvard educated hydrodynamicist (who like so much of this puzzle was intimately known by Oppenheimer). And when Neddermeyer failed, Kistiakowsky was stepping on to the train platform in Santa Fe, NM, ready to be told by Oppenheimer where to go to work.

The strength of this production is in three parts. First the Producer, Director, and the author of the screenplay) Christopher Nolan), took the 2005 biography "American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer (written by Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin over a period of 25 years). And which won numerous awards, including the 2006 Pulitzer Prize for Biography or Autobiography. And they decided the biography should not be edited first and then turned into a screenplay.

Second, they let the story (in the biography) flow into the screenplay and create a motion that a motion picture (all agree) does need.

Third, actors of sufficient gravitas are chosen for their roles large and small, for their talent to be their characters, and fully inhabit their roles. Just think of Sir Kenneth Charles Branagh (as Niels Henrik David Bohr, Danish physicist) of London's Royal Academy of Dramatic Art.

Robert Oppenheimer, the brilliant but troubled scientist who was instrumental in developing the atomic bomb. The story digs into the complicated mix of his scientific breakthroughs, personal battles, and the heavy ethical questions he had to grapple with.

The cinematography is stunning, with each shot carefully crafted to enhance the emotional depth and historical accuracy of the story. The use of lighting and color really pulls the audience into Oppenheimer's world. The set design and world-building do a great job of placing viewers in that era, with authentic recreations of historical settings that enrich the film's narrative. The costume design also fits the period perfectly, helping tell the story without stealing focus from the characters' emotional arcs.

Lighting creatively sets the mood and adds to the atmosphere, making the storytelling even more engaging. The soundtrack blends well to elevate the emotional impact of key scenes, making them stick with you. The lead's acting really adds layers to the characters, making their struggles and victories hit home for the audience.

Christopher Nolan's direction shines, skillfully balancing the intellectual and emotional aspects to create a gripping narrative. The practical effects are integrated so well that they add to the realism seamlessly. The sound design adds to the film's atmosphere, even if it doesn't stand out as much as some other elements.

Though the film takes some artistic liberties, it respects the historical context, capturing the essence of the period and key figures accurately. The plot is engaging and thoughtfully crafted, featuring rich character development and a strong arc that keeps viewers hooked. 10.title: Excellent movie!! Worth the hype
10.content:
The life and times of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the brilliant physicist and central figure of the Manhattan Project, have always fascinated me. Needless to say, the movie surpassed all my expectations and left me absolutely awe-struck.

The casting was impeccable, and the performances were nothing short of extraordinary. The lead actor portrayed Oppenheimer with such depth and authenticity that I felt emotionally connected to the character throughout the film. The supporting cast also delivered stellar performances, bringing to life the complex web of relationships that shaped Oppenheimer's journey.

The visuals were simply breathtaking, and the attention to detail in recreating the historical settings was commendable. From the vast landscapes of Los Alamos to the intense laboratories where groundbreaking scientific discoveries were made, the movie's visual representation was captivating.

The story was masterfully woven, taking us on a rollercoaster of emotions as we witnessed Oppenheimer's struggles, triumphs, and personal conflicts. The film delved into the moral dilemmas faced by scientists during World War II, raising thought-provoking questions about the ethics of scientific advancement during times of conflict.

However, I do have one minor critique. As the movie approached its climax, I expected to see the portrayal of the Hiroshima bombing and its aftermath. Given the immense impact of this event on Oppenheimer and the world, I felt its omission was a missed opportunity to provide a more comprehensive view of the consequences of his work. Nevertheless, I understand that storytelling decisions are often complex, and the focus of the film may have been on exploring Oppenheimer's character rather than the historical events in their entirety.

In conclusion, "Oppenheimer" is a cinematic masterpiece that expertly weaves together the brilliance of science and the intricacies of human nature. It is a gripping tale that delves deep into the mind of a scientific genius while challenging the audience's perceptions of war and its consequences. Despite the absence of the Hiroshima bombing scene, the movie's overall brilliance overshadows this minor flaw. I highly recommend "Oppenheimer" to anyone who appreciates exceptional storytelling and outstanding performances. This movie will leave you with a newfound appreciation for the complexities of the human spirit and the weight of scientific discovery.

10.title: Naive Wonders Bloom Into Dark Understanding
10.content:
I didn't view many films from 2023, but of the few I did see, I'm glad that "Oppenheimer" was one of them. With a three- hour run-time, "Oppenheimer" boasts the slow build (or slow death, whichever is pithier) of a dying star, with all the implosion of such a gravitational collapse.

The First and Second Act

The first act of "Oppenheimer" uses it's long run-time in order to give us time to get familiar with the titular character and the many interconnected characters that make several appearances throughout his grandiose life. This can be overwrought in some films, but it is necessary in this film due to the great entanglement of the characters and pivotal changes in alignment and associations between each other throughout their lives. In the second act, the film revolves around the force of history that is the atomic bomb. The main character Oppie, shifts from a wide-eyed young scientist envisioning the wonders of what science can accumulate into, to life-worn man with a pure focus on doing whatever it takes to get the job done; his job of course being to develop a weapon that forever altered the world as it was known into something unimaginable.

The Final Act

The third and final act is where our bright-eyed scientist develops into the soldier returning home from war. Although he didn't see the battlefield of the world wars as an actual soldier, the gravity of his weapon now weighs on him in the fully hellish nature of war. Oppie is setup to have to endure a kangaroo court, that ends up being nothing more than a witch trial. Like a witch, Oppie must bear the cross of not only his own sins, but also society's as they lay the burden of their own sins onto him as well. This darkly beautiful form of martyrdom allows us to see a very human side of the "father of the atom bomb." In the finale we also get an imagining of the collision of the two great minds of Oppenheimer and Einstein and what their final conversation may have been like. Just like the beauty of a dying star, we see two gifted minds who accomplished some of the greatest heights of man, and get a glimpse to the burden they must have felt in holding the brilliance to truly see the darkest abyss of what man is capable of.

The Silver Lining in the Conclusion

Out of the flaws and triumphs of Oppenheimer, we get a film that paints the messiness of humanity and the mixed capability of good and bad in all of us. Out of the same power that sought to end all wars came the power that may be the perpetual war to humanity's demise. As Oppenheimer and Einstein walk away from their last conversation speechless, seemingly staring into our despair over the loss of our humanity to powers greater than us, we can also see the wonder that lead to great minds such as these in their tenacity to dare to wonder for the very creations that had conquered such demise before. So will we learn from the dark truths in the historic lessons that the atomic and hydrogen bombs or fall into the dark end that Oppenheimer and Einstein saw at the end? Only time will tell...

10.title: THE RAIN DROP WHAT HITS THE PUDDLE HARD: CONFLICTS OF THE GREAT AMERICAN PROMETHEUS
10.content:
"Now I have Become Death, the Destroyer of the Worlds"

The calm view of a tiny drop of rain water hitting a puddle and producing large waves of various wavelengths and the frightening view of a tiny atomic bomb, falling towards mother earth and wreaking havoc, producing astounding shock waves! Both are the inevitable forces of nature and attract the attention of a scientific mind. And amidst the extra-ordinary analogy of these two spectacular powers of nature, master filmmaker Christopher Nolan tries to explore the differences. The falling rain drop hits the puddle hard but doesn't cause any harm to any living beings; it's fundamental. Whereas, the nuclear forces extracted out of a splitting atom on purpose is a force of nature summoned by the Man. And who will take the responsibility and it's inevitable consequences?

"Oppenheimer" is a horror story told in the truest and most delicate form of humanism. It can also be viewed as the character study of a complex Physicist and his inner conflicts juxtaposed by how the top persons in power look at them with wrong perspective. Was very fortunate to see first day first show of this masterpiece.

There are four detonation sequences in the film literally and allegorically. First one was the celebrated Trinity Test of July 16, 1945 in Los Alamos. In order to know, what are the rest of the three, you have to experience this film. As as per as visual depiction is concerned, these are NOT the portrayal of bombing events of Hiroshima and Nagasaki which were ofcourse, the inevitable inhuman consequence of the "detonation". It's deeply philosophical, emotional and concerning; the sensibility what Nolan has mastered over the years. It will chill down your spine.

For cine-lovers, the cross cutting of the scenes and their juxtapositions with picture perfect background score by Ludwig Göransson takes the emotion, tension and further characterisation to a new height. The bombing scene, the use of flash and fire, the words (of consciousness, "I am the death, the destroyer of the world" in the real Oppenheimer's voice) and the sound and shock are something what you have never experienced before. The performances are amazing and no words are sufficient to describe Cilian Murphy (his eyes), Robert Downey Jr and Emily Blunt. Performance of the later one is highly underrated (as I am seeing the reviews) but she did a tremendous job as a person witnessing the nasty politics as an independent individual. The lesser screen time doesn't make the performance no way thinner or lesser.

Rest, there are many great films on Science Fiction but this one can be depicted as a great work on "Scientific Consciousness" , the consciousness what in spite of all the accomplishment tell us to introspect our choice and fate. It will be celebrated in years to come.

10.title: The Best Movie of 2023
10.content: While I was very excited for this movie, I was cautious due to how inconsistent Christopher Nolan has been in the past few years. This movie absolutely blew me away. Seeing this in IMAX was maybe the best theater experience I've ever had, it's up there with Top Gun Maverick. The film keeps and incredibly brisk pace for all three hours of its runtime, which is impressive given how even some of Nolan's recent movies like Tenet or The Dark Knight Rises have dragged at some points. On a technical level, Oppenheimer is perfect. The score, the cinematography, the effects, all look fantastic. Particularly in the first and third hours, when the movie is a barrage of sights and sounds that blend together perfectly. A lot of people complained about the third act of this movie when it came out, and to that I say rewatch the movie. On rewatch the final hour is the most gripping of the whole movie, and the ending hits even harder. 2023 has been a fantastic year for cinema after a decade of tired blockbusters, and movies like Oppenheimer, Barbie, Across the Spider Verse, The Iron Claw, and Killers of the Flower Moon show that people will watch interesting, original movies. Even if 2024 has half as many great movies, it'll be a step above what we've been getting for the past few years.

10.title: A challenging and rewarding epic masterpiece
10.content:
The conflicted story of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the theoretical physicist and director of the Manhattan Project and his development of a potent atomic weapon that could end the course of World War II is told on such an epic manner as it should be told and wasn't before. It's a story that needed to be told and it was done in a most captivating and gripping manner that a film of this magnitude will take a long time to come. Like an atomic bomb, it was a shattering and memorable event that it'll change the world of cinema for ages to come.

Played by an impecable Cillian Murphy, the core of "Oppenheimer" is divided in two fronts: his rise as a physics master all the way until he gets selected by General Leslie Groves (Matt Damon) to head the project to created the atomic bomb where he gathered the most prominent group of minds and scientists to elabore the perfect project with the intention of putting an end to World War II, or if possible, to create such a devastating weapon that could end all wars; and on the second front we have Lewis Strauss (Robert Downey Jr.), chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission, an early ally of Oppenheimer who becomes a ruthless nemesis in the shadow of everything years after the war when Oppenheimer concentrated his efforts to stop the arms race between USSR and USA or prevent the development of more nuclear weapons.

Beyond the scope of Oppenheimer's rise and fall and the whole challenge about the development of the atomic bomb, which was surrounded with secrecy and suspicion from everywhere - let us consider that the man had a brief favoritism to Comunisim and joining the party's meetings - the film deeply analyses the man behind it all, a brilliant mind in a restless quest for learning and applying such learning to test the possibilities and probabilities of creating a breakthrough in the world of physics that he couldn't see it exactly the extension of his creation and how it could affect the whole world, a game-changer weapon that could exterminate human existence on Earth.

When director/writer Christopher Nolan mentioned that Oppenheimer was the greatest figure of the 20th century (and bear in mind I just read that exact description without seeing the reasoning behind) I thought it was an exaggeration. Given some thoughts and after seeing the movie you truly understand why Nolan said that. Not just a century that could be divided in two eras but also the designs of mankind and the fate of men, with the world being divided before and after Oppenheimer. If progress mostly seemed to evolve and prolong our lives for the better, and our planet was thought of being everlasting in the world pre-Oppenheimer and his creation, the future wasn't so bright and a single man could create something that could destroy the world and all lives, literally.

Nolan doesn't take this particular issue lightly, and that final shot of a nearly teared-eye Oppenheimer is incredibly frightening and scares audiences even though it was an event from a distant past. It echoes in our present, and it will echo in the future too. There, he realises the breaking point, with no return.

The terror of knowing that he'd become the destroyer of worlds, the feeling, the pain and agony.

The biggest question mark for audiences comes in trying to figure out the director's real aim: is Oppenheimer a tragic hero or a villain, the actual face of death?

Is Nolan seeking some redemption for the man who never felt sorry for his actions but tried to warn the world about the dangers of uncontrolled use of atomic weapons and how they would affect our lives? Or the idea is merely to show how significant one man could be not in just defining the end of a war but also in defining Cold War strategies, that somewhat persist today? And if the man wasn't discussed enough on media or films before, thanks to this movie he'll be part of discussions a lot more.

A pretty provoking challenge on viewers since the man was a puzzling creature.

It's new but it's not all that new. It had been done before in countless TV movies and miniseries, and the only Hollywood reference "Fat Man and Little Boy" was a failure and ever since the theme hasn't been brought to the big screen. And only a master like Nolan could pull it off in great detail, fashion, a great sense of accuracy (with plenty of dramatic licences, obviously). Immensily absorbing through its 3 hours (those complaining about it know nothing, not a single moment was wasted or was unnecessary), this was one of the most thrilling and most pulsating experiences of all time.

Cast and crew were a spectacle to be witnessed: a knockout performance by Cillian Murphy, with perfect mannerisms and finally a lead on a Nolan movie. It was about time, a well-deserved chance role. Robert Downey Jr. Steals the show and it's his best performance in ages. With a perfect combination of elements - cinematography, editing, music (Ludwig Goransson's non-stop score might be a matter of controversy to some; I loved it), sound (yes, THE explosion, the audience simply lost its breath), everything's is carefully planned, mindblowing and jawdropping. It was worth all the long wait for it! 10/10.

10.title: Nolan's greatest achievement
10.content: I saw 'Oppenheimer' on a huge screen in 70mm when it was released (I think IMAX is great, but I've had issues with how incredibly LOUD films presented in IMAX cinemas can be) and I just watched it for the second time after it won seven Academy Awards. Honestly I can't even begin to describe what an overwhelming cinematic experience this film is. All of the awards are completely deserved. There are very few three hour historical/biopic/war movies that move at such a relentless pace, filled with so many great performances, edited with such precision, shot with so much skill and filled with so many astonishing sights and sounds. Nolan was already at a very high level of filmmaking excellence, but with 'Oppenheimer' he leaps into the class of directors like David Lean, Kubrick and Kurosawa. I think anyone interested in science, history and (obviously) great cinema should see it at least once. People studying how to write and direct and shoot a great film are definitely going to see it many, many times. And actors will be watching the incredible performances of the gigantic cast for a long time, with special attention for Robert Downey Jr., Matt Damon and of course Cillian Murphy. A genuine masterpiece.

10.title: A Masterpiece in Biographical Filmmaking, Yet Yearning for Deeper Exploration
10.content:
"Oppenheimer" stands as a monumental biographical movie that captures the life and legacy of one of the most complex and significant figures in history. While it unquestionably shines as a cinematic achievement, your sentiment that you wanted more suggests a yearning for an even deeper exploration of the subject matter.

The film delves into the life of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the brilliant scientist who played a pivotal role in the development of the atomic bomb during World War II. The portrayal of his genius, his moral dilemmas, and the profound impact of his work on humanity is likely both mesmerizing and thought-provoking. The meticulous attention to detail, historical accuracy, and the portrayal of the era are all testament to the dedication of the filmmakers and the actors involved.

However, your desire for the movie to offer more might stem from a few different factors. Biographical films often face the challenge of condensing a person's life into a limited runtime, which can sometimes lead to the omission of certain aspects or events. As viewers, we might yearn for a deeper dive into the psychological complexities of the character, a more thorough exploration of the historical context, or a deeper understanding of the person's motivations and inner struggles.

"Oppenheimer" seems to have struck a chord by presenting the larger-than-life story of a fascinating individual. Yet, it's not uncommon for biographical films to leave viewers wanting more, especially when the subject's life is rich and multifaceted. This could be an indication of the film's ability to pique your interest and spark your curiosity about J. Robert Oppenheimer's life and the broader historical context in which he operated.

In the world of biographical filmmaking, balancing storytelling, historical accuracy, and the complexity of a person's life is a delicate art. It's possible that the movie's impact on you might lead you to explore further, whether through reading biographies, researching historical accounts, or engaging in discussions about the subject.

In conclusion, "Oppenheimer" appears to have succeeded in crafting a biographical movie that captures the essence of its subject and the historical significance of his contributions. My desire for more depth signifies the film's ability to engage and stimulate my curiosity. While the movie might not provide every detail I was hoping for, it could serve as a steppingstone for deeper exploration and understanding of the remarkable individual and the era in which he lived.

"When I came to you with those calculations, we thought we might start a chain reaction that might destroy the entire world."

"What of it?" Einstein replies.

10.title: I got out of the theater sweating and literally speechless...
10.content:
The film begins with a quote about Prometheus, the figure from Greek mythology who stole fire from the gods to give it to mankind. This analogy is used in the book "American Prometheus" by Martin Jay Sherwin to refer to Jay Robert Oppenheimer, considered the father of the atomic bomb. The book investigates and narrates the creation of the Manhattan Project, which led to the development of the atomic bomb.

Nolan, intrigued for quite some time by subjects such as astronomy, physics, nuclear energy, and war, found in Oppenheimer's life the perfect moment to narrate how this man gave humanity the capacity for self-destruction.

The plot takes us to the time of World War II, where new scientific discoveries, particularly Albert Einstein's findings on quantum physics, led to the creation of the atomic bomb under Oppenheimer's leadership. The movie delves into Oppenheimer's life, from his transformation from an ordinary man to the creator of the bomb, to how he dealt with the consequences of his actions. Kilian Murphy, in a standout role, convincingly and humanely personifies the different moments of Oppenheimer's life.

The film showcases how Oppenheimer had the support of other scientists in his project, giving science a prominent role in the narrative. Unlike Nolan's previous films, "Oppenheimer" focuses more on dialogue and music rather than grandiose settings and action sequences.

The plot explains the creation of the atomic bomb but also delves into the reasons behind its development and the motivations of its creators. The movie avoids focusing on destruction and battle; instead, it concentrates on the characters' emotions and how they face the consequences of their actions.

Cillian Murphy, Robert Downey Jr. And Emily Blunt deserve at least an Oscar nomination for their performances in the film,

The Soundtrack also was gorgeous, Ludwig Göransson really understood the assignment, doing one of the best scores in his career. I think this one complements the film on the best way possible.

Nolan displays his cinematographic prowess in the narrative, immersing the audience in an engaging experience. The use of CGI and visual effects is done elegantly, creating surreal and spiritual moments. Throughout the film, it becomes evident how Nolan has evolved as a director, prioritizing artistic freedom over commercial expectations.

10.title: ummm
10.content:
The film suffered from a lack of engaging dialogue and the quality of the dialogue that was present left much to be desired. Additionally, the excessive use of rapid cuts and an overpowering score detracted from the overall experience. The constant background music seemed unnecessary, especially for a drama centered around a physicist. The film would have benefited from allowing the actors and the set design to convey the story more naturally, without relying heavily on a dramatic score more suited to an action movie like Batman.

Personally, I found the film to be mediocre. It had the potential to be outstanding, but perhaps a different director and writer could have better realized that potential. While I usually appreciate Christopher Nolan's work, a dialogue-driven drama doesn't seem to play to his strengths. In my opinion, he's not particularly adept at writing dialogue. It's unfortunate to see good actors constrained by the film's rapid editing style.

Overall, the film feels like it's a drama tailored for audiences who prefer fast-paced, 90-minute action movies and typically avoid the drama genre.

10.title: I loved it
10.content:
Nolan's direction is meticulous, balancing a non-linear narrative that weaves between Oppenheimer's early academic pursuits and the intense pressures of the Manhattan Project. The film takes its time to explore Oppenheimer's relationships, particularly with fellow scientists, his wife Katherine (played by Emily Blunt), and his mentor, physicist Ernest Lawrence (Josh Hartnett). These relationships add layers to the story, showcasing the personal sacrifices and moral dilemmas faced by those involved in the creation of the atomic bomb.

The supporting cast is equally impressive. Blunt delivers a poignant performance as Katherine, embodying the struggles of a woman caught in the whirlwind of her husband's genius and the societal expectations of the time. Matt Damon shines as Leslie Groves, the military leader of the Manhattan Project, whose pragmatic approach contrasts sharply with Oppenheimer's philosophical musings. Robert Downey Jr. Also stands out as Lewis Strauss, a key figure in the political landscape of the time, whose interactions with Oppenheimer add tension and complexity to the narrative.

Visually, the movie is a stunning achievement. The cinematography, captures both the grandeur of scientific achievement and the intimate moments of personal conflict. The film's use of light and shadow creates a haunting atmosphere that reflects the duality of Oppenheimer's work-its potential for both creation and destruction. The sequences depicting the Trinity Test are particularly breathtaking, blending practical effects with CGI to create a visceral experience that leaves a lasting impression.

10.title: Nolan at his best
10.content:
"Oppenheimer" is more than a biopic about the father of the Atomic bomb. It's a film about the nature of fission, but in an even larger sense than the splitting of an atom and the collision of subatomic particles. It's about the splitting of a man's soul.

It's also about the collision of science and morality, of quantum physics and politics, of ambition and hubris, and of love and responsibility.

In riveting imagery and sound, director Christopher Nolan steers us through the complex story of Robert Oppenheimer's creation of the weaponry that moved civilization to a dangerous new precipice. Nolan employs all his skills to make us see and feel what he imagines Oppenheimer experienced while moving us to the precipice.

"I am become death, the destroyer of worlds," Oppenheimer says, quoting a sacred Hindu text, after his bombs obliterated Hiroshima and Nagasaki to end World War II.

This is the "triumph" of Oppenheimer's genius. It's also the "tragedy" of it.

Nolan based his film on the book "American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer," the Pulitzer Prize winning work of Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin. The movie opens with a title card explaining how in Greek mythology "Prometheus stole fire from the Gods. For this, he was chained to a rock and tortured for eternity."

Nolan shows us how Oppenheimer suffered chained to his own rock.

"I have blood on my hands," Oppenheimer said when he met an unsympathetic Harry Truman after the bombs were dropped. The president mockingly handed Oppenheimer a handkerchief to wipe his hands and then told his secretary of state he didn't want to see that "crybaby" scientist back in his office again.

Nolan's screenplay is crisp and taut but muscular enough to carry the weight of the film's heavy themes, from the basic scientific challenges to the equally complex moral ones. There are portions of the storytelling, the parts told in breakneck dialogue, that bring to mind Oliver Stone's JFK, but they don't make your head hurt the same way. Nolan does a masterful job simplifying the complexities without dumbing them down. There's also some subtle foreshadowing that will take most of us a couple viewings to fully appreciate, including a poisoned apple scene that beautifully sets the table for the moral challenge Oppenheimer faces after creating the bomb.

Nolan uses creative sound effects and an arresting musical score to connect us more viscerally to the emotions percolating at almost every turn of Oppenheimer's journey, with tense string music and dramatic percussion amping up the senses and mood. He uses all those tools he perfected in Interstellar and his Batman movies to make this true story more compelling. He uses sound, like stomping bleachers and shaking walls, to help move us inside Oppenheimer's head.

Cillian Murphy is terrific channeling Oppenheimer's onfidence, as well as his naievete, insecurity and regret. He looks so much like Oppenheimer. It feels like an Oscar winning performance. Emily Blunt is equally terrific as Oppenheimer's wife. Robert Downey Jr. Is difficult to recognize when he first enters the film, but that's fitting, as his character slowly reveals his political nature. Downey reminds us how his range goes way beyond super heroes. Matt Damon is more than solid with so many stars coming and going in supporting roles. It's fun seeing who turns up.

The making of the Atomic bomb is almost too ambitious to fathom, and the making and unmaking of Oppenheimer is equally difficult to grasp. Nolan called Oppenheimer the "most important man in history" but also one of the most "ambiguous." Nolan leaves us unsure how we ought to feel about Oppenheimer. As a scientist, his calculations were so precise, but as a man, he epically miscalculated the heart of the men who would judge him. "How could he see so much and be so blind," Downey's character says.

How much should we admire Oppenheimer? Or pity him? In this three-hour film, Nolan couldn't answer what history's never really been able to answer. Fission, after all, isn't easily fathomed, but it can be spectacularly displayed. Nolan gave us that in his best work yet.

10.title: Oppenheimer is a legendary movie
10.content:
5/5. Here's why: "Oppenheimer" (2023) is a biographical thriller, drawing inspiration from the 2005 biography "American Prometheus." The film intricately explores the life of J. Robert Oppenheimer, an intellectual and charismatic physicist entrusted with leading the Manhattan Project in Los Alamos, N. M., during World War II to develop the atomic bomb. The narrative centers on Oppenheimer's academic pursuits, his pivotal role in the Manhattan Project, and his eventual demise consequent to a 1954 security hearing. Nolan adeptly portrays Oppenheimer as a pivotal historical figure, yet poignantly naive, highlighting the profound gravity of the project and its profound repercussions on humanity.

Cinematography and direction: The cinematography of the film possesses a haunting quality, reminiscent of Christopher Nolan's distinctive style, imbuing it with an ominous atmosphere. Its non-linear storyline, coupled with a swift tempo and skillfully crafted narrative, effectively captivates the audience's attention. Nolan demonstrates his mastery by artfully interweaving revealing segments in lush colors and high-contrast black and white, forming a structure resembling the strands of a DNA double helix.

Employing the terms "fission" and "fusion," he skillfully accentuates the film's themes and introduces an element of complexity through chronological manipulation. Vivid scenes from various periods draw the audience deeply into Oppenheimer's tumultuous life, establishing this movie as unquestionably Nolan's Magnum Opus, showcasing his exceptional vision, meticulous attention to detail, and storytelling finesse. The adept pacing enables both action-packed moments and character-driven scenes to shine brightly throughout the film.

The cast: The film impresses with remarkable performances from its highly skilled ensemble cast. Cillian Murphy's portrayal of the conflicted hero, grappling with duty and personal challenges, is truly captivating. The supporting cast, including Robert Downey Jr., Emily Blunt, Matt Damon, and other accomplished actors, deliver standout performances that infuse the narrative with depth and authenticity. The palpable chemistry among the cast members brings the characters vividly to life. Notably, even the extras are prominent figures, adding to the film's overall quality.

Fantastic Audio Experience: Ludwig Göransson's symphonic score enhances the film significantly by skillfully harmonizing with the on-screen action and intensifying emotional scenes. The expertly crafted sound effects create a captivating auditory experience, immersing the audience in the movie's world. The eerie and dreamlike tone establishes a tense atmosphere, enveloping viewers in the film's narrative. The exceptional score demands a full theatrical IMAX experience, providing an auditory delight that amplifies the film's overall impact.

In conclusion, it's a biographical thriller that pays tribute to the complex life of Oppenheimer and the profound impact of the Manhattan Project. Christopher Nolan's remarkable direction, combined with the stellar cast performances and the enchanting score, results in a film that leaves a lasting impression on its audience.

10.title: Oppenheimer
10.content:
Oppenheimer (2023) is an extraordinary film that captivated my senses from start to finish. This historical drama, directed by the brilliant Christopher Nolan, weaves a mesmerizing narrative that delves deep into the life of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the brilliant physicist whose work changed the course of history during World War II.

From the moment the film begins, the audience is transported back in time to the tumultuous era of the 1940s, and Nolan's impeccable attention to detail immerses us into the historical setting effortlessly. The cinematography is awe-inspiring, and the breathtaking landscapes blend seamlessly with the authentic period settings, bringing Oppenheimer's world to life.

The casting is nothing short of perfection. Cillian Murphy delivers an Oscar-worthy performance as J. Robert Oppenheimer, capturing the complexity and inner struggles of the enigmatic physicist with unparalleled depth. His portrayal is nuanced and compelling, allowing us to empathize with Oppenheimer's moral dilemmas and the burden he carries as the father of the atomic bomb.

The supporting cast, including talented actors like Jessica Chastain, Michael Caine, and Tom Hardy, further enriches the movie, elevating it to cinematic greatness. Each character is beautifully crafted and contributes significantly to the story's emotional weight.

One of the most impressive aspects of Oppenheimer is its intelligent and thought-provoking script. Kudos to the screenwriters for expertly exploring the ethical questions surrounding scientific discoveries during wartime, the moral responsibilities of scientists, and the consequences of unleashing such powerful weaponry on the world.

The film's score, composed by the incomparable Hans Zimmer, is nothing short of a symphonic masterpiece. It amplifies the emotional impact of every scene, pulling at our heartstrings and enhancing the overall experience.

Christopher Nolan's direction is, without a doubt, a work of art. His ability to interweave historical events with human emotions and philosophical musings is nothing short of genius. He masterfully guides the audience through a rollercoaster of emotions, leaving us contemplating the consequences of our actions long after the credits roll.

Oppenheimer is not merely a historical retelling; it's a powerful reflection on the frailty of humanity, the pursuit of knowledge, and the consequences of playing with forces beyond our comprehension. This film will undoubtedly leave a lasting impression on anyone fortunate enough to witness it on the big screen.

In conclusion, Oppenheimer is an unparalleled cinematic experience that deserves every single one of its five stars. Christopher Nolan's visionary direction, outstanding performances, breathtaking cinematography, and emotional depth make this film a true masterpiece. It is a must-watch for anyone who appreciates the power of storytelling and the impact of historical events on the course of human history.

10.title: Nolan's latest masterpiece
10.content:
Oppenheimer was a surprising, pulse-pounding, twisting picture of both the human condition and the condition of all of humanity as we know it. The runtime and pacing of each scene has been constructed carefully, with great attention to detail.

Oppenheimer uses its audio cues to great emotional effect, like rhythmic stomping and split-second explosions cut in at the right times. However, as with many recent Nolan films, it does suffer from poor dialogue volume and dialogue capture. Although not as bad as 2020's Tenet (in that movie every time traveler wears a gas mask that muffles them), I still found myself struggling to piece together sentences in the middle of a crowd or wide echoing room. I did eventually grow to understand these parts better as the movie continued, but I wish I didn't have to.

Christopher Nolan's adaptation of Oppenheimer's struggle with human morality, political scrutiny, and personal decisions effectively throw the audience into his shoes and force them to see what he has seen. I was thrilled by its entirely practical visuals. Dream sequences and cutaways are never gratuitous and always manage to paint the emotions of its characters with a strong contrast to their more subtle expressions.

FOOTNOTE: The movie works surprisingly well juxtapositioned after a showing of Barbie. Both films explored what it means to be human in both a micro and macro sense. Barbenheimer does work.

10.title: Spectacular Movie
10.content:
A movie set during WW2 can sometimes be boring and drawn out. That is not the case in Oppenheimer. While the length of the movie is three hours, the time is filled with a good balance of dialogue and "action" scenes. Cillian Murphy plays Robert Oppenheimer, the physicist responsible for the first atomic bomb. Christopher Nolan does a good job guiding you through a historical period with a theatrical touch. Oppenheimer is designing the bomb and testing it with a group of other great minds while fighting the governmental red tape and pushback for what they were doing. As the history books have told you, the bomb was successful in not only ending the war, but also subsequently ruining Oppenheimer's reputation. Society looked at Robert Oppenheimer differently after the war because he had just set the table for nuclear warfare forever, and he certainly felt differently about himself.

The theme of Oppenheimer can be best described as the history of the atom bomb and the trials of Robert Oppenheimer. I thought of the movie, Lincoln (2012), as far as watching a main character struggle for something against the popular vote. I loved that movie and certain tense moments felt similar. Nolan uses well timed silence to help build tension, especially during the bomb detonation test scene. The countdown and the music build up to the detonation and then right before the climax, the movie goes silent, leaving you suspensefully waiting for the bomb to explode. Another thing Nolan does well in this film is the editing. Without the use of CGI, the explosions look amazing and the dramatic cuts from character close-ups add a layer of personality.

In conclusion, Oppenheimer is a historically accurate film that uses some amazing editing and well -done acting to bring the life of Robert Oppenheimer to the forefront of society once more. The bomb helped end the war but it kickstarted another war in the world between those who agree with the use of atom bombs, and those who don't. Cillian Murphy plays Oppenheimer perfectly and the film, overall, was spectacular to me.

10.title: Classic Movie.
10.content:
There are not many films made, these days, which will become classics, in the traditional sense, but I'll say 'Oppenheimer' is one. We all know it's about the bomb: but when the bomb goes off, there is plenty of time left, as the film is also about the aftermath - which we are still living with today.

There is not one bad camera shot in the whole picture, good framing and some terrific performances from the cast.

The terrific cinemaphotography is by Hoyte Van Hoytema, who has worked with Christopher Nolan before on 'Tenet' and 'Interstellar' to name but two.

You may get a little way through the story, when you realise who the various actors who are playing the roles - some are cameos - and there is a great performance by Robert Downey Jr, who plays Lewis Strauss, who seems obsessed with the quick-word Einstein had with J. Robert Oppenheimer. When people stop a conversation as you approach them, they must be talking about you, as every paranoic person knows, but sometimes they are talking about something more important.

The movie jumps about in time, there are very few clues as to when certain scenes happen, but the excellent make up - and maybe FX - helps, and in the end it all comes together.

We see Oppenheimer in many times of his life, his affairs, his obsession with another woman, Jean Tatlock, sympathetically played by Florence Pugh, a woman his wife, Emily Blunt, also sees, sitting naked across the naked Oppenheimer's lap copulating but only in her mind and, also Oppenheimer's mind, as he is given the third degree by a committee; a committee we learn about later, and we realise that just off the scene, somewhere, lurks the infamous senator from Wisconsin, Senator Joseph McCarthy, who sees many reds under many beds and somewhere, he is accusing Oppenheimer of being a red, a communist, and his henchmen are questioning his integrity and his love of the country.

Senator McCarthy who was the biggest public face during the 'cold war' has no face in this brilliant movie.

Jean Tatlock, his mistress, was a journalist who worked for 'The Western Worker' a communist newspaper, and she was probably the reason he was being questioned in the first place, and must have been on his mind throughout the ordeal and that might have been the reason for Oppenheimers fantasy.

Oppenheimer worked with Niels Bohr, who is played by Kenneth Branagh: Bohr helped develop the Bohr method, he proposed that energy levels of the electrodes can revolve around the atomic nucleus and can jump from one energy level to another.

Oppenheimer looks at patterns in a stream, patterns of rings of water, like a stone has been dropped, and the circles envelop each other and he sees this in the stars too.

It's a moment; a moment a bit like when Alan Turing sees the Fibonacci sequence in a pine cone.

There was always the risk that if there was an explosion from a nuclear device, it could be the end of the world, as the chain reaction might never stop.

There was a very strange fact about Doctor Oppenheimer, in that people didn't think he was 100% sane. They say there were traits such as of dementia praecox, which today is diagnosed as schizophrenia, some say autism and even, these days, Asperger's syndrome.

Some of the traits could be linked with just plain shyness, as he had problems looking people in the eye, but, on the other hand, he got on with people and didn't really think he was better than anybody else, or was part of an elite group of people with a superior attitude and intellect; Einstein suggested that he was. Maybe this all comes from the 'mad professor' theory, who was a stock character such as the father spending all his time in the lab, working on a formula.

There are images in the film which, such as whirlpools, which make him think of the effect of a nuclear explosion.

A fighter pilot, reported images of the U2 rockets, on their way from Germany to England, which he witnessed on the way back from a raid. The scene is shown of the pilot seeing the rockets and later, we also see Oppenheimer in the same scene, making him think that 'The Manhattan Project' needed to be completed quickly before Germany invented the atom bomb.

Oppenheimer was likened to Prometheus, who stole the fire from the Greek gods just as he, Oppenheimer, was stealing his formulas from the stars - the gods.

There are so many brilliant performances in this piece, too numerable to mention, but the brilliant performance of Cillian Murphy makes Oppenheimer into some kind of individual who goes from peaks to peaks to collect knowledge of how to build a nuclear reactor/fusion - who knows where this came from and, in fact, Oppenheimer was a genius, and is the film's director Christopher Nolan a genius too? I think so.

10.title: A Brilliant Cinematic Masterpiece
10.content:
Christopher Nolan has done it again! "Oppenheimer" is a breathtaking cinematic masterpiece that takes audiences on a mind-bending journey through one of history's most pivotal moments. With his signature storytelling prowess and impeccable attention to detail, Nolan crafts a gripping narrative that is both intellectually stimulating and emotionally resonant.

The film centers around the life and work of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the enigmatic physicist and leader of the Manhattan Project during World War II. Nolan's deft direction and visionary approach not only shed light on the scientific brilliance of Oppenheimer but also delve deep into the moral dilemmas and ethical questions faced by those involved in the creation of the atomic bomb.

The cast delivers stellar performances, with the lead character brought to life by a mesmerizing portrayal that captures the complexity of Oppenheimer's character. The supporting cast adds depth and nuance to the story, making it an ensemble performance to remember.

Nolan's artistic vision is evident in every frame, as he seamlessly blends stunning practical effects with mind-boggling visuals that leave the audience in awe. The attention to historical accuracy and the meticulous recreation of the era's settings immerse viewers in the tumultuous world of the 1940s.

What truly sets "Oppenheimer" apart is Nolan's ability to infuse the story with thought-provoking themes. He navigates the ethical implications of scientific advancements, the fine line between duty and morality, and the devastating consequences of humanity's thirst for power. These deep reflections elevate the film beyond a mere biopic, transforming it into a profound exploration of the human condition.

The film's score, composed by the brilliant Hans Zimmer, complements Nolan's visuals perfectly, enhancing the emotional impact of every scene. Zimmer's music becomes an integral part of the storytelling, elevating the entire experience to another level.

"Oppenheimer" challenges the audience's perceptions, leaving them questioning their own beliefs and grappling with profound existential questions. It invites introspection and intellectual engagement, making it an intellectually stimulating and emotionally rewarding cinematic experience.

In conclusion, Christopher Nolan's "Oppenheimer" is a tour de force that excels on all fronts. With its gripping narrative, outstanding performances, stunning visuals, and thought-provoking themes, the film is an unforgettable journey into the heart of one of history's most compelling and controversial figures. Nolan once again proves himself as a master of storytelling, leaving audiences with a film that will linger in their minds long after the credits roll. Don't miss this extraordinary cinematic gem!

10.title: Phenomenal
10.content:
Written and directed by Christopher Nolan, the story centers around physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer (Cillian Murphy) who was appointed as the director of the Manhattan Project by Lt. Gen. Leslie Groves Jr (Matt Damon) during a pivotal time in World War II. They gather a team of scientists who spend years developing and designing the atomic bomb. The aftermath of his creation not only changed the world but also turned his personal life upside down.

Walked out of the theatre, I imagined how it feels like to be able to watch movies that are always considered the best of all time or even define the cinema at its recurring time. Because that's how I felt after watching Oppenheimer, I'm just glad I got to experience the movie to the fullest. From Tenet to this, I don't think that's a comeback anyone can top in years to come. Oppenheimer is Nolan's most significant work thus far, I might need another viewing to make sure this's his magnum opus though it's certainly close. He brings his infamous nonlinear storytelling structure once again and captivates the audience to this epic, dialogue-driven three-hour biopic that delves into the moral dilemmas of a man who's haunted by a burden from something he invented whilst everyone around him keeps glorifying the man for what he has done to the country.

Cillian Murphy reunited with Nolan for the sixth time, but in this one, he finally takes the leading role; he absolutely deserved it. Without a doubt, Murphy delivers a career-best performance. He might be getting that Oscar nomination after all these years, or perhaps he'll bring it home, which I think wouldn't be a surprise for anyone familiar with his work. And I think people aren't giving enough credit to Benny Safdie, who also shines opposite Murphy; the two always clashed throughout the time while developing the bomb in Los Alamos due to their differences. Plus, not to mention Jason Clarke's role as Roger Robb in the intense hearing scene which is great, he succeeded in making me despise the character. He always nailed this type of villainy or bad-guy role. The ensemble cast is probably the most impressive of this year; everyone gave a solid performance and built great chemistry, even the ones with less screen time.

With a hefty 180-minute runtime, writer-director Christopher Nolan wastes no time since most of it consists of a time jump and some people might lose track of the time or events that take place but he didn't let that slide by shooting key sequences in black and white, which is meant to show how different the narrative is from Strauss's point of view and giving more clarity to the narrative as the movie progresses. Nolan teamed up again with his frequent collaborators, cinematographer Hoyte Van Hoytema and composer Ludwig Göransson. Together, they present a technical marvel that'll make moviegoing experience unforgettable, from awe-inspiring cinematography to heart-pounding score.

I highly suggest you to see it at the biggest screen you can get, there's a reason why he shot it with IMAX film cameras, he doesn't want you to just watch but also make sure you get immersed into this very moving story.

10.title: A Subtle Masterpiece
10.content:
In Christopher Nolan's 2023 film 'Oppenheimer', audiences are treated to a masterful cinematic experience that delves into the life and work of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the 'father of the atomic bomb.' The film is a meticulously crafted biographical drama that explores the complexities of Oppenheimer's character and the moral dilemmas faced during the creation of the world's most destructive weapon.

Uncharacteristic of Nolan's filmography, 'Oppenheimer' delivers its narrative through quiet nuances that demand the audience's attention and engagement. For instance, a poignant scene where Oppenheimer (Cillian Murphy) wordlessly observes the destructive potential of his creation, the atomic bomb, beautifully captures this subtlety. The scene speaks volumes about Oppenheimer's internal turmoil, showcasing Nolan's skill in visual storytelling.

The performances in 'Oppenheimer' are nothing short of stellar. Oscar-worthy turns from Robert Downey Jr. And Emily Blunt powerfully anchor the film, with Downey Jr.'s nuanced portrayal of his character adding a remarkable depth to the narrative. Emily Blunt's performance is equally compelling, delivering a magnetic charisma that captivates the audience. Despite her limited screen time, Florence Pugh makes a significant impact, further demonstrating her impressive range as an actress.

In his first leading role in a Nolan film, Cillian Murphy delivers an extraordinary performance that is both deeply nuanced and profoundly moving. His portrayal of Oppenheimer is so compelling, it's hard to imagine anyone else in the role. Murphy's performance is a masterclass in character depth that deserves an Oscar nomination.

Unlike many of Nolan's previous films, 'Oppenheimer' is less about pyrotechnics and more about the character study at its heart. This dialogue-driven narrative creates a palpable tension that simmers throughout the film, giving it explosive energy even in the absence of literal explosions. This thoughtful approach elevates the film to a higher plane of storytelling, making Oppenheimer a richly rewarding cinematic experience.

The screenplay, crafted with meticulous attention to detail, is another impressive aspect of 'Oppenheimer'. It blends historical facts with a deeply personal narrative, creating an engaging and thought-provoking story. The dialogue is packed with meaning, driving the narrative forward and revealing layers of character depth.

This film's success highlights the critical role of writers in the film industry, particularly in light of the recent SAG-AFTRA strike. The strike underscores the need for fair compensation and treatment of writers whose creativity and labor are integral to the production of quality films like 'Oppenheimer'. Without their invaluable contribution, cinema would lack the richness, diversity, and depth that audiences around the world cherish.

The film's one shortcoming, however, lies in the sound score. While the score itself is magnificent, its volume often overshadows the dialogue, making it challenging to discern what the characters are saying at times. This sometimes gives the impression that the characters are mumbling, detracting slightly from the overall experience.

Despite this minor issue, 'Oppenheimer' stands as a testament to Nolan's vision and the cast's stellar performances. It is a thought-provoking, character-driven film that cements Nolan's status as one of today's most visionary directors.

10.title: A Tale of Two Powers
10.content:
In the forces of nature, duality exists. This law governs our humanity. It is the catalyst by which we create...and by which we destroy.

Nolan explores this theme sub-atomically as we enter the mind of our protagonist and the ambition of our antagonist. While we might believe we are witnessing man harness the power of the sun, instead we are witnessing the creation of an equally devastating power - the fallout, the shadows of governance that would usher us into a nuclear winter.

Fusion is created. Both light and darkness burst forth. Can humankind be trusted with this power? Have we as a species reached enlightenment? Or will we repeat Eden? Repeat Babel? Is our reach for divinity the beginning of our fall yet again...

These questions are explored in profound ways. And they are answered with gut-wrenching truth. This work is courageous in that sense - that it does not yield to the desires of man and our ambition, but instead reveals our very nature thereby delivering an existential truth.

Let Nolan's film be praised not as a film, but as a message to the world. Prophetic in its delivery, it foretells of what will come if we continue the current course. It's important that we all take heed of this truth and use it to build a better world - before our power consumes it.

The supporting cast shines, with Robert Downey Jr. And Emily Blunt delivering standout performances. Nolan's non-linear storytelling masterfully weaves together Oppenheimer's rise, the Manhattan Project, and the political fallout, keeping viewers engaged and invested.

With stunning visuals and a haunting score by Ludwig Göransson, "Oppenheimer" is a powerful meditation on science, responsibility, and the human cost of progress. Nolan's masterpiece left this reviewer awestruck, uneasy, and profoundly moved.

10.title: Scientific and biographical perfomance
10.content:
Christopher Nolan's "Oppenheimer" is a cinematic masterpiece that delves into the complex and fascinating life of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the father of the atomic bomb. This epic biographical drama is a thought-provoking exploration of the human cost of genius, the morality of scientific discovery, and the devastating consequences of playing with the fundamental forces of nature.

Cillian Murphy's portrayal of Oppenheimer is nothing short of phenomenal. He brings a depth and nuance to the character, capturing the brilliant physicist's intellectual curiosity, emotional turmoil, and existential dread. Murphy's performance is complemented by an exceptional ensemble cast, who bring to life the complex web of relationships that defined Oppenheimer's personal and professional life.

Nolan's direction is, as always, meticulous and masterful. He weaves together multiple narrative threads, seamlessly shifting between Oppenheimer's early days as a brilliant but troubled student, his rise to prominence as a leading physicist, and his later years as a haunted and isolated figure. The film's non-linear structure adds to the sense of complexity and fragmentation that defined Oppenheimer's life, mirroring the disjointed and often contradictory nature of his own thoughts and feelings.

One of the standout aspects of "Oppenheimer" is its thought-provoking exploration of the ethics of scientific discovery. The film raises important questions about the responsibility that comes with knowledge, the dangers of unchecked ambition, and the devastating consequences of playing with forces beyond human control. Nolan's script is nuanced and balanced, avoiding simplistic moralizing or didacticism, instead presenting a richly textured and multifaceted portrait of a brilliant but flawed individual.

The film's technical achievements are equally impressive. Nolan's use of IMAX cameras adds to the sense of scope and scale, capturing the vast expanses of the New Mexico desert and the claustrophobic intensity of the Los Alamos laboratory. The score, composed by Ludwig Göransson, is a haunting and evocative blend of electronic and orchestral elements, perfectly capturing the mood and atmosphere of each scene.

Throughout the film, Nolan's masterful direction and the outstanding performances of the cast bring to life the complex and fascinating world of J. Robert Oppenheimer. The film is a must-see for anyone interested in the intersection of science, morality, and humanity, and a testament to the enduring power of cinema to inspire, educate, and challenge us.

In conclusion, "Oppenheimer" is a cinematic masterpiece that will leave audiences spellbound and thoughtful. With its outstanding performances, meticulous direction, and thought-provoking themes, this film is a must-see for anyone interested in the life and legacy of J. Robert Oppenheimer.

10.title: Oppenheimer Movie Review

The film has a strong topical message and is sobering in its attempt at an anti-war stance. Based on craftsmanship, the film's screenplay, directing, special effects, editing, set work, costumes, props, and musical score are all well-executed. Based on performance, Cillian Murphy's performance is considered a tour-de-force. Robert Downey Jr.'s performance is also praised, with one reviewer saying he was thoroughly redeemed by taking on the role.

10.title: A Perfect Blending of History & Humanity
10.content:
Oppenheimer was, without a doubt, one of the best movies I've ever seen. I saw it (along with Barbie) on the Thursday of its release, and it took me a couple of days to really understand the extent to which the film affected me.

That's not to say that I left the theater crying, as so many reviewers have claimed to do, but it did leave me somewhat shocked and absolutely awestruck. So very few films are able to convey the reality that historical figures are real, flawed figures while also displaying the gravitas that history is traditionally assigned. Christopher Nolan and crew, somehow, manage to masterfully display both of these facets of the past. All at once, history is both deeply personal and exceedingly grand, but the extent to which the film conveys this isn't entirely clear until its end.

That is to say that, if you're not particularly interested in history or politics, this is not the film for you. I've had a hard time imagining that I would like this three-hour movie if it weren't for my experience with history or interest in nuclear policy. Oppenheimer certainly takes its time to explore the life and world of its namesake, but if you're interested in the man (or The Bomb), I promise you that not once will it feel slow or bogged down with poor pacing. Every scene, action, and piece of dialogue has a purpose in a way that few other pieces of media do. If you are at all interested in history, go see this film NOW, and make sure you see it IN THEATERS.

This is a film that will be remembered for decades much in the same way that Dr. Strangelove has been, and dare I say, it will exceed that film. Oppenheimer is an artistic work that serves as both poetic tribute to the past and prophetic reflection on the human condition. Never before have I seen a film so thematically cohesive. Words alone cannot fully describe its artistic merit.

10.title: Great movie
10.content:
The Oppenheimer movie is a 2023 epic biographical drama film written, produced, and directed by Christopher Nolan. The film follows the life of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the American theoretical physicist who helped develop the first nuclear weapons during World War II.¹

*The Plot*

The movie dramatizes Oppenheimer's studies, his direction of the Los Alamos Laboratory, and his 1954 security hearing. It explores his complex personality, relationships, and the moral implications of his work.

*The Cast*

The film boasts an impressive ensemble cast, including:

_Cillian Murphy_ as J. Robert Oppenheimer
_Robert Downey Jr._ as Lewis Strauss, a member of the United States Atomic Energy Commission
_Emily Blunt_ as Katherine "Kitty" Oppenheimer, Robert's wife
_Matt Damon_ as General Leslie Groves, director of the Manhattan Project
_Florence Pugh_ as Jean Tatlock, a psychiatrist and Robert's romantic interest
*Production and Release*

The film was announced in September 2021, with Christopher Nolan set to write and direct. It was released in theaters on July 21, 2023, by Universal Pictures, after premiering at Le Grand Rex in Paris on July 11, 2023.

*Reception*

Oppenheimer received widespread critical acclaim, with many praising the film's thought-provoking themes, impressive performances, and Nolan's masterful direction. It has grossed over $976 million worldwide, becoming the third-highest-grossing film of 2023.

10.title: The World Forever Changes.
10.content: Christopher Nolan gave cinema one of the most powerful and stunning biopics in history. In his 12th feature length film, Nolan takes on J. Definitely one of the best visual films in Nolans filmography and in recent cinema, "Oppenheimer" manages to turn one of the worlds most destructive weapons, into a mind-blowing, beautiful masterpiece. Nolan used two styles of visuals to portray the story, a first person perspective when the film was in colour and a third person perspective when it came to the black and white scenes, this helped to distinguish the difference between events for viewers especially with how much information was in the picture and really immerse the viewer in J. Robert Oppenheimer's position as these events unfolded and what he now carried with him as "The Father of the Atomic Bomb". I can easily say that Cillian Murphy and Robert Downey Jr. Are clearly in the running for Best Actor and Supporting Actor as they both provide some of their best performances to date. However I will add that the entire cast was on their A-game anytime they were on screen. The fact that Nolan has addressed that there is no CGI used in this picture is phenomenal and after watching this film you can appreciate that so much more, everything was visually beautiful and the sound design on top of that was amazing. I have never watched a film and physically felt the magnitude of what was on screen. Every single explosion was felt as if you were in the observation area with the cast. My only issue that came with this film was the 3 hour runtime actually felt like 4. As some films manage to speed through 3 hours and leave you wanting more, this did not have that affect for me. However it is still a 5/5, it is in my top 3 for Nolan films and is definitely one I can rewatch no problem.

10.title: Oppenheimer Rocks
10.content:
This is a masterwork. Easily on par with the great epics like Lawrence of Arabia, The Bridge on the River Kwai, Ben - Hur, Doctor Zhivago, The Godfather 1 & 2, The Lord of The Rings Trilogy, Amadeus, Schindler's List, Barry Lyndon, Once Upon A Time In America, and Nolan's own The Dark Knight.

The skill with which Nolan and his editor, Jennifer Lame, jump from timeline to timeline is insane. Such a fluid, fast-paced three hours.

The cinematography is some of the most immersive ever put on the big or small screen. Go and watch this in IMAX 70MM and tell me it's not some of the most captivating and involving cinema you've ever seen.

The sound design is outstanding, again, IMAX 70MM, go watch it. Sure, some of it's a little bit difficult to hear, and it wouldn't be a Nolan movie otherwise.

The score by Ludwig Göransson is on another level. Experiencing the "Can You Hear The Music" scene alone is worth the price of admission to an IMAX 70MM screening, or even a regular showing for that matter.

Performances are phenomenal. Robert Downey Jr and Cillian Murphy both knock it out of the park. Emily Blunt is great as well. You know you're watching an epic piece of cinema when even the smallest roles - ones that take up five minutes of screen-time - are played by Academy Award winning calibre (i.e. Gary Oldman as Truman, Casey Affleck as Colonel Pash, or Rami Malek as Dr. Hill).

I'm not afraid to call out Nolan when his movies are flawed, and I still love him as a director. It just so happens that this time, he made a flawless movie. For my money, this deserves more than the majority of the Academy Awards this year, including Best Director and Best Picture - it deserves to go down in history as one of the best movies ever made.

10.title: A Staggering Acheivement
10.content:
Where Tenet failed to rescue post-pandemic cinema, Oppenheimer (along with the very different, eye-wateringly successful, Barbie) may well have succeeded. Christopher Nolan has made a three-hour film, partly in black and white, historical biopic that is mostly men in rooms talking, that grapples with huge moral, ethical and historical issues and turned it into one of the megahits of blockbuster season. In the process, he's rebooted the biopic genre, one of cinema's most creatively moribund genres, an achievement it's hard to imagine any other film-makers taking on.

Two often quoted issues with Nolan's work - a perceived emotional coldness, and poorly served female characters - are worth touching on here. Emotionally this is devastating, daringly empathetic towards such a divisive and complex central character; the women are better written than in some Nolan films, the emotional cost to them of a driven, hero complex man spelled out in ways that may be questionable but certainly asks for thoughtfulness.

Performances are remarkable; Downey Junior layered, Cillian Murphy magnetic and extraordinary. The whole cast is playing in the big leagues here. Technically it's a masterclass; editing, sound design, cinematography and much else working in concert. The almost omnipresent score is sensational; the pivotal test explosion scene is staged unforgettably.

All in all a remarkable, extraordinary, propulsive and utterly gripping film that will demand reward repeated viewings. If it's my favourite Nolan, I'm not sure - but I suspect not; but it's more than likely that history will judge it his best and most important achievement.

10.title: Thrilling story line movie
10.content:
"Oppenheimer" is a biographical thriller film written and directed by Christopher Nolan ("The Dark Knight trilogy", "Inception", "Interstellar", "Dunkirk"), based on the biography "American Prometheus" by Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin. Starring Cillian Murphy in the lead role, in addition to Matt Damon, Robert Downey Jr, Emily Blunt, and Florence Pugh, it subverts the usual biopic formula to create a brilliantly layered examination of a man throughout all of his incredible accomplishments and fundamental flaws.

The one man whom most people pin all the blame on is J. Robert Oppenheimer, whose key role in the development of these weapons led to him being credited as "the father of the atomic bomb", a label which he carried as a heavy burden for the rest of his life. In Christopher Nolan's biopic "Oppenheimer", we are treated to an intricately structured and uniquely tragic analysis of this complex man's legacy and how it still affects everyone several decades later.

Oppenheimer is haunted by the errors of his own judgement, shown to the audience through flashbacks of varying length to pivotal times in his life. These scenes range from his fractured relationship with his wife to the remorse he has for placing his trust in the wrong people. This gives the viewer a first person perspective of what Oppenheimer's mind must have been processing during this intense period of his life, as he contemplates the very real possibility of having all of his hard work mitigated by these powerful government officials.

I may consider myself lucky to be alive to watch Christopher Nolan Works which get better by years.

Oppenheimer is - with no doubt- going to be one of the best movies in the history. Amazing cinematography, Exceptional acting and terrifying Soundtracks.

10.title: "Oppenheimer" offers a unique perspective on the human experience."
10.content: Nolan's bio-pic, based on Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin's Pulitzer-winning biography "American Prometheus," follows the life of physicist and scientist Oppenheimer. Oppenheimer, a student in the 19th century, tours European science capitals before returning to the US and joining Caltech and Berkeley. At Berkeley, he becomes a union organizer and donates to the anti-Fascist cause during the Spanish Civil War. He hangs out with Communist Party members, including his brother Frank and Jackie's wife. Despite not being a Party member, Oppenheimer is spied on by the F. B. I. And meets a Communist medical student named Jean Tatlock, leading to an ill-fated relationship. In 1942, General Leslie Groves (Matt Damon) appoints Oppenheimer to oversee the Army's nuclear bomb development program. Despite political suspicion, Groves supports Oppenheimer, who proves to be a master of both scientific and political aspects. However, the Red Scare and his proximity to Communists make him an easy target. Oppenheimer was stripped of his security clearance in 1954. The movie is structured as a mosaic, intercutting Oppenheimer's life from his rise to fall, connecting his early leftism and later pacifism with the McCarthy era. This fractured chronology makes the film less complex, as events are reduced to their function within a larger morality tale. Nolan's film cuts scenes together like a jigsaw puzzle, leaving out contradictions, subtleties, and random peculiarities, leaving a feeling of experience for both the protagonist and the viewer. The movie is a puzzle to be solved rather than lived. "Oppenheimer" explores the tension between physics and war, focusing on the character of Jewish and leftist researcher Oppenheimer. He is committed to creating an atomic bomb, believing Nazi Germany is ahead in developing one. However, after Germany surrenders in May 1945, work on the bomb accelerates, causing a moral crisis for Oppenheimer. This mission drift determines the rest of the film and his life. Oppenheimer's involvement in the Manhattan Project leaves him compromised, committed to creating a weapon of unparalleled destructiveness without any control over its use. The film ultimately explores the consequences of his actions during the war. "Oppenheimer" is a fascinating film that explores the complexities of individual and collective personality. Despite criticisms of its length, its fascinating physical experience is largely due to its exploration of themes such as Oppenheimer's sex life and Strauss's enmity. The film's focus on governmental hearings, including the third hour, is a testament to its entropic tendencies. The characters appear before a tribunal, bringing to account their contradictions, hypocrisies, and sins. The tribunal is hidden, allowing the audience to make their own decisions, a feature that is as expected of a film. Overall, "Oppenheimer" offers a unique perspective on the human experience. A brilliantly layered examination of a man throughout all of his incredible accomplishments and fundamental flaws.
