I didn't know all of them were so intimately involved in this endeavour.

The interactions between Einstein and Oppie were my favourite moments from the film. One man revealed this huge secret to the mankind and the other man made its application possible.

Nolan devotes lot of time on the consequences and hearings where Oppenheimer's life is dissected brutally. At times, this may seem a bit stretched, but maybe it is necessary to drive home the point.

Overall, July was the month when Tom cruise and Christopher Nolan once again proved why there is no alternative to actual cinematic experience at least for some special movies.

I did not expect this reaction at all. It is a master piece in every sense of the word. Every performance is masterful and the 3 hours evaporates. I didn't believe films like this were made anymore and so pleased I have been proven wrong. The story of a man and a team who were driven to achieve a dream that they knew would become a nightmare but felt duty bound to see it through: only to have the founder taken down because he had a conscience and a reality that he had given the fools their overture. Unfortunately for us the fools still play that melody today, only the orchestra is much, much greater.

10.title: Like witnessing classical music from the greats !
10.content:
Now I don't mean to say that the Marvel movies or the Flash/Mission Impossible/ Indiana Jones aren't any good -despite their criticisms they serve their purpose as entertainment . But every once in a while there comes a film like Oppenheimer and you see exactly what Scorsese meant when he referred to these films like amusement parks . They're fun but largely forgettable

Oppenheimer is the complete opposite - miles and miles ahead of anything that these films could hope to achieve . Every now and then during the movie a part of my mind as an avid movie goer kept saying that this witnessing film history in the making . I was reminded of Scorseses quote that despite a lifetime of watching film we've just seen what cinema could do

In its 3 hour run time there isn't a single frame wasted or.a single character that feels wasted. The acting roster feels like you're seeing the Classic XI coming out to play . The right combination of popularity and acting prowess

I was very happy to see Jason Clarke , Matthew Modine and even Gary Oldman in this .

Robert Downey Jr. Once again proves why he's a living legend and shows us fully the man beyond Iron Man

And as for the man himself - I have no doubts that Cillian Murphy is going to walk away with dozens of nominations and is the first serious contender for this years Best Actor Oscar . A lot of us film nerds have been rooting for him for a long time and were happy to see the man's stellar turn as the iconic Thomas Shelby and now with his portrayal of Oppie he takes that bar of excellence even further. I was reminded of the intensity of classic golden age Hollywood actors time and time again

Very few directors have made me feel strongly about cinema- Stanley Kubrick , Martin Scorsese , Paul Thomas Anderson and Nolan

Watching this film is like witnessing a live rendition of a classic musical piece by Mozart ir Beethoven.

10.title: Beautiful, artful biography from Nolan - his best so far (with spoilers)
10.content:
I've seen this movie three times in theatres and could easily see it three more. It's got incredible scope, breakneck pacing, and a kind of narrative and character-generated complexity you don't see in a lot of Hollywood releases. What I like most, though, is how Nolan continues to treat his well-known themes in new and interesting ways.

I find a lot of Nolan's movies cold. I'm not a huge fan, for example, of Interstellar, Inception, or Tenet. All suffer from a kind of conceptual overload where the narrative framing appears front and centre as "innovative", but often at the expense of my investment. Interstellar looked beautiful, and some of its set-pieces (particularly the black hole) were incredible--but it wanted to tell me directly about love and the scientific/evolutionary benefits of love, and so, in my view, ended up becoming sappy and heavy-handed, particularly by the end. Instead of offering a mystery, the tesseract stood as a great-big, obvious allegory for love and time: of timeless love, actually, which, in my view, *ick*.

Inception, while slick and original and thrilling and "layered" (obviously), completely forgot any sense of place. The whole movie lacked, for me, any kind of texture. While it's true the story "really" takes place on a plane over the ocean--and arguably the movie is about a kind of corporate emptying out of place as a result of globalization--the film embraced this placelessness rather than really offering it as a problem, and so all the sets took on the same colours, tones, and shades. It felt either like I was in a corporate office for the whole film, or maybe even more ironically, it felt like the whole movie was made with CGI: Nolan found a way to give reality the same effect as CGI, to turn reality into a dream--yes, I get it, maybe that was the point. But why dream in so one-note a way? Why dream about corporate offices? I'd level this same critique at Tenet, too. The end battle in the placeless city reminded me of the conceptual dream-space of Inception, and the plane crash near the beginning was more of a concept than a set-piece.

But since this is, in fact, a glowingly positive review of Oppenheimer, I also need to mention there are these other Nolan films, like Dunkirk and The Dark Knight, which care deeply for place and enable the textures of the physical world to do their beautiful, filmic work. Oppenheimer belongs (ambiguously) in a kind of in-between place with respect to these two sides of Nolan's filmography, which is one reason I think it's so fascinating. On the one hand, you've got Los Alamos and the incredible visualizations of scientific concepts that erupt into full force on screen in the Trinity Test. You've also got Oppie's education in Europe and his various classrooms. Lastly, you've got the windowless, government rooms where the law does its work. On the other hand, much of Oppenheimer deals with transforming theory (or abstraction) into reality. Thus, abstraction takes on, for the first time in my opinion, real dimensions in Nolan's story. And while the movie is still cold (a coldness that Murphy's performance excels at) it feels intentional here, rather than a side effect of Nolan's narrative innovations in some of his previous films.

This is his best movie about turning theory into reality (a problem he explores most openly in The Prestige, Inception, Interstellar, and Tenet). At the same time, there's the world that must experience the consequences of this new reality, which is treated with much more care. Los Alamos is gorgeously rendered--though I would have liked to see even more of it in order to tip the movie truly into the second category. The one-note textures of these prior films return in the trial scenes, though again, on purpose here. Oppenheimer's scientific visualizations compel interest in ways that the dreams in Inception never can for me. And the Trinity Test is Nolan's best piece of filmmaking yet. The fire is theory-made-real--but it's distorted, defamiliarized, and its consequences (in the form of sound-engineering) don't hit until a little later.

The movie's three-hour runtime enables characters--rather than theories--to take centre stage. Oppenheimer is complex and certainly not a great man, in terms of the "great man" theory of history. We see him, by turns, as the "great improvisor" (says Dr. Rabi) and as a weak man who cannot look at the consequences of his own actions. The time to make this film is now--with both the threat of nuclear war on the horizon, and as AI technology encroaches with its own theory. The film never judges, which enables the audience to judge. It's so careful in its build-up, and so rapid in its pace, that it never feels slow--or rather, its slowness feels purposeful.

Nolan loves to repeat lines in his films, like refrains. In The Prestige it's the line about love, where a character asks if a woman loves him, and she says: "Not today." In Inception, it's the lines Leo and Marion say on the train tracks. There are many other examples scattered about Nolan's filmography. Here, we get a number of repetitions that never feel contrived. We do sometimes get historical figures speaking in more of an artsy, "foreshadowy" register that real people don't use: "You see outside the world we know, Oppenheimer"; "Don't alienate the scientists in case you need them, Oppenheimer" (which, spoiler, he does); "You are an American Prometheus who gave them the ability to destroy themselves", etc. But I'm more than willing to look past this atificiality because the film does so many other things so well--like the repeated scenes with Einstein. They, to me, give order to Oppie's life as the movie portrays it, and they lead to a beautiful ending that really makes the film for me. I'll probably see it again before it goes out of theatres.

The film is something only Nolan could make, and I love the ways it's a Nolan film, but better than any Nolan film that's come before. Not only is it a great story told so skillfully--but it's also an example of the evolution of an artist I truly admire. Nolan made theory into reality. So did Oppenheimer. And the marriage is fascinating to contemplate--both for its successes and its flaws.

I've felt the movies lacking in reality recently (like MI7, Indiana Jones, and certainly Barbie). Sure, I could go sit under a tree for a while if I want a dose of reality, but I'd probably spend the time making up some idiotic theory anyway.

10.title: Engrossing from beginning to end - wow!
10.content:
Christopher Nolan has once again revealed why he is The One to handle movies of this nature. I was thoroughly enthralled with Dunkirk (I learnt a few extra things that I did not know about it, despite being from there England!) and when "Oppenheimer" was slated to be made, I was ecstatic. Waiting, and waiting, and then the trailer was released... I was in awe. However, the trailer set the a high bar for the forthcoming movie. Those are things I dread... trailers hype up the movie and it ends up being a bore.

Not "Oppenheimer".

From the very beginning to the very end I was hooked. After the end, I wanted more, more!! I hope there is an extended version released as three hours is a short time to cram a lot of information on. If I had to find a fault, it would be there were a lot of characters thrown at you, and sometimes became overwhelming who was who and what their role was in the Manhattan Project. A second viewing (on DVD) will be made.

I absolutely loved the musical score. Ludwig Goransson was a big question mark in my mind as I was vying for Hans Zimmer to be on board (he got stuck with Dune Pt.2) but Ludwig made a wonderful score, very Zimmer-esque.

As others have noted, the ending is a truly cinematic masterpiece. The concluding scene with Oppenheimer talking with Einstein about potentially ending the world coupled with Ludwig's rousing piece (Destroyer of Worlds) brings out such emotion and the fear of what has been created, that a tear or two rolled down my cheek.

Funniest scene: Oppenheimer and Groves near-zero chance of destroying the Earth exchange, prior to first detonation.

By the way, if you have not watched it already, I highly recommend 1989's "Fat Man and Little Boy" (also called "The Shadowmakers" in some countries). That movie with Paul Newman as Groves focuses more on the Project than this one, and is a great companion to "Oppenheimer".

All in all, I loved it. My friend and I each purchased the 600 page book that we shall get through in time... but I truly hope Mr. Nolan released an uncut or extended edition of this movie!

10.title: Oppenheimer: A 10/10 Masterpiece
10.content:
Oppenheimer is a 2023 historical epic film directed by Christopher Nolan and written by Nolan and the late David Kajganich. The film stars Cillian Murphy as J. Robert Oppenheimer, the scientist who led the Manhattan Project to develop the atomic bomb during World War II. The film also stars Emily Blunt, Matt Damon, Robert Downey Jr., Florence Pugh, Benny Safdie, Rami Malek, and Kenneth Branagh.

Oppenheimer is a sweeping and ambitious film that tells the story of one of the most consequential events in human history. Nolan's direction is masterful, and he brings the story to life with stunning visuals and an immersive soundscape. The performances are all top-notch, with Murphy giving a tour-de-force performance as Oppenheimer.

The film is not without its flaws. The runtime is a bit long, and the pacing can be slow at times. However, these flaws are minor compared to the film's many strengths. Oppenheimer is a powerful and thought-provoking film that is sure to stay with you long after you've seen it.

Here are some of the things that make Oppenheimer a 10 out of 10 film:

The direction is masterful. Nolan creates a truly immersive experience that takes you inside the mind of Oppenheimer and the Manhattan Project.

The performances are all top-notch. Murphy gives a tour-de-force performance as Oppenheimer, and the supporting cast is also excellent.

The visuals are stunning. Nolan uses his trademark visual style to create some truly memorable images.

The score is haunting and atmospheric. Ludwig Göransson's score perfectly complements the film's visuals and tone.

The story is both complex and engaging. Oppenheimer is a challenging film, but it is also a rewarding one.

If you are a fan of historical epics, science fiction, or Christopher Nolan, then you need to see Oppenheimer. It is a truly remarkable film that is sure to leave a lasting impression.

Here are some of the specific things that I loved about the film:

The way that Nolan uses visuals to tell the story. The film is full of stunning images that help to convey the scale and complexity of the Manhattan Project.

The performances of the cast. Murphy is excellent as Oppenheimer, and the supporting cast is also very good.

The score by Ludwig Göransson. The score is haunting and atmospheric, and it perfectly complements the film's visuals and tone.

The way that the film explores the moral implications of the atomic bomb.

Oppenheimer is a film that asks difficult questions, and it does so in a thoughtful and nuanced way.

Overall, Oppenheimer is a masterpiece. It is a film that is both visually stunning and intellectually stimulating. I highly recommend it to anyone who is a fan of historical epics, science fiction, or Christopher Nolan.

10.title: The weight of genius
10.content:
Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer (2023) is a cinematic masterpiece that delves into the tumultuous life of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the father of the atomic bomb. This film is not just a biographical drama but a thought-provoking exploration of the human condition, morality, and the consequences of playing with the fundamental forces of nature.

From the outset, Nolan's direction is characterized by its trademark non-linearity, weaving together multiple timelines and narrative threads. This storytelling approach mirrors the complexities of Oppenheimer's own life, where personal and professional relationships, politics, and science intersected in intricate ways.

Cillian Murphy's portrayal of Oppenheimer is nothing short of phenomenal. He brings a depth and nuance to the character, capturing the inner turmoil and conflict that defined Oppenheimer's life. Murphy's performance is complemented by an exceptional supporting cast, including Emily Blunt as Kitty Oppenheimer, Matt Damon as Leslie Groves, and Robert Downey Jr. As Lewis Strauss.

One of the film's greatest strengths lies in its ability to balance the scientific and historical aspects of Oppenheimer's story with the more personal and emotional elements. Nolan's script, penned in collaboration with author Kai Bird, whose book "American Prometheus" serves as the film's foundation, is meticulous in its attention to detail. The film's depiction of the Manhattan Project, the Los Alamos laboratory, and the first nuclear test, codenamed "Trinity," is both accurate and visually stunning.

The film also explores the moral implications of Oppenheimer's work, particularly in the aftermath of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Nolan raises important questions about the responsibility that comes with scientific discovery and the blurred lines between progress and destruction. These themes are timeless and resonate deeply in today's world, where the threat of nuclear proliferation and the ethics of emerging technologies remain pressing concerns.

Visually, Oppenheimer is a feast for the eyes, with Nolan's signature large-format cinematography and a blend of practical and visual effects creating a truly immersive experience. The film's score, composed by Ludwig Göransson, perfectly complements the on-screen action, adding depth and emotional resonance to key moments.

In conclusion, Oppenheimer (2023) is a masterpiece of cinematic storytelling that shines a light on one of the most fascinating and complex figures of the 20th century. Nolan's direction, combined with outstanding performances and meticulous attention to historical detail, results in a film that is both entertaining and thought-provoking. As the world continues to grapple with the challenges of scientific progress and moral responsibility, Oppenheimer serves as a timely reminder of the importance of considering the consequences of our actions.

*Rating:* 5/5 stars *Recommendation:* Oppenheimer is a must-see for fans of historical drama, science, and philosophy. While the film's themes and subject matter may be complex, Nolan's direction makes the story accessible to a broad audience.

10.content:
This movie, no matter how one looks at it, from the first second of it is magnificent. One possibly cannot take the movie in its complete sense after one watch. It craves multiple watches. The movie jumps right into it, and does not let you off for even a second until the very last moment. It's dialogue is maturely written by Mr. Nolan and shows huge respect to its audience. And the visual aspect of it with all of its glory there to see on the 70mm screen, is a treat that leaves to be craved even after a 3hr runtime. The movie with its pace shows the reality of how the US chased after the making of atomic bomb. The audio of this movie, not just dialogue but soundtrack, movie sounds, everything was masterfully managed by. Ludwig Gorannson, it perfectly supplements the visual storytelling while adding weight to each scene in its own right. And the acting is perfect. Mr. Murphy is exceptional, larger than life in this movie. RDJ is exceptional. Matt Damon is exceptional. Emily Blunt is exceptional. This movie has all the Oscar-nominating performances. 10.title: Masterpiece

10.title: Exceptional
10.content:
"I'm not really a movie reviewer or know exactly what to say, but I'll give it a go. First off, I thought the movie was amazing. Cillian Murphy was incredible; he really embodied the character of J. Robert Oppenheimer and sucked you right into the movie. It was amazing to see it in IMAX; you could truly feel the emotions of the characters. The music was insanely beautiful and intense, evoking feelings of fear, anxiety, and sadness. I thought it was brilliant.

I felt really emotional watching the movie, especially considering the times we are in now. Oppenheimer and other physicists definitely created a new world that changed history forever. Robert Oppenheimer was an incredible physicist, and his leadership and contributions to the development of the atomic bomb had a profound impact on warfare and geopolitics.

Cillian portrayed Oppenheimer's internal conflicts after the success of the project so well; it was incredible to watch. His performance felt raw and real, evoking sadness for Robert as I'm sure it wasn't easy for him, particularly after President Truman dropped those bombs on Japan. Moreover, the way Robert was treated by the United States government was quite sad and despicable, in my opinion. It's disheartening how a country could turn its back on a man who dedicated many years of his life to the Manhattan Project, which was initially meant for good, although I believe he later regretted it. I hope he found some peace in knowing that if it wasn't him, it would have eventually been someone else to create the first atomic bomb.

In conclusion, Cillian Murphy's ability to convey emotions with a mere glance or a slight change in expression sets him apart as an actor of remarkable skill and control. His dedication and commitment to delivering exceptional performances that leave a lasting impact are evident in this role as J. Robert Oppenheimer. I hope he wins many awards for his exceptional and stunning performance.

Emily was incredible in this movie; she gave an outstanding performance. Blunt's on-screen presence is captivating, drawing you into the character's life and emotions effortlessly. Her portrayal of Katherine Oppenheimer, the wife of Robert, was versatile and emotionally charged. Moving to the middle of nowhere with a child and dealing with Robert's affair throughout their marriage couldn't have been easy for her. Emily's performance built up brilliantly; it felt real, raw, and emotional.

I did feel for Katherine, and I could truly sense the emotions in the movie. Emily's ability to communicate emotions without relying on dialogue was remarkable, making the character and the film all the more impactful. Her commitment to her roles and her willingness to take on challenging and diverse projects have solidified her position as one of the best actors of our time. I hope she wins many awards for her role in this movie.

I also want to shout out Robert Downey Jr; he was incredible in this movie. What an amazing actor and human being. I hope he wins some awards for his role as well. While I won't deep dive into every character in the movie, I must mention Florence Pugh, who also gave an outstanding performance. Her willingness to be vulnerable and real was astonishing, displaying her ability to convey a wide range of emotions and navigate complex narratives. She is truly an amazing actor who deserves many awards and recognition.

So, would I rate this movie? Absolutely! You must go see it in the cinema; it's just incredible. It's the best movie I've seen in a long time. I give it a 10/10."

10.title: "I Am Become Death, The Destroyer Of Worlds"
10.content:
He was deemed "The Father of the Atomic Bomb"-a man whose core studies on the nature of the universe and the atom itself led to the development of the ultimate Weapon of Mass Destruction; and in his life, he was accused of being a Communist, particularly after his invention (or two of them) atomized Hiroshima and Nagasaki. He was J. Robert Oppenheimer (or "Oppie" to his "fans" in the world), But while his story is fairly well known to anyone who has studied the history of America from World War II through to the Cold War, it took British director Christopher Nolan to truly bring his epic story to the big screen, which he has done so with OPPENHEIMER.

Adapted to the screen by Nolan from the book "American Prometheus" by Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin, OPPENHEIMER stars Cilia Murphy as the legendary and (frequently) legendarily controversial scientist whose studies in quantum physics unlock the great secret of the creation of the universe, but which, in the 1930's, were put to use for a much more disturbing purpose. In order to keep this disturbing purpose totally under wraps, Oppenheimer devised the entire building of a small town in New Mexico called Los Alamos. But both his advocacy for unions inside the professions of professors, teachers, and scientists and his loose associations with people who may have (suspected) ties to the Communist Party make him the subject of scrutiny by the U. S. government, particularly the FBI (very much under the control of J. Edgar Hoover). He nevertheless gets support in the development of The Bomb from legendary General Leslie Groves (Matt Damon), Albert Einstein (Tom Conti), and fellow nuclear physicist Edward Teller (Benny Sadie) and the great Danish scientist Niels Bohr (Sir Kenneth Branagh). Overall, this makes OPPENHEIMER very much a political drama and an historical drama all in one, with Murphy's performance giving us insight into the psychology and psyche of this great and, in many ways, troubled American genius, and also a look at how America, from the 1940's onward, seemed hell bent on containing the evils of Communism with a nuclear weapons program that, if ever used for real, would wipe out every living thing on Earth.

Nolan, known for such great films as 2009's INCEPTION, 2014's INTERSTELLAR, and 2017's DUNKIRK, may have made an incredibly long film out of his subject, with a running time of three hours, but he certainly makes the most of it, particularly in the intense and frightening countdown to the device's test detonation in the New Mexico desert in July 1945. Emily Blunt is quite good as Oppenheimer's wife Kitty; and the supporting turns from Damon, Conti, and Branagh are top-notch all the way. And finally, Murphy's portrayal of Oppenheimer is a portrayal clearly worthy of being awarded, particularly a very likely nomination for Best Actor at the Oscars.

Clearly, this is a masterpiece, and worthy of a '10' rating.

10.title: " I belive we did it "

Who was Oppenheimer? Seemingly, we see an ordinary man, a student who wants to succeed and be somebody. That his knowledge is studied even after him. The development of civilization and its progress. Helping the individual as a human species to rise. What did J. Robert Oppenheimer with his work? He brought death. How and why? To stop more deaths. Did he regret his invention? Not at all. He enjoyed the glory, he gave new energy to humanity. That can help. Tomorrow that weapon can be used to deflect an asteroid that would destroy us. He regrets that he placed his child in the hands of those who did not use that knowledge for the benefit of humanity. To the powerful, for whom human lives are just numbers, and those who realized what they had done are - cry-baby, as one character said. Here, in addition to all that, we see a classic biographical film. Very well woven, with a few flaws. Some of these are the large presence of music in scenes, where it is placed in scenes where someone is talking. It is constantly heard. When characters like the main one are walking, they enter the room and music is there. No need. That's what wasn't needed on that scale. Another minus is that the start is a bit slow. Not meeting him at the university, which was really cool, but all that getting into the story around the Manhattan Project. I get the impression that Nolan did this on purpose to inflate the film to a three-hour running time. Like the old epic classics. But this film, when compared to today's commercials that overwhelm us, can comfortably be called an epic classic despite some flaws. Many singled out the absence of women as one of those. They are even in some way well depicted considering the time and the work the main characters in this story deal with. The tension is brilliantly portrayed by the anticipation of the atomic bomb test and what happens afterwards. After that, you have one scene as well as the ending itself, which can comfortably be called the best in the film. The scenes of testimony before the committee and congress are reminiscent of courtroom dramas and thrillers. Cillian Murphy rocked this role, he portrayed Oppenheimer perfectly. He might even win an Oscar. However, Robert Downey Jr. Stole the show. A great performance of his character, Strauss. I think that if he doesn't win an Oscar now, he never will. It would be completely deserved. Emily Blunt is also good in the scenes where she is represented more. She did a great job on this. Matt Damon, smarmy, brings the humor. Gary Oldman is excellent in that one scene. Rami Malek, very small role and silent. All in, a movie that you will love if you are a Nolan fan and love this genre. I can say - the best movie of the year so far.

10.title: The film is valuable
10.content:
Christopher nolan is one of my role models in filmmaking.

One of the most anticipated films of the year for many people, myself included, Oppenheimer largely delivers. Much of it's great. I feel like I loved two of its three hours, and liked the other hour.... but it's that fact that stops me from adoring the entire thing. I know with Christopher Nolan's Dunkirk, that clicked on a second watch, so maybe Oppenheimer will need one too. That being said, I don't feel the need to rush out and see it again too soon, because it was a long and exhausting film.

But in many ways, I can't deny it was an exceptionally well made one. It looks and sounds as amazing as you'd expect, feeling as though it accurately captures the time period it's set in, and containing amazing sound design and one of the year's best scores so far. Every performance is good to great, but the film belongs to Cillian Murphy, and I feel like he's the lead actor to beat at this stage, if we're talking (early) awards consideration.

The film's at its best when it focuses on being a psychological thriller featuring a famous historical figure, and at one point, it even turns into a psychological horror film. There's one sequence in here involving a speech that's particularly terrifying. It also manages to have some very suspenseful moments, even though its story is commonly known history at this point.

I did really feel the length in the final hour, though, and maybe I wish that final act had been more of an extended epilogue, rather than a whole third of the movie. I currently feel as though I would've loved Oppenheimer more had it been 2.5 hours instead of 3, but nothing about it was bad by any means; just a little patience testing (this is very subjective - I remember feeling like the similarly long Babylon totally justified its runtime, though others didn't feel that way).

I'm left feeling like I watched a film that wasn't a slam dunk, but was incredible for more of its runtime than it wasn't. And that's still worth celebrating, and makes Oppenheimer worth seeing in cinemas for sure.

10.title: Oppenheimer (2023)

Emily Blunt (Kitty) and Florence Pugh (Jean Tatlock) were good, but even better was Robert Downey, Jr. (Strauss) who deserves an award for his performance in the film.

The pacing was perfect, which is vital for a 180-minute long movie. I never felt the story stall or became bored or restless, despite it being such a long movie.

The sounds and visuals in this film are mind-blowing. I was specifically in awe of the detonation scene; the seconds that ticked by between seeing the bomb and hearing the bomb were immensely powerful and moving. The bomb scene, while vitally important to the film, only takes up a few minutes. What's important, though, is that thought and care that went into that scene is present throughout the film.

This is some of Nolan's best work and I'm thoroughly impressed by it. I was worried that it was being overhyped, but it was everything that was promised and more.

10.title: An originally-sinned masterpiece
Fast paced, harsh, naked , brutal , zero judgemental
10.content:
There are numerous occasions where Hollywood has gifted the world the stories that celebrate the human emotion, invention , the lives they lived and historical events which created an impact on human history as we know it but only a few of them have been able to create an impact on the viewer's mind like this. The opening scene of the movie which features a haunting background theme and Oppenheimer facing a bureaucratic enquiry on him against his appeal to revoke his security clearance in Atomic Energy Comission but rejected because of his affiliation with communist community. Seemingly lost in his thoughts , Noland took a dive to Oppenheimer's early days where he could be seen working as a researcher in Cavendish Laboratory under Cambridge University in England. Interacting with Neils Bohr , who suggested him continuing his theoretical research on Quantum Physics which wasn't much popular in the USA back then , he returned to his homeland where he worked with Ernest Lawrence who invented the "Cyclotron" after completing his PhD in physics in Cambridge, until he was approached by General Leslie Groves to get involved in Project Manhattan to develope the first neuclear bomb. Assuring Groves about his zero sympathy towards communism , Oppenheimer takes charge of the project and gathers all of the industrial might available in the USA to develop the first atom bomb before Nazi Germany could make one. The movie then proceeds with further Historical events towards the event where they successfully conducted the "The Trinity Test" . After the Hiroshima and Nagasaki event Oppenheimer finds himself guilty for the reason of the death of the countless people and starts to advocate the adverse effects of neuclear bombs in human civilization which was not received well by Lewis Strauss, a chairperson in Atomic energy commission who ploys his plan to strip Oppenheimer of his political influence.

Ths is the history as we know it. But the benchmark screenplay from which uses a non linear story telling which is a very classic signature style of Nolan gets the audience hooked to the screen from the very fast moment combined with the absolute brilliant musical score that turns the biopic into a historical thriller that will stay as a prime example of brilliance. The cinematography and the editing work of Jenifer Lame will never let you move your eyes from the screen away. The nudity used onscreen could feel a little excessive and unnecessary at the beginning but as the story proceeds , we could see the relevance of it in the movie. When Oppneheimer was being stripped and judged because of his scandalous affairs more than the contribution he made , we can see the scandal sensanization of social structures that makes people vulnerable at their weakest without trying to whitewash the characteristical traits of him, rather Nolan leaves it to the audience. He doesn't judge his characters, he just told the story as it happened. One particular aspect of the movie is using black n white and colour for two main characters, Oppenheimer and Lewis Strauss. Differentiation of the two characters and their mindset by using this technique without commenting on them is the cinematic brilliance of Nolan of giving the audience que to how to receive them.

Cillian Murphy became Openheimer totally. The usual mannerisms of Cillain Murphy was totally missing and when you will think that he stole the show , RDJ just set the fire on screen with his unrecognisable appearance and intense acting prowess. All the other cast did a fabulous job in their respective roles thanks to the brilliant casting.

As usual every Nolan movie is incomplete without a little indecisive ending that leaves so many questions for audience. He asks the question to the audience because this Manhattan project had created a series of events , but was Openheimer ever able to forgive himself for being the god of death ?

In a short conclusion , "Oppenheimer" is a masterpiece in every aspect , the technical aspects such as lighting , set design , sound design, costume design , colour and grading of this movie are too high standard that will always inspire other film makers forever.

P. S. Thai movie is a must watch in Imax screens , especially for the Trinity test sequence. The tension building of that scene just can't be described in words.

10.title: Oppenheimer, The perception of Safety
10.content:
This movie is truly amazing I mean it's very hard to break it down into words

Starting off with the pacing of Oppenheimer this movie feels more like a 2 hour 15 minute movie than a 3 hour movie, part of this is from the switching between timeframes and back & white.

Previously Nolan had done this in his movie Dunkirk with his constant switching and plot shifting and I wasn't a fan of it, however this method is vastly improved in this movie to where plot points matter with the other scenes, the changes are done in well timed spots and don't switch back and forth to a ridiculous degree.

Moving onto the visuals, the practical effect bomb scene is one of, the greatest scenes, we will ever see. The way it's done makes you feel as though you're right there watching this happen. The scene that surrounds this scene is absolutely legendary, to the countdown before detention, to the moments after where Oppenheimer is hallucinating seeing the death and destruction it'll cause. Overall the visuals are fantastic.

Whereas a lot of Nolan movies challenge your perception (Interstellar: Space, Inception: Dreaming/ The Mind, Memento: Memory, Tenet: Time) Oppenheimer challenges the perception of safety. Throughout the movie the theme of safety is pushed through the concepts of 1930s-40s Germany, The possibility that when the bomb goes off the world will end, the safety that the bomb takes away from the world, and the safety that Oppenheimer will have his platform to voice his concerns about the Atomic Bomb

And finally this movie has the greatest villain in Cinema, our country, the United States. As Oppenheimer finishes making the Atomic Bomb he realizes that it will bring the end of the world. In his attempts to bring this to light through his words and policies he is attempted to be silenced by Lewis Strauss played by Robert Downey Jr, and as he sets up a Pseudo Court that's not a trial it seems as if Strauss is the Villain, however he isn't.

Strauss is just the lapdog or symptom of the Villain, of which is the United States. The United States villainization of Communism to start, for a country saying you can have any opinion you want, it makes you into an enemy and treasonous if you even listen about communism. And then comes to the other problem the fact that if the United States has the power to do something, they will do it. For example in the movie once they acquire the power of the Atomic Bomb they turn around and use it on Japan with seemingly no hesitation. And of course when Dr. Oppenheimer shines light on this fact and how dangerous this weapon is, he is silenced.

Overall Oppenheimer is a movie that takes more then a quick thought to decipher, contains Oscar level acting from the likes of Cillian Murphy, Emily Blunt, Robert Downey Jr, Rami Marek, Matt Damon, and Florence Pugh. It has truly incredible visual effects from a director who respects the art and doesn't deliver halfasses to any degree. While also delivering an incredible story, there is no doubt in my mind that Oppenheimer will be remembered as an All Time Great and win many awards.

After a rewatch in the Theaters there's no doubt that this movie is a 10/10 and officially puts Christopher Nolan into the Quentin Tarantino and Stanley Kubrick tier of the greatest Directors of all time.

10.title: Christopher Nolan's Best Film Yet
10.content:
In the world of film, Christopher Nolan holds a high bar for storytelling. With 'Oppenheimer,' he once again proves why he's at the top of his game. The film is a rich tapestry of skill and creativity, leaving the audience captivated from start to finish.

The direction and editing of the film play out like a master class in cinema, turning every moment into a memorable snapshot. The visual appeal of the movie, enriched by the cinematography, is a feast for the eyes, painting each scene in vibrant tones and intricate detail.

The cast is a star-studded line-up of Hollywood's finest, and Nolan expertly uses their talent to add depth to the movie. Even in brief appearances, the performances shine, demonstrating the respect Nolan commands as a director.

The film's claim of avoiding CGI is fascinating, leaving the audience wondering how such effects were achieved. If it's true, it puts 'Oppenheimer' in a unique spot in movie history, celebrating the power of real-world visual magic.

The bomb testing scene is a high point of the movie, creating an immersive experience that outshines even the biggest blockbuster premieres. The spellbound silence of the audience was proof of the scene's impactful execution.

While I won't spoil any more of the movie, I urge you to see 'Oppenheimer.' It's a film that grabs your attention and stays with you long after you've left the theater. Ideally, it should be experienced on the big screen, where its cinematic scope can be fully appreciated.

10.title: "Prometheus stole the fire from the gods and gave it to man. For this, he was chained to a rock and tortured for eternity."
10.content:
The film opens with a quote from the well-known tales of Greek mythology. The story of Prometheus resonates all too well with that of Oppenheimer. Whether prophet or Prometheus, the man behind the atomic bomb will suffer like a Shakespearean tragedy.

The initial scenes of the film consist of montages depicting the workings of quantum mechanics. However, they resemble most what was transpiring in the mind of the then-young student J. Robert Oppenheimer (portrayed by Cillian Murphy). Fragments of thoughts visualized as a nightmare filled with delusions. He saw his ideas taking shape, much like the rain falling into the pond he gazed at. The water represented the world, each droplet a bomb, foreshadowing the inevitable end.

Director Christopher Nolan (known for Inception, The Dark Knight) employs extensive dialogue to unravel the story, music to give voice to the visuals, and visual spectacle to realize gritty realism. As an advocate of shooting on film (the first film recorded in original IMAX black and white scenes) and minimizing CGI, Nolan takes it a step further with this film. The entire 3-hour epic is crafted using 100% practical effects. All of this is masterfully visualized by Dutch cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema and soundtracked by Ludwig Göransson. It's reminiscent of the work of Zimmer, with whom he previously collaborated. Here too, a conscious decision was made to compose the film score independently of the visuals. This means the composer didn't see the footage but created the music solely based on the story's emotions. And it pays off.

Similar to Dunkirk, Nolan once again launches two converging strands, namely Fission & Fusion.

Fission (color) tells the story in the first person from Oppenheimer's perspective. Fusion (black and white) objectively narrates it from the viewpoint of Lewis Strauss, Oppenheimer's opponent, masterfully played by Robert Downey Jr.

The two components serving as storytelling devices have an intriguing merging effect.

Fission involves splitting a heavy, unstable core into two smaller ones, while fusion reactions combine two light cores. The literal definitions in the dictionary reveal a kind of underlying core (no pun intended) to the film's overall picture.

The film is long but never tedious. A dialogue-driven narrative can lose its way, but that doesn't happen here. The script is anything but, and Nolan keeps you on the edge of your seat in this nail-biting and intense retelling of history.

Why would a director like Nolan choose such a film? In 2020, during the filming of Tenet, he received a book from Robert Pattinson. That book was "American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer." Assisted by the authors of the book, Nolan crafts a perfect adaptation script. This is a captivating biography with a weighty message, executed flawlessly by someone in complete control of their work.

The actors also do a superb job. Apart from Murphy's expressive eyes, Emily Blunt delivers a flawless performance, particularly in the climax. Matt Damon remains quintessentially Matt Damon, a standard screen delight. Even Gary Oldman makes a small but noteworthy appearance as President Truman. And we must not overlook Tom Conti as Einstein. While awards may lose their meaning when you hand them out, this film certainly deserves recognition.

VERDICT: Nolan has never delved so deeply into the complex moral issues surrounding his characters. Ethical responsibilities bring forth significant questions, but the answers are complemented by the tight script. This character study, a blockbuster film-noir, is insanely beautiful. Based on its intellectual depth, Nolan's "Oppenheimer" surpasses his Joker arc as the most complicated, psychologically compelling portrayal of humanity, earning it a solid A+.

10.title: The Spectacular Rise and Dramatic Fall of an American Hero
10.content:
Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer film may be best film of 2023. Based on the book American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of Robert Oppenheimer, the film is a tour-de-force that brings to life the rise and fall of the "father of the atom bomb." Like in his films Tenet and Inception, Nolan uses non-linear storytelling. The film is divided into two parts. Part 1. Fission, which covers Oppenheimer's rise in the 1940s, as head of the Manhattan Project, creating the first atom bomb. And Part 2. Fusion, which covers his dramatic fall in the 1950s, after being accused of Communist ties, loses his security credentials.

Nolan, who's directed two Batman films, knows how to create and present a superhero. In one early scene, Oppenheimer, preparing to meet with his project team of scientists, dresses in his suit and tie, puts on his 1940s-style fedora, places his pipe in his mouth, then exits as though he were a superhero preparing to save the world.

The Manhattan Project was a race to build the A-bomb before the Nazis did. The most dramatic scene in the film takes place on 07/16/1945, the day that Trinity, the world's first atomic explosion takes place at Los Alamos, NM. The team of mostly American scientists and engineers party and celebrate the success of three years of experimentation and dedicated, hard work. But it appears that only Oppenheimer sees both the triumph and tragedy of the accomplishment. You can't help but think of a similar day on 07/17/1969, the day Apollo 11 astronauts walked on the Moon. Both celebrate American 🇺🇸 scientific and engineering achievements, but result in dramatically different outcomes.

Sherwin. Starring Cillian Murphy in the lead role, in addition to Matt Damon, Robert Downey Jr, Emily Blunt, and Florence Pugh, it subverts the usual biopic formula to create a brilliantly layered examination of a man throughout all of his incredible accomplishments and fundamental flaws.

During the height of the Second World War, theoretical physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer (Cillian Murphy) is recruited by the United States government to oversee the "Manhattan Project", a top secret operation intended to develop the world's first nuclear weapons. After becoming acquainted with the project's director Major General Leslie Groves (Matt Damon), Oppenheimer and the General come to an agreement that the best place to carry out such an undertaking is the vast desert of Los Alamos, New Mexico. As numerous other scientists and their families are brought in to this discreet location, Oppenheimer works tirelessly around the clock to build this weapon of mass destruction before the Nazis can devise their own. With the War raging and personal troubles mounting, Oppenheimer continues to push himself to his utmost limits, but soon suffers the consequences of his dedication.

10.title: Nolan proves you can still make such movies!
10.content:
Nolan has truly outdone himself with "Oppenheimer," proving that his previous works like Dunkirk, Tenet, and Interstellar were merely warm-ups for this three-hour, R-rated, adult drama filled with intense dialogue. It's a nostalgic throwback to the time when Hollywood used to create such thought-provoking movies. This might even be the last of its kind, or perhaps studios will learn from the underwhelming summer movie slate and start taking more risks instead of sticking to formulaic focus-group-approved films.

"Oppenheimer" delves into mankind's relentless pursuit of technology to better our lives, only to discover that it may ultimately be the thing that leads to our downfall. The timely comparison with AI adds an extra layer of intrigue. Unlike his previous mind-bending film, Tenet, Nolan keeps the plot more straightforward here, but he still plays with timelines to keep us on our toes. However, if you're not familiar with the historical context, some of the fast-paced dialogues may fly over your head as Nolan doesn't spoon-feed the audience. Things like who was the president at the time, what were the foreign policies back then, and some technical things like isotope export to Norway. But don't worry, they're not most important things for you to enjoy this masterpiece.

For those well-versed in the era, "Oppenheimer" feels like a riveting three-hour, 300-million-dollar documentary, providing an insider's view of the Manhattan Project and actual Senate hearings.

Now, some fans may complain about the sound mix and the movie's length. True, IMAX cameras tend to record sound louder than standard ones, and Nolan's aversion to ADR (Dubbing) may lead to some sound issues where the music overshadows the dialogues, especially during IMAX-shot scenes.

As for the runtime, I must say, every minute is justified in "Oppenheimer." Not a single scene feels unnecessary, and each line of dialogue contributes significantly to the story Nolan seeks to tell. In an age when people binge-watch eight hours of shows in a week, a three-hour immersive experience in front of an IMAX screen hardly feels long, especially when it's for what might be the best movie of the year.

10.title: A Remarkable Piece Of Filmmaking Adaptation
10.content:
The first time I watched Oppenheimer during the great Barbenheimer summer of 2023, I pegged it as a really good 9/10 star film-but maybe not the highest tier. It is indeed a departure from director Christopher Nolan's usually trafficking in mind-bending (often time-bending) science fiction or fantasy. But after a pre-Oscars rewatch and a read-through of the "American Prometheus" book it cribs from, I've bumped Oppenheimer up to the full 10 stars. It is truly a landmark achievement in biopics.

For a very basic overview, Oppenheimer tells the story of the famed quantum physicist Robert Oppenheimer (Cillian Murphy) who would go on to create the first atomic weapon. While his work at Los Alamos comprises large swaths of this picture, Oppenheimer is also examined as a young free-thinker (maybe Communist?), as well as his post-WWII views on atomic warfare (away from hawk and towards dove). All the while, new chairman of the Atomic Energy Committee Lewis Strauss (Robert Downey Jr.) schemes to oust Oppie from that body.

The first thing to understand about Oppenheimer is that it isn't just one story. While it certainly portrays Robert's early life, the Manhattan Project, Strauss's wheedling, and the general conversation of atomic warfare post-WW2, the film is a pastiche of all those areas in service of a larger goal. So, when the Trinity Test is completed and there's still an hour of runtime, that is the reason why.

What is that larger goal? Well, besides capturing the Oppenheimer personage, the hallmark of Nolan's work here is examining the shades of gray in Robert's life. Viewers seeing Oppenheimer as "one thing or the other" will be challenged, as Nolan revels in the "middle ground". How can a man support Communist/Fascist causes and create the most destructive weapon of all-time for a capitalist government? How can a man be so brilliant in scientific principles but also so naive when it comes to basic life assumptions? How can the creator of such destruction turn away from nuclear proliferation and towards arms treaties? Finally, how can a government so thoroughly use a man of such prodigious talent and then immediately smear him when his values don't line up with "the state" any longer? Not only are these complex issues compelling through Nolan's specific Oppenheimer lens, but they ring as true today as they ever did in that man's life and times.

Of course, lest you think Oppenheimer sounds a bit too dour and self-serious, it in no way lacks any of a Nolan projects' usual panache. It is expertly shot by Hoyte van Hoytema, the score (Ludwig Goransson) is pulse-pounding yet subtle when needed, and Murphy & Downey are riveting as the leads. Being surrounded by the likes of Emily Blunt, Matt Damon, Josh Hartnett, and Florence Pugh (among others) doesn't hurt either. Simply put, Oppenheimer is as cinematic as, say, Interstellar-just in new and unique ways for Nolan's oeuvre.

I'll also say that reading Kai Bird's "American Prometheus" novel only enhances one's deeper understanding of Robert Oppenheimer's life and times. On first-watch, the film moves pretty fast through Oppie's younger days and it is easy to get a little confused. But armed with the book's deep-dive knowledge, film viewers will be even more privy to how masterful Nolan's portrayals are here.

So, by all means come to Oppenheimer for the expected "big boom" and Manhattan Project material--that's all edge-of-your-seat compelling. But along the way you may also realize that Oppenheimer's unique personality is the true focus of Nolan's creative vision here. In that way, Oppenheimer easily stands out as an achievement rivalling his earlier space, magic/fantasy, or superhero flicks.

10.title: Terrifyingly Awestruck
10.content:
Christopher Nolan has done it again and literally has blown the doors of cinema possibilities off the hinges. Oppenheimer is a masterclass of editing, pacing, scoring, cinematography, and above all, storytelling.

It's taken an entire day of digesting this film to arrive at a headspace where I can finally write down my thoughts-I am mind-blown. This was not just a movie but an experience, and one that will not soon be forgotten.

A week after it dropped into theaters, I secured tickets to witness the 3-hour epic in one of only 30 theaters in the world that was presenting it in true IMAX 70mm 15/70 film print. At the AMC Metreon in San Francisco, the movie was shown on a screen taller than a four-story building which made for a surreal atmosphere. Packed in every seat was 400+ people going on the journey through one man's life trying to delve into his psyche to understand his motivations. In the end, Nolan expresses Oppy's horrors, accomplishments, and regrets beautifully in a rollercoaster of interwoven timelines-looking at you Inception, Tenet, and Interstellar.

Every scene and shot was meticulous and edited to the upmost perfection to make the long odyssey go by in rapid pace-like a countdown clock. Speaking of ticking, the score by the admirable Ludwig Göransson was astounding and, of course, blew us away at times. The standout performances were incredible and telling of how many would drop everything to work with Nolan. Even the smallest of roles were taken by Academy-caliber talent, with surprises in nearly every scene. Nominations are all but confirmed for the awards season this year. An additional gold statue goes to Hoyte Van Hoytema for the outstanding cinematography and the ground breaking special effects working together to make a CGI-less terrifyingly beautiful epic with first-of-its-kind black and white IMAX film.

The extraordinary visuals, booming score, incredible performances, brilliant writing and intricate production design culminate into an enveloping and truly epic story-pushing through the atmosphere and becoming a masterpiece. Though not surprising from Christopher Nolan, Oppenheimer is a masterclass of storytelling and filmmaking in its highest level-and needs to be seen on the largest IMAX screen that you can get to before the countdown finishes.

10.title: Something of a miracle
10.content:
Thousands of events have to conspire for a film to arrive on the screen. The craft takes a lifetime to master, the business is as tough and competitive as any in the world, hundreds of people have to meet, millions of ideas need to merge, and most films die before they're even born. So when we get a movie where such artists join at the pinnacle of their talents, in perfect timing, with the perfect story, and the perfect theme, when age and experience now allow them to give us a piece of work that is so far above and beyond the general output, craft-wise and thematically, then it deserves to be called "something of a miracle".

A striking mastery has been delivered here by the team behind Oppenheimer. The standard of excellence is as high as it can be. The film absorbs and transports us, moves us, and terrifies us in a way only the best do, supplying the most emotional and exciting cinema experience. Nolan has become one of the most sophisticated and exciting dramatists that ever took to the big screen by extracting from such dense material many of the most suspenseful and engaging sequences put on screen. It is the most concentrated, virtuosic, and profound of his films.

Most remarkable is that it manages to make an emotional epic out of minute gestures. Cillian Murphy's performance is perplexing. Every moment he creates, he encapsulates the depth and intensity of every thought pondered by its paradoxical protagonist. The real miracle of this film is that the perfect material finally met this actor to allow his potential to be revealed in its entirety. And part of what allows him to do so is the support of the most amazing ensemble of performances in recent memory; especially Robert Downey Jr's who finally shows us once and for all that he is among the most talented actors of his or any other generation.

Melville wrote that "to produce a mighty book, you must choose a mighty theme", but one thing is to dream of tackling such themes, another is to execute them at the visceral level that this team has. The subject matter here is so crucial that it forces us to face questions about our existence that mind-boggle even the greatest minds in the universe.

Everyone has their personal goals to achieve, everyone has their personal world-view, everyone has their mistakes, setbacks and realizations, and everyone has their insecurities and deep-lying flaws. 10.title: A boom shell of a film

The film is a sweeping epic that explores the intersection of science, politics, and humanity, featuring a tour-de-force performance from Cillian Murphy as the enigmatic and troubled physicist.

From the opening frames, it's clear that Nolan is on a mission to craft a film that's both a tribute to Oppenheimer's genius and a nuanced exploration of his inner turmoil. The director's signature non-linear storytelling style is on full display, weaving together multiple timelines and narrative threads to create a rich tapestry of Oppenheimer's life.

Murphy's performance is nothing short of phenomenal, capturing the essence of Oppenheimer's intellectual curiosity, emotional intensity, and deep-seated vulnerability. He brings a depth and nuance to the character that's both captivating and heartbreaking, making it impossible not to become fully invested in Oppenheimer's journey.

The supporting cast is equally impressive, with standout performances from Emily Blunt as Oppenheimer's wife, Katherine, and Matt Damon as General Leslie Groves, the military leader tasked with overseeing the Manhattan Project. The chemistry between the leads is palpable, adding an extra layer of tension and emotional resonance to the film's already gripping narrative.

Nolan's direction is, as always, meticulous and masterful, coaxing outstanding performances from his cast while balancing the film's complex scientific and historical themes with ease. The cinematography is stunning, capturing the stark.

10.title: Great movie
10.content:
I found the movie difficult to follow at first. I've seen "Fat Man and Little Boy" and "In The Matter of J. Robert Oppenheimer" so I knew pretty much the parameters of the story.

"Fat Man and Little Boy" (with Paul Newman as General Leslie Groves) is a fairly straightforward narration of the development of the atomic bomb in the New Mexico desert. "In the Matter of J. Robert Oppenheimer" a 1968 stage play by Heinar Kipphardt about the security clearance taken away from J. Robert Oppenheimer, for his sympathies for the Communist Party, by Lewis Straus; I believe it became a PBS production. So, I had a fairly good background in the story. I thought to myself, as the movie unfolded with numerous flashbacks, how confusing this film would be without that background information and how easily lost the audience could be.

What is the subject matter of the movie is a more challenging question: is it simply about the development of a destructive bomb or is it about the moral implications of scientists developing a bomb, and their regret for being involved in development of weapons of mass destruction?

The movie starts out with a quote from the Bhagavad Gita: "Now I am become death, the destroyer of worlds." And Oppenheimer quotes the line with the first explosion of the atomic bomb, July 16, 1945. But there is a refrain from the get-go of the film of scientists creating such a destructive weapon. And the response that quiets the argument, "If Hitler had such a weapon, he would not hesitate to use it." And there is something disquieting about a background chant that to me sounded like jackboots of marching Nazis, as if to reinforce the question. Jackboots of any totalitarian state. (And what seemed unthinkable in 1945, now in 2023 so many nations own nuclear weapons, that any flash incident can end in nuclear holocaust. And North Korea insists on developing nuclear weapons for the sole purpose of destroying America.)

Peace comes to Europe in May before the Atom Bomb is finalized, but war continues in Japan. Truman orders the attack on Hiroshima and Nagasaki to bring a final and forceful end to what could be a projected battle to the loss of hundreds of thousands of lives.

Oppenheimer goes to Truman to bemoan the loss of life, that he feels personally responsible for; Truman is less than thrilled and never wants to see the "crybaby" (his words) Oppenheimer ever again.

Subsequent to the war, Lewis Straus, who in reality was indeed a very vindictive, mean spirited, petty person, wants Oppenheimer's security clearance taken away for his sympathies with the American Communist Party, of which his brother Frank is also an active member.

I saw the movie at San Francesco Balboa Theatre (35mm print) and they allowed for two breaks at the hour and 2-hour point of the three-hour movie. (I wouldn't detect the difference between IMax & 35 mm, ...)

It is not so terribly confusing a movie, it soon follows a straightforward narrative, but it is something of a challenge to follow.

10.title: A stunning combination of visual effects, performance and directing - telling the story of a immoral but complex human
10.content:
I've been working my way through the top 250.

You must see this movie in 70mm while you can. I drove over an hour to the one theater near me that is capable of 70mm and I would suggest you do the same.

I can say definitively that this is the greatest film I have ever witnessed, and I will never regret saying that. Watching it in 70mm was undoubtedly the most immersive cinematic experience I have ever had the pleasure of witnessing and experiencing. Nolan undertook what was undoubtedly the most challenging philosophically, morally and character in history. With the presentation of Prometheus and hist story at the beginning with the stunning effects he made possible, we embark upon the stunning story of J Robert Oppenheimer. We understand his beginnings as a scholar, a young man who since the beginning of his life has been challenged by the existence of the universe and what it means exemplified as a protagonists moral struggle with the green apple, as well as the loneliness he endured as a result of his never ending question. While length of the film could be daunting to some, Nolan does not take his time, and does not rush as he seeks to tell the odyssey of Oppenheimer. Oppenheimer was responsible for trinity and the events following, but more importantly the fate of the world. If you feel that the movie should have stopped at the end of trinity, then you simply just do not get the point of the film. Strauss becomes the epitome of evil and greed, and illustrates what Oppenheimer did, the mere mortals hands on celestial power, hands that cannot be trusted with the potential of mutual destruction. Nolan presents the simple fact that Oppenheimer in many ways was too philosophical and tortured by this world, and Nolan presents a fascinating biography of a flawed individual. But despite his wrongdoings, he undoubtedly understood the power of the creation he had hands on, and its effect on the world, the destruction of it. We never escape its grip on our shoulder. With each character in Oppenheimers life, we understand a different piece of humanity, with each character flawlessly performed by each actor and actress, no matter how minor the role. I firmly believe that this is Nolan's masterpiece, simply because of how it gives us so many answers, yet presents so many questions. Additionally, Nolan's masterpiece is the special effects he creates to demonstrate the magnitude and precision and particularity of the bomb created at trinity. Nolan has always looked at Kubricks odyssey as a model for film and innovation and effects, as well as its philosophy. Nolan has in his own way created his own odyssey, but focused on the most one of the most important men in the history of our planet. The ending is perfect. Einstein once fascinated by Oppenheimers bright mind in the field of physics has turned into one tortured by guilt. "Prometheus stole fire from the gods and gave it to man. For this, he was chained to a rock and tortured for eternity."

10.title: What you'd expect from Nolan, delivered in a captivating style
10.content:
STAR RATING: ***** Brilliant **** Very Good *** Okay ** Poor * Awful

J. Robert Oppenheimer (Cillian Murphy) is an awkward, studious trainee professor at Cambridge University, driven to put an unsuccessful attempt on the life of a hard-pressing lecturer within the walls of the educational establishment. Visiting professor Niels Bohr (Kenneth Branagh) admires Oppenheimer's non-conformist style, and invites him to study under his tutelage. On the verge of World War 2, with the aid of the hard edged Major Leslie Groves (Matt Damon), he attempts to split the atom, and design a nuclear device based on implosion rather than explosion, that sets him on course to create the device that will define him. Years later, a courtroom procession plays out, where the head of Oppenheimer's learning establishment, Lewis Strauss (Robert Downey Jr.) must defend his reputation, while Oppenheimer's suspected communist past comes back to haunt him.

By now, it can be safely said that Christopher Nolan has become a household name, with an established filmmaking style. He has become known for all out, lengthy sagas, that leave no stone unturned, and have an art house, eccentric touch to them that singles them out. I've found them largely hit and miss, but at least it can be said that I knew what to expect, and have little excuse to be put off from what has become a signature trademark. And as such, Oppenheimer was a highly pleasing experience, an in-depth examination of the mind and soul of one of history's most controversial figures.

Despite the sprawling length, it's essentially just a life story interspersed with a courtroom drama, with both segments playing out together smoothly and absorbingly. Cillian Murphy is the central player of an all-star cast (including Gary Oldman in a cameo at the end as President Eisenhower), in a film determined to examine the character at the heart of its core, and so it has a beneficial lead star in Murphy, who portrays a quiet, detached individual, with a lot of deeply entrenched internal struggles, but with a focused, determined mindset to his work. A very haunting scene plays out in the third act, where he has to give a speech, and imagines not naked people, but the scarred, charred remains of those who've felt the power of his experiment.

Nolan is a cinematic artiste with a by now very familiar style, and in this true life, historical project of his, it all comes off wonderfully (even with some gratuitous nudity!) and results in a thoroughly absorbing experience. *****

10.title: The moments after the test in Los Alamos felt like scenes straight out of a horror movie.
10.content:
Is it a popcorn flick??? Oh hell no. Watch Barbie instead. Is it dense??? Oh yes!!! It's way too big.

This is undeniably Nolan's best work till date. Here, we get to see, not "Christopher Nolan, The Great Conceptual filmmaker obsessed with literal and empirical representations", but "Christopher Nolan, The Great Dramatist who has unexpected chops for us audiences". It would take years, if not decades, for Indian Cinema to come up with something like this that's made with so much research, sincerity and dedication. The story is legendary, the runtime was perfect, if not asking for more. The camerawork was epic, the dialogues were crisp, the music was intense and the screenplay felt a bit stretched out at times. Specially the interrogation sequences felt a bit dense.

It's all about consequences. Oppenheimer changed the face of global warfare and geopolitics forever. So the cost that he had to pay must also have been equally big. Just like Prometheus was destined to bear torture for eternity, for his love towards humans and for his defiance against the Gods. From being a boisterous advocate of unpopular opinions, to being riddled with self contradictions, Nolan deserves accolades for an immensely thorough dissection of such a controversial personality and serving justice to the stature of his feat by skillfully portraying the horrifying impact it had on him and his life.

Cilian Murphy did a brilliant job which just proves the range of his acting capability. Be it Thomas Shelby, Scarecrow or Oppenheimer, the man can do it all. But take a bow for Robert Downey Jr. I couldn't have imagined in a million years that he would be able to nail such a dramatic role with so much ease. From Tony Stark to being such a method actor, this man was marvelous in the movie. Emily Blunt didn't have much to do, but kudos to the way in which her character stands up for her husband and the awareness that she has of her responsibility. Florence Pugh was there too and Matt Damon's "Cigar Smoking General Uncle Sam" matched well with the conflicting, academic personality of Oppenheimer.

On and all, this is a once in a lifetime experience. And it's meant only for the theatres. It's not an action movie. It's an intense drama about the life of "The Man, The Myth, The Legend". The American who changed the world. Feel your seats vibrate and be on the edge the entire time as the entire cast goes through unfathomable moral dilemmas, confusing questions, world threatening stakes and life-long mountainous guilt. This will definitely be one of my forever favourites.

10.title: The American Prometheus

Also, the brief scenes between Oppenheimer and Einstein were sweet and caught me off guard and provided a layer of comfort to an otherwise perplexing film. Find yourself a friend like Albert Einstein.

Final verdict: 10/10.

10.title: Oppenheimer - Beautifully terrifying Masterpiece
10.content:
Probably the only director of our times whose name is enough to pull the crowd to theaters. His best quality is that he thinks that the audience is smart enough to understand and doesn't spoon feed everything.

Oppenheimer is a biographical thriller which makes Nolan sit in another league of filmmakers. His Nolan ness is stamped in every scene. Caution - don't expect action or masala entertainment here, it's a very serious study of the character of the father of the atomic bomb.

Every time I see a biopic I want to go into the psyche of the protagonist but only a handful of movies were successful in doing that, and this is one of them. From the first frame till the last one you are with Oppenheimer, Nolan grabs you by neck and puts it into the mind of the character. His struggles, his inner turmoil, his guilt you feel it in every frame. This was also possible because of Cillian Murphy, It will be his career defining role. He has just become Oppenheimer. In some of the scenes his acting chops are just masterclass.

Casting is done so perfectly that you cannot imagine any other actor in that role. RDJ makes worthy as a opponent to Cillian Murphys character. His brilliance overshadows his persona. Mat Damon, Emily Blunt, Cassey Affleck, Gary Oldman every one is brilliant in their portrayal. This is Nolan's legacy that great actor's have agreed to appear for one or two scenes just to be associated with Nolan and trust on his filmaking. Everyone has given their best.

Music by Ludwig Göransson is special, it perfectly fits the scenes and makes the movie more immersive. Although I felt the Hans Zimmer mark on it. Cinematography, editing, production design, writing you name it every department has given their best to this project. Highlights are 2 sequences the detonation of the bomb and the gym speech sequence. This is the most refined film making you will get. Hats of to his vision and guts to not to use CGI. But still managing to get emotions out of you.

We in India had something similar to this, the story of Nambi Narayanan. R Madhavan tried his best to make his directorial debut from this story but it felt short on a lot of levels. If you really want to compare, then compare The Nambi effect with Oppenheimer, you will know how much behind we are than Hollywood.

For me by far this is Nolan's best as pure film making point of view. It's 3 hours long, dialogue and conversation heavy but the way it is paced you won't feel the length. But it doesn't have the same re-watchable quality like his other movies. It's not for everyone, normal film audience will be bored. But it's a feast for cinephiles like me. It stunns you with his craft. More power to Nolan. It's an Oscar studded movie, by far the best film of the year. Thank you for this and as always eagerly waiting for your next.

10.title: best
10.content:
"Oppenheimer" is a mesmerizing cinematic masterpiece that delves into the riveting life of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the brilliant scientist behind the development of the atomic bomb during World War II. Directed by the visionary filmmaker, this biographical drama transcends the boundaries of a typical historical documentary, offering an intimate and thought-provoking exploration of Oppenheimer's complex character and his moral dilemmas.

The film's cinematography is breathtaking, capturing both the haunting beauty of the nuclear tests and the somber depths of Oppenheimer's conscience. The narrative brilliantly weaves through his personal struggles, intellectual brilliance, and the grim reality of unleashing the ultimate weapon of destruction. The audience is transported into the era, immersing them in the atmosphere of tension and uncertainty.

What sets "Oppenheimer" apart is the raw and authentic portrayal of its characters. The lead performance is a tour de force, as the actor masterfully conveys Oppenheimer's inner turmoil and the burden of his choices. The supporting cast, including fellow scientists and military personnel, add depth and authenticity to the narrative, breathing life into history.

The film isn't merely a historical account; it raises profound ethical questions about the consequences of scientific discoveries and the responsibility of the scientists behind them. It prompts viewers to ponder the implications of progress and the human cost of such groundbreaking achievements.

While the runtime may feel long for some, every moment is justified as it allows the audience to fully grasp the emotional journey of Oppenheimer. The dialogues are insightful and profound, adding layers of depth to the character dynamics.

In summary, "Oppenheimer" is a captivating film that not only honors the legacy of one of history's most enigmatic figures but also challenges viewers to contemplate the weight of their own decisions. A cinematic triumph that deserves accolades for its storytelling, performances, and thought-provoking themes. This is a must-watch for both history enthusiasts and those who seek cinematic brilliance with substance.

10.title: As close to a perfect movie as I've ever seen
10.content:
So much to say about this remarkable achievement in film, but I will just say that it's quite possibly the best film I have ever seen. Not to be confused with it being my favorite, although I really did enjoy it as well as recognizing it being a pretty flawless film.

I won't delve too much into the story, but will say that similar to his outstanding hit Inception, Christopher Nolan manages to conduct three separate but connected stories in this film, all connected to the title character, J. Robert Oppenheimer.

One story is of Oppenheimer's life leading up to, including, and aftermath of his being put in charge of the US' creation of the atomic bomb in WWII.

The second story is of a sham hearing put together by his nemesis, Lewis Strauss, to discredit him after he speaks out in favor of restraint following the successful detonation of two of his bombs over Japan to end WWII.

The third story follows a few years later when Strauss himself is before a hearing of his own when trying to be confirmed as President Eisenhower's Commerce Secretary.

The film shows the many ironic parallels between the hearings of Oppenheimer and Strauss, mixing in Oppenheimer's life story as it proceeds.

Not going to give all the specifics and spoilers but here's what I found so exceptional about this film - the story itself was incredibly compelling, both collectively and individually among the three aforementioned sub-plots, the cast was as deep and talented a cast as I've ever seen assembled on film, the performances were all perfectly done with no glaring overacting or miscasting, and the writing and directing were brilliant, in typical Nolan fashion. In particular, outstanding performances from Murphy, Downey Jr, Blunt, and Damon stood out.

It's very rare that I give a movie a perfect 10 score but this movie earned every bit of it along with the many Oscar nominations that I'd expect are coming early next year.
