10.title: Hamilton for the nuclear era
10.content:
Hamilton (the musical) is special for many reasons: amazing sung, racially diverse, phenomenally written. But most of all, because it provided our current generations a modern connection to and humanization of the founding of our nation. Though it is about their primary author, the musical is as much a subtle honorific of the Federalist Papers and their philosophy, which in turn shaped the Constitution and our whole way of governance.

Oppenheimer is poised to play a strikingly similar connection and humanization of the US' great international turning point, it's rise as a superpower due to the advent of the atomic age.

Nolan crafts a powerful dramatic documentary of Oppenheimer's adult life. It is beautifully shot; fantastically acted; perfectly written and paced. The music is spectacular.

The plot humanizes the creation of the most inhumane device every created by our species. It did not glorify, yet it also did not expressly vilify, being more content to tell the story of the man who would become known as the father of the atomic bomb, not just the story of the bomb itself. There is the trappings of McCarthyism and anti-communism. There are the mundane flaws of the man and those around him. But Nolan crafts the story and its telling to make these the conduit. Oppenheimer is never actually about the power of communism, or of love, or lust; it's about the power of the atom, and you feel that pull throughout.

When taken in as a whole, Oppenheimer immerses you in the moments when our nation truly entered the stage as a terrifying force of power, and perhaps peace. I left with a sense of awe; amazement; perhaps a dash of fear, at the retelling of that piece of our history.

There is still more to unpack with Oppenheimer- the cinematics, the sound, the production. How the reservations of the scientists ring hauntingly similar to the concerns raised by AI researchers and climate activists. Such a multi-faceted film, that this humble review on IMDB will leave for another time.

Brilliant, brilliant, brilliant.

10.title: Review on openheimer
10.content:
The film Oppenheimer is a mystery to me; here is a movie just over three hours in length, yet there are no gunshots, no car chases, no fist fights, rarely does anyone swear, and we don't actually see atomic bombs being dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. There is some brief sex in it, but the two people involved don't seem to be enjoying themselves. We're left with a tremendous amount of dialogue and very little action.

Don't get me wrong, I've been guilty of a shortened attention span too .I believe superhero films definitely have their place too

Robert Oppenheimer is the hero of this story, and he has been tasked with overseeing the infamous Manhattan Project's Los Alamos lab in New Mexico during World War II. His team's mission is to build the world's first atomic bomb before the Germans do. But make no mistake-this is Oppenheimer's story: every scene is about Oppenheimer, his decisions, and the repercussions of those decisions that will haunt him for the rest of his life.

10.title: Not for everyone!

10.title: Destroyer of worlds
10.content:
Unlike all his other movies, there are no CGI effects in this Nolan's latest. It does have some well placed visual effects which are even more impressive knowing they are real instead of CGI. If you are lucky to have access to an IMAX 70mm cinema, go. I've seen the aspect ratio is cropped in some other cinemas.

Some scenes are in black and white - and if I remember correctly, it's those related to Strauss and his congressional hearing. My interpretation is that those are lifeless moments pertaining to government and bureaucracy as opposed to the achievements of the physicists.

There's a large part of the movie dedicating to the physics and setting up the logistics. Some of the science is obviously explained to the audience. And, how many times does Oppenheimer write the board? A few.

As a non-American the patriotic overtones ring a bit too much but understandable why they are placed. I didn't know that Los Alamos was developed for the research of the A bomb.

The explosion - the first successful test of the atomic bomb - is a triumph of their efforts. But it didn't read as such to the audience or to the protagonist. The silence between the visual presence of the mushroom cloud and the following blast leaves space for agonising moments of anticipation and reflection.

Everyone but Oppenheimer (and the audience? Maybe just me) celebrate; after all their efforts paid off. The moment of reflection arrives when they hear the news Japan had been bombed, when it becomes part of reality not physics experiments. Once released into the hands of the army, the creators no longer have any control over their creation. The movie hints at continuity in search of the ultimate bomb as it brings up the possibility of creating an H bomb - which terrifyingly is today's nuclear bomb.

In the lead up to the movie I came across a video showing all nuclear detonation tests. There are over 2000 of them. Only 2 were ever used as weapons in war. Otherwise world powers have been bombing the hell out of themselves and I can't help but find irony in endlessly testing such a weapon, in the hopes that is never needed.

Oppenheimer gets investigated for political reasons. Can't help but draw parallels between Oppenheimer and Turing, whose governments treated them with scorn following historic achievements. Both only received retractions from officials decades after their demise. Is there perhaps a takeaway here that the government will shield brilliance for as long as they need it and not a second more.

Cillian Murphy is excellent. He'll probably be the top contender for an Oscar. Though I daresay Robert Downey Jr steals the show with his performance of a controlling, narcissistic political figure. Younger viewers may only know RDJ as Iron Man but he has always been an excellent character actor, including biographical roles. It's great to see him use these chops again. The black and white reminds me of Good Night and Good Luck, which takes place in the same era, about suspected communists. Brilliant showing from Matt Damon, too, above my expectations. Florence Pugh and Emily Blunt are underutilised though Blunt gets a satisfying scene towards the end. There's Kenneth Branagh with a trademark stately showing.

10.title: The Galaxy of Nolan
10.content:
At least three different timelines, intricately interwoven. Black-and-white and color sequences, numerous flashbacks, rapid transitions between the scenes. A complicated, probably even impossible task for the most regisseurs and script writers. Not for Christopher Nolan. He does it on everyday basis. He did it even more stunningly. One can think of Tenet, Prestige, Memento... Firstly, it is a drama at its finest. Scientists are not too different from other people, after all, and often have the very same problems in their professional and family life. By no means are they always asexual bookworms. And even being the best physicists in the world, they can be extremely naïve. Several decades ago, they could be easily lured into thinking that some super-powerful weapon could end all wars on our planet forever. But they were definitely not the only ones who thought so. They are just as flawed as everybody, and they also pay dearly for their mistakes.

Secondly, it is a historical film with the meticulously reproduced atmosphere of previous epochs. You can feel the heat of a scorched desert, appreciate the vintage clothing and experience that shuddering, all-consuming paranoia of the hunt for communist spies which ruined so many lives.

It is even a superb detective film. If one hasn't read the story of Oppenheimer before watching the film, one can spend some time guessing whether it was Oppenheimer or someone close to him who leaked secret information to Soviets. The tension builds up gradually, but unrelentingly.

Finally, it excels as a film about science and scientists. It shows the fascinating beauty of science, despite exploring deeply also its destructive side. There is an exquisite scene, where only a pair of phrases and scientific termini are enough for Oppenheimer to reach a conclusion that the Nazis are losing.

It probably would be banal to praise the actors' performance. Who could not predict that Cillian Murphy would be unrivalled in this role? But it is worth mentioning that Matt Damon doesn't look bleak and irritating in Oppenheimer, in contrast to many of his previous films - and it is quite an achievement.

Objectively, Oppenheimer has all characteristics necessary to be worthy of many Oscars. Subjectively, it probably would not win them. Will it at least be nominated? Nolan does not comply with current trends. And it is good that way. The trends can change every day - Nolan will remain. Since The Theory of Everything about Stephen Hawking, there was no such a film. It is enough to say that Nolan manages to awaken empathy for Japanese without even showing any Japanese victims of the nuclear bomb. Who could do more?

10.title: "I believe we did it"
10.content:
There is a moment. Right after the detonation. We see the horrific realisation on his face in a realm of silence. The pure form of terror in its most subtle form as he understands what he has done. And just for a moment you realise along with him that the world has been changed.

When the final scene finished playing and the score came to its conclusion there was a brief period of stillness throughout the audience as everyone momentarily considered what they had just witnessed. And for the first time in my cinematic experience I was just lost for words. As everyone left their seats and my dad and my friend spoke to me I just sat there pondering the meaning of it all, barely replying. And then I realised myself that I'd never been affected by a film in that way before. There are those that I have enjoyed more than this, that have brought out more emotions in me and even those that I consider better made. But the visceral experience that was. It was just phenomenal.

Perhaps I have been blown away to an extent that isn't widely felt. But I think that most of us can agree that Nolan has presented us with his masterpiece no matter how it compares to his previous filmography and what we prefer or not. By placing all the elements of this film together with all the hard work so many have put into it we have been delivered something of brilliance. A hauntingly beautiful score from Ludwig Göransson which gave me chills whenever it played that masterful crescendo of power. The incredible sound design that packs an almighty punch emphasising the true power behind these horrifying creations. The alluring cinematography of Hoyte van Hoytema suitably demonstrating both claustrophobic discomfort and breath-taking pictures of art. The screenplay exhibiting the true power of words both from those spoken by real life figures and Nolan's careful hand. The performances of the cast as a whole bringing these people to the big screen in fascinating ways but most notably of Cillian Murphy and his outstanding and without a doubt Oscar-worthy take on Oppenheimer and of Robert Downey Jr reaffirming his acting prowess in the portrayal of Lewis Strauss. And finally, the considerably fantastic direction of Christopher Nolan to administer this truly wonderful experience which somehow feels like a culmination of all his work that came before.

I can't say it was without flaws unfortunately. I felt at points it became a little dragged out which took me out of the experience and the editing also felt a little too choppy to the point where it was hard to follow sometimes. However, the pacing may have been from my own fault of focusing too much on the adrenaline fuelled sequences of visceral sensation preventing me from admiring the significance of the sections of lower tempo and the editing was clearly deliberate to present the chaotic nature of the reality behind this complex period in modern history.

I spent a few brief instances looking around at the audience And it reminded of my love of the cinematic world. The silence as everyone is completely immersed in what we are being shown. The impossible task of tearing your eyes from the screen. The pure engagement of this new world that you have been transported to. That is what film is about.

But truly, above everything, despite any of my overall opinion of entertainment or issues with the film. It was one of the greatest filmic experiences I've had and I honestly just cannot decide on how I feel about it all. It has completely thrown me.

There are numerous fantastic sequences within the film but the one that stood out to me was the ending. I will not unveil what it is or does but I was so overwhelmed with pure emotion that my eyes just glistened and a tear rolled down my cheek. With one final crescendo after all the symbolism, all the visual cues, all the foreshadowing, all the exploration of humanity, the consequence of action, the power of comradery, the fear of man. Nolan brings the hammer down with a consideration of reality and what we have done.

And it is terrifying.

10.title: A Stark Reminder on Nuclear Energy
10.content:
First off, a masterclass performance by Cillian Murphy. He emphatically captured the personality behind the first atomic bomb and "The Father of The Atomic Bomb". The film delivered on all fronts from Christopher Nolan and gave a great historical overview on Oppenheimer and how he came about the Manhattan Project. The film could have focused more on the war and less about the communist associations of his earlier life. But the film still was incredibly well written, directed and choreographed.

At the end of the day, I hope most people realize the frightening power of nuclear energy. No victor will and can be declared in nuclear warfare, the only victor is the dead.

10.title: Summary
10.content: Not Really a Biopic: As a viewing experience, Oppenheimer is a whole lot of movie, a man's life given the epic treatment - because he did do truly epic things, things that elevate his life story beyond the limitations of genre. Its best moments stand out as some of the most original and exciting filmmaking of the year, highs that do a lot to counterbalance the sequences which dive back into bureaucracy and comparatively petty rivalries. I really love the movie its a good movie and I enjoyed the ride.

10.title: Stunning experience
10.content: Oppenheimer combines both stunning visual and audio experiences! From the beginning of the movie all till the end, you can find yourself on the edge of your seat. The way Christopher Nolan is able to capture the fear in the characters is uncanny. Cilian Murphy delivers extraordinary acting and I'm sure he will be up for an Oscar nomination. 10.title: Oppenheimer: A Cinematic Symphony of Action and Emotion
10.content:
" Oppenheimer" is a breathtaking masterpiece that skillfully combines the elements of action, audio, acting, direction, and scene design into an unforgettable cinematic experience. 2. Audio: The audio design of "Oppenheimer" deserves special accolades for its immersive and evocative quality. The symphonic score, composed by Ludwig Göransson, elevates the movie to a whole new level. It blends perfectly with the on-screen action, accentuating emotional beats and intensifying the adrenaline-pumping moments. Additionally, the sound effects are expertly crafted, creating a dynamic soundscape that draws the audience deeper into the film's world. The combination of the powerful score and well-balanced sound effects makes the audio aspect of the movie a standout feature.

3. Acting: The performances in "Oppenheimer" are nothing short of exceptional. Led by a talented ensemble cast, each actor brings depth and authenticity to their characters. Cillian Murphy shines in the lead role, delivering a captivating portrayal of a conflicted hero torn between duty and personal struggles. The supporting cast, including Robert Downey Jr. And Emily Blunt and Matt Damon and others, deliver standout performances that contribute to the emotional resonance of the narrative. The chemistry among the cast members is palpable, adding further layers to the film's storytelling.

4. Scene Design: The movie's scene design is a visual treat that transports the audience to diverse and imaginative worlds. From sprawling urban landscapes to otherworldly realms, each setting is meticulously crafted to enhance the storytelling. The attention to detail in both practical and digital sets is awe-inspiring, creating a rich tapestry of visual splendor. The scene transitions are seamless and contribute to the overall flow of the film, making it an immersive and cohesive cinematic experience.

5. Direction: Under Christopher Nolan masterful direction, "Oppenheimer" achieves a harmonious blend of action and emotion. The director's vision is evident in every frame, showcasing a keen eye for detail and storytelling finesse. The film's pacing is skillfully managed, allowing both the action-packed moments and the character-driven scenes to breathe. 10.title: Masterful on The Page and The Screen
10.content:
At this point I'm sort of in awe at just now much Christopher Nolan is able to put his own stamp on every single genre he touches. Oppenheimer is a 3-hour long dialogue driven character drama but it still has all of the jaw dropping spectacle of The Dark Knight Trilogy, Inception and Dunkirk. The film just starts at a speed of 100 miles an hour and just keeps at that pace for the entire runtime and I can honestly say couldn't get enough of what Oppenheimer was offering.

Nolan's obviously so well regarded for jaw dropping visuals and this film is no different; the constant shifts between colour and black-and-white never feel jarring but instead purposeful and gorgeously realised. The trinity test scene is as mind blowing as it was built up to be. It's basically a perfect sequence that I can honestly say left me in awe, everything from the visuals, the tension, the little character moments and the performance come together for what I'm sure is going to go down as one of Nolan's all timer scenes. There are very few times I can say my jaw dropped in a theatre but this genuinely was one of them.

But I have to say the movie is just as good from a script perspective as it is from a visual one. The dialogue here is unbelievable, it's almost Shakespearean in how prophetic and atmospheric it is mixed with a good amount of dry humour Nolan's become known for. The script also does a very good job at condensing decades of history into a 3 hour runtime, it's definitely a lot to take in and can be overwhelming at points but despite the quick pace you really do feel the immense passage of time and toll that's being taken on the characters. That's not always easy to do visually and I'm amazed at how well this movie pulled it off.

I was initially disappointed with the rather factual title of Oppenheimer but having seen the film now it's very clear why Nolan chose it. Every single scene features him in some way, shape or form, even when he's not on screen he's usually the topic of conversation and by the end of the film you really do feel like you've seen an entire life play out on screen.

Cillian Murphy is absolutely incredible in this movie, I genuinely could not imagine anyone else playing Nolan's version of this person. He's very subtle and withdrawn for large portions and since Oppenheimer himself was such a flawed person Murphy has a lot that he has to convey emotionally and he hits every single beat perfectly. There's only a few select scenes where the characters psyche starts to break down and they happen just infrequently enough that they leave a lasting impression and that's something I appreciated about all the performances. They didn't feel the need give everyone an Oscar scene or moment; the outbursts are few and far between and most of the work is more subtle and poignant.

When I say that the film starts at a break neck pace I very much mean that as a positive and a negative. I can honestly say I was never bored but I'd also be lying if I didn't say that I wished Nolan would've let some scenes breathe a bit more. A lot of scenes feel like protracted montages and felt like we were flying through scenes so fast that I didn't always have time to register the information and in some cases the emotional beats Nolan was trying to give off.

Nolan works again with the same editor as he did with Tenet and I thought the editing in that film was particularly poor and while it's much improved here it still occasionally feels choppy and too quick cut for its own good. Even if it meant the film was longer I kept wishing Nolan would slow down and let some of these scenes breathe more because all my favourite scenes in the film feel like they have that space to play out in a more organic way.

Oppenheimer might not quite crack top 5 Nolan for me but honestly it's not far off. You have an incredible performance from Cillian Murphy at the centre that ties everything together beautifully, it's just as good on the page as it is on the screen and as break neck as the pace was it never once lost my full attention. This felt refreshingly different for Nolan without ever losing his signature stylistic choices that make him so successful. I'll be seeing it again in a few weeks and this is the first film I'll ever be seeing in IMAX and I could not think of a better one to start out on.

10.title: Incredible storytelling
10.content:
This movie, about J. Robert Oppenheimer and his role in the development of the atomic bomb, is a masterpiece!

For many viewers it mostly likely contains too much information to leave with the feeling that you are done with it after only one watch, but things get much clearer and obvious after a rewatch although it may not ever be entirely understandable. Anyway, the elements are put together in a genius way in every aspect, which makes the movie engaging from start to finish.

The technical aspects are amazing. The cinematography captures the highlight of every shot. The practical effects are so well executed that they make you wonder if they are CGI. The amazing soundtrack by composer Ludwig Göransson varies from being beautiful to epic to terrifying that helps to make the story as an emotional roller coaster. Last, but not least, the sound guarantees an illusion of realism. All of these aspects make sure to deliver an incredible cinematic experience.

The acting is fantastic. You barely think that the characters are played by real actors because you get completely lost in their performances. They really make sure to represent their characters in the most authentic way. And impressively enough, most of the actors look surprisingly similar to their characters, which is both funny and cool.

The story is split into two perspectives; the subjective perspective with its colored scenes, and the objective perspective with its black and white scenes. The movie as a whole is split, basically. The first half focuses mostly on Oppenheimer's subjective journey from being a student to becoming the father of the atomic bomb, and the second half focuses mostly on Oppenheimer's objective journey with the trial and being used by powerful people. First the rise, then the fall. I think the way the movie tells Oppenheimer's story with these aspects is very impressive. As said, there's a lot of information that pops up one after one without any break that forces you to stay engaged throughout the entire runtime. While you try to process every line, you almost get exhausted by it, which is a very clever way to keep the audience engaged in every moment. Before my first watch, I expected much more of the chemical reaction-scenes because I thought the story would be mostly about Oppenheimer and the atomic bomb, like a creator with his/her product, but it turns out it mostly focused on how his role changed throughout his career; he was first a physicist, but then became a political activist. The real deal is the people who decide to use the bomb, not the bomb itself. I think this is very important to keep in mind, and I'm glad with the way the movie told the story.

There was a lot of important characters in the movie, but there is no time to mention them all. Anyway, there were several characters that did the most impression to me. One of them was of course Lewis Strauss. He was the main antagonist against the protagonist Robert. He believed that Robert was a threat to America's nuclear program, and because he was a strong critic of Robert, he tried to dismiss Robert's from Atomic Energy Commission. There wasn't any proof of Strauss' actions being illegal, but wasn't it unfair how he arranged a closed trial and tried to get answers from Robert's privacy? It's very interesting how this "game" was played because there are speculations of Strauss' potential secrets. The second one is Kitty Oppenheimer. Despite her alcoholism, she was a personal fighter and an invincible shield for Robert. I felt that Kitty was socially stronger than Robert, and Robert didn't see his own objective perspective. I think if Kitty was Robert's "advocate", things would go much better for Robert's sake. During her testify, she significantly had much more control compared to Robert, and that says something. The last one is Albert Einstein. He is one of the most important men in the world, and he was a good supporter of Robert. However, one line that interested me was the following: "When they've punished you enough, they'll serve you salmon and potato salad, make speeches, give you a medal, and pat you on the back telling you all is forgiven. Just remember, it won't be for you... it would be for them.". Einstein could see the outcome and warned Oppenheimer, and the exact same thing actually happened.

After thinking about director Christopher Nolan's statement about Oppenheimer as the most important man in the history, he convinced me to believe so, too, especially after watching the movie. Oppenheimer is such an interesting man because of his paradoxical role. He was a fighter for science and a humanist. Oppenheimer wanted to use science to improve people's lives, but he was also aware of the danger of science. During the development there was always something that told him that he shouldn't do it, but he kept on going. After Oppenheimer became the father of the atomic bomb, he realized the destructive effects of it, and it terrified him. His target wasn't to destroy the world, but to help it. Then Oppenheimer had become Death, the destroyer of the worlds.

In conclusion, this movie is a masterpiece that tells the story of a complex and fascinating man. It's technically brilliant, with stunning cinematography, fantastic practical effects, and a beautiful score. The acting is also top-notch, with Cillian Murphy (as J. Robert Oppenheimer) giving a tour-de-force performance. The story is told in a unique and engaging way, with the movie split into two perspectives: the subjective perspective of Oppenheimer and the objective perspective of the world around him. This allows the movie to explore Oppenheimer's inner turmoil as he grapples with the destructive power of the atomic bomb, but also the political conflict between him and AEC. The movie also features a number of memorable characters, including Strauss, Kitty and Einstein. Overall, this is a must-see movie for anyone interested in history, science, or simply great storytelling.

10.title: Future Classic?
10.content:
Oppenheimer, the latest magnum opus by renowned director Christopher Nolan, is a cinematic achievement that transcends the boundaries of both science and history. This epic drama delves into the complex life and work of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the brilliant physicist and key figure behind the creation of the atomic bomb during World War II. Nolan's direction, coupled with a stellar cast and awe-inspiring visuals, delivers a thought-provoking and emotionally charged experience that leaves a lasting impact on the audience.

The film's strength lies in its meticulous attention to historical accuracy while artfully incorporating Nolan's signature storytelling techniques. The narrative chronicles Oppenheimer's personal journey, from his early academic pursuits to his leading role in the Manhattan Project. Through well-crafted flashbacks and dreamlike sequences, the audience gains insight into the physicist's inner struggles, moral dilemmas, and his ultimate realization of the devastating power of his creations.

Cillian Murphy delivers an astonishing performance as J. Robert Oppenheimer, skilfully portraying the character's brilliant mind, emotional turmoil, and the burden of responsibility that weighs heavily on his shoulders. Murphy's portrayal humanizes the enigmatic figure, presenting Oppenheimer not as a cold scientist, but as a man grappling with the moral implications of his inventions, which have forever changed the course of history show the true and important store of a flawed genius.

The supporting cast, including Emily Blunt as Kitty, Oppenheimer's wife, and Robert Downy Jr as Friend and professor turn sourer by the ever present jealousy and blindness to Oppenheimers greatness and character as can be seen in the world peace scene over the transportation of isotopes. RDJ gives us a phenonpnal performance which helps to silence the critics over what seems to be a radical change in character compared to the roles he is used to playing. Provide stellar performances that add depth and dimension to the story. Their relationships with Oppenheimer are portrayed with nuance, contributing to the film's emotional resonance.

Oppenheimer's thematic brilliance lies in Nolan's exploration of the dichotomy between scientific achievement and ethical consequences. As the Manhattan Project gains momentum, the film delves into the ethical debates surrounding the use of atomic weapons and the harrowing aftermath of their deployment in Japan. Nolan does not shy away from depicting the devastation of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, providing a haunting reminder of the consequences of unchecked scientific progress.

Nolan's directorial vision is further elevated by the seamless incorporation of practical effects, setting Oppenheimer apart from contemporary CGI-heavy productions. The authenticity of the explosions and nuclear tests serves as a poignant reminder of the real-world impact of the events portrayed on screen.

Moreover, Oppenheimer's nonlinear narrative keeps the audience engaged throughout, allowing them to piece together the puzzle of Oppenheimer's life while highlighting the complexities of the human mind and the passage of time.

As with any Nolan film, Oppenheimer demands the audience's attention and intellectual engagement. Its dense storyline and non-linear structure may prove challenging for some viewers, but those willing to invest in the narrative will be rewarded with a film that leaves a profound and thought-provoking impression.

In conclusion, Oppenheimer is a triumphant cinematic achievement that cements Christopher Nolan's status as a master storyteller. The film is a compelling exploration of history, science, and morality, driven by stellar performances, mesmerizing visuals, and an evocative score. Nolan's ability to blend fiction with historical accuracy while maintaining emotional resonance is truly remarkable. Oppenheimer is a must-watch for cinema enthusiasts, history buffs, and anyone intrigued by the moral dilemmas posed by scientific advancement. It is a profound and unforgettable experience that will linger in the minds of audiences for years to come. So to answer the question, yes I do believe that Oppenheimer will be cemented as a classic in the future.

10.title: Storytelling at it´s peak
10.content:
Christopher Nolan once said that the first six minutes of a movie can define whether the audience stays to the end. He rolls up the curtains of Oppenheimer with an intro about a battle between humankind and the gods of Olympus. And right after that, starts a great game, that play your senses and mind. So yes, you definitely want to stay.

First you try to set the genre, but it´s far away from a straight road. Horrific visions, retrospective, monochromatic visuals -all diferent timelines. You are focused, because you are jumping from one to another. But to also keep your interest, the individual timelines are connected by key events and characters, bind by the law of causality. So the narrative is dynamic, but not chaotic and you just can´t wait to unfold more. It´s neither that easy with the protagonist - Robert J. Oppenheimer, the leader of The Manhattan Project, who with the invention of the atomic bomb, changed the whole world forever. Challenging story, right? Should we admire him, hate him, or even feel sorry for him? The great thing is that we, the audience, are draged throught a whole spectrum of emotions about him. He is dangerous, unhinged, narcissist, but at the same time, or different times, he is shown as a martyr, genius and loyal to his statements. It works perfectly with the narrative, because you are not biased by what the director/writer wants you to think. He simply tells you the story.

Stylistically, the main character is the dialog. Your focus is guided by a slow camera track-in, beautiful key lighting and camera refocusing on the speaker and listener. Subconscious, elegant.

Another key element is time. You are already focused, not lost, immersed and hungry for more. At last, the dynamic editing and music push you to the limits and you are almost on the edge for the whole journey.

To summarise it, these different layers work perfectly together. Even after the second act, the narration still holds to its tempo and that is something unique. You are taken on a coherent journey and after 180 minutes you just find yourself at its end.

I wanted to stay fully objective (in the sense, that I can somehow argue my statements), but I have to say, that this complexion gave me the feeling, that everybody who worked on Nolan´s Oppenheimer gave a minimum of 100% to its work. The whole star cast, the postproduction, every member of the crew. Just to say that one day, they contributed to this magnum opus.

10.title: An instant classic. A technical wonder. An incredible story.
10.content:
Oppenheimer, almost feels like he was made for Christopher Nolan. For once in a Nolan film, he doesn't have to come up with a larger than life idea, with a complicated man at the helm of it. Because that kind of story, the kind Nolan seems to be so interested in, was Oppenheimer's life.

There's a level of technical prowess to this film that's impressive even for Nolan. People have gotten so used to Nolan's technical ability, they almost ignore it, but this film doesn't allow you to, it is on another level. Without even commenting too much on the obvious 70mm IMAX film (I sadly was unable to see it), which is such an achievement for filmmaking going forward. The faced paced editing, breathtaking cinematography and practical effects so good you forget it's a movie. This movie is a technical masterpiece and that's clear as day even on a first viewing.

And it goes without saying the acting will go down in history. Too many amazing supporting roles to even nominate all of them, and a lead so unbelievably good, it will redefine who people think of when they think of Oppenheimer. Cillian Murphy shows up almost immediately as the film starts, and he doesn't leave your mind for the week after it finishes.

The SOUND, THE GODDAMN SOUND. Wether it's the sound design or the score itself. A score that rivals Zimmer's work with Nolan is score to die for, filling the room with anxiety when it needs to, and a feeling of grandiose when it needs to. The theater shakes and rumbles, the sound of a bomb, the sound of a hand on the shoulder, or the sound of a gust of wind, you can feel all of it. It's sad to say it but outside of the theater this movie will be a bastardized version of itself, and that's mostly because the sounds of an IMAX screening, make this one of the most riveting movies ever made.

All of that is impressive, all of that can make a masterpiece, but at the end of the day, this is Oppenheimer. The story is what makes it all mean something, and what makes it so compelling. A beautifully dramatized version of history, with the truth still intact. Told in classic Nolan fashion, non-linear and labyrinthine. Told at a break-neck speed, through multiples lenses, keeping you guessing, which is nearly unheard of in a biopic. I said it's almost like Oppenheimer was made for Nolan. But in truth, it's stories like Oppenheimer's that make people like Nolan do what he does. I feel as if I've witnessed a classic at it's birth. Which is the first time I can say that in my young life. I went to the theaters and saw something come to fruition, Oppenheimer, a film we will definitely remember.

It isn't an "action a second" movie, but the special effects when the bomb is truly tested later in the movie are amazing.

I see why this film is the talk of the moment; it really is a superbly acted, well written tale that stands alone. Worth seeing, period.

10.title: Spellbinding tale of Creation to Catastrophe
10.content:
"Prometheus stole fire from the gods and gave it to man. For this he was chained to a rock and tortured for eternity!"

Real controllable power stays in the shadows. Imagine a neutron, despite being the most powerful catalyst to a chain reaction never in its purest form compromises the valency of an atom because its innate nature prevents it from turning rogue. But when it gets triggered by externalities, disaster is bound to happen. The genesis of this externality, an obsessive self induced entitlement to change the world, is well explained in one of the verses from Bhagvad Gita "Attachment to sensory pleasures often lead a man spiralling into the abyss of lust, lust leads to anger which further develops into delusion al last destroying all intelligence and bringing him back to the material pool of existence devoid of any reputation".

Dr. J Robert Oppenheimer one of the most influential man to ever live, battered by his pride and lost in the relevance of Manhattan Project, was one such raw mind burst open by the endless desire to change the world. But all his creation led to was a traumatic lifelong battle between the uncontrollable power fueled by monumental stature and the subconscious fear of feeling trapped in the gallows of internal turmoil manifested by the consequences of actions. Amidst the political catharsis his stature is well uplifted by Cilian Murphy's divine portrayal who bends and tears every possible aspect of an already perplexed yet hallucinated mind elevating the notion of an American Prometheus.

All performances including Ludwig Göransson chilling background score are worth remembering with brilliance written all over. Only caveat lies in Nolan's style of filmmaking who builds the experience purely for IMAX. No theatre less will be able to negate somewhat sluggish screenplay at times. Nevertheless, Oppenheimer with its deep scientific and spiritual connotations, fires every neuron in your body and begs you to think what just detonated on screen? Was it an atom bomb or the future of mankind. Highly Recommended!

10.title: Nolan's Unconventional Movie Structure Unveils a Powerful Message
10.content:
I admire Christopher Nolan's audacious decision to place the bomb test in the middle of the film instead of concluding with a grand finale. By eschewing the typical 'big bang' approach, Nolan artfully unveils the subtle yet crucial nuances of Oppenheimer's eventual downfall from grace. This unconventional narrative structure allows us to delve deeply into the complex issues that Oppenheimer encountered during the later phases of his illustrious career.

As the story unfolds, a profound appreciation dawns upon the viewer, showcasing the challenges Oppenheimer faced and the moral dilemmas he wrestled with. Nolan's deliberate choice not to culminate with the Trinity test serves a purpose beyond cinematic bravado. Instead, it crafts a deeper understanding of Oppenheimer's significance-a poignant reflection of the consequences that arise from refusing to resort to violence against our adversaries, as it blurs the lines between 'us' and 'them.'

Had Nolan opted for a more predictable conclusion, the film's powerful message might have been lost. However, by threading Oppenheimer's narrative with finesse and offering an unorthodox perspective, he ensures that audiences are left with an indelible impression of historical significance and the enduring lessons to be learned from this remarkable chapter in human history.

10.title: Explosive Entertainment & Compelling Cinematography
10.content:
A truly remarkable film that, as the poster boasts, will change the world forever.

In our modern political environment fraught with corruption on both sides - while the world teeters towards another global war and the threat of nuclear deployment - I can think of no film more informational and more critical for the American public to watch in this moment, than Oppenheimer.

Nolan delivers a phenomenal film - jam packing a truly foundational moment of American history into a remarkable 3 hour journey.

Arguably dividing the film into two acts, Nolan provides a rare glimpse into the astonishing reality of how America battled through the nuclear program in World War II. Immaculately providing an amalgamation of physics, patriotism, and philosophy Nolan takes a rather scientific effort and transforms it into the astonishing moment of history that it was.

Through the use of bewildering special effects, a star studded cast, and an inspiring score Nolan is able to build to the boom in such a way that keeps the audience wholly engaged and entertained - while Cillian Murphy delivers a performance of a lifetime bringing the emotion, education, and eccentricity of Dr. Oppenheimer to life in a character that will permanently be tied to Murphy.

And yet, the true darkness of the film does not occur until the second act - after the detonation of the bomb. Focusing on the witch-hunt efforts of the jaded Lewis Strauss, Nolan's Act 2 skewers the underbelly of a darker and corrupter time in American politics. Nolan - with stunning accuracy and gripping reality retells the story of how American agencies - particularly our FBI - was weaponized against Dr. Oppenheimer so as to discredit and disengage him from the American public.

But after the second half, I found myself pondering "How much of this has really changed? Have our agencies? Our leaders? Our FBI?" And when I reflect on where our politics and country stand today, I found myself thinking - no.

This is perhaps the most stunning piece of Nolan's puzzle. That he is able to so artfully display American greatness and innovation against corruption and cruelty - without losing a beat.

Much like a nuclear explosion, Oppenheimer blows the viewer away with this amazing storytelling - ignited by a perfected cast and cinematography - but also just as a nuke once it has gone off, it leaves those in its wake in a moment of silence.

10.title: In Witness To Oppenheimer
10.content:
This is an attempt to condense what occurred in a reverent teenage mind, over the course of 180 minutes sat in a cinema theatre (with no seat left empty) witnessing Oppenheimer. I doubt it shall do any justice to the emotions elicited in my own viewing, and I encourage those who read, to see for oneself independent of my own perspectives.

ART Nolan's choice of dividing the movie, splitting it, into scenes of colour and black and white did appear to me, prior to viewing, as an attempt to raise this film to an artistic standard it would not hold upon viewing. I must admit to being incorrect in my predisposition. This choice to divide the colour in the film between monochrome and technicolour is perhaps as useful as it is impressionistic. Not only does it enable the viewer to chronicle the timeline of the film simply, but also present a different theatre, a more complex theatre, to the one the first two parts of the film present. It serves as a useful distinction to the eye, as well as the mind. Where Oppenheimer deals initially with the theatre of science, of creation, of morals, the closing black-and-white post-climax of the film serves to deliver the sickening witch-hunt in the theatre of politics, of immovable institutions, of what shall be called for the rest of this review, the American Justification.

AMERICA I will try to define this term now: and I am sure it will be insufficient to portray what I truly believe it to be, in simply, insufficient words. I believe the American Justification is, put in a pretty, concise words, the ability of 'America' to perpetuate not only its physical existence, but also its image and symbolism by means of justifying itself on the basis of its simple existence and continuation of the 'American way'. Nolan expresses this most beautifully - via his presentation of the aged, the suited, the decrepit, the congruous, the white (ethnically, yes), and their assault on any form of progress that does not follow the route of the American Justification. This path, based purely on opinion and my own personal viewership, is that of winning. And I think winning is different to victory. Victory is a discriminate end goal, while winning is the process, as well as the end goal, if it is ever reached. The story of Oppenheimer is the epitome of the American desire to win, and to never stop winning. Oppenheimer is ultimately persecuted for his delays to American winning. His doubts over the moral credibility of the development of an H-bomb does not coalesce with the American ideal of always winning, of always being ahead.

However, trying to root myself from disappearing into ideals and politics, and whichever way the our world's current political climate turns, I should return to what is upon the screen, what is evident. I shall begin with perhaps the most appalling scene in the film, for me at least, marking one of the six times I moved to tears during the film, and one of the seven times I was moved to tears over the duration of the whole experience of my evening. This scene, to place in context, is after the two A-bombs produced in Los Alamos have been detonated over Hiroshima and Nagasaki to end World War II. We see Cillian Murphy troubled, his name, endearingly shortened to 'Oppy' being chanted by the residents of Los Alamos, calling for his speech in celebration. Perhaps this is pinnacle of the film, to me at least. He walks through his neighbours, haunted by the train-like chugging of their stamping on the wooden boards they are seated upon. If one has watched David Lynch's 'Mulholland Drive' they will pick up on the lighting in this scene. It is shadowy, dark. The wood of the hall is rich, blooming, wet. The faces of those cheering are dark, almost zombified. 'Oppy' stands before his congregation and delivers Americanized sentiments that he does not believe, receiving uproar in applause and cheer and laughter. Here, Nolan cleverly paints Oppenheimer's own fission, his division of his ideals. In this haunting scene we witness the devouring of guilt, airbrushed over by victory, by the cessation of WWII. The zombified Americans feed off the decay of 110,000 dead (initially, 250,000 in the weeks continuing) in the two Japanese cities to fuel their arms to wave small American flags, and to fill their lungs for whoops and cheers. This scene is haunting even before Oppy's visions, where everything becomes muted, and he finds himself stepping through the heart of a burnt husk of one of his bomb's victims. Everything is engulfed in light, everything is swallowed by American victory, the idea of which is on par with divinity. Oppy exits, witnessing some crying, some embracing, all joyous, as well as a couple kissing under the seats, and one of his physicists throwing up outside of the hut. He witnesses all the putridity of America's pulp culture. Americanization devours the intellectual achievement of the creation of such a device, commercialising and lowering it to the level of beer-sodden, vomit-inducing, homecoming partying and cheer. Mass violence is Americanly justified under the guise of winning. Cruelty, gruesomeness, guilt is all admonished by the positive result of victory.

CHARACTERS I feel that now is an opportune moment to depart from the greater ideals that are tackled in the film, and to address the minutiae, of each of the roles tackled by Nolan's stellar cast. Damon plays an intimidating chalk to Oppenheimer's cheese, a shouty, but informed and sympathetic, army general overseeing Los Alamos. The only time his allyship to Oppy, to the audience, is questioned, is in the confined cabinet prosecution room. Blunt plays all but a blunt character, pardoning the pun. Kitty, Oppenheimer's wife, serves a tasteful discord to Oppenheimer's arrogance. To all that he is blind, Kitty is witness to. Blunt's delicate portrayal of Kitty is equally able to be hated and admired by the audience. Her testimony within the cabinet room is a moment of the film where the audience can truly smile. Oppy's science team are perfectly measured, credit to the actors or script writing I do not know, but they do not intrude on the storyline too much and are equally not sidelined. Each is characterised in seconds, and playfully too. They always add the scene, each additional detail is always welcome and never overplayed. I ultimately believe that no word, no moment, is acted incorrectly. There are no times that the acting falls short or feels artificial. You receive an overwhelming sense that each actor enjoys the character that they well and truly live within, unflinchingly. Downey Jr plays a deceptively hurtful role, a political animal. His rupture from his initial portrayal is a betrayal to the audience. We feel deceived, we feel hurt. We feel that we were misfed a character who was simply a fake, and phony, concealing a vain, power-hungry man who aims to succeed and hold control. Cillian Murphy must be mentioned for his role. His depiction of Oppenheimer is not only deeply nuanced, paired with the nuanced characterisation of him by narrative voice throughout the film, he balances Oppy's genius, brilliance and intelligence with his blue-eyed blindness, his naivety. He is flawed, and truly lovable, truly admirable. His impression on the audience is always poignant and touching. His ability to act in silence is as incredible as his ability to deliver lines. He could walk back into the second world war and play Oppenheimer himself.

A BIOPIC? A 'PEOPLE' FILM A striking feature of the film that dawned on me during the cinema walk-home, is how the film is focused. Oppenheimer is a departure from modern filmmaking style: it did help that I watched a 35mm millimetre screening, which removed some HD nature to the viewing, but instilled in it an artistic imperfectness. Nolan chooses not to focus on CGI, on visual spectacle, and while he does not shy away from it completely, his lens it focused on the human, on the being. More shots focus on the eyes, the faces, the bodies, the physicality, the voices, the clothes, the gazes and the actions of those in Oppenheimer than the A-bomb. It is ultimately a film of people, not of explosions, which gives it a great emotional touch. Nolan examines the value of exploring the effect upon the psyche, upon the emotions, upon the relations of people, rather than pure destruction. In fact, Nolan chooses to end upon creation rather than destruction. Avoiding straying into biblical allusions, of which there are many in the 180 minutes, Nolan chooses to instead focus on beginning, rather than ending. WWII is not ended by the A-bomb, instead, the atomic era, the H-bomb race, the age democratic hostility is begun.

CONCLUSION The film is ultimately about fission. Ha-Ha, funny joke, he's trying to be a fancy artistic reviewer. I encourage you to watch, and you shall see, how each ideal, each person, each story explored in this masterpiece is ripped apart, atomised, before the audience. Oppy's communist ideals dissolve and split, ultimately his allegiances to humanity remain, but are smothered by American capitalism and reverent fear of all things Left. Our physicists' relationships with one another are pulled to pieces, and rejoined momentarily by phony formality of a handshake, between Oppenheimer and Teller.

America is split apart. We see an admirable, heroic hunger for academic progression, reduced to greed, and its lust for success and power. I wait for what Nolan has for us next but doubt it will ever be able to succeed his statement that is Oppenheimer. He tackles not only a biopic of such a complex character, but a timeless reincarnation of a time of politics and tension, delivering it all within a three-hour film that will leave you speechless. I encourage you, I implore you, to book your tickets for your local cinema, to experience what shall become a hallmark in cinematic history, to witness Oppenheimer.

10.title: Wonderful
10.content:
_Oppenheimer (2023) Review_

Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer is a cinematic masterpiece that delves into the complex and fascinating life of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the father of the atomic bomb. This epic biographical drama is a thought-provoking exploration of the human cost of scientific progress, the morality of warfare, and the personal demons that haunted one of the most influential minds of the 20th century.

_Nolan's Visionary Direction_

Nolan's direction is, as always, meticulous and masterful. He weaves together multiple timelines, seamlessly transitioning between Oppenheimer's early days as a brilliant and charismatic physicist, his leadership of the Manhattan Project, and his later years as a vocal advocate for nuclear disarmament. The film's non-linear narrative structure adds depth and complexity to the story, mirroring the fragmented and often contradictory nature of Oppenheimer's own thoughts and feelings.

_Cillian Murphy's Tour-de-Force Performance_

Cillian Murphy delivers a breathtaking performance as Oppenheimer, capturing the full range of his subject's emotions, from the ecstatic highs of scientific discovery to the crushing lows of personal loss and moral anguish. Murphy's portrayal is both deeply humanizing and profoundly unsettling, conveying the sense of a man torn apart by the conflicting demands of his conscience, his ambition, and his sense of duty.

_Supporting Cast and Ensemble_

The supporting cast is equally impressive, with standout performances from Emily Blunt as Oppenheimer's wife, Kitty, and Matt Damon as General Leslie Groves, the military leader tasked with overseeing the Manhattan Project. The ensemble cast also includes Robert Downey Jr., Florence Pugh, and Rami Malek, among others, each bringing their own unique perspective and energy to the film.

_Themes and Historical Context_

Oppenheimer is a film that wears its themes and historical context on its sleeve. Nolan is unafraid to tackle the big questions, from the ethics of scientific research to the consequences of unchecked military power. The film is also a powerful exploration of the personal costs of war, as embodied by Oppenheimer's own struggles with depression, anxiety, and addiction.

_Visuals and Cinematography_

The film's visuals are stunning, with Hoyte van Hoytema's cinematography capturing the stark beauty of the New Mexico desert landscapes and the eerie, otherworldly glow of the atomic tests. The special effects are equally impressive, recreating the devastating power of the atomic bomb with haunting realism.

_Conclusion_

Oppenheimer is a masterpiece of cinematic storytelling, a film that will leave you breathless, disturbed, and ultimately, hopeful. Nolan's direction is visionary, Murphy's performance is unforgettable, and the supporting cast is superb. This is a film that demands to be seen, and one that will linger in your thoughts long after the credits roll.

_Rating:_ 5/5 stars

_Positives:_



_Negatives:_ None notable

Oppenheimer is a must-see film for anyone interested in history, science, philosophy, or simply great storytelling. Be prepared for a thought-provoking and emotionally challenging experience, but one that will ultimately leave you inspired and hopeful.

10.title: Oppenheimer (2023, Christopher Nolan) Nolan, master of his craft, brings a pivotal point in history to life with a stellar lineup of acting talent
10.content:
Oppenheimer (2023, Christopher Nolan) Eric's Grade: A

'Oppenheimer' is the latest film from auteur Christopher Nolan whose high profile projects are continuously some of the most popular and critically acclaimed films upon their releases. 'Oppenheimer' is no exception to that. The film is a three hour behemoth that features a star studded cast in a grand, historical biopic about the life of theoretical physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer. The film is based on the book American Prometheus by Kai Bird featuring a screenplay penned by Nolan himself. The film is a commercial and critical success and is likely to be quite present on many year end lists and on Oscar ballots in 2024. 'Oppenheimer' stars Cillian Murphy in the lead role with Matt Damon, Robert Downey Jr., Emily Blunt and Florence Pugh in featured supporting roles. The extended cast is impressive including Josh Hartnett, Casey Affleck, Rami Malek, Jason Clarke, David Dastmalchian, Dane DeHaan, Alden Ehrenreich, Matthew Modine, Jack Quaid and Gary Oldman and the list goes on. Suffice it to say the talent assembled is quite impressive.

'Oppenheimer' surrounds much of the early exploits of the title character spanning the mid 1930's to the 1950's. Predominantly the film details his involvement in the Manhattan Project, which was the United States' secret mission to create an atomic weapon before Nazi Germany. In a parallel plot line the film also details a fall from grace of sorts as the government in the 1950's attacks Oppenheimer, primarily for previous communist affiliations, in a farce of a hearing ultimately resulting in Oppenheimer losing his security clearance which ostensibly removes him from his status as government adviser on all things nuclear.

As a young man Oppenheimer vaults to the forefront of physics research, and as the 1930s wear on it is clear that Germany is pursuing nuclear fission with the aim of making the world's first atomic bomb. Despite some communist ties Oppenheimer is tapped to lead America's secret project to build the bomb. This leads to Los Alamos and a race against time pushing the boundaries of science at the time leading to the Trinity test, Fatman & Little Boy and ultimately, for good or ill, Hiroshima and Nagasaki. While the endeavor at the forefront of science calls to those like Oppenheimer the results of war are haunting, even from afar. After completing their task Oppenheimer goes on to continually promote nuclear deescalation, envisioning what would become the Cold War, which Truman is vehemently opposed to. He has a big stick and wants to swing it. Oppenheimer's political shift, among other reasons, are what lead to the government eventually turning on him and shunning him from the halls of power.

We also get intimate looks at Oppenheimer's somewhat chaotic personal life as he meets and marries Kitty Puening, played by Blunt, who would remain faithful to him, however, Oppenheimer would have affairs the most high profile being with communist Jean Tatlock played by Pugh. There is also an interesting post script of sorts that comes at the end of the film where much is revealed regarding the nature, purpose and ultimately who was behind the railroading of Oppenheimer.

'Oppenheimer' is a stellar film that tells an integral part of not only the history of the United States, but the history of the world. It is fascinating how many times throughout history war and government are what enable science boundaries to be pushed, but we become very much like children handling loaded firearms not truly aware of the ultimate consequences of our actions. I will admit walking into this I knew Oppenheimer's name and I was aware of the Manhattan Project and what it did, but beyond that much of this was an unknown quantity. I was never really a student of this period of history so if you mentioned Oppenheimer, Goddard, and von Braun those names exist in a similar jumbled space in my head. 'Oppenheimer' is a fascinating recounting of the dawning of the nuclear age in American history as well as solidifying and putting face to this famous name now rendered on film wonderfully by Murphy and Nolan as a man in full. The script and acting throughout the film are superlative and will be lauded with awards aplenty come year's end. The direction is impeccable, as always with Nolan, and the use of sound is pronounced which is also a hallmark in technical Nolan films as I recall very much the sound from 'Dunkirk' as well. I will admit that the huge selling point was seeing the trinity explosion in IMAX, and I was a tad disappointed. I am sure it is a technically wonderful shot, but from a passive viewer's perspective I was expecting it to be grander spectacle. That really is about my only qualm with, what is otherwise, an impeccable film. Some might argue there is too much of Oppenheimer's love life bloating the run time, but I think that it is a vital part of understanding him as a man. This is great achievement from Nolan, and a well rendered and accessible film. Many of Nolan's works such as 'Tenet', 'Interstellar' and 'Inception' can bend your mind around difficult concepts, but in the realm of historical biopic 'Oppenheimer' is a truly remarkable film that everyone should appreciate.

10.title: A masterpiece by Chris Nolan
10.content:
Oppenheimer has everything to be the film of the year. One of the few films recorded in Imax, surreal, certainly adds to the experience.

About the film, it is the consecration of Chris Nolan's directing style. The execution of the work with his signature this time was perfect, no narrative slips, nothing exaggerated and nothing omitted, the film uses the techniques in the right measure.

The filmmaker's best film so far brings back the puzzle narrative, in a more spiral format, especially at the beginning of the film. This type of narrative is one that makes you think, build the film along with the execution of it. The beginning of the film demands a lot of attention. Many timelines in quick scene cuts, many new persons introduced, many situations presented out of order: it is the perfect experience for those who enjoy this type of film. Like a puzzle, you're given several pieces that are unlocked for you to piece together the story. If you lose your attention in those first 30-45 minutes of plot and can't put together the narrative, it will be difficult to understand from there. When the pieces fall into place and you understand the timelines (which are few here, when it comes to Nolan), enjoying the art of the film in the next 2:30 hours of film is a great experience!

Oppenheimer brings a new way to watch a biopic unlike anything you've watched before in this genre. The three hours of film pass as if they were one, the pace of the film is electrifying, quick cuts, quick takes, most scenes last a few seconds, before moving on to another point in the story. Very few scenes drag on for more than 30 seconds.

The casting is immense, there are many characters, many actors, many names (which may sound confusing at some point), that the film does not prioritize presenting the trajectory of each one in detail - and it would never have been able to, such a large number of actors -, the performances are of a high level, and the puzzle narrative diminishes in the middle of the film, helping to understand the narrative thread in this large number of actors. Cillian Murphy's performance is extraordinary, by far the best developed character in all of Nolan's filmography, it gave him space to shine and he delivers a lot. Robert Downey Jr also delivers a great performance, in fact the best or one of the best of his career. Emily Blunt manages to dominate the dramatic scenes throughout the film. In my opinion, a cohesive script, with the perfect screen time for each character, given the relevance of each one in the story.

Cinematography, visual effects (no cgi), editing, original score and sound editing are categories with a high probability of awards. The original score and editing of this film, in particular, caught my attention too much, quick cuts, great editing, non-linear at times, and when linear, with short scenes, in addition to the original score that holds you in your chair and gives a frantic pace to the film are exceptional.

In summary, this film has Nolan at his best (debuting in a new studio, Universal), in his best film, managing to overcome all the negative nuances that hovered over his other works (little tenacity with the characters and exaggeration in his non-linear narrative vices). Far surpassing his last work, Tenet, which is his worst film.

Oppenheimer is finished, mature, and Nolan's best yet. It has a chance in virtually all award categorias o Oscars. 10/10.

10.title: Oppenheimer in-depth review - new Christopher Nolan masterpiece
10.content:
It is safe to say that this film is exceptional in every aspect: acclaimed director Christopher Nolan does not disappoint and brings to the big screen not only a film with a good historical narrative, but also a superb cast and, of course, a mind-blowing visual experience. However, it is important to keep in mind two aspects that for many could be negative and that I will discuss in this review after commenting on the positive aspects.

The cast of the film is composed of exceptional actors and actresses such as Cillian Murphy, Matt Damon, Emily Blunt, Florence Pugh, Robert Downey Jr and more. Along with that, the film is directed by Christopher Nolan, author of great movies such as Interestellar, The Prestige, Memento, TENET... The entire team enhances the quality and credibility of the film through exceptional performances and an unparalleled visual and audio experience.

The film's narrative is perfect, showing the reality of the historical events that took place in a detailed, dark and credible way, plus the perfect use of time by means of different chronological entry points. To bring this narrative to the big screen, Christopher Nolan once again surprises on a visual level without the use of CGI, reinterpreting on a smaller scale what happened in history thanks to his superb direction.

Going into what could be negative aspects, even though the plot is superb, the pacing may not be perfect for many, as the film has a long running time, and is somewhat complex in its implementation of many characters and subplots. Moreover, especially for fans of the director, the film does not take the same approach as his previous films, but is different in that it deals with a detailed historical perspective rather than delving into fiction and final plot twists (there is something similar to this kind of plot twist, but in a different way).

Having said all that, the film is a masterpiece that everyone should see and definitely will enjoy.

10.title: My Thoughts on Oppenheimer Directed by Christopher Nolan
10.content:
Oppenheimer is a very good movie, starring Cillian Murphy as Robert J. Oppenheimer, the father of the atomic bomb. The film is rated R for nudity and sexual themes, so many women are walking out of the theater for what they perceive to be patriarchal oppression. Though that part didn't personally bother me, Christopher Nolan could've deleted those scenes to get a PG-13 rating so the film could've grossed more money. Anyway, Oppenheimer's runtime is 3 hours 15 minutes.

Now I really think Oppenheimer would be difficult for non-American audiences to fully appreciate and non-native English-speaking audiences to catch all the dialogue. The film is very dialogue heavy and the beat in the background is loud enough that you'll have to strain your ears. The film in general is difficult to fully grasp because of the huge cast of characters and the fractured narrative of the script. Lots of times, the film is in black and white. Nolan is also fixated on the historicity of the script such as when a general said, "I don't want to drop the bomb on Kyoto because of its huge cultural significance and because my wife and I honeymooned there." Or when Oppenheimer said, "Now that we've finished our work at Los Alamos, I plan to give the land back to the Indians." Anyone not familiar with the history of the Manhattan Project would probably miss those lines of real-life lore.

What really impressed me was how the film was basically broken up into three parts. The first part was about Oppenheimer's personal and academic life and how he theorized the atom bomb thanks to Albert Einstein's work in the field. The second part was when the general (Matt Damon) built a town in the New Mexico desert at Los Alamos so Oppenheimer could make and test the bomb. The third part was about the government interrogation of Oppenheimer's ties to communism and the bad guy named Strauss (Robert Downey Jr.) who wanted to be appointed to a presidential cabinet position and gain bureaucratic powers setting Oppenheimer up for failure. Thus the movie's themes and subplots wove together like an elegant tapestry. My only problem is that the film is so dialogue heavy, you can't lose focus for a single scene. Cillian Murphy who I enjoyed as Thomas Shelby from Peaky Blinders stole the show.

10.title: A Modern Masterpiece
10.content:
I don't know where to start with this behemoth of a film, this gigantic technical achievement, this incredibly intricate study of a man's consciousness as he changes the world forever.

Perhaps the most impressive thing that Nolan has done, is that this is a biopic. Throughout the film, I never felt like I was reading a Wikipedia page or that it was a conventional attempt at telling someone's story. Nolan puts you right into the mind of J. Robert Oppenheimer, and Cillian Murphy puts you right into his soul.

This is the greatest performance of this decade so far in my opinion, the way Cillian embodies the tiredness and weight that is present behind Oppenheimer's eyes is just magnificent, incredible voice work too. All of the cast is phenomenal, Nolan brought out everyone he could and they all brought their highest calibre of acting performances, great short performances by Oldman and Affleck too. RDJ and Blunt were incredible, wished to have seen more of Pugh though.

Every once in a while, a film presents technical abilities that are unheard of, and it is often Nolan who does that with his work. I felt like I was watching a film made with technology we didn't have, I think it is because everything was practical and our eyes have been bombarded lately with terribly noticeable and rushed CGI, that this felt incredibly fresh and lively. The bomb test and the speech scenes are both masterful works in every aspect of filmmaking, a masterclass in how a climax should be executed. The cinematography maaaaaaaaaaan, so crispy and sharp and beautiful in IMAX, Hoyte is definitely top two in the industry. The score by Ludwig too, incredible work there are no weak aspects here.

As for the pacing, Nolan's usual fast paced style of directing and editing helped the 3-hour runtime go unnoticed. The first hour felt like two in a good way, I was surprised that I was still one hour into the film because of how wrapped up I became in its world. There may have been an imbalance of pacing at times, but nothing that hindered the film for me.

The weakest element throughout the film for me were the court hearings which took centre stage during the last act of the film, I felt like it was getting a bit too much of a court-room drama and a bit convoluted, compared to the rest of the film's engaging events. I feel like a rewatch is necessary to fully comprehend those scenes because of how fast everything happens. Another problem was the sound mixing, especially at the beginning, I was not able to understand a lot of the dialogue unfortunately.

Overall, this is one of Nolan's finest accomplishments as a director, one who is often known for his technical prowess and nonlinear style of storytelling, where he often explores how time connects us all one way or another. Here, he brings the audience with him to explore one of the most important aspects of the new world, a fate that could unite humanity in the most disastrous of ways, nuclear armageddon brought forth by the American Prometheus.

10.content:
"Oppenheimer" is a masterclass in filmmaking, boasting exceptional cinematography, an engaging story, and a stellar cast that leaves a lasting impression.

The cinematography in "Oppenheimer" is nothing short of breathtaking. From breathtaking wide shots in stunning locations to intimate close-ups that capture the characters' emotions, every frame is meticulously composed. The film beautifully captures the mood and atmosphere of each scene, immersing the audience in the world of the story.

Speaking of the story, "Oppenheimer" weaves a compelling narrative that keeps viewers captivated from start to finish. The screenplay is both thought-provoking and emotionally resonant, delving into complex themes and ethical dilemmas. It explores the life and work of J. Robert Oppenheimer, taking us through his involvement in the development of the atomic bomb and the personal and moral turmoil he faces along the way. The story is expertly crafted, striking a balance between historical accuracy and engaging storytelling.

What truly sets "Oppenheimer" apart is its exceptional cast. Each actor gives a truly standout performance, fully embodying their characters and adding depth and nuance to the story. The cast's chemistry is palpable, adding an additional layer of authenticity to the film. From the lead role to the supporting characters, every performance is impeccable and contributes to the overall brilliance of the film.

In summary, "Oppenheimer" is a cinematic gem that excels in every aspect. With its breathtaking cinematography, gripping story, and stellar cast, it becomes an unforgettable viewing experience. It is a must-watch for anyone who appreciates great filmmaking and wants to be transported into a captivating and thought-provoking narrative.

10.title: Cinematic Masterpiece
10.content: Christopher Nolan movies have always been an acquired taste. I remember when Inception was released and there were mixed responses from the audience from "Absolutely brilliant" to "What on Earth did I just watch?" I love this about Nolan. His movies are designed to make us ask questions, to make us use our brains. We have become lazy in our viewing of entertainment. We want action packed explosions and everything handed on a plate and tied up in a little bow at the end. This is not that. Acting performances were superb from all parties. It is a theatrical, cinematic masterpiece. This movie is not about Oppenheimer being put on trial. This movie is about humanity being put on trial. It's a movie that needs to be watched more than once, like all Nolan movies, to truly be able to take in all of the amazing creativity, writing, music and acting. Is it essential to view in IMAX? Perhaps not. But, I really think this movie is something to be experienced, not to just be watched. That is what makes cinema special. Cinema isn't just watching a movie, it's experiencing a movie. Oppenheimer in an IMAX cinema was an experience that I am unlikely to forget.

10.title: An all-star acting tour de force backed by Nolan's brilliant directing.
10.content:
Christopher Nolan's filmography has been building to this movie. Over decades, Nolan has had gimmicks in his films that make them stand out. Oppenheimer (2023) uses many of them to create a compelling story that's half scientific discovery and half political drama. That a movie like this-about unleashing the Pandora's box of nuclear weapons-hadn't been made like this before is perhaps the more impressive feat. The way Nolan weaves the two halves of the story together is masterful. However, the actors definitely do a lot of heavy lifting here.

It took me a second viewing to piece together that the black-and-white segments followed Lewis Strauss (Robert Downey Jr.) while the color segments focused on J. Robert Oppenheimer (Cillian Murphy). This visual stylization hearkened back to the way Nolan made Memento (2000) unique. The shifted timelines between the black-and-white/color segments evoked Dunkirk (2017)., I'm just glad that I could actually understand what everyone was saying, unlike in Tenet (2020). Ultimately, the way Nolan films his movies with practical effects adds a layer of realism that can't be faked. The emotional realization of what they had just released on the world still gives me chills.

Of course, the style and way a movie looks can only take it so far toward greatness. The actors in Oppenheimer all turned in excellent performances. It would surprise me if Robert Downey Jr. And Cillian Murphy didn't receive nominations for acting Oscars when awards season hits. Similarly, Emily Blunt and Florence Pugh helped to showcase the scientist's womanizing tendencies. Even the minor characters like Niels Bohr (Kenneth Branagh), General Groves (Matt Damon), and Ernest Lawrence (Josh Hartnett) were portrayed to their fullest. Overall, Oppenheimer is a timeless film that builds upon Christopher Nolan's already successful cinematic career.

An all-star acting tour de force backed by Nolan's brilliant directing, I give Oppenheimer 5.0 stars out of 5.

My first 10! During World War II, Lt. Gen. Leslie Groves Jr. Appoints physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer to work on the top-secret Manhattan Project. Oppenheimer and a team of scientists spend years developing and designing the atomic bomb. Their work comes to fruition on July 16, 1945, as they witness the world's first nuclear explosion, forever changing the course of history.

Just a little heads up before I start, I would like to make sure you know that I found it difficult to write this review. Anything stated as a review of its magnificence would be an understatement. Words truly can't describe the brilliance of this movie.

Christopher Nolan has established himself as one of, if not the best director in Hollywood nowadays. He was able to transform a biography into a brilliant mind-bending movie that leaves the audience thinking about every frame for a very long while. The movie just leaves you in a statet of disbelief; no one could directly leave the theatre right after the movie ended. The timeline and the story in general were so messed up and confusing but it came together like puzzle at the end. The cast was so good. Everysingle cast member had one of the best performances of their life. The dialogue was so good. The visuals were stunning (0 CGI was used according to Christopher Nolan). It was all just so good. I can go on and on but I can stop by just saying that this is my first 10/10 review.

Score:10/10.

10.title: A (meta)philosophical, ethic, physical, artistic and historic masterpiece by Christopher Nolan!
10.content:
Tbh., this has to win every Oscar there is... Cillian Murphy is a genius actor and one of our generation's finest. The cinematography, the plot, the acting, the historic accuracy: just everything is perfect.
