I love Nolan as much as the next guy; his films feel purposeful rather than so much of the pointless cinema that exists today... but this movie was so drab. I love historically-based dramas, true stories, etc. But I'm at an honest loss for words. Maybe it's because it's the weekend and I wasn't as into it as a mindless watch, but I found myself dozing off throughout most of it. It's as if Nolan filmed hours of random scenes and just spliced them together in a hurry to make an excessively long, boring film. I suppose shooting it this way was to give the viewer insight into the way he felt Oppenheimer's brain worked, and the film is meant to reflect that? I honestly don't know. I'm no pyromaniac, but even the bomb detonation sequence was entirely anticlimactic. I guess the whole awful thing just went over my head. 1/10.

1.title: Horrible Confusing Movie - Too Bad!
1.content: "Oppenheimer" was a confusing mess. I expected much better. There were flash forwards, flash backs - even a few flash sideways. There were scenes in color, scenes in black and white. 1.title: Confusion
1.content:
It seems like Nolan read the book American Prometheus on Oppenheimer, the overseer of the Atomic bomb project, and then tore out the pages and reshuffled them in a waste basket, the result being a script for his 3-hour dirge, Oppenheimer. Adding insult to the confusion of the film with its mind numbing dialog was that the movie ended with whimper instead of an expected BANG, namely the Bang of the A bomb explosions over Hiroshima and Nagasaki never seen in the movie. The official excuse according to Nolan was it would have distracted from the interior point of view of Oppenheimer. But really, I suspect it was worries about the Japanese film market where the film was initially banned.

If any movie ever needed events presented in chronological order for those unfamiliar with the history, this movie was it. What the viewer got was confusing flashbacks and flash-forwards of critical plot points, enough to make your head spin.

Also Nolan should have used ID supers for the names of the many historical figures presented, mostly unidentified. Actually, you probably need a program guide to follow this movie.

While the Irish Actor Cillian Murphy was flawless in portraying Oppenheimer, the average movie goer should save his money and watch the movie Fat Man and Little Boy (1989) in order to understand what really happened in the building of the atom bomb and its controversial usage.

Or better yet read American Prometheus. Just don't tear the pages out.

1.title: Um, no Japanese actors in it. Wonder why? Bohring.
1.content:
This is a 3-hour long, drama-documentary about the scientist behind the US atomic bomb - emphasis on the drama. Except there is no drama, it's a courtroom flashback to a long succession of meetings, attended by actors on the up doing impressions of famous people from the past. Who were, on the whole, very unpleasant. Chain-smoking, philandering, swotty show-offs, some of them.

Because there is no drama, Nolan has to introduce sex scenes; without them, 'Oppenheimer' would be like The West Wing set in 1943. Matt Damon and Cillian Murphy certainly deliver the thespian goods (no chain-smoking for Oppie or daily booze for Grovesy, mind), but there are only two sources of tension:

1, Will the Nazis develop The Bomb first?

2, Was Oppenheimer a Comyanist?

Since everybody knows the answer to both those questions - well, No.1, even if you weren't paying attention - this film is more about 'how well is history dramatised?' Yes, the History Channel will be gnawing its heart out, but even they don't squeeze out 3 hour-shows.

This. Movie. Has. No. Story. There are far better movies, and far better books. Nolan tries to cram everything, including quantum theory, in and the result is a long and tedious firework display. By the end, you're wishing you'd never been Born.

1.title: Floppenheimer: Overwhelmingly Disappointing
1.content:
Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer was one of the most anticipated films of the year, promising a deep dive into the life of J. Robert Oppenheimer and the moral complexities of creating the atomic bomb. However, what audiences received was a bloated, convoluted, and surprisingly dull experience.

At over three hours, the film feels like a marathon of courtroom drama interspersed with brief glimpses of scientific breakthroughs. While Nolan's trademark nonlinear storytelling works in films like Memento, here it creates confusion and makes it difficult to emotionally connect with the narrative. Instead of focusing on the monumental stakes of building the bomb, the film spends an inordinate amount of time on political intrigue and bureaucratic disputes, which, while historically relevant, lack the dramatic tension one would hope for.

The much-anticipated explosion sequence is visually stunning but lasts only a few minutes in a film that should have been centered around such moments. The rest feels like an overly academic exercise, alienating viewers who aren't already well-versed in the history and physics involved. It's a missed opportunity to bring one of history's most complex figures and his controversial creation to life in a truly engaging way.

1.title: Quietly fizzles and peters out rather than providing any kind of explosion
1.content:
Unfortunately for me this film was a total failure.

I can't fault the actors who mostly do a good job (apart from RDJ who despite the prosthetics never convinces that he is anyone expect RDJ.) The blame here lies solely with Nolan who in his signature style creates an overlong, convoluted, poorly edited, tedious slog of a film.

Although there are good scenes, they are a few and far between. Most are over in a matter of minutes and erratically jump to the next, sometimes spanning across multiple timelines, causing unnecessary confusion. We never spend enough time with any of the characters to learn much about them or form any kind of connection, thus leaving the film devoid of any kind of emotional impact.

The main focus of the film is also on Oppenheimer's trial and communist connections post-war rather than the actual building and detonation of the bomb. A complete bait and switch from what was advertised to us. This would be fine if any of it was interesting but it's really not. It's dull as dishwater and it lasts for THREE HOURS.

The score is too loud and overbearing, often drowning out the dialogue and not fitting in with the scene. Many have commented that the first 30 mins feel like an extended trailer, of which I agree. It really doesn't get much better after that.

We actually left the cinema half an hour early because it had become completely intolerable at that point (having already contemplated leaving around 90 mins in). I should point out, I've been going the cinema for 25 odd years and I've only ever walked out on one other film. Can you hazard a guess as to what it was? Yep, Nolan's previous effort...Tenet.

The mass praise and hysteria surrounding this is clearly unwarranted. It is a BAD movie no matter how you look at it, pure and simple. A snoozefest that will send even the worst insomniac to sleep. I'm astonished by all the positive reviews.

After yet another dud, I personally will never see anything directed by Nolan again.

1.title: Not appreciable for me
1.content:
"Oppenheimer," directed by the esteemed Christopher Nolan, explores the life of Dr. Julius Robert Oppenheimer, a pivotal figure in history who played a crucial role in the development of the nuclear bomb during World War II. However, while the film boasts Nolan's visionary storytelling, I find it difficult to celebrate this particular biopic.

My reservations stem from the fact that Dr. Oppenheimer's work ultimately resulted in immense devastation, with the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki leading to the loss of approximately 226,000 lives, predominantly civilians who continue to endure the consequences. This dark chapter in history raises important ethical questions about the development and use of nuclear weapons.

While Christopher Nolan's directorial prowess is unquestionable, I struggle to reconcile with the idea of endorsing a movie that centers around a figure whose actions had such catastrophic consequences. It is essential to remember that a film's merit goes beyond the talent of its director or the performances of its actors.

As audience members, we have a responsibility to engage with art and cinema critically, recognizing that certain stories may evoke conflicting emotions and moral dilemmas. "Oppenheimer" may offer a compelling narrative and showcase Christopher Nolan's cinematic brilliance, but the subject matter raises valid concerns about the human toll of scientific advancements.

In conclusion, "Oppenheimer" poses a challenging dilemma for viewers like myself, torn between appreciating the artistry of the film and grappling with the moral implications of its subject matter. While Christopher Nolan's name alone draws considerable attention, the content of the movie prompts us to reflect on the ethical complexities that lie at the heart of historical events and the impact of scientific advancements on humanity.

Any part of the movie that I can think of , be that visual sound or story , was always eclipsed by unexplained chaotic take over by something else. If it's a story then music. 1.title: Disappointing and Uninspiring
1.content:
I was eager to watch "Oppenheimer" with high hopes of experiencing an engaging and insightful depiction of one of the most critical scientific figures in history. However, I was left deeply disappointed by the film, which fell far short of my expectations.

The movie fails to capture the essence and complexity of J. Robert Oppenheimer's life and contributions to the world. Rather than delving into the intriguing details of his scientific genius and the moral dilemmas surrounding the development of the atomic bomb, the film becomes an incoherent mess of disconnected scenes and poorly developed characters.

One of the most glaring issues with "Oppenheimer" is the lackluster portrayal of the protagonist himself. The character development is superficial, and we are left with a one-dimensional portrayal of Oppenheimer that does no justice to his intellect, ambition, or internal struggles. The film misses a golden opportunity to showcase the man behind the science, leaving audiences unattached to the central figure and disengaged from the story.

Furthermore, the pacing of the film is disjointed, making it challenging to follow the narrative coherently. It jumps from one event to another without proper context, leaving the audience perplexed and struggling to connect the dots. The lack of a well-structured timeline makes it difficult to grasp the significant historical events surrounding Oppenheimer and the Manhattan Project.

While the cinematography is visually appealing, it is not enough to compensate for the film's numerous shortcomings. The director seems more focused on artistic aesthetics rather than delivering a compelling and meaningful narrative. As a result, the film feels more like a collection of visually pleasing shots than a coherent and captivating storytelling experience.

Additionally, the supporting characters are underdeveloped and do not add any depth or substance to the overall plot. The interactions between characters lack authenticity and fail to evoke any emotional connection with the audience.

In conclusion, "Oppenheimer" falls short of being a gripping historical drama, failing to bring life to the fascinating story of a brilliant scientist in the tumultuous times of World War II. The lack of character development, disjointed storytelling, and underutilized supporting cast render this film unimpressive and forgettable. Regrettably, I must give "Oppenheimer" a one-star rating for its inability to live up to its potential and engage its viewers.

Save your time and seek out other well-crafted historical films that do justice to the subjects they portray. "Oppenheimer" fails to leave a lasting impression, making it an unfortunate disappointment for those seeking an enriching cinematic experience.

1.title: Oppenheimer: A Dud Of Historical Fiction
1.content:
This film prominently features highly regarded male actors, accompanied by a limited presence of esteemed actresses such as Florence Pugh and Emily Blunt, who portray characters that align with Christopher Nolan's tendency for charismatic yet volatile female roles.

Criticism of Nolan's portrayal of women has been persistent over time. These female characters often possess an alluring and intelligent demeanor, yet their narratives often end tragically-reminiscent of the marginalized and ill-fated wives in "The Prestige," "Inception," and "Memento."

In contrast, the role of Florence Pugh, an exceptional talent within her generation, is regrettably constrained to moments of emotional distress and nudity. Her character, Jean Tatloc, a politically influential psychiatrist with her own compelling backstory, seems underutilized. Similarly, Emily Blunt's portrayal of Kitty, Oppenheimer's belligerent wife, primarily involves offering encouragement to her husband or displaying frustration towards her crying infant. Her sole redemption moment involves an engagingly acerbic exchange with one of Oppenheimer's adversaries.

The film progressively revolves around heated discussions among white male figures within boardroom settings. This focal point not only marginalizes other characters but also positions white men at the forefront of the narrative, relegating other perspectives to the periphery and classifying them as mere distractions or collateral.

However, a glaring omission is evident in the film's historical context-Japan. The absence of any substantial focus on Japan in a narrative that centers on Oppenheimer is not only glaring but ethically concerning. The film's neglect of the Japanese perspective renders it morally incomplete, particularly considering it purportedly presents Oppenheimer's perspective on the trauma he experienced.

Moreover, Nolan's treatment of renowned figures like Einstein and the exclusion of John von Neumann's involvement in the Manhattan Project underscores a concerning oversight in the film's historical accuracy.

The film's tendency toward over-dramatization is evident in its portrayal of Oppenheimer as an unparalleled force in history, capable of deciphering the intricacies of the strong force. This characterization borders on the risible, and its audaciousness aligns with the self-absorption often attributed to Nolan.

The film's final act places undue emphasis on Oppenheimer's security clearance and endeavors to evoke a sense of moral empathy for a man who played a central role in the deaths of thousands. This focus on portraying Oppenheimer as a victim seems misplaced, as historical accounts suggest he grappled less with his moral responsibility and more with personal entitlement.

Rather than addressing the experiences of those who endured war crimes, the film places undue importance on the emotions of those who contributed to such actions. Biographical films that prioritize the perspectives of instigators, especially when told predominantly by white men, prove inadequate vehicles for recounting narratives of imperial aggression and genocide. These narratives inevitably sideline critical aspects of history, limiting the storytelling potential.

Throughout the film, a sense of pretension prevails, reminiscent of Nolan's reputation. The filmmaker appears to have succumbed to his own acclaim, reflected in the film's execution.

While the film's success can be attributed partly to riding on popular trends and the loyalty of Nolan's followers, its critical shortcomings remain evident. This is not the kind of film that warrants repeated viewing. Claims to the contrary may stem from an attempt to project intellectualism rather than a genuine appreciation of the film's merit.

The movie is plagued by significant flaws, primarily stemming from its writing. Regardless of the visual and auditory elements, the inadequacies of the script are undeniable. Dialogue rarely engages, character development is virtually non-existent, and the plot proves insipid. Even the inclusion of A-list actors cannot salvage the screenplay's shortcomings. Hollywood tropes designed for Oscar-worthy performances make an appearance in the film's final moments, emphasizing the film's inclination toward self-indulgence.

Regrettably, the film's perspective remains fixated on the experiences of a privileged white man. The movie refrains from offering insights into the internal lives of the Japanese or depicting the mass casualties inflicted upon them.

The film's neglect of the Trinity test's repercussions on Indigenous and Mexican-American populations is an egregious omission that denies the audience a complete understanding of history.

The film's disregard for the plight of those affected by the Atomic bomb fallout is starkly apparent. Families spanning generations, still grappling with the consequences, continue to seek justice from the U. S. government.

Furthermore, Oppenheimer's deliberate choice to detonate the bomb over United States citizens in New Mexico, neglecting the option to do so in Tennessee, underscores the film's lack of acknowledgment regarding this racially charged decision. Such oversights contribute to a narrative that distorts historical realities and sustains a heroic portrayal of Oppenheimer despite his morally questionable choices.

In conclusion, the film's pretentious perspective aligns with its director's persona. Its success can be attributed to strategic associations and a dedicated fanbase, but it fails to overcome its significant deficiencies. The narrative's shortcomings, coupled with its historical and ethical omissions, underscore the need for a more comprehensive and sensitive approach to storytelling.

1.title: "Openheimer: A Disaster of Epic Proportions"
1.content:
Where do I even begin with this trainwreck of a movie? "Openheimer" was supposed to be a cinematic masterpiece, exploring the fascinating life of J. Robert Oppenheimer and the development of the atomic bomb. However, it turned out to be an utter disappointment, leaving me questioning why I wasted my precious time and money on this cinematic catastrophe.

First and foremost, the screenplay was a complete mess. The story lacked coherence and failed to provide any meaningful insights into Oppenheimer's character or the historical events surrounding the atomic bomb project. It felt like the writers had no idea what they were doing and were merely patching together random scenes without any logical connection.

The pacing of the film was torturous, to say the least. It dragged on for what seemed like an eternity, with scenes that were either excessively long and tedious or confusingly rushed. The lack of a clear narrative arc left me struggling to maintain interest throughout the movie.

The casting choices were equally disastrous. While talented actors can sometimes elevate a mediocre script, that was not the case here. The lead actor's portrayal of Oppenheimer was bland and unconvincing, failing to capture the complexity and intensity of the renowned physicist. Supporting characters were poorly developed and often served as mere placeholders, with their talents wasted in this forgettable production.

To make matters worse, the film's production value was abysmal. The shoddy cinematography and lackluster set designs made it difficult to immerse oneself in the period the movie was attempting to portray. The lack of attention to historical accuracy was jarring, and it felt like the filmmakers were indifferent to doing justice to the real-life events they were trying to depict.

Perhaps the most insulting aspect of "Openheimer" was its treatment of the atomic bomb's moral implications. The movie barely scratched the surface of the ethical dilemmas surrounding the development and use of such a devastating weapon. It was a missed opportunity to explore the complex and profound impact that this momentous event had on humanity.

Overall, "Openheimer" is an unmitigated disaster that fails on almost every level. Its lackluster script, poor pacing, subpar performances, and disregard for historical accuracy make it one of the worst cinematic experiences I have ever endured. Save yourself the agony and avoid this film at all costs.

Title: "Openheimer: A Cinematic Catastrophe"

I hope you don't take it personally, but "Openheimer" is quite possibly the most dreadful movie I've ever had the misfortune of watching. From start to finish, it was an unmitigated disaster that left me questioning the very nature of filmmaking and how this monstrosity ever saw the light of day.

The plot, if one can call it that, is an incoherent mess of random scenes and inexplicable occurrences. I couldn't discern a clear storyline if my life depended on it. It felt like the filmmakers were trying to be profound and thought-provoking, but instead, they delivered a pretentious jumble of half-baked ideas that left me more confused than enlightened.

The characters in "Openheimer" are as lifeless as a sack of potatoes. I had absolutely no emotional connection to any of them, and their motivations were about as clear as mud. It's as if the actors themselves were bewildered by the script and had no idea how to portray their poorly written roles. Watching their lackluster performances was a painful exercise in endurance.

The direction and editing were so haphazard that I couldn't tell if the film was going backward or forward half the time. Jump cuts and awkward transitions were used in an attempt to be edgy, but they only succeeded in making the film feel like a choppy mess. It's evident that the filmmakers were aiming for an avant-garde approach, but instead, they achieved a level of incompetence rarely seen in cinema.

The cinematography in "Openheimer" is nothing short of an eyesore. It's as if the director of photography had never operated a camera before and decided to experiment during the actual shoot. The result is a visual nightmare of poorly framed shots, out-of-focus scenes, and an overuse of shaky cam that made me queasy.

As if the cinematic abomination wasn't enough, the soundtrack added insult to injury. The music, if you can call it that, consisted of discordant noises that assaulted my ears and made me wish for the sweet sound of silence. It felt like the composer was playing a prank on the audience, trying to see how much auditory torture we could endure before walking out of the theater.

"Openheimer" is a prime example of filmmakers trying to be "artsy" and "intellectual" without having a clue about storytelling or the craft of filmmaking. It's a slap in the face to moviegoers who expect even a modicum of coherence and entertainment value from a film. This cinematic catastrophe should be avoided at all costs, and I can't help but feel sorry for anyone involved in this embarrassing disaster, from the actors to the crew who wasted their time and talent on such an appalling project. Save yourself the agony and find something else to watch-anything else would be a step up from "Openheimer."

1.title: Disappointed
1.content:
A Failed attempts to profound exploration of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the man behind the atomic bomb. However, it stumbles into tedium and self-indulgence, leaving audiences stranded in endless dialogue and lacking engaging storytelling.

The film revels in its own seriousness, with a glacial pace and heavy dialogue on weighty topics. Unfortunately, the execution is lacking. The dialogue feels unnatural, missing the flow that brings characters to life.

Nolan's choice of a fragmented, non-linear narrative alienates the audience rather than allowing a connection with Oppenheimer's journey. The constant time shifts make it hard to follow and emotionally invest in the characters.

Clocking in at over three hours, Oppenheimer feels like an interminable slog due to its lack of action and visual stimulation. Endless talking heads make it unbearable.

Most notably, the film lacks self-awareness. Nolan appears oblivious to its flaws, lingering on shots and indulging in lengthy monologues, expecting captivation that never arrives.

Expectations of an action-packed blockbuster intensify the disappointment. Instead, audiences get a meandering, self-indulgent exploration of the human psyche.

Oppenheimer (2023) fails with its convoluted narrative, stilted dialogue, and slow pace. Its self-indulgent nature and lack of self-awareness leave audiences profoundly disappointed, despite its attempt at exploring complex themes.

I'm afraid the film "Oppenheimer" fell flat in more than a few areas. The most noticeable issue was the pacing; the movie was an exhausting, drawn-out affair that rarely managed to hold my interest. Rather than focusing on the most poignant parts of Oppenheimer's life and work, it was bogged down in needless minutiae.

The characterization of Oppenheimer himself was another major flaw. For such a complex and historically significant figure, the movie offered a disappointingly one-dimensional portrayal. The acting was passable but lacked the depth and nuance necessary to truly capture the essence of this troubled genius.

All in all, "Oppenheimer" missed the mark on several counts and ended up being a disappointing depiction of an otherwise fascinating historical figure.

1.title: Oppenheimer: A Tedious Historical Misfire
1.content:
When I first heard about the film "Oppenheimer," I was genuinely excited. The subject matter, exploring the life and contributions of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the father of the atomic bomb, seemed like a promising premise. However, my enthusiasm quickly turned into disappointment as I endured what can only be described as a dull and misguided cinematic experience.

First and foremost, the pacing of "Oppenheimer" was excruciatingly slow. The film stretched on for what felt like an eternity, with lengthy scenes that added little to the narrative or character development. The director seemed more interested in showcasing their supposed artistic vision than in creating a coherent and engaging story. The result was a plodding and monotonous narrative that failed to hold my attention throughout its unnecessarily long runtime.

Furthermore, the character portrayal in "Oppenheimer" was uninspiring at best. While J. Robert Oppenheimer was undoubtedly a complex figure, the film failed to capture his essence and instead reduced him to a one-dimensional and uninteresting protagonist. The script lacked depth and failed to delve into the inner conflicts and moral dilemmas that Oppenheimer faced. As a result, the character felt detached and distant, preventing any meaningful connection between the audience and the protagonist.

The supporting cast, unfortunately, suffered the same fate. The talented actors were given little material to work with, and their performances felt wooden and lifeless. It was as if they were merely going through the motions, lacking the emotional depth and nuance necessary to bring the characters to life. This lack of character development left me feeling disconnected and uninvested in their fates.

While historical accuracy is not always the most crucial aspect of a biographical film, "Oppenheimer" took too many liberties with the facts. It seemed more interested in presenting a distorted version of events rather than providing a nuanced exploration of Oppenheimer's life. The film played fast and loose with the historical timeline, distorting significant events and omitting crucial details. This disregard for accuracy undermined the film's credibility and left me questioning the validity of the story it sought to tell.

In addition to the film's pacing and character flaws, the visual presentation was also underwhelming. The cinematography lacked creativity and failed to capture the grandeur and significance of the subject matter. The drab color palette further contributed to the overall dullness of the film. It felt as if the filmmakers had little interest in creating visually striking scenes or memorable imagery, which ultimately made the viewing experience even more forgettable.

Lastly, the thematic exploration of "Oppenheimer" fell flat. The film failed to engage with the ethical and moral implications of Oppenheimer's work adequately. It barely scratched the surface of the profound questions surrounding the development and use of nuclear weapons. Instead, it seemed content with a superficial examination of the events, leaving me longing for a more thought-provoking and intellectually stimulating experience.

In conclusion, "Oppenheimer" was a tedious and disappointing film. Its sluggish pacing, lackluster character development, historical inaccuracies, uninspired visual presentation, and superficial thematic exploration all contributed to a movie that failed to deliver on its promising premise. I cannot recommend this film to anyone seeking an engaging and meaningful cinematic experience.

1.title: This was the one film where music should have supported the film instead of muffling key dialogues in the final act!
1.content:
I wanted to love this film but this is a film where dialogues are vital. However, that music, which cannot hold a candle to classical music or any type of fusion pretentious music, blazing up left right and centre to the point where in the final act, horribly muffles and drowns key dialogues being bantered back and forth main characters, breaks your patience and you thus lose interest in the film!

For somebody who is very good at innovating new realms visually, Nolan seems to be brilliantly handicapped sonically in the whole sound department. When the music is too loud that even when you increase the volume on your headphones to hopefully and seamlessly hear dialogues in a dialogue-driven film but sadly realise that it would never help; so to ensure you are hearing what you think are hearing, turn on subtitles... that's where it annoys and loses me entirely!

Go absolutely bananas on Dark Knight and the likes but not on a movie of this nature, please don't!

Technically, yes, breathtaking but it is not a visual effects film. It is a chapter from history, so even if it may not be tad dull as a facts-driven documentary, it still needs to be equally engaging and informative. And those who understand English, would want to hear the dialogues decently and clearly, in order to thus appreciate the whole package!

Imagine too much subwoofer rumble when listening to Beethoven's Ninth or Mahler's Resurrection symphonies or even Sibelius' Violin Concerto... The horror is unimaginable even to suppose such a tragedy!

Balance is everything; SIr Nolan just needs to learn about moderation!

This is not a film where visually the film can propel forth with just music alone. The redemption / closure of most characters on screen is through key dialogues in a dialogue-driven film. If you invest close to 3 hours of your life for a film, you would definitely want to experience closure in a preferred manner - without losing patience over loud noisy garbled music and then to rely on subtitles that cover the lower half of the screen ruining the visual splendour spectacularly!

If you have seen Indiana Jones and The Dial of Destiny, in the final act, that main lady character keeps yapping endlessly. That was the first time I was ever annoyed with a British character on film or tv show. Imagine that spread forth gloriously for close to 20-25 minutes (Indy's was just about 3 minutes or so). Yeah, not ideal!

They could have fixed it a little for home media but I guess that wasn't done either.

Also the constant jumping back and forth may work for an action film, but not for a film / subject of this nature.

Ergo, technically brilliant but overall, brilliantly annoying! Watch it once, only if you get cheaper tickets or home media / online price because you would be disappointed if you pay full price!

I loved every other Nolan film, including his first short film but this is the first one that makes me go meh and leave it at that because technically, it has some good spots and that too just here and there but overall, I MAY watch it just once more.

1.title: A Lackluster, Mediocre Cinematic Endeavor
1.content:
Oppenheimer, directed by Christopher Nolan, is a film that falls disappointingly short of its potential. While it attempts to delve into the intriguing life and contributions of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the renowned physicist and key figure in the development of the atomic bomb, the execution of the film leaves much to be desired. Here are a few reasons why Oppenheimer fails to deliver on its promise.

First and foremost, the pacing of the film is sluggish, making it difficult for the audience to fully engage with the story. The narrative unfolds at a leisurely pace, often getting bogged down in unnecessary details and lacking a cohesive structure. As a result, the film struggles to maintain momentum, leaving viewers disinterested and disconnected from the subject matter.

Moreover, the screenplay of Oppenheimer leaves much to be desired. The dialogue often feels forced and contrived, lacking naturalness and authenticity. The interactions between characters lack depth, and the exchanges fail to evoke genuine emotion or intellectual stimulation. As a result, the film feels flat and fails to fully explore the complex themes and ideas it aims to tackle.

Lastly, the editing and overall structure of the film contribute to its mediocrity. The transitions between scenes are often abrupt and disjointed, hindering the flow of the narrative. Additionally, certain sequences feel unnecessarily prolonged, while others are hastily wrapped up, resulting in an uneven pacing that disrupts the film's coherence.

In conclusion, Oppenheimer falls short of its potential due to its sluggish pacing, shallow character development, lackluster cinematography, weak screenplay, and flawed editing. While the subject matter holds immense intrigue and potential for a captivating film, this particular rendition fails to engage and inspire its audience. Despite its aspirations, Oppenheimer ultimately proves to be a lackluster cinematic endeavor.

1/10.

1.title: Oppenheimer's Insensitive Portrayal: A Reckless Misstep
1.content:
Hold onto your seats, movie enthusiasts, because "Oppenheimer's Insensitive Portrayal" takes you on a bewildering journey through historical misrepresentation and sensationalism. This film attempts to merge the scientific legacy of J. Robert Oppenheimer with the timeless wisdom of the Bhagavad Gita, but ends up veering into tasteless territory.

The premise seems intriguing: delving into Oppenheimer's struggles during the atomic bomb's development while drawing parallels with the Bhagavad Gita's teachings. However, the execution falls flat.

From the start, it's clear that shock value overshadows genuine storytelling. The Bhagavad Gita, a revered philosophical text, is carelessly reduced to a plot device involving explicit content. Rather than honoring its depth, the film offensively equates its teachings with intimate scenes.

Cultural sensitivity should have been vital. Yet, the film dismisses the Gita's sanctity for controversy's sake. It raises questions about the filmmakers' intent: genuine exploration or deliberate provocation?

This movie sparks reflection, but not as intended. Instead of bridging science, spirituality, and ethics, it leaves us pondering media's state, prioritizing shock over respect.

"Oppenheimer's Insensitive Portrayal" is a cautionary tale on approaching these themes. Let's hope future filmmakers honor history, science, and spirituality with respect, rather than choosing tasteless offense.

1.title: Insult to Bhagwat Geeta
1.content:
Title: Oppenheimer - A Misguided Fusion of Themes [⭐]

As a movie enthusiast, I approach films with an open mind, appreciating the art of storytelling and the diverse perspectives they offer. Unfortunately, Oppenheimer left me deeply disappointed and disheartened. While it attempted to delve into the life of the renowned physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, the inclusion of an insensitive and inappropriate scene involving the Bhagavad Gita during a sexual encounter was an utter misstep that marred the entire film.

The movie itself had the potential to be a captivating biographical drama, exploring the complexities of Oppenheimer's life and the moral dilemmas he faced during his work on the atomic bomb. Regrettably, the film veered off course, resorting to shock value by including a scene that was clearly intended to provoke controversy rather than add any meaningful depth to the narrative.

To further exacerbate the situation, the scene in question incorporated the sacred and revered text, the Bhagavad Gita, into an intimate moment. Such a disrespectful portrayal not only trivializes a profound spiritual scripture but also demonstrates a lack of cultural sensitivity. It is crucial to understand that religious texts are sacred to millions and should not be misused for sensationalism or shock factor in any context.

As an audience member from the region that the Bhagavad Gita holds significant importance for, I felt deeply offended by this blatant disrespect. It is essential for filmmakers to be responsible and thoughtful about the cultural implications of their work, especially when it involves elements so deeply intertwined with people's faith and beliefs.

Despite any positive aspects the film might have had, the inclusion of this offensive scene completely overshadowed them, leaving a bitter taste that is hard to overlook. As a result, I cannot, in good conscience, recommend Oppenheimer to others. It is a shame that the potential for a compelling exploration of a remarkable historical figure was overshadowed by such careless and harmful choices.

In conclusion, Oppenheimer had the opportunity to be a thought-provoking and respectful biopic, but it failed to live up to its potential. The inappropriate use of the Bhagavad Gita during a sexual scene has deeply insulted our region and undermined the credibility of the film. I urge filmmakers to exercise caution and sensitivity when handling religious and cultural elements in their storytelling, as such irresponsible decisions can alienate audiences and tarnish the reputation of otherwise promising works of art.

1.title: if time would be money, i would be poor!
1.content:
I'm a big fan of Christopher Nolan's films. I love long-form movies, I'm deeply interested in science, and I love film. This is a personal review, I'm not trying to be unbiased - just raw and authentic with my feelings towards the movie. Enjoy or hate as you will:

Here are my reasons why I think Oppenheimer is a bad movie:

Insane amounts of dry exposition: Some of it was creatively weaved in, but the majority felt very pace-breaking and unnatural. This is a common trope in Nolan movies, but this is by far the worst hyperbolic version of it. It completely breaks the characters, pacing, and immersion of the reality he is trying to establish. It felt quite lazy and uncreative a lot of the time.

Terrible pacing: Besides the main hooks in the movie, Ludwig and the editing team made some amazing sequences, but for the most part, it's largely quite boring. However, the hooks of the movie keep you grounded in your seat long enough not to fall asleep when trying to trench through the shallow characters and exposition avalanche, until you come to another hook in the movie which tie you back down in your seat for another avalanche of uncreative exposition.

A lot of the dramatization of the characters and perspective felt very pretentious at times: Yes, it is profound to harness the strong force, and make a film about it - but there is a subtle self-importance to the film. It's the feeling of an artist knowing they create profound art, and the self awareness seeps into the art and you can feel it. It's hard to explain, but I feel it's tangible in this film. I do enjoy that it teaches newer generations about history and the dangers of humanity with such technology - but it felt self indulgent at times and it's hard to explain; for that I apologize -- I wish I was better with my words. I'm sure someone out there feels what I feel.

CGI dust on the screen completely ruining the continuity of the film and image: This is obviously something only some people will notice, but it's just absolutely wild that post production thought it was a good idea to have floating particles cover up the beautiful scape of Los Alamos. Cheap, uncreative, and unnecessary CGI atmosphere. Usually these visual effects can blend quite well in majority CGI films, but something so grounded with such high dynamic range, shot on film with this ridiculous atmospheric effect added just breaks the aesthetic of film entirely.

Florence Pugh's character was very shallow and was used uncreatively as an narrative tool: Yes, we're used to this with many Nolan films, shallow characters used to drive the main characters motivations in an obvious way. You can use your characters more creatively and mask the plot tools that they truly are; have them feel more authentic as characters and not just shallow story telling tools.

Jack Quaid's cameo was an awkward choice of casting: He says a few lines and plays bongos in the background of a few scenes and whenever I saw him on screen, it felt so wrong. Maybe there was potential to have him fit in another way, but there's something about his acting and presence that is super unconvincing and unfitting. This is likely just a bias that I cannot explain due to association of him in outside media - but there's something tangibly wrong with him being in this film lmao.
